hierarchy.lvl2: The parameters that carry a clinical hypothesis
The parameters that carry a clinical hypothesis

records.content:
The parameters and their semantics are defined fully in 

The Inference Agent; they are summarised here only insofar as the directional hypotheses depend on getting their meaning exactly right.

The agent has six parameters in total, but the symptom-driven hypotheses concern only the four original ones, listed below. The two parameters added later, cue_sensitivity and placement_noise, were mainly introduced for reasons internal to the model (isolating associative cue learning and absorbing undirected within-state placement scatter, respectively) and neither carries an a-priori clinical prediction (to be discussed - however, the prediction would not be a priori atp). cue_sensitivity is in fact expected to eventually dissociate from the internalizing scales (it indexes a learning ability rather than an affective bias), and placement_noise is an execution-noise term. Both are still entered into the exploratory trait x parameter grid further down, but they do not appear among the primary hypotheses, and the current empirical results (N = 34) bear this out: neither shows a meaningful correlation with any questionnaire scale.

Parameter

Meaning

Direction that matters

precision_weighting

allocation concentration / stacking

high → tighter, more concentrated placement

noise_reactivity

stochasticity-attribution bias (Piray & Daw)

high → surprises attributed to noise → weaker learning

belief_momentum

inertia in latent-state inference

high → sluggish state switching

h_switch

perceived environmental volatility

high → readier to entertain a state change

The two emphasised rows are the ones whose direction is counter-intuitive from the name alone, and getting them backwards inverts every downstream prediction - a clarification worth stating explicitly here because it is easy to get confused here (this is of course not stated because it is driven by my own experience - would never happen to me for sure).

hierarchy.lvl2: Theory-motivated primary hypotheses (H1–H3) TO BE DISCUSSED!!!
Theory-motivated primary hypotheses (H1–H3) TO BE DISCUSSED!!!

records.content:
The three primary hypotheses

H1 (Piray & Daw, 2021): trait anxiety (STICSA-T) → lower noise_reactivity. Anxious participants over-attribute surprising outcomes to genuine structural change rather than to noise, i.e. they have a lower noise-attribution setting.

H2 (Zika et al., 2023): intolerance of uncertainty (IU-18) → higher belief_momentum. Difficulty tolerating uncertainty manifests as reluctance to commit to a stable state belief, i.e. sluggish, inertial state inference.

H3 (volatility over-estimation): intolerance of uncertainty → higher h_switch. Over-estimation of how often the environment changes.

Each is a single directional prediction, tested with a Spearman correlation, a two-sided p, a one-sided p in the predicted direction, and a within-family Holm flag. Holm (family-wise) is applied only within this three-member family, since these are the primary tests and are not folded into the exploratory grid, which would over-penalise them at current N (to be discussed how to adjust this at final N).

For every (trait, parameter) pair the script fits, on standardised variables:parameter ~ trait                       [+ covariates]      (main effect)
parameter ~ trait * condition_L         [+ covariates]      (moderation)

and, where a posterior SD column ({param}_std) is available, a precision-weighted main-effect model with weights 1/\text{SD}^2, so that participants whose parameter is poorly identified contribute less. The weighted estimate is reported alongside the unweighted one. The full main-effect grid is FDR-corrected as an exploratory family.

Because the internalizing scales are strongly inter-correlated (see 

overview), the script computes partial Spearman correlations between each anxiety-core trait and each parameter, controlling for the other core traits. This separates the unique contribution of, say, intolerance of uncertainty from general trait anxiety. The partial results are the more informative readout when the question is whether or which specific construct drives an association or if the effect is potentially driven by a transdiagnostic latent factor; the exploratory family is FDR-corrected.

At N = 32 the three primary hypotheses behave as follows. H2 (IU → belief_momentum) and H3 (IU → h_switch) reach one-sided significance uncorrected (p₁ ≈ 0.04 and ≈ 0.06) but do not survive within-family Holm; H1 (STICSA-T → noise_reactivity) is null at the bivariate level (r ≈ −0.19).

The instructive result is what the partial correlations reveal. Once the shared internalizing variance is removed, STICSA-T → noise_reactivity becomes the strongest single association in the table (partial r ≈ −0.37, p ≈ 0.04), i.e. the H1 effect is present but is masked at the bivariate level by IU-loaded shared variance. Within the exploratory regression grid, the inhibitory subscale of IU carries the strongest association with belief_momentum (β ≈ 0.43), more than the prospective subscale, which is theoretically coherent, since inhibitory IU (the action-paralysing facet) maps naturally onto reluctance to commit to a new state.

None of these survive multiplicity correction at the current N, and none should be reported as established. They are recorded here as the associations most likely to firm up toward the target N, and as a demonstration that the partial-correlation step changes which trait looks responsible for a given parameter association. So please take all of this with a grain of salt :)

records.content:
This book documents the TAMBI project, a computational psychiatry study of how people infer hidden structure in an uncertain environment, and of how this inference relates to symptoms of anxiety, intolerance of uncertainty, depression and obsessive-compulsive symptoms. It contains the task, the analysis pipeline, the computational model and its validation, and the current results, and it is the reference for anyone who joins the project or needs to reproduce an analysis.

Note

Status of this page: 12 October 2026. Behavioural N = 68 (None = 24, Partial = 30, Full = 14), questionnaire analyses N = 65 (None = 23, Partial = 29, Full = 13), from the analysis run of 12 October 2026 with the adopted computational model (run tag 12_10). Data collection is ongoing, with a target of N = 90 to 100. The study is exploratory and not preregistered; targeted tests are to be preregistered for the planned online replication.

records.content:
RQ1. Does instruction about the latent structure change how participants infer it? The three instruction conditions differ in what participants are told about the task structure, and the question is whether this shifts behaviour from gradual, outcome-driven learning toward inference about the latent state.

RQ2. Are questionnaire scores associated with how participants infer the latent structure? The focal measures are state and trait anxiety, intolerance of uncertainty, depression and obsessive-compulsive symptoms, which are always analysed alongside each other.

RQ3. Does a latent-state model describe the behaviour, and do its parameters reflect the behavioural measures? This concerns the six-parameter inference agent, its validation, and the relation of its parameters to behaviour and questionnaires.

records.content:
Task

Mosquito Defense Task, a spatial predictive-inference task implemented in PsychoPy. On each trial, participants place 7 nets on 32 positions of a circle to intercept an attack after one of two colour cues.

Latent structure

Two latent states alternate across nine episodes of 16 to 24 trials. At each transition, the attack directions of both cues rotate by 120°. The direction for the second cue is 70° from that for the first.

Events

Oddballs (about 10% of trials, attack 120° from the current target without a change of state) and omissions (about 10% of trials, no attack shown).

Manipulation

Three instruction conditions, between participants. None: how to place nets. Partial: additionally, that rules might determine the attack direction. Full: additionally, the cue offset and the rotation.

Questionnaires

STICSA (state and trait), IU-18, BDI-II, OCI-12 (focal); ERS, PCL-5, SIAS, ACE, EAT-26 (wider battery).

Further data

Eye tracking (EyeLink 1000), pupil size, mouse tracking, physiology (BIOPAC), in-task affect ratings.

Computational model

A two-state hidden Markov model with von Mises emissions and six free parameters, fitted by amortized simulation-based inference (BayesFlow), preceded by an amortized comparison of five candidate models.

records.content:
Each participant contributes three data streams that the analyses bring together: the trial-by-trial behaviour (net allocations) and the measures derived from it, the questionnaire scores, and the posterior distributions of the six model parameters. Eye-tracking, pupil, mouse-tracking and physiological data are analysed in separate sub-projects.

Participant flow (recruitment, exclusions, and the sample size at each stage) is not documented in this book. It is maintained during data collection in the shared project folder on Google Drive, which is the single source for these numbers.

Every model signal relates to the feedback pupil (all p < .001), and the surprise of the change-point observer describes it somewhat better than the surprise of Nexus (ΔAIC −69). The model-free error relative to the participant’s own nets describes it far better than any model signal (ΔAIC −755). The attack pupil is smaller after larger errors, most clearly for the model-free error.

The participant’s own placement is the most direct trace of what they expected, so the feedback pupil follows how far the outcome lay from the participant’s own expectation. None of the three models describes the trial-by-trial pupil better than that, and the models do not differ in a way that singles out one of them.

records.content:
Not specific to Nexus. The link between the scores and the pupil is carried by surprise as defined by a model of the task’s statistics, and three different models give nearly the same result. The data do not single out the latent-state mechanism of Nexus.

Model-based beyond the participant’s own error. The pupil itself follows the participant’s own prediction error most closely, but the part of the pupil response that relates to the scores is the part that follows how unexpected an outcome is under the task’s statistics, beyond the distance to the participant’s own nets. Higher scorers’ pupils respond more to outcomes that are statistically surprising, with the participant’s own expectation held constant.

Consequence for the score prediction. The model-based pupil couplings predict the scores better than the model-free pupil summaries because they index this sensitivity to statistically surprising outcomes. Any of the three models provides such an index; the choice among them does not change the association.

Correction (Benjamini-Hochberg): per pupil window, the eight signals are one family. No signal relates to the anticipation pupil (all p ≥ .62). In the ISI, the window in which the attack is already on its way and its outcome cannot be known yet, the pupil is larger when the change-point observer is more uncertain (U q = .007, entropy q = .013); the n-state model (q = .094) and Nexus (q ≥ .21) point the same way without passing the correction. During the placement of the nets, the pupil is smaller when Nexus and the change-point observer are more uncertain (all four q ≤ .011). No signal relates to the baseline after correction (all q ≥ .31). With the Nexus signals, the change-point observer’s entropy, the n-state model’s entropy and the own allocation entropy entered together, the ISI pupil keeps a positive contribution of the change-point observer’s entropy (0.013, p = .012) and a negative one of the own allocation entropy (−0.020, p < .001).

Within the conditions (family: one signal in the three conditions), the ISI slope is positive for the n-state model’s uncertainty with partial instructions (0.025, q = .019; entropy 0.028, q = .012); for Nexus state uncertainty without instructions (0.018, p = .036, q = .11) and the change-point observer’s entropy with full instructions (0.021, p = .023, q = .070) it does not pass the correction. With full instructions the ISI pupil is smaller when the participant’s own allocation is more spread (−0.035, q = .013). The baseline pupil is lower with more states of the n-state model with partial instructions (−0.15, q = .001) and not in the other conditions.

Participant level and questionnaire scores. Per participant, the slope of the ISI pupil on each signal (also controlling the entropy of the own allocation) was related to the general factor and STICSA trait as above (83 participants). No slope relates to either score (all p ≥ .19, all q ≥ .53; family per score: the eight slopes, and separately the seven controlled slopes; largest: change-point observer U and the general factor, 0.17).

Reading.

The anticipatory pupil follows model uncertainty only weakly (β ≤ 0.016 per SD in the ISI, against 0.06 to 0.11 for the surprise signals of the three models in the feedback window), and the uncertainty of the change-point observer describes it at least as well as that of Nexus.

The entropy of the participant’s own allocation, the model-free counterpart, does not increase the ISI pupil; with full instructions a wider spread of the own nets goes with a smaller ISI pupil.

Unlike the response to surprising outcomes, the coupling of the pupil with uncertainty before the outcome carries no individual differences related to the scores. The score-related pupil signal is the response to the outcome, not the state of uncertainty while waiting for it.

The surprise response is a response to bites. Within bites, where the flash, the shake and the text are the same on every trial, the pupil is larger the more surprising the bite, under every model and for the model-free error. Within blocks the relation is weakly negative.

The surprise response grows from the early to the late part of the feedback and is as large after the feedback screen has ended (2000 to 3000 ms). It is therefore not the light response to the early flash.

The surprise of trial t does not carry over into the anticipation or the baseline pupil of the next trial (model signals all p ≥ .24).

records.content:
Pupil features predict the general factor out of sample: ridge r = .25 (95 % range over 10 CV repeats .17–.35), R² = .05 (−.02 to .12), permutation p = .006 (1,000 permutations within condition). The result holds across models: elastic net r = .26, R² = .06 (p = .010); random forest r = .27, R² = .07 (p = .010); PLS r = .28, R² = .02 (p = .006).

The same pupil block predicts STICSA trait (r = .27, R² = .06, p = .002), STICSA state (r = .22, R² = .04, p = .012) and BDI-II (r = .17, R² = .02, p = .010), but not IUS-12 (r = .04, p = .054) or OCI-12 (r = .08, p = .064).

Gaze features predict STICSA trait (r = .19, R² = .03, p = .004) and STICSA state (r = .15, R² = .00, p = .024); for the general factor they are at the permutation threshold (r = .07, p = .052).

Cursor, gaze–cursor, placement and model-parameter blocks do not predict any score (all p ≥ .08; R² ≤ 0). Combining all blocks does not improve on the pupil block: general factor r = .07, R² = −.02 (p = .048); STICSA trait r = .19, R² = .02 (p = .008).

The pupil prediction rests mainly on a few features, stable across folds: the feedback-pupil response to surprise, the pupil before the outcome (ISI), the feedback pupil on the trial after an event and the coupling of the attack pupil with the subsequent placement shift. The 9 model-based pupil couplings alone give r = .28, R² = .07 (p = .001); the 17 model-free pupil summaries alone r = .14, R² = .00 (p = .022).

The variance explained is small (R² ≤ .07): the scores can be predicted above chance from the pupil, but not precisely enough to estimate an individual’s score.

Self-report measures (affect ratings, post-task questions) are not used as features. The condition is entered as two dummies in every model.

Pipeline (integration/scripts/score_prediction_cv.py), fitted inside each outer training fold: columns without training data dropped, median imputation of missing values (participants without pupil or gaze data are imputed, not dropped), standardisation, condition dummies, model. Models:

ridge (penalty chosen by efficient leave-one-out inside the training fold);

ridge with condition × feature interactions;

elastic net (penalty and l1 ratio by inner 3-fold CV);

PLS (1–5 components by inner 5-fold CV);

random forest (300 trees, minimum leaf size 5, a third of the features per split; not tuned).

Baseline: linear regression on the condition dummies alone.

Evaluation. Outer CV: 5 folds stratified by condition, repeated 10 times. For each repeat, out-of-sample r is the correlation of the pooled out-of-fold predictions with the observed score, and R² = 1 − SSE / SS around the observed mean. Reported: the mean over repeats and the 2.5–97.5 % range.

Permutation test. The whole pipeline is rerun after permuting the score within condition: 1,000 permutations for the general factor with ridge, 500 for the scales, PLS and the interaction model. Elastic net and random forest got 100 permutations with 2 CV repeats each; a mean over fewer repeats has a wider null, so these tests are conservative. p = (1 + number of null values ≥ observed) / (1 + permutations), on the mean r.

Reading r. With no signal, cross-validated r is biased below zero. The training-fold mean shifts in the opposite direction to the left-out participants, so predictions and observations are anti-correlated. Here the null means lie between −.15 and −.23, and the condition-only baseline gives r = −.07 to −.34. The relevant comparison for r is therefore the permutation null, not zero; R² > 0 is the stricter criterion.

Importance (integration/scripts/score_prediction_importance.py). In each outer test fold, a feature (or a whole block) is permuted among the test participants (5 times). The drop of the pooled out-of-fold r is averaged over the 10 repeats. Stability: share of the 50 outer fits in which a feature is among the 10 largest absolute standardised ridge coefficients.

records.content:
Earlier results. The pupil features that carry the prediction include measures whose associations with the scores were reported in the synthesis chapter for these same participants (feedback pupil × surprise, ISI pupil, attack pupil → shift). The prediction does not add a new finding about which measures relate to the scores. What it adds is that these measures, together, predict the scores out of sample better than chance, and the rest of the process data does not add to it. The feature set itself was not chosen by association with the scores: it is the complete set of pupil summaries and couplings of the pupil analysis. Whether the model-based couplings are specific to Nexus is tested in 

Pupil and the Latent Signals of Three Models: the surprise signals of the change-point observer and the n-state model give couplings with the same association with the scores.

Scales. The pattern by scale follows the loadings of the general factor: STICSA trait, STICSA state and BDI-II are predicted, IUS-12 and OCI-12 are not. The gaze block predicts STICSA trait more than the general factor.

Missing data. Participants without pupil or gaze data (7–9) are predicted from imputed medians plus condition. The share of usable pupil trials is itself among the weighted features.

Size. With R² ≤ .07, an individual’s predicted score has an error almost as large as the spread of the scores.

The participant-level feature table and predictions are kept in a local cache outside the repository.

This chapter asks how the events of the last trials carry over into what a participant reports and does next. The predictors are the outcomes of the attacks (bites, and among them bites without a net and bites despite a net in the attack slot), oddballs, transitions, the model-free prediction error and the surprise and uncertainty of three models: the latent-state model (Nexus), the change-point observer and the n-state model (

Alternative Models). The outcomes are the next in-task affect rating, the response to the next oddball, and the placement, gaze, cursor movement and pupil on the next trials. In the reverse direction, the affect rating is related to the placement on the trials after the rating screen. All effects are estimated within participants; the participants’ own lag slopes are then related to the general factor and to STICSA trait.

Run 23_11: 96 participants, 17,241 trials, 15,550 attacks (11,180 bites: 8,541 without and 2,639 despite a net in the attack slot), 1,507 oddballs, 768 transitions. Gaze for 87, pupil for 85 participants. Script: tambi_time_lag.py --tag 23_11 (analysis repository), figures tambi_time_lag_figures.py --tag 23_11; output in stats_results/23_11/time_lag/ (pipeline steps timelag, timelagfigs).

Summaries of the past. Lag 1, 2 and 3: the value on the trial one, two or three trials before the measured trial. Weighted: exponentially weighted mean over the preceding trials (half-life 3 trials, up to 10 trials, at least 3 with a value). For the ratings, the summaries cover the trials since the previous rating: the last trial with a value (lag 1), the plain mean (window) and the weighted mean ending at the rating trial.

Models. Linear mixed models (maximum likelihood) with the predictor split into its within-participant part (participant-mean-centred, divided by its pooled within-participant SD) and the participant mean (z). Outcomes are divided by their pooled within-participant SD, so β is the change of the outcome in within-participant SD per within-participant SD of the predictor; tables also give β in the outcome’s unit. Every model contains trial number, condition and the previous value of the outcome; random intercept and random slope of the within-participant predictor per participant. If the random slope does not converge, the model is refitted with a random intercept; for the pupil outcomes, whose participant means are zero after the per-trial baseline, the random-intercept variance is zero and the models are OLS with participant-clustered standard errors.

Next-trial models also contain whether a rating screen preceded the trial. Pupil windows on trials after a rating or break screen are left out. The pupil models of the oddball family contain the outcome type of the oddball (blocked, bite despite a net, bite without a net), so that the feedback animation of the outcome is held constant. The rating screen follows trial 7 or 14 of an episode and never a transition trial, so the lag-1 transition models of the affect family are not estimable; the trial before an oddball is never an oddball or a transition, so the corresponding lag-1 models of the oddball family are not estimable.

Multiple comparisons. Benjamini–Hochberg FDR. A family is the set of models that answer one question about one measure: one outcome (a rating, a next-trial measure, a response to the oddball), one lag summary (lag 1, 2, 3, window or weighted) and one class of predictors. The classes are the outcome events (bite, bite without a net, bite despite a net, oddball, transition; 5), the surprise and error signals (model-free |prediction error| and the surprise of the three models; 4), the uncertainty signals (4), and, for the rating → next trials models, the six ratings. The score tests use the same families, separately per score. All families are defined in tambi_time_lag.py (fdr).

Participant slopes and scores. For the next-trial lag-1 models, each participant’s slope comes from an OLS fit of the same model (at least 30 trials) and is related to the score: slope (z) ~ score (z) + condition, HC3; β is the SD of the slope per SD of the score. The affect and reverse families have 8 or 9 ratings per participant (the nine in-task ratings, each with the previous rating as control; the first in-task rating has a previous rating only for the 23 participants whose results file contains the pre-task rating), the oddball family about 16 oddballs per participant; there the score enters the mixed model as a cross-level interaction (within-participant predictor × score), and β is the change of the within-participant slope (in the units of the main β) per SD of the score. With so few observations, the participant slopes from the random effects of these models (participant_slopes.csv, method blup) follow the participant’s mean rating (median |r| = .83, up to .98 for valence), so a regression of these slopes on the scores mainly reflects the relation of the mean rating to the scores; the cross-level interaction tests the dependence of the within-participant slope itself. Tested for the weighted summaries (affect, oddball) and for all reverse models. FDR within the families above, per score.

24 of the 234 affect models reach q < .05 (32 p < .05); the table shows a selection, all are in lag_models.csv. Frustration rises and valence falls with the share of bites since the previous rating; the weighted summary, which gives the last trials the most weight, describes both better than the plain window mean and better than the last trial alone. Bites without a net and bites despite a net both raise frustration. Of the model signals, the surprise of the change-point observer relates most clearly to frustration, the surprise of Nexus (q = .005) and of the n-state model (β = .08, q = .042) less. Arousal rises after a higher predictive entropy and state uncertainty of Nexus (q = .016 and .045), and frustration after a higher uncertainty of the change-point observer (q = .038). Stress and fatigue show no effect with q < .05.

Most events change the placement, gaze and cursor movement on the next trial: q < .05 for 136 of 208 placement models, 172 of 312 gaze models, 73 of 208 cursor models and 35 of 156 pupil models (all lags and the weighted summary).

Placement. After a bite without a net participants use more slots on the next trial (β = .11 [.09, .13], +0.13 slots; net entropy .09 [.07, .11]); after a bite despite a net they use fewer (−.11 [−.12, −.09], −0.13 slots; net entropy −.10 [−.12, −.08]). Both effects remain at lag 2 and lag 3 (slots .06 and −.06) and are largest for the weighted summary (.10, −.12). The surprise of each model and the model-free error are followed by more slots and a higher net entropy (β .04 to .09 at lag 1, all q < .001), and by longer placements (Nexus surprise .05 [.04, .07]). After a transition, split placements with nets at both state locations are more frequent (lag 1 .09 [.05, .12], lag 2 .05 [.03, .07], lag 3 .02 [.00, .04]). Of the uncertainty signals, the state uncertainty of Nexus and the uncertainty of the n-state model are followed by more slots and longer placements (.03 to .05); the predictive entropy of Nexus by slightly shorter placements (−.02 [−.04, −.01]).

Gaze. After an oddball, the gaze during placement rests less on the location of the current state (lag 1 −.13 [−.15, −.11], lag 2 −.08, lag 3 −.06, weighted −.15) and more on the other state’s location (.05 [.03, .08]) and on locations beyond the two states (.09 [.07, .12]). After a transition the share at the other state’s location rises on the next trial (.08 [.05, .11]) but not at lag 2 (−.01). Surprise of all three models has the same pattern as an oddball (current state −.11 to −.13; beyond the states .09 to .12) and raises the gaze entropy during placement (change-point observer .08 [.06, .10]); the gaze entropy is also higher after a bite without a net (.08) and lower after a bite despite a net (−.06). In the cue window the effects are smaller (|β| ≤ .06).

Cursor. After a bite without a net, an oddball or a surprising outcome, the first cursor movement starts earlier (initiation time −.02 to −.03) and is more curved and changes direction more often (.03 to .05); the bite-without-net effect on direction changes is confined to lag 1 (lag 2 −.00, lag 3 .01). A higher predictive entropy of Nexus is followed by fewer direction changes (−.05 [−.07, −.03]), less curvature (−.04) and a lower cursor entropy in the cue window (−.06).

Pupil. The placement pupil on the next trial is smaller after a bite (−.06 [−.08, −.04]), after an oddball (−.05) and after a surprising outcome (−.04 to −.05); the effect weakens at lag 2 (bite −.03, q = .044) and is absent at lag 3 (−.01). The ISI pupil is larger after a surprising outcome (Nexus .05 [.02, .07], q = .005; change-point observer .04 [.02, .07], q = .005). No outcome event changes the cue pupil with q < .05; the cue pupil is slightly larger two and three trials after a high model uncertainty (Nexus state uncertainty and n-state uncertainty, .02 to .03, q ≤ .031; weighted n-state uncertainty .03, q = .003).

Of the 221 next-trial lag-1 slopes, nine relate to the general factor with q < .05 and 13 to STICSA trait (family: one measure × predictor class, per score; all in slope_scores.csv). STICSA trait adds gaze entropy at the cue after an oddball (.29, q = .034), fixations at the cue after the surprise of the change-point observer and of the n-state model (q = .020 and .007) and a smaller cue pupil after the surprise of Nexus (−.25, q = .038). Higher scorers spread their nets more after an oddball, look at more locations during the next cue and the next placement after a bite without a net, a large error or a surprising outcome, and have a smaller cue pupil on the next trial after a large prediction error; on average across participants these within-participant effects are small or absent (slots after an oddball .05, gaze entropy in the cue window after a bite without a net .02, cue pupil after a large error −.01), so the scores relate to how strongly a participant’s next trial depends on the event rather than to the average effect.

The within-participant effects of the outcome events and the surprise signals on the affect ratings do not depend on the scores. The uncertainty signals do: in higher scorers, anxiety rises less with the uncertainty of the change-point observer and of the n-state model (general factor −.09 and −.07, both q = .012; STICSA trait q = .034 and .012), frustration less with the uncertainty of the n-state model (−.11, q = .027) and arousal less with the state uncertainty of Nexus (−.09, q = .043; STICSA trait −.10, q = .023). These are 4 of 78 cross-level terms per score with q < .05 (family: rating × predictor class, per score). In the oddball family, the shift toward the oddball increases with the preceding uncertainty of the n-state model in higher scorers (general factor +.08, q = .035; 1 of 65). The rating → next trials effects do not depend on the scores (0 of 30).

Three follow-ups of the lag slopes (tambi_broadening_followups.py, pipeline step broadening; outputs in stats_results/<tag>/broadening/).

Feedback pupil and the next trial. For consecutive trials t and t+1 (t not after a rating or break screen), the next-trial measure was regressed on the feedback pupil of trial t. The model was y_{t+1} ~ pupil_w + surprise_w + |prediction error|_w + y_t + trial + bite type + condition + (1 + pupil_w | participant), a linear mixed model (ML).

pupil_w is the feedback pupil of trial t (500–2500 ms, pre-feedback baseline), centred within the participant and divided by its within-participant SD. The Nexus surprise and the model-free |prediction error| of trial t enter in the same form, so that pupil_w is the pupil response beyond the two signals it follows.

Outcomes (z-scored): slots with nets, net entropy, split placement, gaze entropy at the cue and gaze entropy during placement.

Score form: + q + q × pupil_w (cross-level), with the general factor or STICSA trait.

BH within each trial subset (all trials; bites without a net) over the five outcomes, separately for the within-participant effect and for each score’s cross-level term.

Results:

A larger feedback pupil goes with a higher gaze entropy during the next placement (all trials: +0.032 SD per SD [0.010, 0.055], p = .005, q = .025; bites without a net: +0.038, p = .010, q = .052; 85 participants).

Slots and net entropy tend in the same direction (+0.017, p = .051; +0.015, p = .085).

Split placements and gaze entropy at the cue do not (p ≥ .73).

None of these couplings depends on the general factor (cross-level terms |b| ≤ .018, all p ≥ .15, q ≥ .70) or on STICSA trait (all q ≥ .65).

Bites despite a net. After a bite through a correctly placed net, participants use fewer slots on the next trial (−0.11 within-participant SD per SD, q < .001; see above). The participant slopes of this narrowing are not related to the general factor (lag-1 participant slopes against the score, OLS with condition and HC3; BH within measure × predictor class, per score): slots −0.12 [−0.27, 0.03], p = .12, q = .31; net entropy −0.10, p = .13, q = .33; split placements −0.18, p = .072, q = .18. The estimates point to a slightly stronger narrowing in higher scorers.

Pre-cue baseline after a large error. The pre-cue baseline of trial t+1 (not baseline-corrected) does not depend on the |prediction error| of trial t within participants (+0.006 SD per SD, p = .63). Its participant slopes are not related to the general factor (+0.12, p = .31) or STICSA trait (+0.18, p = .10). Model: covariates as above, random slope; participant slopes from OLS with at least 30 trials, related to the score with OLS, condition as covariate, HC3. In the same data, the cue pupil of t+1 (corrected to the 200 ms before the cue) has participant slopes on the error that are lower with the general factor (−0.28 [−0.47, −0.09], p = .004; STICSA trait −0.24, p = .020). The smaller cue response of higher scorers after large errors is therefore not a higher pre-cue level carried over from the error trial; it is a smaller dilation to the next cue.

Affect follows the recent outcomes. Frustration and valence at a rating screen follow the bites of the last trials, weighted toward the most recent ones; one SD more bites in the weighted window corresponds to 3.6 points more frustration and 1.5 points less valence. Both kinds of bites contribute. Among the model signals, outcome surprise relates to frustration; model uncertainty relates weakly to arousal and frustration.

The two kinds of bites have opposite consequences for the next placement. A bite without a net is followed by wider placements, a broader gaze and more cursor direction changes; a bite despite a net, where the nets already were at the attack location, by more concentrated placements and a narrower gaze. Both persist over at least three trials.

Oddballs and surprising outcomes move the gaze away from the current state. On the next placement the gaze rests less on the current state’s location and more on the other state and on locations beyond both, decaying over three trials; transitions shift the gaze to the other state’s location for one trial.

Little build-up toward the next oddball. The events of the preceding trials do not change the pupil response to the next oddball or the shift toward it; only the placement after the oddball takes longer after high uncertainty of the change-point observer and after larger errors.

Rating and the next trials. The rating itself is followed by slightly wider placements when frustration is high and valence low (both q = .037).

Scores. The scores relate to the strength of individual carry-over effects on the next trial — the net spread after an oddball, the gaze entropy and the number of fixations at the next cue and the gaze entropy during the next placement after a bite without a net, a large error or a surprising outcome, the cue pupil after a large error — and not to how affect follows the outcome events. Affect follows model uncertainty less in higher scorers (anxiety, frustration, arousal).

This chapter summarises the latent-state model: its generative assumptions, its six free parameters, and the way the parameters are estimated and validated. It gives the defining equations only. Derivations, all constants and the complete update rules are in 

The Inference Agent and in 

Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants.

Status

The equations describe the model adopted on 11 October 2026: the six-parameter agent with a commitment gain of 3, estimated with a network trained on 100,000 simulations and the 54 summary features of feature_extraction_v3.py. The decision, the validation and the alternatives examined are documented in 

Model Selection and Validation. The participant results in this book come from run 12_10, obtained with this model.

The model is a two-state hidden Markov model with von Mises emissions on the circle of 32 slots. An agent filters the latent state trial by trial, tracks the attack directions with gated delta-rule updates, and converts its predictive distribution into an allocation of seven nets. Six parameters govern this process. Because the mapping from parameters to allocations has no closed-form likelihood, the parameters are estimated by amortized simulation-based inference: a neural network is trained once on simulated sessions and then returns the posterior distribution for each participant.

Latent state. A binary state z_t \in \{0, 1\} determines which of two attack regimes is active. Before each outcome, the belief is propagated with the switch probability h:p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1) = p_{t-1}(z = 1)\,(1 - h) + \big[1 - p_{t-1}(z = 1)\big]\,h .

Emissions. Given the state, the attack direction \omega_t follows a two-component von Mises mixture. The regular component is centred on the believed direction \hat{\mu}_{c,z} for cue c in state z, and the oddball component is displaced by the believed rotation \hat{\Delta}:L^{(z)} = (1 - \rho_{\text{eff}})\, f_{\text{vM}}(\omega_t;\, \hat{\mu}_{c,z}, \kappa_{\text{fixed}})
          + \rho_{\text{eff}}\, f_{\text{vM}}(\omega_t;\, \hat{\mu}_{c,z} + \hat{\Delta}, \kappa_{\text{fixed}}),
\qquad \rho_{\text{eff}} = \rho_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{nr} .

State update. The state belief is updated by exact forward filtering and then smoothed with the belief momentum \text{bm}:p_t^{\text{Bayes}}(z = 1) =
\frac{p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1)\, L^{(1)}}
     {p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 0)\, L^{(0)} + p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1)\, L^{(1)}},
\qquad
p_t(z = 1) = (1 - \text{bm})\, p_t^{\text{Bayes}}(z = 1) + \text{bm}\, p_{t-1}(z = 1) .

Direction updates. The directions are point estimates. The direction of the dominant state \hat{z}_t is updated by a delta rule whose step is reduced when the outcome is attributed to the oddball component:\hat{\mu} \leftarrow \hat{\mu} + \eta_\mu \, g_t \, \text{PE}_t,
\qquad
\eta_\mu = c_\eta \cdot \text{pw},
\qquad
g_t = 1 - \frac{\rho_{\text{eff}}\, L_{\text{odd}}^{(\hat{z}_t)}}
               {(1 - \rho_{\text{eff}})\, L_{\text{reg}}^{(\hat{z}_t)} + \rho_{\text{eff}}\, L_{\text{odd}}^{(\hat{z}_t)}} ,

with \text{PE}_t = \angle(\omega_t - \hat{\mu}_{c_t, \hat{z}_t}) and c_\eta = 0.10. On a trial on which the dominant state changes, the direction is realigned to the outcome with rate \max(\eta_\mu, 0.85) and without gating. The offset between the two cues, \hat{\delta}_B, is learned from cue B outcomes and is drawn toward the target \text{cs} \cdot 70°, so that its steady-state value scales with the cue sensitivity \text{cs}.

Predictive distribution and action. The predictive distribution over the slots mixes the two states with weights that commit to the more probable state,\pi_s \propto \sum_{z \in \{0,1\}} w_z
\Big[(1 - \rho_{\text{eff}})\, f_{\text{vM}}(\phi_s;\, \hat{\mu}_{c,z}, \kappa_{\text{eff}})
   + \rho_{\text{eff}}\, f_{\text{vM}}(\phi_s;\, \hat{\mu}_{c,z} + \hat{\Delta}, \kappa_{\text{eff}})\Big],
\qquad
w_1 = \sigma\!\big(\beta_z\,[\,p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1) - 0.5\,]\big),\quad w_0 = 1 - w_1 ,

where \kappa_{\text{eff}} = \kappa_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{pw}, \sigma is the logistic function and \beta_z = 3 is the commitment gain. The distribution is shifted on the circle by a draw from \mathcal{N}(0, \text{pn}^2), raised to the power 1 + \text{pw}, renormalised, and converted into seven nets by largest-remainder rounding.

Three constants of the equations above are fixed for all participants: \kappa_{\text{fixed}} = 4.0, \rho_{\text{fixed}} = 0.10 and \beta_z = 3. The likelihoods of the belief update use \kappa_{\text{fixed}}; only the predictive distribution is scaled by \text{pw}.

All priors are independent and uniform. The recovery correlation r is the correlation between true values and posterior means in 500 simulations drawn from the priors (adopted network).

Precision weighting enters at three points by design, so that a higher value yields a narrower predictive distribution, a more concentrated allocation and faster direction learning. The three effects cannot be separated within this model.

Step

Procedure

Simulate

Parameters are drawn from the priors, one of the 20 trial schedules is drawn at random, and the agent is run on it.

Summarise

Each simulated session is reduced to a fixed vector of summary features. The same code computes the features of simulated and of participants’ sessions.

Train

A conditional density estimator q_\phi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) (flow matching with a small summary network, BayesFlow 2) is trained on the pairs of parameters and features (

Radev et al., 2020; 

Radev et al., 2023).

Apply

For each participant, 4,000 posterior samples are drawn conditional on the participant’s features. No further fitting takes place.

Before the parameters are interpreted, an amortized classifier compares the model with four alternatives (random allocation, two tracking models without latent states, and coverage of both state directions without state inference). The parameters are meant to be interpreted only for participants for whom the latent-state model has the highest posterior probability (

Model Comparison).

The summary features are not sufficient statistics. Whether they carry enough information about each parameter is an empirical question, which the recovery and calibration analyses answer.

Calibration. In simulation-based calibration (

Talts et al., 2018) with 1,000 simulations, the rank distributions of all six parameters remain inside the simultaneous 95% band of the graphical test (

Säilynoja et al., 2022). Rank means and rank dispersions lie within 1.5 standard errors of their expected values.

Recovery. Recovery is high for precision weighting and placement noise, good for belief momentum, cue sensitivity and the switch probability, and moderate for noise reactivity (table above). In the range of precision weighting that participants occupy, the recovery of noise reactivity is .86. Estimates of one parameter are nearly uncorrelated with the true values of the others (at most .21). Within posteriors, noise reactivity and belief momentum are negatively correlated (mean −.64).

Posterior predictive check. For the 62 participants classified as the latent-state model, the fitted agent reproduces the differences between participants in the main behavioural summaries (rank correlation between observed and predicted values of .87 to .96 for net entropy, trial-to-trial shift, angular error, placement variability and defense rate). The observed value lies inside the central 95% predictive interval for 56% of all features and participants; the intervals are narrow, and most deviations are offsets below half a between-participant standard deviation. The largest offsets concern the variability of the trial-to-trial shift.

The details are in 

Model Selection and Validation. The analyses that are still missing are listed on the 

front page.

Placement noise is a general measure of placement variability. Participants alternate between precise placements and discrete moves to the other state’s direction or to the location of a preceding oddball. The agent represents all off-target placements by a Gaussian shift, so that placement noise includes these moves, and the variability of the trial-to-trial shift is underestimated.

Noise reactivity is the least well-identified parameter (r = .79), and its posterior is correlated with that of belief momentum. Conclusions about it are drawn with its posterior uncertainty.

The switch probability is bounded by saturation. Above h = \rho_{\text{eff}} a single oddball changes the dominant state, and higher values produce nearly the same behaviour. The upper bound of the prior reflects this (

h_switch Identifiability; that analysis predates the adopted model).

The model comparison is confounded with action noise. Among the directed models, only the latent-state model has placement noise and cue sensitivity. A comparison with matched action noise is outstanding, and the classifier for the adopted agent is being retrained.

Estimates near the prior bounds. Posterior samples are clipped to the prior bounds, and several participants have estimates of cue sensitivity, placement noise, noise reactivity and the switch probability close to a bound.

records.content:
On each trial, with probability \lambda the allocation is centred on one state z drawn from the agent’s predicted belief P(z); otherwise the allocation is that of the adopted model (commitment-weighted mixture, commitment gain 3, single-stage allocation). The belief update, and therefore the meaning of the six Nexus parameters, is unchanged. The prior of the additional parameter is \lambda ~ U(0, 1); the other priors are those of 

Notation and Priors.

With the sampled state, a participant who places all nets at the other state on some stable trials can be described without a change of belief: the belief stays mostly on the current state, and the other state is occasionally sampled. In the adopted model, such placements require the belief itself to move, which is expressed by noise reactivity and belief momentum.

The latent-state agent (Nexus) explains the attacks with a small set of latent rules between which the environment switches. The models on this page explain the same attacks with other generative assumptions, and they are fitted with the same amortized workflow, the same 54 summary features and the same readout from belief to nets. A comparison therefore concerns the inference about the attacks and not the mapping from belief to allocation.

The alternative models are run with their own script (run_alt_models_overnight.ps1, see below), and their simulations, networks and results are stored in their own folders (bayes_flow/alt_models/<model>/). The results on this page are from run 23_11 (96 participants).

The reduced Bayesian observer of Nassar et al. (2010, J Neurosci; 2019, eLife) keeps one believed attack direction per cue and no latent states. After each attack it weighs three explanations of the attack.

Explanation

Assumed cause

Likelihood of the attack

Prior probability

change-point

the direction has changed, the new direction is unknown

uniform on the circle

H

oddball

a single displaced attack, the direction is unchanged

uniform on the circle

O

regular

scatter around the current direction

von Mises with the predictive variance \sigma^2 + U

1 - H - O

With the posterior probabilities W_{cp}, W_{odd} and W_{reg} of the three explanations, the believed direction moves toward the attack with the learning rate\alpha = W_{cp} + W_{reg}\,\tau, \qquad \tau = \frac{U}{U + \sigma^2},

where U is the observer’s uncertainty about the direction and \sigma^2 the assumed scatter of attacks around it (\sigma^2 = 1/\kappa, the scatter Nexus assumes). U is updated as the variance of the three-component posterior mixture (change-point centred on the attack with variance \sigma^2, regular centred on \mu + \tau\delta with variance \tau\sigma^2, oddball centred on \mu with variance U). Without oddballs this reduces to the update of Nassar et al. (2010), and without change-points to the oddball condition of Nassar et al. (2019).

Cue B is represented as a learned offset from the direction of cue A. As in Nexus, cue_sensitivity sets the initial offset and the asymptote toward which the offset is anchored, and the part of a regular prediction error on a cue-B trial that is not absorbed by the direction update moves the offset.

Two properties separate the observer from Nexus. Because change-points and oddballs have the same likelihood, a single displaced attack is divided between the two causes in the ratio H : O, and only the following attacks decide which cause was at work. And because the observer stores no previously learned directions, it cannot return to a former direction after a change-point and has to relearn it.

The predictive distribution is a von Mises around the believed direction of the current cue with concentration\kappa_{pred} = \frac{\text{precision\_weighting}}{\sigma^2 + U},

which equals the concentration of Nexus (\kappa \cdot precision_weighting) when U = 0 and widens with the observer’s uncertainty. The distribution is shifted by Gaussian placement noise and sharpened with exponent 1 + \text{precision\_weighting} before the seven nets are allocated (allocate_nets of reduced_agent_v3.py). The observer therefore hedges by widening the allocation around one direction and cannot place nets on two separate directions.

records.content:
Zika, Wiech, Reinecke, Browning and Schuck (2023, Nature Communications 14, 4203) modelled shock-probability ratings in an aversive reversal-learning task with an n-state model. The model learns within a currently active state, tracks how surprising the outcomes are under that state, and switches to another known state or creates a new state once the surprise exceeds a threshold. The present adaptation keeps this mechanism and replaces the beta distributions over shock probabilities by believed attack directions on the circle.

Each state s holds a believed direction \mu_s (for cue A, cue B through the learned offset as in the other models) and an amount of evidence n_s. Its uncertainty about the direction is U_s = \sigma^2 / n_s. Only the active state learns from an attack, with the count-based learning rate 1/(n_s + 1), and the evidence of every state decays by \lambda on every trial, as in Eqs. 7 to 10 of Zika et al. The decay sets the learning rate the active state approaches, about 1 - \lambda.

The model keeps a recency-weighted surprise of the active state (Eq. 11 of Zika et al.), with the prediction error scaled to [0, 1],S_t = (1 - \pi)\,S_{t-1} + \pi\,\frac{|\delta_t|}{\pi_{rad}} .

The surprise is compared with two thresholds, both scaled by the predictive standard deviation of the active state in the same units, \sigma_s = \sqrt{\sigma^2 + U_s}/\pi_{rad}.

Threshold

Condition

Consequence

basic (Eq. 12)

S > \sigma_s\,\eta

existing states whose predicted direction lies within S\,\pi_{rad} of the attack are polled, and the model switches to the most likely one or stays in the current state

compound (Eq. 13)

S > \sigma_s\,\eta\,q_K

existing states within \sigma_s\,\eta\,\pi_{rad} of the attack are polled, and if none fits a new state is created at the attack

The most likely state is the one with the highest likelihood of the attack under its predictive distribution, weighted by its evidence. After a switch or a new state the surprise restarts with the prediction error of the newly active state.

The difficulty q_K of creating a new state grows with the number of existing states K through a Chinese restaurant process. Counting each existing state once, the probability of a new state is \theta/((K-1)+\theta), and relative to K = 1q_K = 1 + \frac{K-1}{\theta} .

With one state (K = 1) the compound threshold equals the basic threshold, so the concentration \theta only acts on the creation of a third and every further state. The number of states is capped at six.

Zika et al. derived q from a two-parameter Chinese restaurant process with fixed values (\theta = 0.25, discount 1). The model is implemented in two versions. In M_ZIKA (--model zika) \theta is fixed at 0.25 as in Zika et al. In M_ZIKA_CRP (--model zika_crp) \theta is a free parameter. \theta is not identified on the task schedules (see below), so M_ZIKA is the version used for the participant fits, the model comparison and the questionnaire models.

The readout is that of the Nassar observer with the uncertainty of the active state. The model commits to one state at a time, so it hedges only by widening the allocation around the direction of that state.

Model and networks behind the current results

The participant results in this book come from run 12_10 (12 October 2026), obtained with the model adopted on 11 October 2026: the agent with the single-stage net allocation and a commitment gain of 3, the 54 summary features of feature_extraction_v3.py, and a posterior network and a model classifier each trained on 100,000 simulations. The decision and the validation are documented in 

Model Selection and Validation. The earlier run 09_09 used the networks of 8 June 2026 (commitment gain 8, 40 features); the chapters of that state are kept in archiv/run_09_09/.

Formally, we seek the posterior:p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto p(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \cdot p(\boldsymbol{\theta})

where \boldsymbol{\theta} = (\text{pw}, \text{nr}, \text{bm}, h, \text{cs}, \text{pn}) \in \mathbb{R}^6 are the cognitive parameters (precision_weighting, noise_reactivity, belief_momentum, h_switch, cue_sensitivity, placement_noise) and \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{54} is the feature vector. Rather than computing this posterior analytically or via sampling, we train a conditional density estimator q_\phi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) parameterized by neural network weights \phi to approximate p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) across the full joint space (\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{x}). The priors p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and all fixed constants of the simulator are listed in one place in Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants.

We approximated the posterior using neural posterior estimation (NPE) with learned summary statistics (

Radev et al., 2020), as implemented in the BayesFlow 2.0 framework for amortized Bayesian inference (

Radev et al., 2023a).

Specificially, the implemented inference pipeline uses the following architecture:



Figure 1:The Amortized Bayesian Inference Workflow.Agent Simulation → Feature Extraction → DeepSet(64) → FlowMatching → Posterior
     (CPU)            (deterministic)     (summary)    (inference)   (6 params)

Summary Network: A DeepSet (

Zaheer et al., 2017) maps the 54-dimensional feature vector (reshaped to a 1-element set) to a 64-dimensional summary representation. The DeepSet architecture is used (instead of an MLP) to comply with BayesFlow’s internal architecture requirements for condition passing. With a single set element it is functionally an MLP encoder of the feature vector and should be read as such.\mathbf{h} = \text{DeepSet}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{64}

Inference Network: FlowMatching (

Lipman et al., 2022; 

2024) with optimal transport and an MLP subnet (4 layers × 256 units, 5% dropout) learns a conditional normalizing flow from the 64-dimensional summary to the 6-dimensional posterior over parameters. FlowMatching was chosen over coupling flows for its faster convergence and better handling of multimodal posteriors.

How this works: the 64-dimensional summary \mathbf{h} conditions a Flow Matching model that learns a continuous normalizing flow from a standard normal base distribution to the conditional posterior:\boldsymbol{\theta} = F_\phi(\mathbf{z}; \mathbf{h}), \quad \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_6)

The flow F_\phi is parameterized by an MLP with 4 hidden layers of 256 units each, 5% dropout, and mish activation. We use optimal transport coupling (

Tong et al., 2023) to improve training efficiency.

The total number of trainable parameters is approximately 850,000.

The network is trained on 100,000 simulated sessions:

Data generation. N_{\text{train}} = 100{,}000 simulations are generated in parallel. For each simulation:

Parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} are drawn from the uniform priors

A trial schedule is randomly selected from the 20 available schedules

The agent runs the full session, producing allocations \{\mathbf{g}_t\}

The 54-dimensional feature vector \mathbf{x} is extracted

The pre-generated feature vectors are then used to train the DeepSet + FlowMatching network:

Training. The network is trained offline (i.e., on the pre-generated dataset, not with on-the-fly simulation) for up to 300 epochs with:

Batch size: 256

Initial learning rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}

Optimizer: Adam (this is the default Keras settings)

Early stopping: patience 50, restoring best weights (monitored on validation loss)

Validation split: 10% (10,000 held-out simulations)

Loss function. BayesFlow’s default training objective for Flow Matching is the conditional flow matching loss (

Lipman et al., 2022; 

2024), which minimizes the expected squared error between the learned and target velocity fields:\mathcal{L}(\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{t, \boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x}} \left[ \| v_\phi(t, \boldsymbol{\theta}_t; \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})) - u_t(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \|^2 \right]

where t \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1), \boldsymbol{\theta}_t = (1-t)\mathbf{z} + t\boldsymbol{\theta} (with optimal transport pairing), and u_t is the target velocity field.

How our loss curve looks like:



Figure 2:Training Loss and Validation Loss

Calibration and recovery are produced by run_agent_v3.py --mode validate, which writes sbc.json, recovery.json, validation_arrays.npz and validation_settings.json; tools/fig_validation.py turns the arrays into the report (recovery, cross-recovery, contraction, graphical calibration). The numbers below are those of the adopted posterior network (bayes_flow/rf_validation_gain3/). A comparison with the earlier networks and the remaining open analyses are in 

Model Selection and Validation.

Following 

Talts et al. (2018), we verify posterior calibration via SBC. For M = 1000 simulations with known parameters the posterior is sampled and the rank of the true parameter within the posterior is computed:

Draw \boldsymbol{\theta}^* \sim p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) from the prior

Simulate data \mathbf{x}^* from the agent with \boldsymbol{\theta}^*

Draw K = 1000 posterior samples \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^K \sim q_\phi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}^*)

Compute the rank statistic: r_i = \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{I}[\theta_i^{(k)} < \theta_i^*] for each parameter i

Under correct posterior calibration, r_i \sim \text{Discrete Uniform}(0, K), with mean K/2 and standard deviation \sqrt{((K+1)^2 - 1)/12} \approx 289. A rank mean that differs from its expected value indicates a systematic shift of the posterior relative to the true value, and a rank standard deviation above 289 indicates posteriors that are too narrow. With M = 1000 simulations, the standard error of a rank mean is 289/\sqrt{1000} \approx 9.1. Beyond these two moments, the empirical distribution function of the fractional ranks is compared with the uniform distribution using simultaneous 95% bands (

Säilynoja et al., 2022).

The confidence intervals are Fisher-transformed intervals for n = 500. The slope is that of the regression of posterior means on true values; a slope below 1 indicates shrinkage toward the prior mean. RMSE / prior SD compares the estimation error with the error of reporting the prior mean. Contraction is one minus the ratio of posterior to prior variance.

Five of the six parameters achieve recovery correlations of 0.92 or higher. Parameter recovery of this kind is the standard check that a model’s parameters can be estimated from data of the available size (

Wilson & Collins, 2019). Noise reactivity (r = 0.785) is the least well recovered parameter. Its target behaviour (oddball attribution) is governed by few informative events per session (see Oddball-Response Diagnostics), and its recovery is lowest at low precision weighting (0.64 in the lowest third of the prior range), where participants are not found; in the range of precision weighting occupied by participants it is 0.86.

Cross-recovery. The correlation between the estimate of one parameter and the true value of another does not exceed 0.21 in absolute value. Within posteriors, noise reactivity and belief momentum are negatively correlated (mean −0.64), so that for a single participant the two are not determined independently of each other.

For real participants, the pipeline:

Parses net allocations from the all_slot_barriers column of the behavioral results CSV

Extracts the trial schedule from the same file (episode, cue_identity, actual_vector_angle, outcome_occurred, is_oddball)

Computes the identical 54 features used during training

Passes the feature vector through the trained network

Returns 4,000 posterior samples per parameter, from which means, standard deviations, and credible intervals are computed*

Clips samples to prior bounds to prevent out-of-support estimates

*Posterior means, standard deviations, and central 95% credible intervals (the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles) are computed from the clipped samples. The SBC and recovery checks above use unclipped samples.

hierarchy.lvl2: Why we decided to take a feature-based approach
Why we decided to take a feature-based approach

records.content:
Rather than feeding the raw 32-slot allocation time series to the neural network (which caused training instability due to sparsity, variable sequence lengths, and the curse of dimensionality), we extract a fixed-size vector of 54 behavioral summary statistics per session. This approach eliminates variable-length padding issues, replaces sparse integer inputs with continuous, bounded features, ensures identical feature computation for simulated and real participant data (no domain shift) and thus reduces the neural network’s task from “learn to extract behavioral patterns from raw sequences” to “learn to map extracted patterns to parameters” - which also best aligns with the core research focus.

Furthermore, this approach simplifies the integration of multimodal data while maintaining the same network architecture; and - even more interestingly - it potentially allows for generalization to various tasks rather than being limited to a single paradigm.

All 54 features satisfy the following requirements (to ensure traceability and computational stability):

Continuous and bounded: No discrete or unbounded values that could destabilize training

Deterministic: Given the same allocation sequence \{\mathbf{g}_t\} and schedule, the features are identical

Domain-invariant: The same extraction code operates on both simulated agent output and real participant data (to avoid preprocessing differences that could create domain shift)

Information-preserving: Each feature is designed to capture a specific aspect of behavior that distinguishes between parameter values, based on prior sensitivity analysis (see The inference agent, associated behavioral features in the parameter definition section)

The 54 specified features are organized into 11 groups, each targeting different aspects of behavior:

The single direct marker for the belief-to-action execution noise parameter placement_noise. It measures undirected, memoryless placement scatter on stable mid-episode trials, separated from structured inference.

Feature

Description

within_state_placement_var

Mean absolute deviation of allocation from the local same-cue, same-episode circular mean on regular mid-episode trials (trial-in-episode > 4), in degrees

1. mean_net_entropy — Mean Shannon entropy (base 2) of the net allocation over all trials: \bar{H} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T H(\mathbf{g}_t), where H(\mathbf{g}) = -\sum_s p_s \log_2 p_s and p_s = g_s / \sum_j g_j.

2. std_net_entropy — Standard deviation of per-trial entropy: \text{SD}(H(\mathbf{g}_1), \ldots, H(\mathbf{g}_T)).

3. mean_slots_occupied — Mean number of slots with \geq 1 net: \frac{1}{T} \sum_t |\{s : g_{t,s} > 0\}|.

4. mean_max_nets_slot — Mean maximum stacking depth: \frac{1}{T} \sum_t \max_s g_{t,s}.

5. frac_stacking — Fraction of trials where any slot has \geq 2 nets: \frac{1}{T} \sum_t \mathbb{I}[\max_s g_{t,s} \geq 2].

6. mean_circ_variance — Mean circular variance of the allocation: \bar{V} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_t (1 - R_t), where R_t = \|\sum_s p_s e^{i\phi_s}\| is the resultant length.

7. entropy_change_halves — Difference in mean entropy between the second and first halves of the session: \bar{H}_{t > T/2} - \bar{H}_{t \leq T/2}.

8. mean_angular_error — Mean unsigned angular distance (degrees) between the allocation circular mean and the actual outcome: \frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}|} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{O}} |\angle(\omega_t - \bar{\phi}_t^g)|, where \mathcal{O} is the set of outcome trials and \bar{\phi}_t^g is the circular mean of \mathbf{g}_t.

9. std_angular_error — Standard deviation of per-trial angular errors.

10. mean_defense_rate — Fraction of outcome trials where the attacked slot has \geq 1 net: \frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}|} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{O}} \mathbb{I}[g_{t, s(\omega_t)} > 0], where s(\omega) = \text{round}(\omega \cdot S / 2\pi) \mod S.

11. defense_rate_improvement — Defense rate in the last 3 episodes minus the first 3 episodes.

12. mean_tracking_error — Mean angular distance (degrees) between the allocation center on trial t and the previous outcome \omega_{t-1}. Measures how closely the agent tracks the most recent observation.

13. oddball_entropy_spike — Mean entropy on trial t+1 after an oddball, minus mean entropy on regular trials.

14. oddball_angular_shift — Mean angular shift (degrees) of allocation center from trial t-1 to t+1 around oddball trials.

15. oddball_angular_shift_regular — Same metric computed around non-oddball outcome trials (baseline).

16. oddball_shift_ratio — Feature 14 divided by Feature 15. Values > 1 indicate the agent reacts more strongly to oddballs than to regular outcomes.

17. oddball_recovery_speed — Mean angular distance of allocation center on trials t+1, t+2, t+3 from the pre-oddball position (t-1), averaged across oddballs.

18. frac_oddball_followed — Fraction of oddballs where the allocation on t+1 is closer to the oddball direction \omega_t than the allocation on t-1 was.

19–21. transition_angular_error_t1/t3/t5 — Mean angular error on trials 1, 3, and 5 after episode transitions (z-state switches).

22. transition_recovery_slope — Linear regression slope of angular error over trials 1–5 after transitions. Negative slope = error decreasing = fast recovery.

23. transition_entropy_peak — Maximum entropy in the first 3 post-transition trials.

24. transition_entropy_recovery — Number of trials until entropy returns to baseline (\leq \bar{H} + 0.5 \cdot \text{SD}(H)) after a transition.

25. mean_angular_error_late_episode — Mean angular error on trials 6+ within each episode (baseline accuracy after initial learning).

26. transition_recovery_improvement — Linear slope of recovery speeds across the 8 transitions. Positive = recovery gets faster over the session (meta-learning).

27. cue_offset_learned — Mean angular offset (degrees) between allocation centers for Cue A vs. Cue B, computed per episode and averaged. True value: 70°.

28. cue_offset_std — Standard deviation of per-episode cue offsets.

29. cue_defense_rate_diff — Mean absolute difference in defense rate between Cue A and Cue B trials, per episode.

30. cue_entropy_diff — Mean absolute difference in entropy between Cue A and Cue B trials, per episode.

31. mean_trial_shift — Mean angular shift (degrees) of allocation center between consecutive trials.

32. std_trial_shift — Standard deviation of trial-to-trial shifts.

33. frac_large_shifts — Fraction of consecutive trial pairs with > 45° shift (proxy for perceived state switches).

34. autocorr_lag1 — Circular autocorrelation at lag 1: \frac{1}{T-1} \sum_t \cos(\bar{\phi}_{t+1}^g - \bar{\phi}_t^g). High values = stable allocation direction.

35. autocorr_lag3 — Same at lag 3 (captures stability across cue alternations).

36. omission_entropy_change — Mean entropy change from trial t-1 to t+1 around omission trials.

37. omission_shift — Mean angular shift of allocation center from t-1 to t+1 around omissions. Should be near zero for a normative agent (no information received on omission trials).

38. defense_rate_slope — Linear regression slope of per-episode defense rate over the 9 episodes.

39. angular_error_slope — Linear regression slope of per-episode angular error.

40. odd_even_episode_diff — Absolute difference in defense rate between odd-numbered and even-numbered episodes. Captures asymmetry in learning across alternating episodes.

records.content:
All shifts in this block are cue-corrected: the post-oddball allocation is compared to the nearest same-cue trial before the event.

41. oddball_shift_early_episode — Mean cue-corrected oddball-driven allocation shift (degrees) for oddballs occurring early in episodes (trial-in-episode 0–5).

42. oddball_shift_late_episode — Same for oddballs occurring late in episodes (trial-in-episode 12+).

43. oddball_shift_early_late_ratio — Ratio of feature 41 to feature 42. Indexes the temporal prior on switching (how much episode position modulates the oddball response).

44. oddball_shift_odd_episode — Mean cue-corrected oddball shift in odd-indexed (non-confusable) episodes.

45. oddball_shift_even_episode — Mean cue-corrected oddball shift in even-indexed (confusable) episodes, where the oddball outcome can coincide with the alternative state.

46. oddball_shift_parity_ratio — Ratio of feature 45 to feature 44. Indexes sensitivity to cue-confusability of the oddball.

hierarchy.lvl3: Block 10: Oddball-Following and Switch Dynamics (7 features)
Block 10: Oddball-Following and Switch Dynamics (7 features)

records.content:
47. oddball_persistence — Mean angular distance (degrees) maintained from the nominal state across the post-oddball trials, averaged over oddballs.

48. spontaneous_switch_rate — Rate of large allocation jumps (>45°) that are not preceded by an oddball, i.e. false-alarm switching.

49. switch_lag_after_evidence — Mean lag (in trials) between the accumulation of switch-consistent evidence and a committed allocation switch.

50. belief_lability — Mean magnitude (degrees) of belief-direction changes across trials. Captures large, structured jumps; this is the feature most sensitive to the structured template-inference jumps the agent deliberately does not model, and is the hardest residual in posterior-predictive checks.

51. late_episode_shift_buildup — Build-up of allocation shifts toward the end of episodes (anticipatory switching).

52. oddball_follow_raw — Cue-agnostic next-trial movement toward the raw oddball location: (d_{\text{pre}} - d_{\text{post}}) / \pi, where d is the angular distance from the allocation to the raw oddball angle on the trial before / after the oddball. Normalised to [-1, 1].

53. oddball_follow_switch — Cue-aware next-trial movement toward the switch-interpretation location: the raw oddball angle shifted by the cue offset when the next trial’s cue differs from the oddball trial’s cue. Distinguishes cue-aware from cue-blind switching. Normalised to [-1, 1].

54. within_state_placement_var — Mean absolute deviation (degrees) of the allocation circular mean from the local same-cue, same-episode circular mean, computed on regular mid-episode trials (trial-in-episode > 4). This is the direct behavioural marker for placement_noise: it isolates undirected, memoryless placement scatter from structured inference. It increases monotonically with placement_noise (≈ 17° at placement_noise = 0 to ≈ 42° at the prior upper bound).

records.content:
This section documents the identifiability analysis of the perceived-volatility
parameter h_switch, the rationale for its prior bound, and the relationship
between h_switch and noise_reactivity observed in the participant data. The
analysis is fully reproducible via h_switch_grid.py.

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling

records.content:
In an initial fit with the h_switch prior extended to [0.005, 0.35], a large
share of participants had posteriors pressed against the upper bound: 59% had
their 97.5% credible limit pinned at 0.35, and 68% had posterior means above
0.30. Taken at face value this would imply that most participants believe the
latent state switches on roughly every third trial — far more often than the
true switch rate (~0.05 per trial; episodes are 16–24 trials long). This was
implausible on its face and motivated a systematic investigation rather than
simply accepting the values or extending the bound further.

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
hierarchy.lvl2: The switch mechanism and why behaviour saturates

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
hierarchy.lvl2: The switch mechanism and why behaviour saturates

records.content:
In the v2 agent, a single oddball produces an outcome at the other latent
state’s location (the oddball displacement of +120° coincides with the
alternative state). Working through the Bayesian belief update with a
freshly-committed prior, the raw posterior over the alternative state crosses
0.5 — i.e. the agent commits to a full state switch — exactly whenh_{\text{switch}} > \rho_{\text{eff}} = \rho_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{noise\_reactivity},

with \rho_{\text{fixed}} = 0.10. This is the Piray & Daw (2021)
volatility-versus-stochasticity trade-off emerging directly from the mixture
likelihood: whether a surprising outcome is attributed to a changed rule
(volatility, h_switch) or to noise (stochasticity, noise_reactivity).

The crucial consequence is that the switching behaviour is governed by whether
the agent is above or below this threshold, not by the precise value of
h_switch. Once h_switch exceeds 0.1 · noise_reactivity, the agent switches
at essentially every oddball, and there are no further switching opportunities
to exploit. Behaviour therefore saturates: higher h_switch values become
behaviourally indistinguishable.



Figure 1:Switch-interpretation behaviour (oddball_follow_switch) as a function of
h_switch at four noise_reactivity levels. Each curve rises sharply at its
own threshold h = 0.1 \cdot nr (dotted vertical lines) and then plateaus.
Above threshold, behaviour is flat — h_switch is no longer identifiable from
behaviour. The highest informative region is reached at h \approx 0.30, the
threshold for the largest noise_reactivity in the prior (nr = 3.0).

Because noise_reactivity ranges up to 3.0, the largest informative value of
h_switch is approximately 0.10 \cdot 3.0 = 0.30. Beyond this, no
noise_reactivity value leaves the behaviour unsaturated, so additional prior
mass above 0.30 contributes only non-identifiable parameter space — precisely
the region that produces the ceiling artefact.

records.content:
We swept candidate upper bounds and measured the recovery of h_switch and
noise_reactivity, plus the recovery slope in the upper 20% of the prior (a
slope approaching zero indicates the ceiling/saturation regime).



Figure 2:Recovery as a function of the h_switch upper bound. As the bound admits more
of the saturated region, noise_reactivity recovery degrades (the two
parameters become harder to separate where behaviour is saturated). A bound of
0.30 keeps the prior within the behaviourally informative range while retaining
solid recovery of both parameters.

Note that the apparent improvement in r(h_switch) at larger bounds is
mechanical: a wider prior spreads more variance across the range, inflating the
correlation even though the upper portion is poorly resolved. The behaviourally
principled criterion is the saturation analysis, not the raw correlation. Both
converge on the same conclusion.

Decision: the h_switch prior upper bound is set to 0.30, the point at
which the switch threshold for the maximum noise_reactivity is reached. This
is the largest bound for which the entire prior remains behaviourally
identifiable, and it avoids the implausible near-ceiling values while preserving
the joint recovery of h_switch and noise_reactivity.
