hierarchy.lvl2: The h_switch–noise_reactivity coupling is genuine, not an artefact

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
hierarchy.lvl2: The h_switch–noise_reactivity coupling is genuine, not an artefact

records.content:
Across participants, posterior h_switch and noise_reactivity are positively
correlated (r = +0.60). This is theoretically expected: a person who perceives
the environment as more volatile (high h_switch) and simultaneously attributes
surprising outcomes more readily to genuine change rather than noise is
expressing a coherent, correlated cognitive style. Because the two parameters
sit on either side of the same switch threshold, a positive association across
individuals is exactly what the volatility/stochasticity framework predicts.

A coupling of this kind could, in principle, also arise as an inference
artefact — if the network compressed the two parameters along the threshold
line. We tested this directly. In simulation, noise_reactivity and h_switch
were drawn independently; if the inference induced a spurious coupling, the
estimated parameters would correlate despite the independent ground truth.
They do not: the estimated correlation is ≈ 0 (and slightly negative), while the
real-participant correlation is strongly positive.



Figure 3:Left: simulated data with noise_reactivity and h_switch drawn
independently. The estimated parameters show no spurious correlation
(estimated r ≈ 0), confirming the inference does not manufacture coupling.
Right: real participants. The posteriors show a clear positive coupling
(r = +0.60), and all participants lie above the single-oddball switch threshold
h = 0.1 \cdot nr (dashed line) — i.e. they reliably treat oddballs as state
switches. The coupling is therefore a genuine psychological effect.

Because the simulated check rules out an inference-induced artefact, the
correlation observed in the real data reflects genuine individual differences in
cognitive style. This is a substantive finding rather than a nuisance, and it is
consistent with the prior theoretical expectation that perceived volatility and
the propensity to attribute change (rather than noise) covary.

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling

records.content:
All 34 participants lie above the single-oddball switch threshold
h_{\text{switch}} > 0.10 \cdot \text{noise\_reactivity}. The model therefore
infers that every participant reliably interprets oddballs as state switches —
consistent with the originally observed posterior-predictive behaviour, in which
participants made sharp, full-magnitude allocation jumps following oddballs. The
participants pressed toward the (previous) ceiling are specifically those with
high noise_reactivity: to reproduce their observed switch behaviour at high
noise_reactivity, the model requires a correspondingly high h_switch to keep
them above the threshold. This is the mechanistic origin of the coupling and of
the former ceiling.

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling

records.content:
h_switch is well identified up to the switch threshold; above it,
behaviour saturates and the parameter is only weakly constrained from above.
The bound of 0.30 keeps the prior within the identifiable range.

The high h_switch values seen with the 0.35 bound should not be read as
evidence that participants believe in literally frequent latent-state
switching. They indicate that the participant sits above the switch threshold;
the precise value above threshold is not behaviourally determined.

The positive h_switch–noise_reactivity correlation is a genuine,
artefact-free psychological effect and can be reported as such, with the
simulated independence check as supporting evidence.

For downstream individual-difference analyses, the behaviourally robust
quantity is whether and how strongly a participant treats oddballs as
switches (captured by the switch-interpretation behaviour and the joint
position in the noise_reactivity–h_switch plane), interpreted together
rather than as two fully independent dimensions.

The hybrid switch model describes a participant as a cue-wise direction tracker that switches, at some trial, to inference over latent states, and then relies on that inference with a weight w. It answers two questions that the Nexus model takes for granted: when a participant starts to use the task structure, and how fully the placements then follow it. An extension (hybrid7) also asks which structure is used after the switch: two latent states coupled across the colour cues, as in Nexus, or four independent states, two per cue. The model is used to describe participants and to relate the switch, the reliance and the type of structure to the questionnaire scores (

A General Questionnaire Factor, section 8; 

Structural Inference Under Uncertainty, section 1). It is not part of the model comparison.

Scripts (analysis repository, bayes_flow/online_mc/): omc_sim6.py and omc_sim7.py (simulators), omc_hybrid.py (network, validation and inference; OMC_MODEL=hybrid7), omc_coverage.py (coverage of the participants by the simulations); questionnaire tests: tambi_hybrid7_factor.py.

Three systems, all learning from every attack.

System

Learns

Acts

Tracker

one direction per colour cue by a delta rule with learning rate \alpha (model M_TRACK_CUE of the model comparison)

centred on the cue’s tracked direction

Coupled latent states

identical to the tracker until it creates a second state from evidence; then a Nexus agent (

The Inference Agent) with one latent state shared by both cues

Nexus action: with probability \lambda centred on one state sampled from the predicted belief (state guessing s: P(\text{state 1}) = (1 - s)\,b + s/2), otherwise its commitment-weighted mixture

Four independent states

per cue two direction modes updated by online k-means (rate \alpha), no state belief, no coupling between the cues, no transitions (model M_STRUCT4)

one of the cue’s two modes, each with probability ½

The second state (or, for the four-state system, each cue’s second mode) is created from evidence: after the first five attacks, two consecutive attacks that are both more than 90° from the system’s prediction and lie within 45° of each other. Until then the structured systems act like the tracker, so all three systems act identically in the first episode.

Switch and reliance. Before the switch trial, the placement follows the tracker. From the switch trial on, the predictive distribution is\pi_t = (1 - w)\,\pi^{\text{tracker}}_t + w\,\big[(1 - v)\,\pi^{\text{coupled}}_t + v\,\pi^{\text{four}}_t\big].

The switch trial is t_1 + \tau, where t_1 is the first transition; \tau beyond the end of the session means that the participant never switches. w is the reliance on the structured systems and v the share of the four-state system among them.

Shared action layer. Whatever system acts, the same non-structural responses are added: an exact repeat of the previous placement for the same cue (probability rep), centring on a surprising attack, i.e. more than 60° from the previous placement (phi), hedging as an equal mixture of \pi_t and the previous placement direction (eta), a placement shift per trial (placement_noise), random-direction trials (trial_lapse), random nets (lapse), and the participant’s own number of nets per trial.

The priors put more mass on precise, early-switching, high-reliance agents than a uniform prior would (variant B of omc_sim6.py), because the participants lie in that region.

Network. 100,000 simulated sessions on the task’s trial schedules. A time-series summary network (convolution and bidirectional GRU) reads the per-trial features of the whole session, and a flow-matching network gives the joint posterior of all parameters (logit of the prior-scaled value); 80 training epochs. Per participant, 4000 posterior draws. The switch is summarised as P(switch), the share of draws with a switch within the session; w, v and the posterior probability of the four-state system, P(four) = P(v > .5), are summarised over the draws with a switch.

Figure 1:Recovery (posterior median against the true value) and simulation-based calibration (rank histograms) of hybrid7 on held-out simulations.

The rank histograms are close to uniform (precision weighting has fewer ranks at the two extremes), and the 90 % intervals contain the true value in 89 to 94 % of the simulations. Recovery differs strongly between the parameters:

Well recovered: precision weighting (r = .99), exact repeats (.96), random nets (.89), tracker learning rate (.87), placement noise (.84).

Switch and reliance: for simulated agents with a switch, the recovery of w is r = .78, and of the product of switching and reliance r = .83. A switch within 25 trials after the first transition is located with a median error of 5 trials; later switches are located less precisely (median error 19 to 22 trials). With true w below about .2, the posterior medians of w lie around .3 to .4, so low reliance is not resolved.

Type of structure: v is identified only at high reliance. With true w ≥ .7, the four-state and the coupled system are told apart with AUC = .96 (r = .77); with w between .4 and .7, AUC = .74; below .4, not at all (AUC ≤ .58).

Not recovered: the Nexus parameters noise reactivity (r = .09), belief momentum (.22), switch probability (.14) and cue sensitivity (.35), and state guessing s (−.02). In the hybrid, the structured system shares the placement with the tracker and the action layer, and these parameters leave too little trace in the data. They are not interpreted.

Coverage. 31 of the 96 participants lie outside the 99th percentile of the simulations in the embedding of the summary network (omc_coverage.py). Their estimates are reported but marked, and the questionnaire tests are repeated without them.

All 96 participants switch (P(switch) > .5), in a median of the second episode in every condition. The median reliance after the switch is .90 to .91 in every condition, and 88 participants have w ≥ .7, the range in which the type of structure is identified. The median share of the four-state system is .23 without, .38 with partial and .05 with full instructions; P(four) > .8 holds for 6 participants without, 9 with partial and 2 with full instructions, and P(four) < .2 for 11, 11 and 13 (bayes_flow/online_mc/results_hybrid7/participant_estimates.csv).

Tests: ordinary least squares with HC3 standard errors and the condition contrasts as covariates, per SD of the score (tambi_hybrid7_factor.py; stats_results/<tag>/questionnaire_factor/general_factor/hybrid7_factor.csv and hybrid7_factor_by_condition.csv).

Reliance. In the participants with high reliance (w ≥ .7, n = 87 with a factor score), w is lower with higher general-factor scores (−0.023 per SD, p < .001; within the simulation range, n = 58: −0.016, p = .013). The slope comes mainly from participants without instructions (−0.029, p < .001; Partial −0.015, p = .20; Full −0.022, p = .36; differences between the conditions p ≥ .31).

Type of structure. v and P(four) are unrelated to the general factor (all participants: p = .60).

Split placements. v goes with split placements at t+2 after transitions (high reliance: ρ = .42, p < .001), and the general-factor slope on split placements changes little when v is added (all participants: +0.037, p = .038 → +0.034, p = .051). w is unrelated to split placements in the high-reliance sample (p = .85), and the general-factor slope on split placements does not decrease when w is added (+0.034 to +0.040 per SD). The lower reliance of higher scorers is therefore separate from their splitting of the nets. It depends on the Nexus parameters of the coupled system being free: with them fixed (hybrid7f, below), w is unrelated to the general factor.

hierarchy.lvl2: Variant with the unrecovered parameters fixed (hybrid7f)
Variant with the unrecovered parameters fixed (hybrid7f)

records.content:
In hybrid7f the five parameters that hybrid7 does not recover are fixed: the Nexus parameters of the coupled system at the medians of the adopted Nexus fits of the 96 participants (noise reactivity 1.304, belief momentum 0.246, switch probability 0.108, cue sensitivity 0.828) and state guessing s at 0. The other 12 parameters, the priors, the network and the training are those of hybrid7 (omc_sim7.py with OMC7_FIX=1, OMC_MODEL=hybrid7f).

Validation. Recovery is similar to hybrid7, slightly better for the reliance and the type of structure: w r = .64 (hybrid7 .61), w in agents that switch .79 (.78), v .64 (.56), switch trial .60 (.65), tracker learning rate .87 (.87), precision weighting .99 (.99). The four-state and the coupled system are told apart with AUC = .98 at w ≥ .7 (.96) and .82 at w between .4 and .7 (.74). Switches within 25 trials after the first transition are located with a median error of 4.8 trials (5.4). 30 of the 96 participants lie outside the 99th percentile of the simulations (31).

The participants’ estimates agree with those of hybrid7 for precision weighting (Spearman ρ = .96), the tracker learning rate (.81) and v (.88), less for w (.69) and the switch trial (.58). hierarchy.lvl1: Overview Computational Modeling: Amortized Bayesian Parameter Estimation
Overview Computational Modeling: Amortized Bayesian Parameter Estimation

records.content:
This chapter describes the computational modeling pipeline used to estimate participant-specific cognitive parameters from behavioral data. A short, self-contained tour of the model is given in Modeling at a Glance, and all symbols, priors and fixed constants are collected in Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants. The pipeline combines four components:

The inference agent, a parametric belief-update model with six free parameters (precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum, perceived volatility, cue sensitivity, placement noise) that maps these parameters to observable behavior. It is implemented in reduced_agent_v3.py.

A feature extraction module, the deterministic extraction of 54 behavioral summary statistics from the net allocations of a session, computed by the same code for simulated and observed sessions.

An amortized model comparison, a neural classifier that assigns each participant posterior probabilities over five candidate models, from random allocation to full latent-state inference. It identifies participants whose behavior is indistinguishable from random allocation and participants who do not perform latent-state inference.

An amortized Bayesian inference network, a neural density estimator (BayesFlow) that inverts the agent model, mapping the 54 observed behavioral features to a posterior distribution over the six parameters.

The key advantage of this methodological approach is that inference is amortized. Specificially, a neural network is trained once on a large corpus of simulated agent–environment interactions, after which posterior estimation for any real participant takes approximately 3 seconds. The likelihood of the agent is defined only through its simulator and cannot be evaluated in closed form, so that sampling-based methods that require the likelihood are not available, and amortized simulation-based inference provides full posterior distributions from forward simulations alone.

Whether the resulting posteriors can be trusted is addressed in three places. Calibration and parameter recovery of the inference network on simulated data are reported in Amortized Bayesian Inference. The agreement between the fitted agent and participants’ behavior is reported in Posterior Predictive Checks. The two parameters with limited identifiability are examined in Oddball-Response Diagnostics (noise reactivity) and h_switch Identifiability (perceived volatility).

The particle-filter simulation models documented in the section The Simulation Models are not part of this pipeline and are no longer used for parameter inference.

Further information about Amortized Bayesian Inference and BayesFlow 2.0 can be found in 

Radev et al. (2020), 

Radev et al. (2023) and on the 

BayesFlow website.

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task

records.content:
Participants in the TAMBI mosquito defense task face a complex learning problem: they must infer hidden environmental regularities (latent state transitions, cue-dependent directional offsets, and the distinction between noise and genuine change) from noisy, intermittent outcome feedback. Not all participants approach this problem in the same way. Some may engage in latent structure inference, tracking hidden states and attributing surprises to their appropriate sources. Others may rely on simpler strategies: following the most recent outcome direction, learning the association between cue colours and attack directions without ever building a model of the latent state dynamics, or covering all structured attack locations without inferring which state is currently active. A small number may not engage meaningfully at all.

Before we can interpret the cognitive parameters estimated by our inference agent (

Amortized Bayesian Inference), we need to establish which type of learning strategy each participant is using. This is essential for three reasons:

Validity of parameter estimates. The six parameters of the inference agent (precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum, perceived volatility, cue sensitivity, placement noise) are defined within a latent-structure-learning agent. Estimating these parameters for a participant who is not performing structure learning would be scientifically inappropriate (analogous to fitting a linear regression model to non-linear data).

Participant exclusion. Participants who clicked randomly or without meaningful engagement should be identified and excluded from subsequent analyses. Here, model comparison provides an objective, data-driven exclusion criterion.

Characterisation of the learning strategy spectrum. The distribution of winning models across participants provides insight into the prevalence of different learning strategies in the sample, and can be related to instruction condition and trait-level measures.

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task

records.content:
We employ BayesFlow’s ModelComparisonApproximator (Radev et al., 2023; Schmitt et al., 2023) to perform amortized Bayesian model comparison. The approach follows the same simulation-based inference logic as the parameter estimation pipeline: a neural classifier is trained on a large corpus of simulated behavioral data (generated from all candidate models), and then applied to real participant data to estimate posterior model probabilities.

Compared with model comparison by information criteria or by Bayes factors obtained with bridge sampling, both of which require a tractable likelihood that the present simulators do not have, amortized model comparison:

Operates on the same 54 behavioral summary features used for parameter estimation (ensuring consistency)

Returns posterior probabilities over models, whose calibration can be checked on simulated data

Requires no per-participant optimization or sampling at inference time

Can be validated via confusion matrices, calibration curves, and model recovery analyses before application to real data

The posterior model probabilities are conditional on the candidate set and on the prior over each model’s parameters. They state which of the five candidate models best accounts for a participant’s feature vector, and they do not state that this model describes the participant well in absolute terms. That question is addressed by the 

Posterior Predictive Checks.

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task

records.content:
Rather than comparing a large number of models that differ in subtle ways, we define a compact set of five models that span the qualitative spectrum from disengaged behavior to full latent structure inference. Each successive model adds a qualitatively distinct cognitive capability.



Figure 1:The candidate models. (The figure shows the original four-model set and has to be regenerated to include M_STRUCT4.)

Model

Strategy

Free parameters

M_RANDOM

Uniform random allocation

0

M_TRACK_SIMPLE

Tracks one direction, no cue differentiation, no latent states

2

M_TRACK_CUE

Tracks one direction per cue via a learned cue offset, no latent states

2

M_STRUCT4

Knows both attack directions of each cue and covers both permanently, without inferring the active state

2

M_STRUCT

Infers the active latent state and commits to it

6

The rationale for limiting the set to these models is twofold. First, the cognitive transitions (no learning → outcome tracking → cue association → knowledge of the four structured locations → state inference) capture the most important qualitative distinctions in learning strategy. Second, model variants that differ only in continuous parameter settings within the structure-learning agent (e.g. with or without oddball attribution, with fixed or free volatility) are better handled by the parameter estimation pipeline, where these differences manifest as different parameter values rather than as discrete model classes. Maintaining them as separate models would test the same cognitive dimension at both the model and the parameter level.

M_STRUCT4 was added to the original four-model set to separate two things that M_STRUCT combines, namely knowing that each cue has two possible attack directions and inferring which of the two is currently valid. A participant who has learned the four locations but hedges between the two directions of the current cue on every trial has acquired the structure of the task without performing latent-state inference, and should not be classified as M_STRUCT.

records.content:
Purpose: Tests whether behavior can be explained by exponential moving average (EMA) tracking of the most recent outcome direction, without any cue differentiation or latent state inference.

Mechanism: The agent maintains a single direction estimate \hat{\mu}, initialised at the first observed outcome and updated after each observed outcome \omega_t via a circular EMA:\hat{\mu} \leftarrow \left(\hat{\mu} + \alpha \cdot \angle(\omega_t - \hat{\mu})\right) \mod 2\pi

where \alpha is the learning rate and \angle(\cdot) denotes the signed angular distance in [-\pi, \pi]. The agent does not distinguish between cue colours: outcomes from both cues update the same direction estimate. No update occurs on omission trials.

Free parameters:

Parameter

Prior

Description

precision_weighting

\text{Uniform}(0.1, 5.0)

Controls allocation concentration (same role as in M_STRUCT)

\alpha

\text{Uniform}(0.01, 0.5)

EMA learning rate

What this model cannot capture: Cue-specific behaviour, latent state transitions, or oddball attribution.

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task

records.content:
Purpose: Tests whether behaviour can be explained by trial-by-trial tracking with a learned cue-colour association. This is a form of associative learning that does not require inferring hidden states.

Mechanism: Identical to M_TRACK_SIMPLE, with the addition of a cue-specific angular offset \hat{\delta}_B (initialised at 0) that is learned online. The prediction for Cue A is \hat{\mu}_A and for Cue B (\hat{\mu}_A + \hat{\delta}_B) \mod 2\pi. When a Cue B outcome is observed, the offset and the base direction share the prediction error:\hat{\delta}_B \leftarrow (\hat{\delta}_B + \alpha \cdot 0.3 \cdot \text{PE}_B) \mod 2\pi\hat{\mu}_A \leftarrow (\hat{\mu}_A + \alpha \cdot 0.7 \cdot \text{PE}_B) \mod 2\pi

where \text{PE}_B = \angle(\omega_t - [\hat{\mu}_A + \hat{\delta}_B]).

Free parameters: Same as M_TRACK_SIMPLE (precision_weighting, \alpha). The offset \hat{\delta}_B is a learned internal state, not a parameter with a prior.

What this model cannot capture: Latent state transitions (the agent has no concept of alternating hidden states), oddball attribution (all surprises are treated as signal), or the coexistence of two directions per cue.

hierarchy.lvl3: 2.4 M_STRUCT4: Four-Location Coverage Without State Inference

records.content:
Purpose: Tests whether behaviour reflects knowledge of the four structured attack locations (two cues × two latent states) without inference about which latent state is currently active.

Mechanism: For each cue, the agent maintains up to two direction modes by circular online k-means. An observed outcome is assigned to the nearest existing mode of its cue and moves that mode toward the outcome at rate \alpha,m_j \leftarrow \left(m_j + \alpha \cdot \angle(\omega_t - m_j)\right) \mod 2\pi .

If the outcome lies more than 50° from every existing mode of that cue and fewer than two modes exist, it creates a second mode at its own location instead. On each trial, the predictive distribution is an equally weighted von Mises mixture over the available modes of the current cue (uniform over the 32 slots before the first outcome of that cue), without a state belief and without temporal weighting. The agent therefore covers both directions of the current cue on every trial and never commits to one of them.

Free parameters:

Parameter

Prior

Description

precision_weighting

\text{Uniform}(0.1, 5.0)

Controls allocation concentration

\alpha

\text{Uniform}(0.01, 0.5)

Learning rate of the direction modes

The separation threshold for creating a second mode is fixed at 50°.

What this model adds over M_TRACK_CUE: The simultaneous representation of two attack directions per cue. Because an oddball outcome lands on the other state’s direction, the second mode can also be created by an oddball.

What this model cannot capture: Commitment to one latent state, the change of that commitment at a transition, and the attribution of a displaced outcome to noise versus a change of state.

Mechanism: The six-parameter inference agent described in The Inference Agent and implemented in reduced_agent_v3.py. It implements a two-state hidden Markov model with cue-dependent offsets, an oddball mixture observation model, belief momentum, and placement noise. model_zoo_v3.py imports its parameter list and priors directly from reduced_agent_v3.py, so that the model comparison and the parameter estimation always use the same agent.

records.content:
All five models produce integer net allocations \mathbf{g}_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{32} on every trial. These allocations are processed through the same 54-feature extraction pipeline used for parameter estimation (see the 

Feature Extraction chapter). This ensures:

Identical processing of simulated and observed data: The classifier sees the same feature representation for training (simulated data from all five models) and inference (real participant data).

Consistency with parameter estimation: A participant classified as M_STRUCT by the model comparison has their parameter estimates computed from the same features.

Interpretability: The features that drive classification can be inspected directly.

Identical processing does not guarantee that the feature vectors of real participants lie within the region of feature space covered by the simulations. Whether they do is a separate check (see Section 5.6).

records.content:
The model comparison uses BayesFlow 2.0’s ModelComparisonApproximator, implemented in run_model_comparison_v3.py. The architecture consists of:

Adapter: Renames the model index to inference_variables, applies one-hot encoding (\mathbb{R}^1 \to \mathbb{R}^5), and converts to float32. The summary variables are standardised by the approximator.

Summary Network: A DeepSet (Zaheer et al., 2017) with summary_dim=8 and depth=1 processes the feature vector, reshaped to a 1-element set, and maps the 54-dimensional feature vector to an 8-dimensional embedding. With a single set element, the DeepSet is functionally an MLP encoder.

Classifier Network: An MLP with two hidden layers of 64 units each (SiLU activation, no dropout) maps the 8-dimensional embedding to 5 logits, which are passed through a softmax to produce posterior model probabilities.

The network is deliberately small relative to the 100,000 training simulations, given the low complexity of a five-class classification problem on 54 features.

records.content:
Data generation. N = 100{,}000 simulations are generated in parallel (run_classifier_training.ps1; the default of the script is 40,000). For each simulation:

A model is selected uniformly at random from the five candidate models

Parameters are drawn from the model’s prior

A trial schedule is randomly selected from the 20 available schedules

The model simulates the full session

The 54-feature vector is extracted

Because the model index is drawn at random for every simulation, the classes are balanced in expectation (8,000 simulations per model) and not exactly. The realised counts are written to mc_data/meta.json. A uniform prior over the five models is thereby built into the classifier.

Training. The classifier is trained via cross-entropy loss for 200 epochs with:

Batch size: 512

Adam with cosine learning rate decay starting at 

10-4

90% of the simulations used for training, with the remaining 10% used only to report held-out accuracy after training

No early stopping

Loss function. The standard categorical cross-entropy:\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{m=1}^{5} y_{i,m} \log \hat{p}_{i,m}

where y_{i,m} is the one-hot encoded true model index and \hat{p}_{i,m} is the predicted probability for model m.

Near-perfect closed-world accuracy shows that the five simulators occupy almost non-overlapping regions of the 54-dimensional feature space. It also means that the classifier has seen almost no ambiguous cases during training, so that its output for a feature vector that lies between or outside these regions is an extrapolation. Three checks address this: a test of whether participants’ feature vectors lie within the simulated feature distribution (model misspecification in summary space; Schmitt et al., 2023; open), the comparison with placement noise in all directed models (Section 5.7; implemented, not yet run), and the stability of the participant classification across independently trained classifiers (open; the classifier of Section 5.7 partly serves this purpose, because it is trained on new simulations). They are listed on the

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
hierarchy.lvl3: 5.7 Sensitivity analysis: placement noise in the alternative models

records.content:
Question. Of the five models, only M_STRUCT contains placement noise. Participants’ placements vary considerably within a latent state, so that M_STRUCT could be preferred because it reproduces this variability, not because participants infer the latent state. Conversely, a free noise parameter could make the models harder to distinguish, because it can absorb differences in the mean placement pattern. The sensitivity analysis tests both possibilities.

Design. M_TRACK_SIMPLE, M_TRACK_CUE and M_STRUCT4 receive the placement noise of M_STRUCT: a free parameter with the same uniform prior (0 to 0.873 rad, i.e. up to 50°), applied in the same way (on every trial, the predictive distribution over the 32 positions is shifted by one zero-mean Gaussian displacement before the allocation is sharpened and converted into seven nets). M_RANDOM and M_STRUCT are unchanged, and so are the features, the classifier architecture and the training settings (100,000 simulations in equal proportions, 200 epochs). The switch is the environment variable NEXUS_COMPETITOR_NOISE=1, set by run_model_comparison_v3.py --competitor-noise; without it, all models and their random-number streams are identical to the primary analysis (checked by simulating with fixed seeds against the previous version of model_zoo_v3.py). Cue sensitivity is not added to the alternative models: M_TRACK_CUE learns the cue offset as a free quantity, and M_STRUCT4 learns the directions of the two cues separately, so that both can represent any cue offset.

Analyses.

Model recovery in the extended model space. The new classifier is validated on 5,000 new simulations (1,000 per model): confusion matrix, accuracy, expected calibration error, and the proportion of sessions assigned to the generating model by quintile of the generating placement noise. A drop of recovery at high placement noise would show that the noise parameter absorbs the differences between the models.

Cross-classification. 1,000 sessions per model from each model space are classified by both classifiers. The key quantity is the proportion of sessions of the alternative models with placement noise that the primary classifier assigns to M_STRUCT: if it is substantial, a classification as M_STRUCT in the primary analysis could reflect placement noise alone.

Participants. All participants are classified with the new classifier. Reported are the agreement of the assigned models with the primary analysis (cross-table, by condition), the participants whose assignment changes, and random-effects Bayesian model selection over participants for both classifiers (expected model frequencies, exceedance probabilities, Bayesian omnibus risk and protected exceedance probabilities; 

Rigoux et al., 2014), with the log posterior model probabilities, floored at log 10⁻⁶, as log model evidences.

Criteria, specified before the analysis was run (12 October 2026). The conclusion that participants’ behaviour is best described by latent-state inference is retained if (a) in the extended model space every model is recovered with an accuracy of at least .90, also in the highest quintile of placement noise; (b) the primary classifier assigns fewer than 5 % of the sessions of each alternative model with placement noise to M_STRUCT; and (c) M_STRUCT remains the model with the highest protected exceedance probability under the new classifier. If (a) fails, the models cannot be distinguished once all have placement noise, and the primary comparison is reported with this limitation. If (b) or (c) fails, the classification as M_STRUCT cannot be attributed to latent-state inference, and the participants concerned are reported. Either way, both analyses are reported.

Running it. bayes_flow/run_competitor_noise_sensitivity.ps1 -Tag <tag> runs all steps (validation of the primary classifier with a per-simulation record, simulation, training, validation, participant inference, cross-classification, report). Outputs: mc_validation_gain3_compnoise/, mc_checkpoints_gain3_compnoise/, mc_results/<tag>_compnoise/ and mc_results/<tag>_compnoise/sensitivity_report/ (summary.txt, recovery_by_model_space.csv, accuracy_by_placement_noise.csv, cross_classification.csv, participant_comparison.csv, assignment_crosstab.csv, group_level_bms.csv, fig_competitor_noise_sensitivity). The adopted validation in mc_validation_gain3/ is not overwritten.

records.content:
The three instruction conditions differ in what participants are told about the structure before the task (see 

Instruction Conditions).

Condition 1 (basic instructions): Participants are told how to place nets and must discover all regularities through experience.

Condition 2 (rules mentioned): Participants are additionally told that rules might determine the attack direction, without being told what the rules are.

Condition 3 (rules explained): Participants are additionally told the cue offset (about 70°) and the rotation of both directions (about 120°) at irregular intervals.

The distribution of the model classes across the three conditions serves as a manipulation check, namely whether instruction shifts participants toward strategies that use more of the task structure. In run 12_10, the latent-state model was assigned to 21 of 24 participants in None, 25 of 30 in Partial and 13 of 14 in Full (Section 6.3).

hierarchy.lvl2: Why the commitment gain was changed
Why the commitment gain was changed

records.content:
The commitment gain determines how strongly the allocation commits to the more probable state (see 

The Inference Agent). Three observations led to the change from 8 to 3.

Participants place nets at the other state’s direction. For each session, the nets within ±2 slots of the direction of the other latent state and of a matched third direction were counted on stable regular trials (trial in episode above 4, no oddball on this or the previous trial). The 62 participants classified as M_STRUCT place a median of 0.41 more nets at the other state’s direction than at the third direction (interquartile range 0.17 to 0.90; 87% of participants above zero). The difference is present in every instruction condition (medians 0.41, 0.60 and 0.17). A corresponding difference for the direction in which oddballs land is absent (median 0.08).

With gain 8, the simulated agent does not. For parameters drawn from the priors, the median difference is 0.08 with gain 8, 0.26 with gain 4, 0.44 with gain 3 and 0.73 with gain 2. Gain 3 matches the participants’ median and quartiles.

A lower gain makes the switch probability and noise reactivity more identifiable. With a lower gain, the allocation carries graded information about the state belief, on which both parameters act. A screen with a feature-based regression (4,000 simulations per gain) and the trained networks agree on this (table above).

The commitment gain is a fixed constant of the model, like \kappa_{\text{fixed}} and \rho_{\text{fixed}} (

Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants).

Alternative

The screens in the last three rows use a gradient-boosting regression from the features to each parameter with five-fold cross-validation as a proxy for recovery. The proxy lies below the recovery of a trained network (for the current agent: .58 against .71 for noise reactivity) and serves only for comparisons between variants.

A joint amortized inference over a larger space of candidate models with model-specific posterior networks was considered as a different route to the same problem and is not part of the present analysis. The present pipeline implements the bounded form of this idea in two steps (amortized classifier, then the posterior network of the latent-state model; see 

Model Comparison).

Figure 3:Deviation of the centre of each allocation from the target direction, for participants and for the agent simulated from each participant’s posterior (control network, 20 draws; 62 participants; mean and standard error across participants; logarithmic scale). Deviations are oriented so that the other state’s direction lies at +120°.

A trial-level comparison locates the difference. On stable trials, participants’ allocations are centred on the target with a smaller spread than the agent’s (10.6° against 13.7°), and they are centred on the other state’s direction more often (6.4% of trials against 2.7%). The agent instead produces more allocations that are centred on no structured direction (21% against 10%). After an oddball, participants centre their allocation on the location where it landed on about 20% of the following trials, in both states; the agent does so on 8%. Trial-to-trial shifts above 90° make up 19% of participants’ stable trials and 10% of the agent’s, while a quarter of participants’ shifts are below 5° (agent: 14°).

Participants thus alternate between precise placements and discrete moves to a small number of locations, whereas the agent represents all off-target placements by a Gaussian shift of the allocation. Across participants, the estimated placement noise correlates with the share of allocations centred on the other state’s direction (Spearman \rho = .58). The pattern does not change between the first and the second half of the session.

What the parameters describe. The agent is a low-dimensional description of behaviour along six interpretable dimensions. It reproduces the level and the between-participant ordering of the main behavioural summaries and not every placement. Its parameters are read as measures of these dimensions.

Placement noise summarises all placements away from the predicted direction. This includes discrete moves to the other state’s direction and to oddball locations, so that it is a measure of placement variability in general.

Noise reactivity is recovered with r = .79 over the prior range and with about .81 to .86 in the range occupied by participants. Its posterior is correlated with that of belief momentum. Conclusions about noise reactivity are drawn with its posterior uncertainty.

Several participants have estimates near a prior bound (cue sensitivity: 10 near the upper bound; placement noise: 8 near the upper bound; noise reactivity: 8 near the lower bound; switch probability: 6 near the lower bound).

Model and networks behind the current results

The participant results in this book come from run 12_10 (12 October 2026), obtained with the model adopted on 11 October 2026: the agent with the single-stage net allocation and a commitment gain of 3, the 54 summary features of feature_extraction_v3.py, and a posterior network and a model classifier each trained on 100,000 simulations. The decision and the validation are documented in 

Model Selection and Validation. The earlier run 09_09 used the networks of 8 June 2026 (commitment gain 8, 40 features); the chapters of that state are kept in archiv/run_09_09/.

hierarchy.lvl1: Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal
Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal

records.content:
This section documents how participants respond to oddball outcomes - the behaviour that the noise_reactivity (nr) parameter is designed to capture - and explains, on the basis of that behaviour, why the nr signal is intrinsically weak in the current paradigm. The analysis aims a fine-grained characterization of participant behaviour
in the present data. It is fully reproducible via oddball_diagnostics.py.

hierarchy.lvl1: Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal
Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal

records.content: noise_reactivity is the parameter on the stochasticity side of the Piray & Daw (2021) volatility-versus-stochasticity trade-off: it governs whether a surprising oddball outcome is attributed to noise (the rule is unchanged) or to a genuine state change. In parameter recovery it is consistently the weakest of the six parameters (BayesFlow correlation ≈ 0.63, against ≥ 0.82 for every other parameter), with a classic  regression-to-the-mean error profile. Before accepting this as an irreducible property, we characterised the underlying behaviour directly, i.e. what do participants actually do after an oddball, how informative are those events, and what about the task structure limits the signal.

hierarchy.lvl1: Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal
Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal

records.content:
On an oddball trial the observed attack location (actual_vector_angle) sits approximately 120° away from the nominal state (target_vector_angle); the oddball displacement of +120° coincides with the other latent state for that cue. On regular trials the same difference is only the von-Mises sensory noise (≈ 8°). The behaviourally meaningful references for the next same-cue placement are therefore:

STAY is defined as placement near the nominal state (target_vector_angle of the   oddball trial), i.e. the participant treats the oddball as noise (high nr)

FOLLOW is defined as placement near the displaced attack location   (actual_vector_angle), i.e. the  participant treats the oddball as a state switch (low nr).

Note

The oddball location must be referenced to actual_vector_angle, not target_vector_angle. Using the target collapses STAY and FOLLOW onto the same point and makes the classification meaningless. The feature-extraction pipeline and the agent both use actual_vector_angle throughout; this was verified end-to-end (see the agent and feature-extraction sections).

records.content: Across 1490 clean oddball events (those with valid same-cue placements both before and after the oddball) from 96 participants, the next same-cue placement moves on average 66.1° relative to the pre-oddball placement, with a mean signed move of +23.4° toward the oddball location. This net movement is modest: participants do not, on average, chase the displaced outcome, but neither do they fully ignore it.

records.content:
The decisive finding is that the post-oddball response is not the binary stay-or-follow decision that the nr mechanism assumes. Classifying each next same-cue placement with a 35° threshold gives:

Figure 1:Left (A): the three-way response distribution. About two fifths of responses are neither a clean stay nor a clean follow. Centre (B): distance of the next same-cue placement to the nominal state. The distribution is bimodal with a large peak near 0° (STAY) and a second peak near 120° (FOLLOW, i.e. on the other state), with substantial mass in between (the diffuse/hedge responses). Right (C): the per-participant oddball-follow rate, the individual-difference signal noise_reactivity is meant to track. It is broadly spread (0 to ≈ 0.81) but estimated from few events per participant.

About two fifths of oddball responses (39%) carry no clean stay-versus-follow information. Of these OTHER responses, 43% lie near the midpoint between the stay and follow locations, indicating that participants frequently split their nets between the two hypotheses rather than committing to either. This hedging is a qualitatively different behaviour from the binary attribution the nr parameter encodes, and it directly dilutes the nr signal.

records.content:
Two structural features of the data combine to limit nr identifiability:

Few clean informative events per participant. Oddballs are rare (≈ 10% of trials), giving a median of 16 clean events per participant (range 10–18). With about two fifths of those being uninformative hedges, only about ten clean stay-versus-follow decisions remain per participant from which to estimate nr.

About two fifths of the behaviour is off-axis. The nr mechanism maps onto a binary stay/follow axis, but 39% of responses are diffuse or hedged. This off-axis behaviour is partly absorbed by placement_noise (action-level scatter) and does not inform nr, so the effective signal is smaller than the raw event count suggests.

Together these explain the flat, distributed feature-importance profile observed for nr (no single behavioural feature dominates) and the regression-to-the-mean recovery: with little per-participant information, the posterior is pulled toward the prior mean except for participants with unusually consistent stay or follow behaviour. So this is an intrinsic property of the paradigm and not an implementation issue. The agent and feature pipeline reproduce nr-dependent following in the correct direction (the simulated follow rate decreases monotonically with nr).

hierarchy.lvl1: Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal
Oddball-Response Diagnostics and the Weak noise_reactivity Signal

records.content:
noise_reactivity should be reported with its posterior uncertainty rather than as a precise point estimate. However, its calibration is sound (clean SBC) and the posteriors are honest; the limited signal manifests as appropriately wide posteriors (not as miscalibration).

Additionally, the three-way response structure (stay / follow / hedge) is itself a substantive behavioural description and can be reported as a model-agnostic characterisation of how participants treat surprising outcomes.

Downstream individual-difference analyses involving nr should weight by posterior uncertainty and check robustness to the small number of low-nr participants who anchor the low end of the distribution (working on it)

This chapter reports how well the fitted model reproduces participants’ behaviour. It describes what the check is meant to establish, how it is computed, and the results for the adopted model (run 12_10). The figures and tables are produced by ppc_all_features.py and ppc_report.py at every pipeline run.

hierarchy.lvl2: What the check is meant to establish
What the check is meant to establish

records.content:
The latent-state agent is a low-dimensional description of behaviour. Its six parameters are meant to capture informative and interpretable tendencies of each participant, such as how concentrated the nets are, how quickly a change of the latent state is adopted, how strongly the colour cue is used, and how variable the placements are, and to order participants reliably along these dimensions, so that the parameters can be related to questionnaire scores. The model is not meant to reproduce every placement of a participant, and no model of this size can. The parameters are estimated from 54 summary features of a session by simulation-based inference (

Amortized Bayesian Inference), so that the relevant standard is how well the model reproduces these behavioural summaries, at the level at which they are used.

Three questions follow from this use of the model:

Size of systematic deviations. Where the fitted model predicts a different value than observed, is the deviation small relative to the differences between participants?

Individual differences. Does the fitted model reproduce the ordering of participants on each feature, and how close does it come to the agreement that would be expected if the model had generated the data?

Consistency across conditions. Does the reproduction of individual differences hold within each instruction condition?

A frequently used summary, the share of participants whose observed value falls inside the central 95 % interval of their own posterior predictive distribution, answers none of these questions. That interval reflects only the simulation variability of one session at the participant’s posterior. With 171 to 188 trials per session, the summary features are estimated precisely, and the intervals are narrow: for the main features they are 0.6 to 0.8 between-participant standard deviations wide. A small offset that is shared by all participants then places many observed values outside the interval, even when the model reproduces the differences between participants almost perfectly. The share is reported for completeness, but it is not used to judge the model.

For each participant, 100 parameter vectors were drawn from the posterior, and the agent was simulated with each of them on the participant’s own trial schedule (ppc_all_features.py). The 54 summary features were computed from each simulated session in the same way as from the participant’s session. The analysis includes the 59 participants for whom the latent-state model had the highest posterior probability in the model comparison.

Intervals for the mean offset and for \rho are 95 % bootstrap intervals over participants (2,000 resamples).

In Full they reach 63 %, although the expected rank correlation in Full is as high as in the other conditions (median .90). The smaller between-participant variation in Full therefore does not explain the lower correlations: with the Full participants’ own posteriors and schedules, the model would order them as well as in None and Partial. The difference is largest for the error relative to the hidden-state target (ρ = .55, expected .86), the proportion of large shifts (.46, expected .92), the rate of switches between the two state directions without an event (.52, expected .87) and the learned cue offset (.53, expected .88). With 13 participants each of these correlations is uncertain, but the pattern is consistent over features. It concerns the participants who were told the structure; the differences between them in how often they move their placement by large amounts are captured less well than in None and Partial.

Figure 4:All features in one view: absolute mean offset (between-participant SD) against the share of the expected rank correlation that is reached. Features in the upper left are reproduced in value and in the ordering of participants.

Trial-to-trial variability. The standard deviation of the trial-to-trial shift (std_trial_shift, +1.68 SD), belief_lability (+1.68), the standard deviation of the error (std_angular_error, +1.63) and of the net entropy (std_net_entropy, +0.99) are higher in participants than predicted. The ordering of participants on these statistics is still reproduced in part (ρ = 0.61, 0.61, 0.12 and 0.46). A trial-level analysis locates this difference (

Model Selection and Validation): participants alternate between precise placements and discrete moves to the other state’s direction or to the location of a preceding oddball, whereas the model represents all off-target placements by a Gaussian shift of the allocation on every trial. The mean variability of the placements is reproduced (within_state_placement_var, ρ = 0.92), but the variability of that variability is not.

Relations. Differences, ratios and slopes, such as the change of the defense rate over the session or the ratio of the shift after oddballs to the shift on regular trials, are reproduced in value (median offset 0.57 SD) but only partly in the ordering of participants (median ρ = 0.27, at 46 % of the expected agreement). These statistics combine two estimates from one session and are less reliable than the levels from which they are formed; the expected rank correlation is correspondingly lower (median 0.70). For five features it is below .60, so that even the data-generating model would order participants on them only weakly: odd_even_episode_diff (.29), defense_rate_improvement (.43), defense_rate_slope (.49), cue_defense_rate_diff (.50) and oddball_shift_odd_episode (.55). These features carry little information about differences between participants in sessions of this length. Part of the remaining gap reflects the same discrete moves after oddballs that the model does not represent.

Distribution of the placement errors. The excess variability is located in the upper part of the distribution of the placement errors (diagnose_placement_error_tails.py; regular trials, 20 posterior draws per participant). The median error of the placement centre relative to the hidden-state target is reproduced (observed minus predicted, median over participants −0.5°), but the 75th and 90th percentiles are 17° and 29° higher in participants than predicted (for 81 % and 93 % of participants), and the share of placements more than 90° from the target is 21 % against 13 %. The same holds for the change of the placement centre from one trial to the next (90th percentile 26° higher). Participants’ errors are thus more often either small or very large (close to the direction of the other latent state, 120° away), whereas the Gaussian placement noise of the model produces intermediate errors. The positive offsets of the mean error (+0.59 SD) and of the within-state variability (+0.69 SD) follow from the same upper tail.

Response to oddballs. Among the level features, those of the response to oddballs are reproduced least well (ratio 0.34 to 0.70), consistent with the discrete moves to the location of an oddball described above.

hierarchy.lvl3: Consequences for the use of the parameters
Consequences for the use of the parameters

records.content:
The behavioural dimensions on which the parameters are defined are those on which the model reproduces the ordering of participants closely: the concentration of the allocation (precision weighting), the variability of the placements (placement noise), the learned cue offset (cue sensitivity), and the trial-to-trial change and the switching of the placement (belief momentum and the switch probability). The construct-validity check confirms the corresponding associations between each parameter and its behavioural measure (

Results by Research Question). The systematic deviations concern the trial-to-trial variability of the placements and statistics of the response to oddballs. They are reported as a limit of the model: placement noise summarises all placements away from the predicted direction, including discrete moves, and noise reactivity, whose behavioural measure is the response to oddballs, is interpreted with its posterior uncertainty.

The share of participants inside their own 95 % posterior predictive interval is 55 % on average over all features (share_inside in ppc_feature_metrics.csv), for the reason given above.

hierarchy.lvl2: Deviations that could be addressed without a new mechanism
Deviations that could be addressed without a new mechanism

records.content:
Two deviations follow from the prior ranges rather than from the mechanism of the model, and could be addressed by widening the range and retraining the posterior network (no new parameter):

Upper bound of cue sensitivity. The believed cue offset approaches cue sensitivity × 70°, so that offsets above the true 70° cannot be represented. For the 27 participants whose 95 % posterior interval reaches the upper bound of 1, the predicted learned cue offset is about 10° below the observed one (medians 64° to 67° against 73° to 78°, in all three conditions). Widening the prior to, for example, 0 to 1.3 would let the parameter represent an overestimated offset, and would be expected to remove the offset of cue_offset_learned (+0.30 SD) and to improve its rank correlation in Full, where 10 of 13 participants are at the bound.

Upper bound of placement noise. For 11 participants the 95 % interval reaches the bound of 0.873 rad (50°). Their offsets on the variability features are not larger than those of the other participants (for example +0.77 against +0.67 SD for within_state_placement_var), so that the bound does not explain the deviations, but their placement noise is estimated with an upper limit, which compresses the differences at the top of the distribution used in the questionnaire analyses (RQ3). A wider range (for example to 1.2 rad) would remove this.

In addition, the five features with an expected rank correlation below .60 could be removed from the feature set at the same retraining, since they add noise to the summary network without information about differences between participants.

The deviations in the variability and upper tail of the placements, in the response to oddballs, and in Full share one source, discrete moves of the placement to the other state’s direction or to an oddball location. The mechanisms that would reproduce them (allocation centred on a sampled state, following an oddball with a free probability) were examined and not adopted because they reduce the identifiability of the parameters or overlap in meaning with noise reactivity (

Model Selection and Validation).

The posterior predictive checks motivated the sixth parameter of the agent. The five-parameter agent placed its nets at the predictive mean on every trial and was too stable: for nearly all participants, the features of trial-to-trial change lay above the predictive interval. The excess variability was identified as variability of the placement within a latent state that is not explained by the outcome noise of the task, and placement_noise was added as a circular Gaussian shift of the predictive distribution before the nets are allocated (see 

The Inference Agent). The checks of that development step were computed with an earlier network at N = 34; the chapter of that state is kept in modeling/archiv/posterior_predictive_checks_until_2026-10-12.md. The trial-level analysis of October 2026 refines its conclusion: the remaining variability is not only undirected scatter but includes discrete moves to a small number of locations.

Zika, Wiech, Reinecke, Browning and Schuck (2023, Nature Communications 14, 4203) compared, per participant, how well a model with several latent states and a model with a single state explained shock-probability ratings in an aversive reversal-learning task. The difference in fit correlated with trait anxiety in the session with the most reliable outcomes (90/10 contingencies, r(36) = 0.39, CI [0.07, 0.63], p = .017, Fig. 6c). They found no association in the 75/25 and 60/40 sessions. This page applies the same logic to the TAMBI task. It asks whether the participants whose allocations are better predicted by a model with latent states than by a model with one direction per cue differ in their questionnaire scores.

The fits and the statistics are the pipeline steps relfit, relfitmodels (five scales) and grelfitmodels (general factor). The results on this page are from run 23_11 (96 participants, 95 with questionnaire scores).

All four models update their beliefs deterministically from the attacks a participant saw. They differ only in how they explain the attacks.

In the simulations of all models the only random element of an action is one circular shift of the predictive distribution \pi_t by a draw from N(0, \text{placement\_noise}^2). The shifted distribution is sharpened with exponent 1 + \text{precision\_weighting}, and the seven nets are then placed deterministically. For a likelihood the deterministic placement is replaced by multinomial draws, and a lapse rate \varepsilon mixes the distribution with a uniform one,p_k(t) = (1 - \varepsilon)\,\text{sharpen}\big(\text{shift}(\pi_t, s_k)\big) + \frac{\varepsilon}{32},
\qquad
L_t = \sum_k w_k \,\text{Multinomial}\big(g_t \mid n_t, p_k(t)\big),

where g_t are the nets a participant placed in the 32 sectors on trial t, n_t their number, and s_k, w_k the 15 Gauss-Hermite nodes and weights of the placement shift. \varepsilon is free in every model (range 0.0001 to 0.5). Trials without nets are excluded.

The parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood (Nelder-Mead on a logit transform of the prior ranges, at most 400 evaluations per start). The starts are the BayesFlow posterior mean of the participant (for Nexus, Nassar and Zika) and three random draws from the priors.

Relative fit is cross-validated. The parameters are fitted on the odd episodes and evaluated on the even episodes, and vice versa. Beliefs are always replayed on the full trial sequence, so only the evaluation is split. The held-out log-likelihood of both folds is summed and divided by the number of held-out trials. The relative fit of a participant is the held-out log-likelihood per trial (nats) of a model with latent states minus that of a model without latent states. Positive values mean that the model with latent states predicts the held-out allocations better.

hierarchy.lvl3: Relation to behavioural measures and parameters
Relation to behavioural measures and parameters

records.content:
Spearman correlations of relative fit with the structural signatures, the state-selectivity measures, the coverage of the allocations and the Nexus BayesFlow parameters (96 participants, file relative_fit_redundancy.csv).

The relative fit of Nexus (against either reference) correlates with hedging between the trained directions after a transition (ρ = 0.52 and 0.53) and after an oddball (ρ = 0.62 and 0.63), with the mass of the allocation on the other learned state (ρ = 0.50 and 0.46) and on no learned state (ρ = 0.43 and 0.41), and with the Nexus parameters noise_reactivity (ρ = 0.40 and 0.42) and belief_momentum (ρ = 0.23 and 0.40). Nexus predicts those participants better whose nets are spread over more than one direction. The two references concentrate their allocation around one direction per cue and cannot produce such a spread.

The relative fit of the n-state model against the tracker correlates with the Nexus parameter h_switch (ρ = 0.36) and negatively with belief_momentum (ρ = −0.39), noise_reactivity (ρ = −0.26) and transfer_I_e_abs (ρ = −0.32). Against the Nassar observer it correlates with the noise weight of the state-selectivity model (ρ = −0.22).

Controlling the score slopes for the three behavioural measures most strongly related to each outcome, the covariates explained 67 % of the variance of nexus_vs_track and 61 % of nexus_vs_nassar, and all score slopes of these two outcomes were then |slope| ≤ 0.13 (BDI-II with nexus_vs_nassar −0.13, p = .054; all others p ≥ .22). For zika_vs_track the OCI slope became 0.23 [0.02, 0.44] (p = .034) with transfer, consolidation after transitions and snap-back after oddballs as covariates.

Across the three instruction conditions the advantage of a model with latent states over a model with one direction per cue was unrelated to the general factor (slopes −0.12 to 0.17) and, with one exception (OCI with Nexus against the tracker, 0.21, p = .047), to the five scales. This holds for both models with states, for both references, with and without the reference fit as covariate, and for the direct counterpart of the analysis of Zika et al. (2023). With 95 participants the power to detect a correlation of 0.39 at α = .05 (two-sided) is .98, and that to detect a correlation of 0.2 is .49. A correlation of the size reported by Zika et al. would therefore very likely have been detected, whereas smaller associations cannot be excluded.

In Full, higher OCI and general-factor scores went with a better fit of Nexus relative to the references, and higher STICSA trait and general-factor scores with a worse fit of the n-state model relative to the Nassar observer. The Nexus slopes in Full depend on two participants with high OCI scores whose allocations Nexus predicts far better than any other participant’s; the rank correlations keep the OCI association with nexus_vs_track (ρ = 0.63).

The relative fit of Nexus is largely accounted for by how much a participant hedges between learned directions (61 to 67 % of its variance by three behavioural measures). It is therefore a model-based summary of behaviour that the structural signatures already measure and not an independent measure of state inference.

This variant keeps the belief dynamics of the adopted Nexus model (

The Inference Agent) and adds one response to surprise to the action rule. After a surprising outcome, the next allocation of nets is wider, and the widening decays over the following trials. The belief update, and therefore the meaning of the six Nexus parameters, is unchanged. The variant describes participants who spread their nets after surprising attacks without changing their belief. It is fitted to all participants as a second description, and its additional parameter is related to the questionnaire scores. It is not part of the model comparison.

Scripts (analysis repository): bayes_flow/variant_screen/spread_variant.py (agent and simulator), bayes_flow/variant_screen/run_spread_network.py (recovery proxy, network, validation, inference, posterior predictive check, parameter table), tambi_rq3_alt_models.R (score models; stats_results/<tag>/rq3_spread/, general factor in general_factor/), tambi_spread_variant.py (summaries and figures; stats_results/<tag>/spread_variant/). Pipeline steps: spreadinfer, spreadppc, spreadtable, spreadrq3, gspreadrq3, spreadfigs.

Surprise. Before each update, the agent computes the surprise of the observed attack direction \omega_t under its predictive distribution, with the same definition as in the pupil analyses (

Pupil and the Latent Signals of Three Models):S_t = -\log\Big(2\pi \sum_{z} P_{\text{pred}}(z)\,\big[(1-\rho_{\text{eff}})\,\text{vM}(\omega_t;\mu_z,\kappa) + \rho_{\text{eff}}\,\text{vM}(\omega_t;\mu_z+\Delta,\kappa)\big]\Big),

with \kappa = 4 and \rho_{\text{eff}} = 0.1 \cdot noise reactivity. S_t = 0 means that the attack was as probable as under a uniform guess. Trials without an attack and the first attack of the session have no surprise.

Spread state. A spread state s rises with the positive part of the surprise and decays geometrically:s_t = d\,s_{t-1} + g\,\max(0, S_t).

Allocation. The allocation on trial t+1 sharpens the predictive distribution (commitment-weighted mixture, commitment gain 3, Gaussian placement shift) with the exponent (1 + \text{precision weighting})/(1 + s_t) instead of 1 + \text{precision weighting}. A spread state of 1 halves the exponent. The centre of the allocation is unchanged. With g = 0 the agent reproduces the adopted agent exactly; this was checked on 50 simulated sessions.

Parameters. The six Nexus parameters with the priors of 

Notation and Priors, plus the spread gain g ~ U(0, 2). The decay is fixed at d = 0.5, so the widening halves on each trial. With a free decay d ~ U(0, 0.9), the decay was not recovered: in a recovery proxy (8000 simulations, five-fold cross-validated gradient boosting from the 54 summary features), r = .39 for the decay and .61 for the gain. With the decay fixed, the proxy gives r = .62 for the gain.

The network has the settings of the adopted network: 54 summary features, 100,000 simulations on the 20 trial schedules, a DeepSet summary network with flow matching, 150 epochs, seed 42. It was validated on 500 recovery simulations and 1000 calibration simulations.

Status

This chapter describes the six-parameter agent reduced_agent_v3.py with the single-stage net allocation. The model adopted on 11 October 2026 uses a commitment gain of \beta_z = 3; the participant results in this book (run 12_10) were obtained with it. The earlier run 09_09 used \beta_z = 8; the agent is otherwise identical. All constants are listed in 

Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants, and the decision and the validation of the adopted model are in 

Model Selection and Validation. Recovery values quoted in this chapter that are not marked otherwise are those of the network of 8 June 2026; the values of the adopted network are in 

Amortized Bayesian Inference.

The TAMBI task generates rich trial-by-trial behavioral data (32-slot net allocations over ~180 trials). To connect this behavior to latent cognitive processes, we require a generative model that:

Retains the scientific structure of the task (2-state HMM, cue offset, oddball mixture, von-Mises observation model)

Has parameters that directly and transparently affect behavioral output

Produces behavioral patterns that match the range observed in human participants

Is computationally efficient enough to generate the tens of thousands of simulations required for amortized inference training

The reduced-form agent satisfies all four requirements. It replaces the particle filter approximation (used in the simulation models for model comparison) with analytically tractable update rules, ensuring that each parameter has a direct, measurable effect on the allocation output without being “washed out” by particle dynamics. Additionally, the simplified action selection allows to focus on the underlying process of inference and belief updating - implementing inference with free parameters for both at a time would cause critical ambiguity and uncontrolable parameter-interaction effects in the inference process.

The agent maintains point estimates of the following latent state variables, updated on each trial:

State Variable

Symbol
