Cue A direction

\mu_A

Believed attack direction for Cue A under the current z-state

Cue offset

\delta_B

Angular offset between Cue A and Cue B directions

State rotation

\Delta

Angular rotation between z-states (~120°)

z-belief

p(z_t = 1)

Soft belief over which latent context state is active

Two structural parameters are fixed across all participants:

Fixed Parameter

Value

Justification

\kappa_{\text{fixed}}

4.0

Calibrated so that precision_weighting produces the full range of VP-observed allocation patterns (1–7 occupied slots, with realistic stacking)

\rho_{\text{fixed}}

0.10

Baseline oddball probability matching the TAMBI design (~10% oddball rate)

Fixing \kappa and \rho ensures that the six free parameters have strictly monotone, uncompensated effects on behavior throughout the entire session. Online learning of \kappa and \rho was found to create compensatory dynamics that reduced parameter identifiability. Importantly, the update-step likelihoods (

Likelihood Computation) use \kappa_{\text{fixed}} directly, while the predictive distribution (

Predictive Distribution) uses \kappa_{\text{eff}} = \kappa_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{pw}. This prevents a confound where precision weighting would simultaneously make the agent more confident in its predictions and more responsive to prediction errors.
The agent has six free parameters estimated per participant via BayesFlow:

\text{pw} \in [0.1, 5.0]

Controls how tightly the net allocation follows the agent’s learned direction. Mechanically, precision weighting controls three aspects of the agent’s behavior:

Predictive concentration:
\kappa_{\text{eff}} = \kappa_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{pw}


This scales the von Mises concentration used in the predictive distribution, determining how sharply the predicted attack distribution peaks around the believed direction.

Allocation sharpening:
\alpha = 1 + \text{pw}


The predictive slot probabilities \pi_s are raised to the power \alpha before integer rounding, controlling how concentrated the net placement is.

Direction learning rate:
\eta_\mu = c_\eta \cdot \text{pw}, \qquad c_\eta = 0.10


This scales the prediction-error-driven update of \hat{\mu}_A, determining how quickly the agent adjusts its direction estimate after each observation.

These three mechanisms are intentionally coupled to represent a certain mechanistic behavioral pattern. An agent with high precision weighting believes outcomes are precise (narrow predictive distribution), places nets precisely (high sharpening), and updates its direction estimate quickly (high learning rate). This coherence reflects the theoretical construct of precision weighting in predictive processing (Friston, 2008; Mathys et al., 2014).

Associated behavioral features: Net entropy (bits), number of occupied slots, stacking depth.

Identifiability: r = 0.996 (parameter recovery), primary behavioral signature: net entropy, slots occupied, stacking fraction.

\text{nr} \in [0.1, 3.0]

Controls how the agent attributes surprising observations to noise (oddballs) versus genuine environmental change (state switches). (This is inspired by the computational formalization of the Piray & Daw (2021) “broken unpredictability estimator” hypothesis)

The effective oddball rate \rho_{\text{eff}} = \rho_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{nr} modulates the likelihood mixture:L(z) = (1 - \rho_{\text{eff}}) \cdot f_{\text{vM}}(\omega_t; \mu_z, \kappa) + \rho_{\text{eff}} \cdot f_{\text{vM}}(\omega_t; \mu_z + \Delta, \kappa)

That way, higher \rho_{\text{eff}} increases the weight of the oddball component in the marginal likelihood, reducing the evidence for state change when a surprising outcome is observed.

Additionally, noise reactivity gates the direction update via the oddball responsibility:\gamma = \frac{\rho_{\text{eff}} \cdot L_{\text{odd}}}{(1 - \rho_{\text{eff}}) \cdot L_{\text{reg}} + \rho_{\text{eff}} \cdot L_{\text{odd}}}

The oddball responsibility \gamma_t determines how much the direction update is dampened after a surprising observation. The direction update is scaled by (1 - \gamma). That means, when noise reactivity is high, \rho_{\text{eff}} is high, \gamma is high for surprising observations, and the update is dampened (the agent treats the surprise as noise and shows weaker learning from this trial). When noise reactivity is low, \rho_{\text{eff}} is low, \gamma is low, and the agent fully updates its direction estimate (treating the surprise as a real signal). Low noise reactivity (\text{nr} < 1) corresponds to an agent that underestimates the oddball rate, causing unexpected outcomes to be interpreted as state changes rather than random fluctuations, which produces a behavioral pattern that is characterized by excessive belief updating, abrupt state switches, and elevated perceived volatility. The complementary case (high noise reactivity (\text{nr} > 1)) describes an agent that over-attributes surprising outcomes to noise, potentially missing genuine state changes.

(My idea was that this parameter could seperate anxiety and depression in a reasonable manner)

Associated behavioral features: Oddball shift ratio, fraction of oddballs followed, oddball recovery speed.

Identifiability: r = 0.636. Noise reactivity is the least well recovered parameter. In this version of the agent the oddball component of the predictive distribution receives almost no nets after sharpening, so that \rho_{\text{eff}} has little effect on the allocations; its remaining signature lies in the oddball shift ratio, the fraction of oddballs followed and the oddball recovery speed. No conclusion is drawn from associations with this parameter until the revised allocation has been validated.

\text{bm} \in [0.0, 0.95]

Controls resistance to z-state belief revision. After computing the standard Bayesian posterior p(z=1 \mid \text{data})_{\text{raw}}, the agent applies exponential smoothing:p(z=1)_t = (1 - \text{bm}) \cdot p(z=1 \mid \text{data})_{\text{raw}} + \text{bm} \cdot p(z=1)_{t-1}

At \text{bm} = 0, the agent is a perfect Bayesian updater (instantaneous belief revision). At \text{bm} = 0.9, only 10% of the new evidence is incorporated per trial, requiring ~10 trials to approach the new posterior. This parameter captures individual differences in cognitive flexibility versus rigidity, and may relate to intolerance of uncertainty or perseverative tendencies. It is distinct from noise reactivity in that it applies to all belief updates (including those following genuine state changes), not only to oddball attribution.

Note on how to distinguish belief momentum from h_switch: Both parameters affect the dynamics of p(z = 1) over time. However, they operate at different stages of the update. h (perceived volatility) acts in the prediction step, pulling p(z = 1) toward 0.5 before each observation, which creates a baseline drift that is constant across trials. \text{bm} (belief momentum), on the other hand, acts in the update step, dampening the posterior revision after each observation, which creates sluggish transitions that are most visible around episode boundaries.

Associated behavioral features: Transition recovery slope, angular error in early post-switch trials, allocation autocorrelation.

Identifiability: r = 0.910, primary behavioral signature: transition recovery slope, angular error in first trials after episode transitions, allocation autocorrelation.

h \in [0.005, 0.30]

This is the HMM transition probability used in the prediction step (the agent’s prior belief about how frequently the latent state switches):p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1) = p_{t-1}(z = 1) \cdot (1 - h) + [1 - p_{t-1}(z = 1)] \cdot h

Higher h means the agent expects more frequent state switches, which manifests as a persistent pull of p(z = 1) toward 0.5 (maximum uncertainty). Agents with high h may hedge between both possible directions, placing nets at two locations simultaneously.

The true transition rate in the TAMBI task is h_{\text{true}} = 1/20 = 0.05 (one switch per ~20 trials). Participants who over-estimate h perceive the environment as more volatile than it is.

Associated behavioral features: Fraction of large allocation shifts, mean trial-to-trial angular shift, defense rate trajectory across episodes.

Identifiability: r = 0.825. The prior upper bound is set to 0.30 because behaviour saturates above the single-oddball switch threshold h = \rho_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{nr}: once the agent switches at essentially every oddball, higher h is behaviourally indistinguishable. The bound, the saturation analysis, and the genuine (non-artefactual) positive coupling between h and noise_reactivity (r = +0.60 across participants) are documented in h_switch Identifiability.

\text{cs} \in [0, 1]

Cue sensitivity captures the degree to which the participant has resolved the cue-colour dimension of the task structure, i.e. that the two cues (A and B) are attacked from directions offset by a fixed angle (true offset ≈ 70°). It scales the target, the learning rate and the initial value of the believed cue offset \delta_B (see 

Direction Update with Oddball Gating). Because \delta_B is drawn toward the target \text{cs} \cdot 70° after every cue B outcome, its steady-state value is an approximately linear function of \text{cs}:

\text{cs} = 0 means that the cues are never separated; the agent tracks a single location regardless of cue (associative tracking with offset ≈ 0°, as observed in the cue-blind participant VP 5272).

\text{cs} = 1 means that the full cue offset is learned and initialised (≈ 70°, as in VP 9247).

Cue sensitivity deliberately isolates associative cue learning from the structural latent-state inference captured by the other parameters. This separation matters theoretically, since it is a cognitive-ability dimension (whether the participant uses the cue) rather than an anxiety-related inference style, and it dissociates cleanly from the clinical questionnaire scales in the present data.

Associated behavioral features: Learned cue offset, cue offset variability, cue defense-rate difference, cue entropy difference (Block 5).

Identifiability: r = 0.934. In simulation-based calibration the rank mean of cue sensitivity is 544 (expected 499.5, a deviation of 3.4 standard errors), which indicates posteriors that lie too low on average. A boundary effect near \text{cs} = 1, where posteriors cannot spread above the upper bound, is a possible cause; this has not been tested.

\text{pn} \in [0, 0.873] (radians; ≈ 0–50°)

Placement noise is the standard deviation of a zero-mean circular Gaussian jitter applied to the predictive mean before net placement (in the action-selection step). It models the noisy belief-to-action mapping — the undirected, trial-to-trial scatter in where nets are placed within a state — independently of the structured inference, which remains deterministic. With \text{pn} = 0 the agent is bit-identical to the earlier five-parameter agent.

Placement noise was added to resolve a systematic posterior-predictive misspecification: the deterministic agent was too stable on within-state placement, underproducing the scatter participants actually show (see Posterior Predictive Checks). It is an action-level noise parameter, distinct from the inference-level stochasticity governed by noise_reactivity. Diagnostics confirmed that the within-state placement scatter participants show is genuine (≈ 32°, far exceeding the ≈ 8° sensory noise), undirected, and memoryless - exactly the structure this parameter generates.

Associated behavioral features: Within-state placement variability (Block 11), and indirectly the action-level oddball-following features.

Identifiability: r = 0.985, the highest recovery after precision_weighting. In simulation-based calibration the rank mean is 467 (expected 499.5, a deviation of 2.5 standard errors in the direction opposite to cue sensitivity). In the development runs, allowing placement_noise to vary reduced the recovery of noise_reactivity by about 0.17, because the jitter masks the action-level features that carry the noise_reactivity signal. The parameter trade-offs have not yet been quantified with a cross-recovery analysis.

Given the current state estimates, the agent computes the predictive slot probabilities as a mixture over the latent state z:\pi_s = \sum_{z \in \{0,1\}} w_z \left[ (1 - \rho_{\text{eff}}) \cdot \text{vM}(\phi_s; \hat{\mu}_{c,z}, \kappa_{\text{eff}}) + \rho_{\text{eff}} \cdot \text{vM}(\phi_s; \hat{\mu}_{c,z} + \hat{\Delta}, \kappa_{\text{eff}}) \right]

where \text{vM}(\phi; \mu, \kappa) \propto \exp(\kappa \cos(\phi - \mu)) and the summation is over the S = 32 slot angles \phi_s. The slot probabilities are normalized: \pi_s \leftarrow \pi_s / \sum_j \pi_j.

The mixture weights are not the predicted state probabilities themselves but a sharpened version of them (commitment):w_1 = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\big(-\beta_z\,[\,p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1) - 0.5\,]\big)}, \qquad w_0 = 1 - w_1, \qquad \beta_z = 3 .

With a decisive belief the allocation is weighted toward one state, and with a belief near 0.5 it is divided between the two directions. For p^{\text{pred}}(z = 1) = 0.9 the weight is w_1 = 0.77, for 0.6 it is 0.57. Because the predictive distribution is subsequently raised to the power 1 + \text{pw}, the allocation itself is more concentrated on the more probable state than these weights. The commitment gain \beta_z is a fixed constant. Until 10 October 2026 it was 8 (w_1 = 0.96 and 0.69 for the two examples), which made the allocation nearly all-or-nothing. With \beta_z = 3 the allocation carries graded information about the state belief, which improves the recovery of the switch probability and of noise reactivity (

Model Selection and Validation).

This predictive distribution incorporates:

Uncertainty over the latent state (via the commitment weights w_z)

Uncertainty about whether the next trial will be an oddball (via \rho_{\text{eff}})

The agent’s confidence in its direction estimate (via \kappa_{\text{eff}})

The agent converts its predictive distribution to a net allocation. When \text{placement\_noise} > 0, a jitter step precedes the standard two-step conversion:

Placement jitter (placement_noise): The entire predictive distribution \pi is circularly shifted by a single zero-mean Gaussian draw \delta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \text{pn}^2) (in radians), implemented by interpolating \pi onto the rotated slot angles and renormalising. This applies an undirected, trial-to-trial scatter to where the nets are placed, independent of the structured belief. With \text{pn} = 0 this step is skipped and the agent is bit-identical to the five-parameter version.

Sharpening: The (optionally jittered) predictive probability per slot \pi_s is raised to the power \alpha = 1 + \text{pw}: \tilde{\pi}_s = \pi_s^\alpha / \sum_j \pi_j^\alpha

Integer rounding: The continuous allocation \tilde{\pi}_s \cdot 7 is rounded to integers via largest-remainder rounding, ensuring the total equals 7.

This produces realistic stacking patterns: at \text{pw} = 1.5, the agent places nets in ~5 slots with pattern [2,2,1,1,1]; at \text{pw} = 3.0, in ~3 slots with pattern [3,2,2]; at \text{pw} = 5.0, in ~2 slots with pattern [6,1]. These patterns match the range observed in human participants. Because the jitter acts on the predictive distribution before sharpening, it shifts the centre of the allocation without by itself changing its concentration, separating action-level placement scatter from the inference-level precision governed by precision_weighting.

On omission trials (no attack outcome), only the HMM prediction is applied:p_t(z = 1) \leftarrow p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1)

No direction or state updates occur. The oddball gate defaults to \gamma_t = 0 (gate = 1), and the prediction error is undefined.

hierarchy.lvl3: Latent State Update with Belief Momentum
Latent State Update with Belief Momentum

records.content:
The dominant state is \hat{z}_t = \mathbb{I}[p_t(z = 1) > 0.5]. The prediction error is:\text{PE}_t = \angle(\omega_t - \hat{\mu}_{c_t, \hat{z}_t})

where \angle(\cdot) denotes the signed angular distance in [-\pi, \pi].

The oddball responsibility under the dominant state is:\gamma_t = \frac{\rho_{\text{eff}} \cdot L_{\text{odd}}^{(\hat{z}_t)}}{(1 - \rho_{\text{eff}}) \cdot L_{\text{reg}}^{(\hat{z}_t)} + \rho_{\text{eff}} \cdot L_{\text{odd}}^{(\hat{z}_t)}}

The gating factor is g_t = 1 - \gamma_t. When g_t \approx 1 (low oddball responsibility), the observation is treated as regular and the full prediction error drives the update. When g_t \approx 0 (high oddball responsibility), the observation is likely an oddball and the direction update is suppressed.

For Cue A observations:\hat{\mu}_A \leftarrow (\hat{\mu}_A + \eta_\mu \cdot g_t \cdot \text{PE}_t) \mod 2\pi

For Cue B observations:\hat{\delta}_B \leftarrow (\hat{\delta}_B + \eta_\mu \cdot g_t \cdot \text{PE}_B \cdot c_\delta \cdot \text{cs}) \mod 2\pi

\hat{\delta}_B \leftarrow \hat{\delta}_B - \lambda_\delta \cdot \angle(\hat{\delta}_B - \delta^{*} \cdot \text{cs})

where \text{PE}_B = \angle(\omega_t - [\hat{\mu}_A + \hat{z}_t \cdot \hat{\Delta} + \hat{\delta}_B]), \eta_\mu = c_\eta \cdot \text{pw} with c_\eta = 0.10, c_\delta = 1.5, \lambda_\delta = 0.15 and \delta^{*} = 70°.

The first line is the error-driven update of the cue offset, scaled by the cue sensitivity. The second line is an anchor step: after every cue B outcome the offset moves toward the target \delta^{*} \cdot \text{cs} by the fraction \lambda_\delta of the remaining distance. Without the anchor, the offset would converge to the full 70° for any \text{cs} > 0 over a long session, and \text{cs} would only determine how fast. With it, a cue-blind agent (\text{cs} \to 0) is held near 0° and a cue-aware agent (\text{cs} \to 1) near 70°. Cue B outcomes do not update the base direction \hat{\mu}_A.

hierarchy.lvl3: Realignment on an Inferred State Switch
Realignment on an Inferred State Switch

records.content:
The trial on which the dominant state changes, that is, on which p(z = 1) crosses 0.5 between t - 1 and t, is treated as the agent’s inference that the latent state has changed. On this trial the direction update above uses the learning rate \max(\eta_\mu, \eta_{\text{sw}}) with \eta_{\text{sw}} = 0.85 and the gate g_t = 1, so that the direction of the newly dominant state is realigned to the outcome that caused the switch within one trial. On all other trials the update uses \eta_\mu and the oddball gate g_t.

With the mixture likelihood, a single displaced outcome changes the dominant state if h > \rho_{\text{eff}} (for \text{bm} = 0). This is the condition that links the switch probability and noise reactivity (

h_switch Identifiability).

The state rotation \hat{\Delta} is updated only when the agent is uncertain about the current state (i.e., near state transitions):z_{\text{unc}} = 1 - |2 \cdot p_t(z = 1) - 1|\hat{\Delta} \leftarrow (\hat{\Delta} + 0.01 \cdot z_{\text{unc}} \cdot \angle(\omega_t - \hat{\mu}_{c_t, 1 - \hat{z}_t})) \mod 2\pi

The small learning rate (0.01) and the uncertainty gating ensure that \hat{\Delta} is updated primarily during state transitions, when the agent has access to observations from both states in close temporal proximity. The rotation is not updated before the sixth observed outcome.

The state belief starts at p_0(z = 1) = 0.5 and the rotation at \hat{\Delta} = 120°. The first observed outcome only initialises the directions and produces no update: \hat{\mu}_A is set to \omega if the trial shows cue A, and to \omega - \delta^{*} \cdot \text{cs} (with \hat{\delta}_B = \delta^{*} \cdot \text{cs}) if it shows cue B.

The agent produces two types of output per trial:

Net allocation \mathbf{g}_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{32}: The observable behavioral response, identical in format to participant data.

Latent summary features (5 per trial):

\sin(\bar{\phi}_t), \cos(\bar{\phi}_t): Circular mean direction of the predictive distribution (before action selection)

V_t^{\text{circ}}: Circular variance of the predictive distribution (= 1 - R, where R is the resultant length)

p_t(z = 1): State belief before the trial’s update

g_t: Oddball gate value (1 - \gamma_t)
These latent quantities are returned by the simulator for inspection and for the belief trace replay. They are not an input of the inference network, which receives only the summary features computed from the net allocations (

Feature Extraction).

Friston, K. (2008). Hierarchical models in the brain. PLoS Computational Biology, 4(11), e1000211.

Mathys, C. D., Lomakina, E. I., Daunizeau, J., Iglesias, S., Brodersen, K. H., Friston, K. J., & Stephan, K. E. (2014). Uncertainty in perception and the Hierarchical Gaussian Filter. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 8, 825.

This page is the reference for all analyses of the behavioural and questionnaire data: what is measured, which models are fitted, how they are coded and tested, which script runs them and where the results are. The task is described in 

The Task, the computational model and its fitting in 

Fitting the Models to Participant Data, and the commands that run everything in 

Reproducing the Analysis. The text of 

Results by Research Question is the draft of the manuscript’s methods; this page gives the same content as an overview.

How to use this page. Sections 1 to 3 define the data, the measures and the conventions that hold for every model. Section 4 lists the analyses, grouped by question, each with its unit of analysis, outcome, model, script and the page with its results. Section 5 maps the names used in code, outputs and manuscript draft. Section 6 lists where the outputs are.

Participants

86 with behavioural data (run 13_11); 85 with questionnaires (84 for STICSA state and OCI)

Instruction conditions

None (no rules given): 31; Partial (rules mentioned): 33; Full (structure explained): 22 (21 with questionnaires)

Session

9 episodes, 171 to 188 trials (median 181; 20 trial schedules); two colour cues per episode (cue B = cue A + 70°); about 9 % oddballs and 10 % omissions (attack not shown); 8 transitions per participant

Events analysed

688 transitions (first trial of episodes 2–9), 1,356 oddballs

Raw data

tambi-analysis/results/<participant>_results.csv (one file per participant)

Questionnaires

questionnaires/q_results/questionnaire_scores.csv (scored by questionnaire_scoring_pipeline.R)

Questionnaires. Five focal questionnaires enter every questionnaire model: STICSA state and STICSA trait (anxiety), IU (intolerance of uncertainty, IUS-18), BDI (BDI-II, depressive symptoms) and OCI (OCI-R, obsessive-compulsive symptoms). Five further questionnaires are analysed in some places and corrected separately: PCL-5, ACE, SIAS, ERS, EAT. Total scores are used; in every model they are z-scored within the participants of that analysis.

In-task affect. After each episode, six ratings from 0 to 100: valence, arousal, anxiety, stress, frustration, fatigue.

records.content:
Topic

Convention

Instruction condition

unordered factor with two sum-to-zero contrasts: Full vs None + Partial (−1/3, −1/3, 2/3) and Partial vs None (−1/2, 1/2, 0). All other terms are evaluated at the unweighted mean of the three conditions.

Condition differences

contrasts of estimated marginal means (emmeans); the two contrasts are reported unadjusted, all pairwise comparisons Holm-corrected

Questionnaire scores

one model per questionnaire; score z-scored within the analysed participants; slopes per SD

Two forms of each questionnaire model

across conditions: condition + questionnaire (slope estimated from all participants); moderation: condition × questionnaire, from which the slopes within each condition, in None + Partial, and their contrasts are derived. The questionnaire main effect of the moderation form is the unweighted mean of the three condition slopes and is not used as the across-condition estimate.

Within-participant factors

event type (oddball −1/2, transition +1/2), placement (t+1 −1/2, t+2 +1/2), session half (−1/2, +1/2); continuous covariates centred

Linear mixed models

lme4/lmerTest, REML, Satterthwaite df, Type III F-tests

Generalized mixed models

binomial (logit) with glmmTMB or glmer, Wald z-tests

Random effects

by-participant intercepts and slopes of the within-participant predictors, plus random intercepts of events or episodes nested in participants; if singular, reduced stepwise (correlations removed, then slopes); the structure used is reported with each model

Robust tests

every test of a linear mixed model is repeated with cluster-robust CR2 standard errors (clustered by participant); participant-level linear models with HC3

Event-level binary outcomes (strategies)

logistic GEE, exchangeable working correlation, clustered by participant (robust sandwich SEs)

Multiple comparisons

Benjamini–Hochberg across the five focal questionnaires, separately per term and model form (q); further questionnaires corrected separately; condition effects of a family of measures BH across the measures; simple slopes and contrasts derived from a model unadjusted

Diagnostics

tambi_model_diagnostics.R for every model: residual QQ plots and moments, heteroscedasticity, random-effect normality, singularity, VIF; simulation-based quantile residuals for GLMMs; Cook’s distance for participant-level models (

Model Diagnostics)

Reporting

all results on equal footing (estimate, test statistic, p, and q where computed); the study is exploratory

Software

R 4.5.1 (lme4, lmerTest, glmmTMB, emmeans, clubSandwich, sandwich); Python 3.13 (pandas, statsmodels, scipy); BayesFlow 2 for the model fits

This chapter documents the analysis pipeline for characterising the latent dimensions of inter-individual variation in behaviour. The approach takes the per-participant random-effect estimates (Best Linear Unbiased Predictors, BLUPs) from 

Primary GLMMs and submits them to a factor analysis after standardisation and redundancy pruning.

The pipeline is implemented in participant_factor_structure.py.

Each participant produces a vector of behavioural traits via the random-effect BLUPs from M1, M3, M4, M5, M6, and M7. These traits include things like overall accuracy (M1.Group), oddball reactivity (M4.oddball_lag1), generalisation quality (M5.Group), and so on. The hypothesis is that these traits are driven by a small number of underlying trait-level dimensions. The factor analysis aims to:

Recover these dimensions empirically from the BLUP matrix.

Provide per-participant scores on each dimension.

Enable later cross-validation against the BayesFlow parameter posteriors fit to the same trials. If the GLMMs and the generative model are capturing the same individual differences, the same low-dimensional structure should emerge from both.

Each model that successfully fits with random slopes writes a M{n}_blups.csv file with one row per participant and one column per random-effect term. The factor structure script discovers and loads all such files in the input directory.

A theoretically-motivated subset of BLUPs is retained (not all random effects are included because this would dilute the factor structure with measurement noise); including only those with named theoretical interpretations preserves the signal. The current inclusion list is:

Models that fall to OLS or cluster-robust OLS (and therefore have no extractable random effects, see 

Cross Cutting Methods) contribute NaN columns; these are dropped before standardisation.

Each retained BLUP column is z-scored across participants:\tilde z_{p,k} = \frac{b_{p,k} - \bar{b}_{\cdot,k}}{\mathrm{SD}(b_{\cdot,k})}.

This is essential because BLUPs from different models live on different scales (M5 is in degrees, M4 is on a log scale, M7 is in logit units). Without z-scoring, M5 would dominate any unrotated factor solution purely because of its scale.

The matrix is checked for collinear feature pairs with \lvert r \rvert > 0.95. When such pairs are detected, the lower-priority member of each pair is dropped, where the priority order is fixed to preserve features mapping onto the focal theoretical constructs:PRIORITY = [
    "oddball_reactivity",          # focal Factor 1
    "inference_intercept",          # focal Factor 2
    "inference_learning_rate",
    "accuracy_intercept",
    ...
]

The full priority list appears in participant_factor_structure.py. The motivation for this step is the following: the M4 random-effect covariance (Group-oddball_lag1-transition_lag1) is typically near-singular at small N because the three components share much of the same participant-level variance. The corresponding BLUPs are then near-perfectly correlated (e.g., \lvert r \rvert > 0.99 in pilot data), which makes the correlation matrix singular, breaks KMO and Bartlett, and destabilises the factor solution. Auto-pruning preserves the factor most directly tied to the focal hypothesis (oddball_reactivity) and removes the redundant indices (belief_shift_intercept, transition_reactivity). Thus this approach allows to preserve methodological rigor, regardless of the sample size (and it also allows for a more nuanced and sophisticated analysis with the same code as soon as more data is available).
Three diagnostics are computed and reported:
A near-zero determinant indicates remaining collinearity even after the explicit pruning step. We report \det(\mathbf{R}) in the diagnostics file as a transparent indicator.

KMO (

Kaiser, 1974) is the ratio of the sum of squared correlations to the sum of squared correlations plus the sum of squared partial correlations:\mathrm{KMO} = \frac{\sum_{i \neq j} r_{ij}^2}{\sum_{i \neq j} r_{ij}^2 + \sum_{i \neq j} a_{ij}^2},

where a_{ij} are entries of the anti-image correlation matrix. We compute a_{ij} from the inverse correlation matrix as\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\, \mathbf{R}^{-1}\, \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}, \quad \mathbf{D} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{R}^{-1}),

following the standard formulation. Per-feature KMO (“MSA”) values are also reported. Conventional interpretation thresholds (Kaiser 1974; Hutcheson & Sofroniou 1999):

KMO

Interpretation

\geq 0.90

marvellous

\geq 0.80

meritorious

\geq 0.70

middling

\geq 0.60

mediocre

< 0.60

unacceptable

Bartlett’s chi-square test (

Bartlett, 1951) tests the null hypothesis that the correlation matrix equals the identity matrix:\chi^2 = -\Big(N - 1 - \tfrac{2p + 5}{6}\Big) \cdot \log\det(\mathbf{R}), \quad \mathrm{df} = \tfrac{p(p-1)}{2}.

A significant result (typically p < 0.05) is a necessary but not sufficient condition for FA to be appropriate.

hierarchy.lvl4: Step 5: Factor count via parallel analysis
Step 5: Factor count via parallel analysis

records.content:
We use Horn’s parallel analysis (

Horn, 1965) to determine the number of factors. The procedure:

Compute the eigenvalues of the observed correlation matrix.

Generate n_iter = 500 random matrices of the same shape with i.i.d. standard-normal entries.

Compute the eigenvalues of each random matrix and take the per-rank 95th percentile across iterations.

Recommended k = the number of observed eigenvalues exceeding the corresponding random-data 95% quantile.

A scree plot (fa_scree_parallel.png) shows both the observed and random-data quantile curves with the Kaiser cutoff (eigenvalue = 1) and the recommended k marked.

Parallel analysis is the methodological consensus choice over the older Kaiser eigenvalue-> 1 criterion or the visual scree elbow, both of which over-extract in noisy data (

Zwick & Velicer, 1986).
The factor analysis is fit at multiple values of k for sensitivity inspection, by default at k = 1, k =  recommended-by-parallel-analysis, k = 2, and \min(k_{\max}, p - 1).

We use principal axis factoring (PAF) for the unrotated loadings:

Initial communalities h^2_j are set to the squared multiple correlations: h^2_j = 1 - 1/[\mathbf{R}^{-1}]_{jj}.

Substitute communalities on the diagonal of \mathbf{R} to form \mathbf{R}^*.

Take the top-k eigen-decomposition of \mathbf{R}^*: \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{D}^{1/2}.

Update h^2_j = \sum_{m=1}^{k} L_{jm}^2.

Iterate steps 2–4 until \max_j \lvert \Delta h^2_j \rvert < 10^{-6} or 50 iterations.

We decided to use PAF for this factor analysis pipeline, since it is the standard fitting method when distributional normality of the input is questionable (Fabrigar, Wegener, MacCallum, & Strahan, 1999) and works well with the standardised but possibly non-Gaussian BLUPs.

We use direct oblimin rotation with \gamma = 0 (the quartimin criterion; 

Carroll, 1953). Oblique (rather than orthogonal) rotation is appropriate when there is no theoretical reason to assume the underlying factors are uncorrelated (and in this case, the M4 random-effect covariance structure already shows that they are not).

The rotation is implemented via the gradient-projection algorithm (

Jennrich, 2002). Convergence threshold is 

10-6 on the projected gradient norm; backtracking line search (Armijo condition) controls the step size. Maximum 500 outer iterations.

The returned objects are:

\mathbf{L} (the pattern matrix): L_{jm} = unique loading of feature j on factor m.

\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \mathbf{T}^\top \mathbf{T} (the factor inter-correlation matrix): off-diagonal entries are the correlations between rotated factors.

hierarchy.lvl5: Why we implemented the factor analysis “from scratch”
Why we implemented the factor analysis “from scratch”

records.content: The factor analysis is implemented in-house (numpy + scipy only) rather than using the factor_analyzer Python package. The decision was forced by a known compatibility break between factor_analyzer 0.5.1 and scikit-learn ≥ 1.6 (check_array(force_all_finite=...) was renamed to ensure_all_finite=...). Rather than pinning to outdated dependencies (which could lead to compatibility issues with the dependency requirements for the other analyses), we implement PAF, oblimin rotation, KMO, and Bartlett directly. This also makes the framework self-contained and easier to audit.

Per-participant factor scores are computed via regression method:\hat{\mathbf{F}} = \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}\, \mathbf{R}^{-1}\, \mathbf{S}, \quad \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{L}\, \boldsymbol{\Phi},

where \tilde{\mathbf{Z}} is the standardised feature matrix, \mathbf{R} is the correlation matrix, \mathbf{L} is the pattern matrix, \boldsymbol{\Phi} is the factor inter-correlation matrix (identity if rotation is orthogonal), and \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\Phi} is the structure matrix. Saved as fa_factor_scores.csv for the recommended k.

These scores are intended to support downstream analyses, including correlation with BayesFlow parameter posterior means, with state and trait questionnaire scores, and with the change-point and survival analysis outputs. Most notably, the factor scores could be used for cross-validation of the BayesFlow pipeline and the respective estimated parameters.

To quantify uncertainty in the loadings (at the currently small-medium N typical of this study), we bootstrap the loading matrix:

For b = 1, \ldots, B = 200, sample N participants with replacement.

Re-fit the factor model on the bootstrap sample.

Sign-align each factor to the reference solution: if \mathbf{L}^{(b)}_{:,m} \cdot \mathbf{L}^{\text{ref}}_{:,m} < 0, flip the sign of factor m in iteration b.

Compute mean, SD, and 95% bootstrap quantiles of each loading across iterations.

A loading is flagged as stable and substantial (•) in the heatmap if its bootstrap SD < 0.20 and \lvert \hat L_{jm} \rvert > 0.30. Loadings without this marker should not be interpreted at the current N.

(The sign-alignment step is necessary because factor analysis is identified up to sign and column permutation; without alignment, the bootstrap mean and SD are inflated by sign flips that have no substantive meaning.)

This is a heatmap of correlations between the factor scores and a small set of model-free per-participant summary statistics (mean angular error, mean circular variance, mean defense rate, mean placement duration, mean \Delta_t). The idea is, that each factor should correlate with theoretically related summaries; if it does not, the factor labelling is unreliable (or it captures another latent structure that might not be meaningful and interpretable in our context).

This chapter documents an analysis that is no longer part of the pipeline (archived on 10 October 2026). Its script is in old_scripts/ of the analysis folder, and its numbers come from an earlier, smaller sample. See 

Reproducing the Analysis for the reason and the replacement.

These analyses are conceptually (partially) adjacent to M5 in 

Primary GLMMs (both ask “when does behaviour change relative to ground truth?”) but they use entirely different statistical machinery and rest on different operationalisations. Again, the aim is to provide convergent evidence (a finding that emerges both under the parametric M5 specification and under at least one of the non-parametric / semi-parametric alternatives is much more credible than any alone).

The two analyses are:

Change-point analysis (M_CP) (Layer 5A), which is an offline change-point detection algorithm that is run per participant on the trial-by-trial trajectory. Detected change-points are compared to the true episode episode boundaries.

Time-to-recovery survival analysis (M_SURV) (Layer 5B). Here, for each true transition, the number of trials elapsed until the participant’s net mean falls within a tolerance window of the new target (episode mean for the respective color cue) is treated as a time-to-event outcome with right censoring.

Both are implemented in temporal_dynamics_analysis.py.

For each participant, the per-trial signal is the signed angular distance of the participant’s net mean from a per-participant reference angle (signed difference is wrapped to get the euclidean distance instead of circular one).

We use Pruned Exact Linear Time (PELT) segmentation (Killick, Fearnhead, & Eckley, 2012) implemented in the ruptures Python library (Truong, Oudre, & Vayatis, 2020). PELT minimises a penalised cost function\sum_{k=1}^{K+1} \mathcal{C}\!\big(s_{t_{k-1}+1:t_k}\big) + \beta \cdot K,

over all possible numbers (K) and locations (t_1, \ldots, t_K) of change-points, where \mathcal{C} is a per-segment cost function and \beta is the penalty per added change-point. PELT solves this exactly in \mathcal{O}(n) amortised time under mild conditions (Killick et al., 2012), via dynamic programming with a pruning rule that discards dominated candidate change-points. model='l2' (sum of squared deviations from segment mean) is used as the default cost function.

By default, the penalty is set per participant via the BIC-style heuristic\beta = 3 \cdot \log(T) \cdot \widehat{\sigma}^2,

where T is the participant’s number of trials and \widehat{\sigma}^2 = \mathrm{Var}\!\big(\mathrm{diff}(s)\big) is a noise scale estimated from the first differences of the signal. This adapts the penalty to each participant’s own signal scale and length. Sensitivity to the penalty can be inspected by overriding via --cp_penalty <value>.

Given a participant’s set of detected change-points \{\hat{t}_k\}_{k=1}^{\hat{K}} and the set of true episode-boundary trials \{t^*_j\}_{j=1}^{J} (transitions only, episode 1 has no preceding boundary), four per-participant metrics are computed:

Per-transition signed latency is computed for each true transition t^*_j. This is the signed distance to the nearest detected change-point: \ell_j = \hat{t}_{k^*} - t^*_j, where k^* = \arg\min_k \lvert \hat{t}_k - t^*_j \rvert. Negative values are anticipatory; positive values are reactive.

Per-transition hit indicator is True if \lvert \ell_j \rvert \leq \text{tolerance} (default tolerance: 5 trials).

Per-participant hit rate is the proportion of true transitions correctly detected within tolerance.

False-alarm rate per 100 non-transition trials is the number of detected change-points not matched to any true transition within tolerance, normalised by (T - J) / 100.

Mean unsigned latency is \frac{1}{J}\sum_j \lvert \ell_j \rvert, computed over transitions where a latency is defined (NaN for transitions never matched).

The per-transition signed latency is the unit of analysis for the parametric test. A linear mixed model is fit on the long-format per-transition table:latency ~ condition_L + condition_Q
          + episode_index_c
          + condition_L : episode_index_c
          + condition_Q : episode_index_c
          + transition_dir_sum
          + condition_L : transition_dir_sum

Random effects: (1 + episode_index_c | participant_id).

The structure deliberately mirrors M5 so that interaction signs and magnitudes can be compared coefficient-by-coefficient between the two analyses (for cross-validation). Transitions where no detection occurred (NaN latency) are excluded from this model and tracked separately in the companion model below.

records.content:
Per-transition hit indicators are modelled with a binomial GLMM (logit link), using the same predictor structure as M_CP. The fitting strategy mirrors M7’s: BinomialBayesMixedGLM (variational Bayes) is the preferred fit, with plain logistic regression as a fallback.

This companion model is informative because a participant who fails to detect a transition does not contribute a “long latency” - they contribute no latency. Treating the hit rate separately (rather than imputing latency for misses) can (hopefully) handle this in a pricipled manner.

For each (participant, episode) with episode_index >= 1:

The target angle for episode e is computed as the circular mean of actual_vector_angle over all delivered-outcome trials in episode e. Averaging across cues produces the latent-state-induced reference (rather than a cue-specific reference), which is the relevant target for “did the participant reach the new state?”. Episodes with fewer than 3 delivered outcomes are excluded. #CHECK

The time-to-recovery is the smallest trial_in_episode value \geq 1 such that\big\lvert \mathrm{wrap}_{[-180°, +180°]}\!\big(\theta_t - \theta^{\text{target}}_e\big) \big\rvert \leq \text{threshold}.

If the threshold is never reached within the episode, the observation is right-censored at the episode length.

The event indicator is 1 if the threshold was reached, 0 if right-censored.

The analysis is run at two thresholds: 15° (strict) and 30° (lenient), both reported. The two thresholds are implement to represent two layered questions. The 30° threshold asks “did the participant reach the right region?” while the 15° threshold asks “did the participant consolidate tightly?”. Consistent vs divergent effects between the two thresholds could themselves be informative.

The semiparametric Cox proportional hazards model (Cox, 1972) is fit at each threshold:\lambda(t \mid x) = \lambda_0(t) \exp\!\big(\beta^\top x\big),

where x comprises:condition_L + condition_Q
+ episode_index_c
+ transition_dir_sum
+ condition_L : episode_index_c

Implementation: lifelines.CoxPHFitter (Davidson-Pilon, 2019).

Each participant contributes 7 (8! CHECK) transitions. The Cox partial likelihood treats observations as independent, which understates SEs in the presence of within-participant correlation. We use cluster-robust standard errors (Lin & Wei, 1989) with cluster_col="participant_id". This is a sandwich-type robust variance estimator analogous to those used in GEE, and is the standard alternative when frailty terms are not natively supported (which they are not in lifelines at the time of writing).( (So this is the survival-analysis analogue of the cluster-robust OLS fallback used in the GLMMs in the framework)

In the Cox model, \beta_k > 0 corresponds to a higher hazard, i.e., faster recovery (the recovery event happens sooner). The exponentiated coefficient \exp(\beta_k) is the hazard ratio per unit increase in the covariate.

The central test is condition_L (a positive coefficient means recovery is faster in higher-instruction conditions, on the unit-contrast scale).

Two Kaplan–Meier survival curve plots accompany the Cox model:

By condition (M_SURV_kaplan_meier.png), where survival means “not yet recovered”

By transition direction (M_SURV_kaplan_meier_by_direction.png) separates away vs toward_baseline transitions, with an embedded log-rank test (Mantel, 1966) per panel. This directly addresses / allows to control for potential structural-asymmetry effects (return-to-baseline transitions might be reached faster than away-from-baseline transitions because baseline is the perceptually familiar configuration)

records.content:
Overall, each addresses a different facet of the same underlying construct (latent-state inference / cross-cue generalisation):



What it asks

Operationalisation

M5

At the focal first-c_2 trial, how close is the participant’s net to the new target?

Parametric, requires defining I_e and the previous-episode reference; cue-specific

M_CP

When does the participant’s trajectory show a discontinuity?

Non-parametric (PELT detection), no cue-specificity

M_SURV

How long until the participant’s net mean reaches the new target?

Semi-parametric (Cox PH), defines an explicit event with censoring

Findings that converge across all three are robust to operationalisation. Dissociations are themselves diagnostic. (e.g., a participant with low M_CP latency (detects transitions quickly) but long M_SURV recovery time (slow to consolidate) has a different cognitive/behavioral profile from one with the opposite pattern, mapping onto separate model parameters in the BayesFlow generative-model fits (h_{\text{switch}} vs \Delta updating rate) again)

Blinks are the EyeLink blink events of the recorded eye. tambi_eye_convert.py writes them to stats_results/eye_tracking/converted/<pid>/blinks.parquet.

Blink: an event of 50–500 ms that starts inside a trial’s recording block.

Artefacts: shorter events (11 % of all events).

Long closures or tracking loss: longer events (4 % of all events).

Pupil gaps. Pupil gaps were also built from the 20 ms bins of the sample stream (bins with a share of valid samples below 1). 99.8 % of the blinks overlap a gap of 50–500 ms, and 99.9 % of these gaps overlap a blink, so both sources mark the same events.

Relation to the pupil preprocessing. The pupil preprocessing (

Pupil Preprocessing) treats every bin with an invalid sample as missing. It pads these bins by 100 ms before and 160 ms after and interpolates gaps up to 500 ms. A blink as defined here is therefore an interpolated stretch of the pupil signal. Only tracking loss longer than 500 ms stays missing.

Observed time. Observed time is time inside the recording, outside gaps longer than 500 ms and outside long closures. It is the denominator of all blink rates. An event window is used when at least 75 % of it is observed.

The events are those of the pupil preprocessing:

cue onset: ANTICIPATION_START;

attack onset: MOSQUITO_ANGLE;

feedback onset: attack onset + 2,300 ms, when BLOCKED! or BITE! appears with a sound.

The blink windows were read off the grand-average blink rate over all trials and participants (

Figure 2) before any contrast was computed.

Trial variables.

Bite: the attack got past the nets.

Outcome type: transition (first trial of an episode after episode 1), oddball, or regular (all other trials).

Nexus quantities (pupil_model_trials.csv; see 

Pupil Analysis):

after the outcome: surprise, belief update and oddball attribution;

before it: state uncertainty and predictive entropy.

Each quantity enters as the within-participant deviation (x_w, in SD) and the participant mean (x_b, z-scored).

As in the pupil analyses, the trials after a rating or break screen are left out of the trial-level models.

Trial level. Generalised estimating equations (GEE) clustered by participant, with an exchangeable working correlation:

binomial (logit) for 0/1 measures;

Poisson (log link, offset log observed minutes) for blink counts;

Gaussian for latency.

Covariates: trial number (centred) and condition, coded as Full vs None + Partial (c3) and Partial vs None (c21).

Participant level. OLS with HC3 standard errors, as in tambi_factor_strategies.py. The measure and the score are z-scored: measure ~ score + c3 + c21. The score × condition interaction is the Wald test of the two interaction terms in measure ~ score × (c3 + c21). The main score is the general factor (gf_item_sl_g_oos_total), and the second score is STICSA trait.

Correction. Benjamini-Hochberg q within families. Each family is one question about one measure and is named with each result. The reference window, the outcome-type interactions and the pupil confound checks are controls and carry p values.

Sample. 90 participants have gaze data. Two are not analysed: 15265 (excluded participant) and 5272 (13 trials recorded). The sample is 88 participants (None 33, Partial 35, Full 20), 87 of them with questionnaire scores.

Blinks and observed time.

95,455 blinks fall inside trials.

The median blink duration is 111 ms.

The median observed share of the trial time is .99 (minimum .74).

The median blink rate over the whole trial is 18.5 per minute (IQR 12.4–29.9).

Blink rate and pupil data loss. The blink rate goes with pupil data loss: Spearman ρ = .76 with the share of missing pupil samples, and ρ = −.73 with the share of usable pupil trials (

Figure 1).

The pupil exclusion criterion (fewer than 50 % usable pupil trials) applies to three of the 88 participants.

These three blink 34, 44 and 50 times per minute. The median of the others is 18 per minute (Mann-Whitney p = .013).

The pupil sample therefore leaves out participants who blink often.

Figure 2) has three features:

The blink rate falls from about 0.35 to 0.07 per second within 250 ms of the attack onset and stays low for about 1 s, while the mosquito approaches.

After the feedback onset it rises from about 0.2 to 0.9 per second at 350–500 ms.

After the cue onset it peaks at 1.2 per second at 400–500 ms.

Result of the check. Blinks in the pupil windows do not differ with the scores or with Nexus surprise, and blink control leaves the score effect on the feedback-pupil surprise slope at the same size. Right: effect of the general factor on the participant slope of the feedback pupil on Nexus surprise, with all trials, with the blink count as covariate and with the trials without a blink (estimate and 95 % CI).

Defensive blink. Blinks are suppressed while the mosquito approaches and occur in a burst 350–500 ms after the feedback. A bite raises the probability of a blink 250–750 ms after the feedback from .21 to .37 and brings the first blink 86 ms earlier. Oddballs and transitions do not change the post-feedback blink. This bite effect is the candidate defensive blink reflex.

Blink rate. The blink rate is lowest during the net placement and highest in the ISI, and rises over the session. It does not follow the Nexus uncertainty before the attack or the surprise of the outcome after correction.

Scores and condition. The general factor and the instruction condition are not associated with any blink measure. Higher STICSA trait scores go with fewer post-feedback blinks after blocked attacks.

Pupil results. Blinks do not account for the stronger coupling of the feedback pupil with surprise at higher general-factor scores. The pupil exclusion criterion removes participants who blink often.

records.content:
With gaze and cursor on one clock (

Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Synchronization), this chapter compares where participants look with where they move: how far the gaze runs ahead of the hand, whether gaze and cursor visit the other latent state before the first net, how the gaze and the cursor at the end of the anticipation phase relate to the first net, and how the spread of the gaze compares with the spread of the cursor. Each measure is related to the instruction condition, the questionnaire scores and the general questionnaire factor.

Scripts (analysis repository): tambi_eye_mouse_questionnaire.py (pipeline step eyemouseq) and tambi_eye_mouse_figures.py (step eyemousefigs; talk versions in stats_results/13_11/eye_mouse_sync/figures/talk/). Input: sync_trials.csv and sync_tokens.csv of tambi_eye_mouse_sync.py, the mouse-tracking trials (curvature and direction changes of token 1), the fixation-based gaze entropy of the eye-tracking analysis, the questionnaire scores and the general questionnaire factor, and the strategy rates after events. Output: stats_results/13_11/eye_mouse_sync/.

Data. 87 participants (None 32, Partial 35, Full Instructions 20), 15,177 usable trials; 86 with questionnaire scores, 77 with a general-factor score. Measures are defined in the synchronization chapter.

Statistics as in the 

eye-tracking analysis: GEE across trials clustered by participant (binomial for 0/1 measures, Gaussian otherwise); contrasts Full vs None + Partial (c3) and Partial vs None (c21); score slope per SD across conditions (y ~ score + c3 + c21), and slopes within each condition and their pairwise differences (y ~ score × (c3 + c21)). Benjamini–Hochberg q values across the measures of one score, measure set (eye–hand, competition, anticipation, entropy) and trial set, are in the CSV files; the text gives estimates and p, with the general factor as the main score. Stable trials are neither event trials nor the trial after one (sync_condition.csv, sync_questionnaire.csv, sync_questionnaire_by_condition.csv).

records.content:
Figure 1:Left and middle: gaze lead over the cursor (cursor arrival − gaze arrival at the token’s location) for token 1 and for later tokens that need a movement of more than one slot, by condition. Right: mean angular difference between gaze(t) and cursor(t + lag) during placement (mean and SE across participants); the minimum near 0 ms shows that gaze and cursor are at the same slot most of the time.

Token 1. From placement onset, the gaze reaches the location of token 1 after a median of 508 ms and the cursor after 590 ms; the gaze arrives first in 66 % of the trials with both arrivals. Median lead 95 ms; participant means 134 ms (None 147, Partial 117, Full 144 ms). The press follows the gaze arrival by a median of 643 ms.

Later tokens (movement of more than one slot): median lead 75 ms, gaze first in 64 %; participant means 162 / 185 / 205 ms (None / Partial / Full).

At the click the gaze is at the pressed slot in 87 % of the token-1 presses and 83 % of the later presses (median distance 0.8–1.0°), and already at the next token’s location in 7–9 %.

Condition. No differences in lead, gaze at the click, gaze ahead, gaze–cursor distance or lag (all p ≥ .09).

Questionnaires. With higher STICSA trait scores the lag at which gaze and cursor agree best is shifted toward the gaze leading (general factor +16 ms per SD, p = .030; STICSA trait +23 ms, p < .001). The token-1 lead is longer with higher general-factor scores (+20 ms per SD, p = .019), and within Full Instructions with higher STICSA trait (+39 ms, p = .002), STICSA state (+33 ms, p = .006) and general-factor scores (+33 ms, p = .006).



Figure 2:Distance between gaze and cursor during the movement to token 1 over normalised time (placement onset to the press), stable trials: by condition, and by median split of STICSA trait within each condition (mean and SE across participants).

During the first movement the gaze is about 6–7° from the cursor (it is already at the target while the cursor leaves the centre) and the distance closes to 1.5–2° at the press. The mean distance is not associated with the condition or any score (all p ≥ .38). In None, participants with high STICSA trait show a larger distance at the end of the movement on average, with a wide spread across participants.

records.content:
On trials on which token 1 goes to the current state (6,902 trials, 5,358 stable), gaze and cursor can visit the other latent state before the first net is placed.



Figure 3:Trials with token 1 at the current state. Left: share of trials on which gaze and cursor, only the gaze (covert), or only the cursor visit the other state before the press of token 1, by condition (stable trials; the rest: neither). Middle: share of trials on which the other state receives a later net in the same trial, by visit class (participant means). Right: cursor toward the other state on trials with and without gaze at the other state (participant means by condition).

Frequencies (participant means, stable trials): the gaze visits the other state on 4.0 % of these trials, the cursor on 7.6 %. Classes: both 1.5 %, gaze only (covert) 2.5 %, cursor only 6.1 %, neither 90 %. About half of the gaze visits (51 %) begin before the cursor starts to move.

Gaze and cursor go together. When the gaze visits the other state, the cursor does so as well on 37 % of the trials, against 3–9 % otherwise (+2.24 log-odds, odds ratio 9.4, p < .001; sync_competition_models.csv), and the deviation of the first movement toward the other state is larger (log(1 + maximum deviation) +0.59, p < .001). On the same trials, more fixation time at the other state in the prediction window goes with more pull (+0.041 per SD, p = .003, stable trials), and a first fixation at the other state goes with token 1 at the other state (+1.16 log-odds, p < .001; eye_mouse_models.csv of the eye-tracking analysis).

Relation to later splits. On 18 % of these trials the other state receives a later net in the same trial. Gaze at the other state before token 1 makes a later net there more likely (+0.36 log-odds, p = .033, with the cursor visit in the same model), the cursor visit does not (−0.11, p = .40). Gaze at the other state in the anticipation phase predicts a later net there more strongly (+0.61, p < .001). Between participants, the rate of later splits goes with the split strategies after events (split at t+1 ρ = .67, at t+2 after transitions ρ = .64, transitions followed at t+1 ρ = −.55; sync_participant_correlations.csv); the rate of covert visits is not related to any strategy (|ρ| ≤ .18).

Condition. Cursor-only visits are more frequent with instructions (Partial vs None +0.68 log-odds, p = .014; Full vs None + Partial +0.53, p = .014), as is the pull (Partial vs None +0.13, p = .006; Full +0.12, p = .030). Gaze visits to the other state do not differ between conditions (p ≥ .19).

Questionnaires. Across conditions none of the visit measures is associated with a score (all p ≥ .095). Within conditions:

None: higher STICSA trait and BDI-II scores go with more cursor-only visits (+0.28 and +0.24 log-odds per SD, p = .007) and more pull (STICSA trait +0.068, p < .001; BDI-II +0.048, p = .005); gaze visits are not associated (p ≥ .05).

Full: higher STICSA trait and BDI-II scores go with fewer cursor visits (−0.33, p = .003; −0.46, p < .001); higher STICSA state scores go with more gaze visits (+0.22, p = .022) and more covert visits (+0.27, p = .013); higher OCI scores with more later splits (+1.46, p < .001).

Gaze and cursor do not show opposite entropy effects: within None, neither gaze nor cursor entropy is associated with STICSA trait. The lower gaze entropy with higher scores across conditions comes mainly from Partial Instructions and from fewer fixations.

Which of these questionnaire effects hold across conditions and which are carried by one condition is shown for all gaze, gaze–cursor and mouse measures in

records.content:
Alignment. Gaze and cursor are aligned to about ±1.5 ms at placement onset after correcting a clock drift of 60 ppm.

Eye leads hand. The gaze reaches the location of the next net before the cursor (participant means 134 ms for token 1 and 181 ms for later tokens; medians across trials 95 and 75 ms) and stays there until the click; with higher STICSA trait and general-factor scores the gaze runs further ahead.

Competition. Gaze and cursor visits to the other state before the first net are rare (4 % and 8 %) and strongly coupled; covert visits (gaze only) are as rare as visits by both. Gaze at the other state predicts a later net there, the cursor visit does not. Instructions increase cursor visits, not gaze visits. In None, higher STICSA trait and BDI-II go with cursor visits and pull, not with gaze visits.

Anticipation. The last fixation before placement predicts the location of the first net better than the cursor does.

Entropy. Gaze and cursor entropy agree during placement and are unrelated in the anticipation phase. The anxiety-related spread of the first movement in None is curvature and direction changes, not entropy, and it has no counterpart in gaze entropy.

Gaze was recorded by the EyeLink on its own clock, the cursor by the task on the task clock. This chapter describes how both are put on one clock per trial, how precise the alignment is, and the measures computed from the synchronised streams. The results are in 

Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Analysis.

Script (analysis repository): tambi_eye_mouse_sync.py (pipeline step eyemouse). Input: the cursor files raw_data/mouse_tracking/<pid>_session1_*_mousetrap.csv, the converted gaze stream stats_results/eye_tracking/converted/<pid>/samples.parquet, the phase table, drift offsets and geometry of the 

eye-tracking preprocessing, the trial features and fixations of the 

eye-tracking analysis (eye_trial_features.csv, eye_example_fixations.csv.gz) and stats_results/13_11/mouse_tracking/mouse_trials.csv. Output: stats_results/13_11/eye_mouse_sync/.

records.content: The 87 participants with usable eye-tracking data all have a cursor file: 15,177 usable trials with 97,778 tokens (net placements; None 32, Partial 35, Full Instructions 20 participants).

records.content:
Cursor. The task writes a cursor sample on every frame it polls (every 33–50 ms), with timestamps (task clock, ms), time_from_trial_start, the position xpos, ypos in task units (degrees of visual angle; the slots lie at radius 8), the phase (anticipation, placement, ISI) and the button state. The cursor is not recorded during the outcome. Within a trial, timestamps − time_from_trial_start is constant (SD 0.004 ms), so both columns share one clock.

Gaze. The EyeLink stores the phase messages (ANTICIPATION_START, PLACEMENT_START, ISI_START, …) on its clock (ms). The gaze stream is the 50 Hz stream of the conversion (20 ms bins).

hierarchy.lvl1: Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Synchronization
Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Synchronization

records.content:
The task writes the first cursor sample of a phase at the first frame of that phase, and sends the phase message at the same point. For every trial, the time stamp of the first placement sample (task clock) is paired with PLACEMENT_START of the same trial (EDF clock), and a straight line

EDF time = a + b × task time

is fitted per participant. Pairs more than 20 ms off the first line are left out and the line is refitted (2 of 15,636 pairs in all). Every cursor sample is mapped to the EDF clock with this line.



Figure 1:Clock alignment per participant. Left: drift of the EDF clock relative to the task clock. Middle: residuals of the placement onsets after the linear fit (bars: 5th–95th percentile; dots: largest absolute residual). Right: first anticipation and first ISI sample, mapped to the EDF clock, minus ANTICIPATION_START and ISI_START (median, 5th–95th percentile).

Per participant (sync_clock_participants.csv; median and range across the 87 participants):

Quantity

Value

Trials used for the fit

181 (163–188)

Drift of the EDF clock relative to the task clock

+59.9 ppm (58.6–62.6), i.e. about 0.2 s per hour

Residual at placement onset, SD

0.82 ms (0.64–1.18)

Residual at placement onset, 5th / 95th percentile

−1.4 / +1.2 ms

Largest absolute residual

3.0 ms (1.6–8.4)

First anticipation sample − ANTICIPATION_START

−10.0 ms (−10.9 to −9.6); within participants 5th–95th percentile ±1 ms

First ISI sample − ISI_START

−10.2 ms (−11.1 to −9.7); within participants ±1 ms

Drift. The two clocks run at slightly different rates (60 ppm). Over a session of about 55 minutes this adds up to about 0.2 s, so a single offset would not be enough; the linear fit removes it.

Precision. After the fit, placement onsets agree within about ±1.5 ms; the time resolution of the cursor (33–50 ms per sample) is far coarser than this.

Phase onsets. The anticipation and ISI onsets, which are not used for the fit, agree within ±1 ms around a constant −10 ms: relative to the placement anchor, the first sample of these phases is written about 10 ms before the message is sent. This constant does not change the alignment within the placement phase, which all eye–hand measures use; for the anticipation phase the cursor times are therefore accurate to about 10 ms.

Gaze bins with at least half of the 1000 Hz samples valid are converted to degrees from the screen centre (33.7 px per degree, y upwards, as the cursor) and corrected with the drift offset of the trial’s block. Their time is the centre of the 20 ms bin. Gaze and cursor then share the clock and the coordinates: at the press of a token, the gaze lies a median 0.8° from the pressed slot, and within one slot of it in 87 % of the token-1 presses (

Figure 2).

records.content:
Tokens are reconstructed as in the 

mouse-tracking analysis: a left press in the placement phase at a radius of 5–11; token 1 starts at placement onset (cursor reset to the centre), token j at the press of token j − 1. Task locations (current state, other state, third direction, the other cue’s states, elsewhere, centre) are those of the eye-tracking analysis (22.5° around each direction).

Eye–hand coordination, per token (sync_tokens.csv):

Measure

Definition

Gaze arrival

start of the first fixation within one slot (11.25°; 4–12° from the centre) of the token’s location that is still going on at the token’s start or starts before its press (ms from the token’s start; negative: the gaze was already there)

Cursor arrival

first cursor sample after the token’s start within one slot of the location at a radius of at least 5°

Gaze lead

cursor arrival − gaze arrival (ms; positive: the gaze arrives first)

Gaze lead to the press

press − gaze arrival (ms)

Gaze at the click

the gaze at the press lies within one slot of the token (0/1)

Gaze ahead at the click

the gaze at the press lies within one slot of the next token’s location and more than one slot from the current one (0/1; tokens whose next token is at another slot)

Movement token

the token lies more than one slot from the previous one (token 1: always); lead times of later tokens use only these

Per trial (sync_trials.csv):

Measure

Definition

Gaze–cursor distance, token 1

mean distance (°) between gaze and cursor from placement onset to the press of token 1; and over normalised time (101 points)

Angular gaze–cursor difference, token 1

mean absolute difference of the angles (°), samples with gaze and cursor at least 3° from the centre

Lag

lag (−1000 to +1000 ms, 20 ms steps) at which the angular difference between gaze(t) and cursor(t + lag) during placement is smallest (samples with both at least 4° from the centre, at least 25 pairs); positive: the gaze is ahead

Gaze at the other state before token 1

a fixation at the other state starts between placement onset and the press of token 1 (trials with token 1 at the current state); also whether it starts before the cursor moves (movement initiation: 0.3° from the start) and whether the other state was fixated in the anticipation phase

Cursor toward the other state

the cursor comes within 45° of the other state at a radius of at least 2° before the press of token 1 (same trials)

Visit class

both, gaze only (covert), cursor only, neither

Later split

the other state receives a later token in the same trial (tokens 2–7)

Pull toward the other state

log(1 + maximum deviation of token 1 toward the other state) of the mouse-tracking analysis

Gaze and cursor at the end of the anticipation phase

task location of the last fixation of the anticipation phase, and of the cursor at the last anticipation sample (centre if the radius is below 3°); agreement of the two and of each with the location of token 1 (trials with the location away from the centre)

Gaze and cursor entropy

Shannon entropy (bits) of the angular position in 32 sectors weighted by time, positions within 3° of the centre left out, for the gaze stream and for the cursor (= entropy_antic, entropy_place of the mouse analysis), anticipation and placement phase

The gaze entropy here is computed from the 20 ms gaze stream in the same way as the cursor entropy, so the two are directly comparable; the fixation-based gaze entropy of the eye-tracking analysis (over task locations or slots, fixations only) is reported alongside.

The task screen shows the circle of 32 slots and, in the anticipation window, only the colour cue at the centre. Where participants look before any outcome is visible indicates which locations, and thus which hypotheses about the next attack, they consider. This chapter describes the gaze features computed from the preprocessed fixations (

Eye-Tracking Preprocessing) and their relation to the instruction condition, the questionnaire scores, the general questionnaire factor, the net allocation, the latent-state model and the mouse trajectories.

Scripts (analysis repository): tambi_eye_features.py (pipeline step eyefeat), tambi_eye_questionnaire.py (step eyeq) and tambi_eye_figures.py (step eyefigs; talk versions of the main figures in stats_results/13_11/eye_tracking/figures/talk/). Input: the fixations, usable trials and participant flags in stats_results/eye_tracking/ (eye_fixations.csv.gz, eye_trials.csv, eye_quality_participants.csv), the result files results/<pid>_session1_*_results.csv, the posterior means of the latent-state model (bayes_flow/bayesflow_vp_results/13_11/all_participants_posteriors.csv), the replayed belief traces (bayes_flow/belief_traces/13_11/belief_traces_trial.csv), the mouse-tracking trials (stats_results/13_11/mouse_tracking/mouse_trials.csv), the questionnaire scores and the general questionnaire factor. Output: stats_results/13_11/eye_tracking/.

The analysis uses the 87 participants with usable eye-tracking data (eye_usable and not excluded; None 32, Partial 35, Full Instructions 20) and their usable trials (usable in eye_trials.csv: 15,177 trials). Of these, 86 have questionnaire scores, 77 a general-factor score of run 13_11 and 78 posterior estimates of the latent-state model.

Features are computed separately for three windows of each trial:

Window

Task phase

Duration

Anticipation

colour cue shown, net placement not yet possible

4 s

Prediction

net placement possible

up to 7 s

Outcome

attack revealed (or no attack shown)

until the end of the trial

A fixation belongs to the window in which it starts. Positions are drift-corrected, in degrees from the screen centre.

Task locations. Each colour cue has two target directions, its two latent states; the two cues change state together, and their targets are about 70° apart. The possible outcome locations of a trial are:

Location

Definition

Current state

target direction of the trial for the shown cue

Other state

the other target direction of the shown cue

Third direction

the direction opposite the circular midpoint of the two states (about 120° from both)

Other cue, current

target direction of the other cue in the current latent state

Other cue, other

target direction of the other cue in the other latent state

Elsewhere

the remaining part of the circle

Centre

less than 2.5° from the centre (colour cue)

A fixation 4–12° from the centre is assigned to the nearest of the five directions if it lies within 22.5° (two slots) of it, otherwise to elsewhere. Fixations 2.5–4° or more than 12° from the centre are not at a task location. The pairing of the two cues’ targets is read from the episodes (within an episode both cues are in the same latent state). For the 32-slot measures, fixations 5–11° from the centre (the circle of slots) are assigned to the nearest slot.

What the locations stand for. In this task an event moves the next attack one step, to the other state or to an oddball location:

the current state: the attack comes from here if the state stays;

the other state: after a transition, or an oddball at the other state (57 % of the oddballs);

the third direction: an oddball outside the two states (43 % of the oddballs);

the other cue’s two states: not a possible outcome of the shown cue; gaze there reflects the joint structure of the two cues.

Gaze beyond the current state is the fixation time at the other state, the third direction and the other cue’s states. After an event (t+1, t+2), gaze back at the location of the previous state is analysed with the event measures below.

Gaze entropy follows the definition of stationary gaze entropy (Das & Maiti, 2024; Harris et al., 2025; Iaconis et al., 2021), with the task locations or the slots as the areas.

Comparison quantities for each trial:

Net entropy: Shannon entropy (bits) of the net allocation over the 32 slots.

Entropy of the model’s predictive distribution: the latent-state model (ReducedFormAgent, as in the belief trace replay, step 7 of 

Reproducing the Analysis) is run with the participant’s posterior means over the observed outcomes; before the update of each trial its predictive distribution over the 32 slots gives the entropy (bits).

Replayed state uncertainty: 1 − |2z − 1| of the same model before the trial, averaged over the posterior draws (belief_traces_trial.csv).

The mouse measures of the same trial (pull of token 1 toward the other state, spatial entropy of the cursor, location of token 1).

Event trials (eye_events.csv). As in the 

mouse-tracking analysis: t0 is a transition (first trial of a new episode) or an oddball; k = 0 is the event trial itself (before its outcome), k = 1, 2 the next two trials if they show the same cue and no further event occurred before them. Old is the circular mean of the participant’s own nets at t0, new the direction of the displaced attack at t0; events with the own t0 placement within 45° of the attack are left out. Measures: share of fixation time at old and new (22.5° around each), first fixation at old or new, at least one fixation at old.

Trial sets. Stable trials are neither event trials nor the trial after an event (11,206 of the 15,177 usable trials).

Generalised estimating equations (GEE) across trials, clustered by participant (exchangeable correlation; binomial for 0/1 measures, Gaussian otherwise), as in the mouse-tracking and factor analyses:

Condition: y ~ c3 + c21, with c3 = Full vs None + Partial (−1/3, −1/3, 2/3) and c21 = Partial vs None (−.5, .5, 0).

Score: y ~ score + c3 + c21 (slope per SD of the score across conditions), and y ~ score × (c3 + c21) for the slopes within each condition and their pairwise differences; for the general questionnaire factor and the five questionnaires. The general factor is the main score; the five scales are shown alongside it. Each score is reported with its estimate and p (Benjamini–Hochberg q values across measures are in the CSV files).

Events: the same models per event type, k and window; transitions vs oddballs: y ~ tr + c3 + c21 and y ~ score × tr + c3 + c21 (tr = 1 for transitions, 0 for oddballs).

Session: y ~ trial × (c3 + c21) with trial = (trial_index − 90)/100 (slope per 100 trials; across conditions = mean of the three condition slopes), y ~ score × trial + c3 + c21, and y ~ trial in episode × (c3 + c21) (per 10 trials), stable trials.

Entropy and mouse comparisons: y ~ x_within + x_between + c3 + c21, with x_within the predictor centred within the participant and x_between the participant mean (both divided by the SD of the predictor across trials).

Participant level: Spearman correlations of the participant means (stable trials) with the strategy rates after events, the mouse measures and the posterior means of the latent-state model.

The score slopes above are averaged across conditions. Within each condition fewer participants contribute (None 32, Partial 35, Full 20), so a slope can reach p < .05 in one condition only, even when the other conditions show the same direction. This section therefore puts, for every measure and score, the across-condition slope next to the three within-condition slopes and their pairwise differences, all from the score × condition GEE models above, for the gaze measures, the gaze–cursor measures (

In short:

Gaze before and after the placement (anticipation and outcome window): the associations hold across the three conditions, for the general factor (gaze at slots without nets, outcome entropy, the other state without a net at the outcome) and for the scales, most of them for STICSA trait. Participants with higher scores direct their first fixation to the current state, look less at slots without nets and at the other state when it has no net, and spread their gaze less.

Gaze during the placement (prediction window): the associations are condition-specific. With Partial Instructions, higher scores go with less gaze beyond the current state; with Full Instructions, higher STICSA state, OCI and general-factor scores go with more gaze at the other state without a net there, and more gaze shifts between the states.

Mouse: the anxiety-related curvature, direction changes and pull of the first movement are specific to None, and the cursor’s visits to the other state go in opposite directions in None and Full.

This section asks whether the questionnaire effects above are present from the first episode on, or whether they appear, weaken or change direction as participants learn the latent structure. It covers the gaze effects of the previous sections, the gaze–cursor lag and lead (

Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Analysis), the mouse measures of the first movement (

Mouse Tracking) and two placement strategies after transitions (transition followed at t+1, split at t+2; 

Follow-up Analyses).

Over the task gaze becomes more concentrated: gaze entropy changes by −0.20 bits from episode 1 to 9 in the anticipation window and by −0.12 bits in the outcome window (both p < .001, in every condition).
