In short:

Most questionnaire effects are stable over the task. They are present in the first half and of similar size in the second half: the first fixation at the current state, less gaze at slots without nets, lower gaze entropy, the gaze lag behind the cursor, the mouse effects in None, the gaze effects of the prediction window in Partial and Full, and the placement strategies after transitions (less following at t+1, more splitting at t+2).

None of them reverses. The few changes are small:

the entropy effect of STICSA trait and the gaze lead at token 1 grow in the second half;

with BDI-II, splitting at t+2 and gaze at the other state during the placement weaken;

in Full, gaze at the other state during the placement weakens with STICSA state.

The measures themselves change. While gaze and mouse movement change markedly over the task, especially from episode 1 to 2, the differences between low and high scorers keep roughly the same size (

Figure 31).

Do participants look back at where something happened on earlier trials, beyond the current trial’s task locations? Two targets are used:

Last oddball: the location of the most recent oddball attack 1–5 trials back, if the attack was shown. The attack of the previous trial lies away from the current task locations almost only when that trial was an oddball (248 of 252 trials), so it is included here at lag 1.

Nets of trial t−1: the slots that received nets on the previous trial.

A target counts only if it lies at least 33.75° (the 22.5° task window plus the 11.25° target window) from the current state, the other state and the two states of the other cue of the current trial. The control location is the target mirrored about the current state, so it lies at the same angular distance from the current state. If the mirrored location falls on a task location, the target rotated by +90°, −90° or 180° is used instead; for the nets, all target nets are moved together. Target and control windows are ±11.25° wide at a radius of 4–12°. Replay is the share of fixation time at the target minus the share at the control, in percentage points (pp).

The measure is taken in two windows of the current trial: the anticipation window, before the placement, and the ISI, after the placement and before the outcome. Usable trials: 1,122 trials with an oddball target and 1,432 with a net target, from 87 participants (median 13 per participant for each target). Script: tambi_eye_replay.py (pipeline step eyereplay). Output: stats_results/13_11/eye_replay/. Models: GEE as above.

Figure 34:Replay in the anticipation window: at the nets of t−1 by the type of trial t−1; at the last oddball by the number of trials since it; and both over the task (participant means; 95 % CI, episode: SE).



Figure 35:Replay and questionnaire scores: slope per SD across conditions (diamond, 95 % CI; filled: p < .05) and within each condition (dots).

Gaze returns to the last oddball location. In the anticipation window 4.4 % of the fixation time falls on the target and 1.9 % on the control (+2.5 pp, p < .001). At least one fixation lands on the target on 19.6 % of trials and on the control on 12.8 % (+0.51 log-odds, p < .001). In the ISI the difference is +2.4 pp (p < .001).

The oddball replay is short-lived. In the anticipation window it is +8.0 pp one trial after the oddball (p < .001), +2.1 pp two trials after (p = .007), and +0.6, +0.3 and +0.2 pp three to five trials after (p ≥ .56). It decreases by −2.0 pp per trial (p < .001). In the ISI the pattern is the same: +5.2 pp, +3.0 pp, then +1.6 pp (p = .056) and less. Because the locations at lags 3–5 are of the same kind as at lags 1–2, the effect is not a general preference for these locations.

Gaze returns to the previous trial’s nets when they lie away from the current task locations: +3.3 pp in the anticipation window (5.0 % vs 2.2 %, p < .001; at least one fixation 24.8 % vs 13.8 %, +0.73 log-odds, p < .001) and +2.1 pp in the ISI (p < .001).

This holds after stable trials (+3.6 pp, p < .001) and after transitions (+4.7 pp, p = .001; 62 trials of 38 participants), but not after oddballs (+0.2 pp, p = .94; 126 trials of 55 participants). After an oddball, gaze goes to the oddball location instead.

The differences between these trial types are not significant (p ≥ .28).

The control matches the distance from the current state, not the location itself, so this replay may also reflect a preference for the locations a participant tends to use.

Condition. Replay of the nets in the anticipation window is larger with Full Instructions (Full vs None + Partial +3.6 pp, p = .007; participant means: None +3.3, Partial +0.6, Full +5.6 pp). For the oddball replay the conditions do not differ (p ≥ .34).

Over the task, replay does not change (episode 1 to 9: oddball −2.4 pp, p = .19; nets +0.5 pp, p = .77; ISI p ≥ .48).

Questionnaires. Replay is not related to the scores across conditions. General factor: −0.7 to +0.2 pp per SD, p ≥ .24 for both targets and windows. Of the five scales, one slope has p < .05: IUS with the oddball replay in the ISI, −1.1 pp per SD, p = .035. Within conditions, replay of the nets in the ISI increases with STICSA state in None (+2.0 pp per SD, p = .015; differs from Full, p = .016). The replay measure rests on about 13 trials per participant and target, so these participant-level slopes are imprecise.

The working interpretation (see 

Pupil Analysis) has three parts:

Higher scores go with relying more on an internal representation of the structure, and with treating surprises as noise until they are confirmed.

This pays off under structural ambiguity (Partial).

With the structure explained (Full), participants with higher scores may consider more hypotheses and end up more uncertain and slower.

How the gaze, gaze–cursor and mouse results relate to each part:

Internal structure, surprises as noise.

Fits: before and after the outcome, gaze of participants with higher scores stays closer to the current state. It shows a first fixation there more often, less gaze at slots without nets, lower gaze entropy, and less looking at the other state when it has no net (general factor and scales, in all three conditions).

Fits: the strategies after transitions go the same way: fewer transitions followed at t+1 (general factor −0.26 log-odds, p = .022) and more splits at t+2 (+0.45, p < .001).

Fits: at t+2 after a transition the first fixation returns to the previous state more often (general factor +0.28, p = .076; IUS +0.37, p = .015).

Fits: these associations are present in the first half of the task.

Does not fit or stays open:

Gaze at the other state in stable phases is not related to the scores.

The lower anticipation entropy goes together with fewer fixations.

Gaze replay of oddball locations does not differ with the scores, so the gaze shows no separate processing of surprises.

Partial.

Within Partial, higher scores go with more concentrated gaze: less gaze beyond the current state during the placement (general factor −.043, p = .001) and lower anticipation entropy (STICSA state −0.10 bits, p < .001).

Whether this pays off cannot be read from the gaze measures; it depends on the performance measures in the other chapters.

Full.

Fits: within Full, higher scores go with signs of considering the other state during the placement:

more looking at the other state without a net (general factor +0.42, STICSA state +0.43, OCI +0.45 log-odds);

more gaze shifts between the states (OCI +0.96);

more later nets at the other state (general factor +0.66, p = .019);

a longer gaze lead before the cursor reaches the first net (general factor +33 ms, p = .005).

Does not fit:

Gaze entropy before the placement is not higher with higher scores in Full (IUS: lower over the 32 slots).

The gaze associations before and after the placement have the same direction in Full as in the other conditions.

The looking at the other state with STICSA state weakens over the task.

Uncertainty. Gaze entropy before the placement is lower with higher STICSA state and trait and OCI scores; this goes together with fewer fixations and is no longer significant when the number of fixations is controlled. In the outcome window gaze entropy is lower with higher STICSA and general-factor scores also with this control. Gaze entropy decreases over the session and does not differ between conditions in the anticipation window. On a given trial, gaze is more spread when the nets are more spread and when the replayed state uncertainty is higher.

Representation of the other state. Gaze at the other state in stable phases is not related to the instruction condition or to the questionnaire scores, but between participants it goes with the strategies and model parameters that describe treating surprises as noise (noise reactivity) and splitting after transitions. Within a trial, gaze at the other state goes with the pull of the mouse toward it (

Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Analysis).

Considered but not acted upon. With higher STICSA trait (and the general factor), gaze goes less often to locations that receive no net, and the first fixation more often to the current state.

Within and between conditions. The questionnaire associations of the gaze in the anticipation and outcome window hold across the three conditions (same direction, no differences); those in the prediction window are carried by Partial or Full Instructions.

After events. One trial after an event gaze goes to the new location regardless of whether it was a transition or an oddball; transitions and oddballs separate at t+2. With higher IUS the first fixation at t+2 after transitions goes back to the previous state more often. At the outcome of a transition, participants with higher scores look less at their own nets.

Over the task. Gaze and mouse movement change, mostly between the first and second episode: gaze becomes less spread and the first movement straighter. The questionnaire effects on gaze, the gaze–cursor lag, the mouse (in None) and the strategies after transitions are mostly stable from the first to the second half. None reverses, and the few changes are small.

Replay. Gaze returns to the location of an oddball attack on the next one or two trials, and to the previous trial’s nets. This replay does not change over the task and is not related to the questionnaire scores.

Gaze and pupil size were recorded with an EyeLink 1000 (camera “EyeLink CL”) during the task. This chapter describes the conversion of the EyeLink files, the segmentation of the trials and phases, their alignment with the behavioural result files, the drift correction, the data quality per participant and the first area-of-interest (AOI) measures.

Scripts (analysis repository): tambi_eye_convert.py and tambi_eye_quality.py (pipeline steps eyeconv and eyequal; reproducing step 8.8). Input: the EDF files <pid>_S<k>_<date>_<time>.EDF (pipeline parameter -EdfDir, default raw_data/eye_tracking) and the result files in results/. Output: stats_results/eye_tracking/.

All EDF files available on sciebo have been converted. EDF and result file are matched by participant ID; the session number in the file names (1 or 2) differs where the task had to be restarted, and there was one session per participant. Of the 97 participants with a lab session, 92 have an EDF file:

90 files are complete.

2 files exist only as truncated uploads (.EDF.tmp): the transfer stopped in the middle of a record. They are read up to the last complete trial: 11872 trials 1–163 of 176, 5272 trials 1–13 of 182 (see 

Conversion).

In 2 of the 92 sessions the eye tracker crashed, and the files contain no gaze data (16060, 9820: every trial is a single blink event, no fixations).

90 participants have gaze data (None 35, Partial 35, Full 20), 89 of them included in the analyses (15265 is excluded; see 

Data Collection Status).

5 participants have no EDF file: in 4 sessions eye tracking did not work (11218, 13654, 15025, 16093); the file of 16390 is in the lab and not yet on sciebo.

Two EDF files have no result file and are not used: 11623 (pilot participant with a different trial schedule, excluded) and 15454 (the task PC crashed, no result file).

The task code (conrad_fixed.py) starts the recording before and stops it after every trial, so each trial is one recording block. The tracker recorded one eye at 1000 Hz (the left eye in 87 sessions, the right eye in 5), with gaze in screen pixels (GAZE_COORDS 0 0 1919 1199) and pupil size as diameter. The trial messages are:

The outcome phase runs from OUTCOME_START (or NO_OUTCOME) to TRIAL_END. Further messages mark the state ratings (RATING_START / _END) and the post-task questions (POST_QUEST_*). The calibration takes place before the EDF file is opened, so its result is not in the file. Drift checks at the screen centre after the breaks are stored as DRIFTCORRECT messages with their offset; in two files (9031, 9820) a recalibration during the session is stored as !CAL messages.

tambi_eye_convert.py reads the EDF files with the EyeLink EDF API (edfapi64.dll), which ships with the Python package eyelinkio; the SR Research Developer Kit is not needed. Each file is read once and written to stats_results/eye_tracking/converted/<pid>/:

An EDF file of 43–54 MB becomes 2.6–3.4 MB (0.9 MB for the two files without gaze data) and takes 12–24 s. Participants already converted are skipped. With --delete_edf_after the EDF is deleted once all tables are written and read back; the pipeline step keeps the EDF files. --sample_hz 0 writes the events only.

Truncated files. A file left as .EDF.tmp is read when the participant has no .EDF. The EDF API cannot open a file that ends in the middle of a record. The EDF stream has no index; a complete file ends with its last record followed by two zero bytes. The script therefore writes a temporary copy that ends after the last complete TRIAL_END_<n> message, followed by two zero bytes, converts it and deletes it; the .tmp file itself is not changed. info.json records edf_truncated and the last complete trial. If the copy cannot be read either, only info.json is written, with the status incomplete.

tambi_eye_quality.py segments the trials from the messages and matches them to the result file by trial number. For each trial it checks the episode, the cue colour, whether an attack was shown, and the attack angle against the result file, and compares the onsets of placement, ISI and outcome (relative to the anticipation onset) and the placement duration with the times in the result file.

Of the 16,542 trials in the result files of the 92 participants with an EDF file, 16,360 are found in the EDF files, each once. The 182 missing trials are the trials after the truncation of 11872 and 5272. No EDF trial is missing from the result files.

Episode, cue colour, attack shown and attack angle agree in every trial in which the message is present. In 12 trials of 12 participants one message is missing (8 × EPISODE, 4 × CUE_COLOR; these are sent in the same millisecond as TRIAL_START). The tracker marks such losses with ERROR MESSAGES LOST <k>, where k is a signed 16-bit count: messages that arrive out of order produce LOST 1, LOST 65534 (= −2), LOST 1, a net loss of 0, and are present in the file. The phase messages are complete in every trial.

The phase onsets agree with the result file within −7 to +2 ms (−1 to +2 ms in all but 2 trials), the placement duration within −1 to +2 ms.

The trial onsets on the EDF clock and the unix time stamps of the result file (whole seconds) differ by at most 0.57 s after a linear fit, within the resolution of the time stamps.

The task draws in degrees of visual angle around the screen centre. The slots lie on a circle of radius 8° at 0°, 11.25°, …, 348.75° (counter-clockwise from the right, as slot_angles in the result file), and the colour cue is a disc of radius 1.5° at the centre. With this convention, 82 % of the placement fixations on the circle (after drift correction) lie within half a slot of a slot that received a net in the trial; with the angles mirrored or rotated by 90°, 5–16 % do.

The pixels per degree are estimated from the placement phase: fixations whose angle lies within 5° of a slot that received a net in the trial have a median distance of 269 px from the screen centre, which gives 33.7 px per degree (89,750 fixations of the participants with gaze data who are not excluded; eye_geometry.json). The fixation density shows the circle of slots at 8° (

Figure 1).



Figure 1:Fixation density (weighted by fixation duration, after drift correction) by phase, all participants with gaze data. The white circle marks the circle of slots (8°).

The drift checks after the breaks could not always reduce the offset: some were repeated many times and accepted with large offsets (participant medians of the accepted checks 0.28–28°). The offset is therefore estimated from the data and subtracted from the gaze positions.

Blocks. A block runs from one drift check or recalibration to the next (median 4 blocks per participant, 1–5).

Estimate. During the placement phase the participants look at the nets they place. For every placement fixation on the circle (5–11° from the corrected centre) within half a slot (5.625°) of a slot that received a net in the trial, the difference between the raw fixation position and the slot position (8° at the slot angle) is computed. The offset of a block is the median of these differences; blocks with fewer than 30 such fixations take the participant median (9 of 322 blocks). The selection depends on the offset, so the estimate is iterated four times, starting from no offset.

Correction. The block offset is subtracted from the fixation positions (xd, yd; raw positions in xd_raw, yd_raw). The offsets per block are in eye_drift_offsets.csv, so that the same correction can be applied to the 50 Hz gaze stream. The median correction is 1.03° per participant (0.32–3.41°).

Check. The anticipation phase is not used for the estimate. There, the colour cue is at the centre, and the median position of the fixations within 3° of the centre gives an independent offset. Before and after correction (participant medians, 90 participants with gaze data):

Fixation positions are converted to degrees relative to the screen centre and corrected for drift, with radius r and angle. The AOIs are:

Centre: r < 2.5°.

Ring: 5° ≤ r ≤ 11°, with the nearest of the 32 slots.

Current, other, third: r ≥ 4° and within 22.5° (two slots) of the direction. As in the 

mouse-tracking analysis, each cue has two target directions (its two latent states); current is the target direction of the trial, other the other target direction of the cue, and third the direction opposite the circular midpoint of the two.

Attack: within 22.5° of the attack direction of the trial (actual_vector_angle).

Per trial and phase, eye_trial_aoi.csv holds the share of fixation time in each AOI and the AOI of the first fixation outside the centre; eye_fixations.csv.gz holds every fixation with its trial, phase, block, raw and corrected position, and AOIs.

This chapter relates the trial-locked heart rate to the outcome types, to Nexus surprise and state uncertainty, to the model-free prediction error and to the instruction condition. The session-level heart rate and heart-rate variability are related to the general factor (gf_item_sl_g_oos_total) and STICSA trait. Heart rate is set against the pupil, and the feedback response is tested as a predictor of the next placement and gaze. The analyses use the predictors and model forms of the pupil analyses (

Pupil Analysis, 

Pupil and the Latent Signals of Three Models, 

Time Lags), so the two signals can be compared directly. The measures are described in

Outcome type: the response is 0.44 bpm smaller after a bite despite a net than after a blocked attack. In this outcome, heart rate first falls by about 0.6 bpm in the first second and then rises (

Measures:

Each is tested as z(measure) ~ z(score) + condition, OLS with HC3 standard errors. Within each condition: z(measure) ~ z(score) (HC3). Correction (Benjamini-Hochberg), per score: the three measures (mean heart rate, ln RMSSD, ln HF power) of the task, the three measures of the time before the first trial, and the three trial means, each as one family; each measure across blocks 1 to 4 as one family; within the conditions, each measure of each segment across the three conditions. A BIOPAC MP160 with an ECG100C amplifier recorded the ECG during the whole session. This chapter describes how the ECG is aligned with the task, how R peaks are detected and corrected, the heart-rate measures per trial and per session, and the data quality.

Script (analysis repository): tambi_ecg_preprocessing.py --tag 23_11 (pipeline step ecg). Input: raw_data/ecg/<pid>_<ddmm>.acq, the BIOPAC event logs raw_data/ecg_events/<pid>_*_biopac_events.csv, the result files and the EyeLink messages. Output: stats_results/23_11/ecg/. Settings: ecg_settings.json.

There are 96 AcqKnowledge files, one per participant. Each has two channels sampled at 2000 Hz: the ECG (ecg - ECG100C, mV) and a digital trigger line (Digital (STP Input 0), 0 or 5 V). Recordings last 56 to 103 min, of which the task takes 53 to 75 min. The ECG is resampled to 1000 Hz (polyphase filter with anti-aliasing). Participants 11218 and 16390 of the analysis sample have no ECG file. Participants 11623 (old trial schedule) and 15265 have an ECG file but are not in the analysis sample.

hierarchy.lvl2: Triggers and alignment with the task
Triggers and alignment with the task

records.content:
The task sets the trigger line high for 100 ms at every event: experiment start, trial start, cue onset (ANTICIPATION_START), placement onset, ISI onset, attack onset (OUTCOME_ANGLE) and the end of the feedback screen (OUTCOME_BLOCKED / OUTCOME_NOT_BLOCKED). All events give the same pulse, so the pulses carry no event code. Trial start and cue onset are 102 ms apart, and their two pulses can merge into one pulse of about 200 ms; a pulse longer than 150 ms is split into two onsets.

The expected event times on the task clock come from the result files: trial start (trial_start_timestamp) plus the onsets of the cue, placement, ISI and outcome relative to it, in ms. The offset between the task clock and the ECG clock is the mode of all differences between pulse onsets and expected events. The ECG clock runs about 23 ppm fast relative to the task computer (about 80 ms per hour), so the offset is estimated in each quarter of the session as a starting value. Each expected event is then matched to the nearest pulse (within 50 ms, then within 15 ms), and ECG time = a + b × task time is fitted by least squares. The windows below use the matched pulse onsets (the fitted time where no pulse was matched).

Attack onset: the outcome pulse + 100 ms. The pulse holds the task for 100 ms before the EyeLink message MOSQUITO_ANGLE; in the EyeLink data, MOSQUITO_ANGLE − OUTCOME_START = 101 ms.

Feedback onset: 2300 ms after the attack onset (end of the approach animation), as in the 

pupil preprocessing.

Blocks of the task are separated by the self-paced breaks, which are scheduled every 40 to 60 trials. The EyeLink message BREAK_END_TRIAL_<0-based trial index> marks them; it is sent after the break that follows that trial. For 13654, 15025 and 16093, who have no EyeLink file, a break is a gap of more than 60 s between two trials when the earlier trial was not followed by a state rating. 89 participants have four blocks, 3 have five, and 4 have one to three.

Step

Rule

1. Polarity

nk.ecg_invert (NeuroKit2) on 20 windows of 60 s spread over the recording; the signal is inverted when most windows are inverted

2. Filter

nk.ecg_clean, method neurokit: 0.5 Hz high-pass (Butterworth, 5th order) and 50 Hz notch

3. R peaks

nk.ecg_peaks, method neurokit

4. Beat quality

correlation of each beat (−200 to +300 ms around the peak) with the participant’s median beat; peaks with r < .50 are removed

5. Runs

the peak series is split where two retained peaks are more than 2.5 s apart (signal loss)

6. Correction

within each run of at least 10 beats, nk.signal_fixpeaks, method Kubios, iterative (Lipponen & Tarvainen, 2019): ectopic, missed, extra and long/short beats

7. Inter-beat intervals

intervals between consecutive corrected peaks of a run are valid when 300 to 2000 ms (30 to 200 bpm)

Instantaneous heart rate = 60,000 / inter-beat interval, assigned to the whole interval (step function at 1 ms resolution). The heart rate of a window is the time-weighted mean over the window (Velden & Wölk, 1987). Time not covered by a valid interval is missing.

Trial-locked heart rate (ecg_trials.csv, epochs in ecg_epochs.parquet). One heartbeat lasts about 850 ms, so the baselines are the 1 s before the event; the pupil uses 200 ms.

During the task the cursor position was recorded together with the button states and the task phase. The nets are placed by clicking on the slots of the circle, so the recording shows, for every net (token), the movement that led to it, the order in which the nets were placed, and where the cursor rested before the placement phase began. This chapter describes the extraction of these measures and their relation to the instruction condition, the questionnaire scores, the placement strategies and the parameters of the latent-state model.

Scripts (analysis repository): tambi_mouse_tracking.py (pipeline step mouse), tambi_mouse_questionnaire.py (step mouseq) and tambi_mouse_figures.py (step mousefigs; talk versions of the main figures in stats_results/13_11/mouse_tracking/figures/talk/). Input: raw_data/mouse_tracking/<pid>_session1_*_mouse_tracking_mousetrap.csv of all participants with a result file in results/ (95 participants: None 36, Partial 36, Full 23). Output: stats_results/13_11/mouse_tracking/.

The cursor is sampled every 33–50 ms. Positions are in task units; the slots lie on a circle of radius 8 around the centre. Each trial has an anticipation phase, a placement phase and an inter-stimulus interval. At the onset of the placement phase the cursor is reset to the centre, so the movement to the first token starts at the centre on every trial.

A token is a left-button press during the placement phase at a radius between 5 and 11; its location is the angle of the press. Token 1 starts at the onset of the placement phase, token j > 1 at the press of token j − 1.

count_trial of the mouse file equals trial_index of the result file. Per participant there are 171–188 trials and 1,076–1,228 tokens (median 1,161).

In 87 % of the trials (participant range 63–100 %) every slot that holds a net in the result file is within one slot of a press. The remaining trials contain nets that were placed on a neighbouring slot of the press (stacked nets).

Triangle: current state; orange: other state; violet: third direction. From left: token 1 straight to the current state; token 1 at the current state after a movement toward the other side; after an event, nets on both states; token 1 at the other state.

Trajectory of each token. The movement from the token’s start to its press is time-normalised to 101 points and compared with the direct path between start and press:

Measure

Definition

Maximum deviation

maximum absolute perpendicular deviation from the direct path (signed)

Area (curvature)

signed area between trajectory and direct path (shoelace area of the trajectory closed by the direct path); absolute version: absolute deviation integrated over the progress along the path

Direction changes

reversals of the movement along the direct path (steps below 0.1 units ignored), and the time of the first one

Initiation time

time until the cursor has moved 0.3 units

Response time

time from placement onset to the press of token 1

Latent states. Each colour cue has two target directions, its two latent states. On every trial, current is the target direction of the trial, other the other target direction of the cue, and third the direction 120° from both. Token 1 is classified as at the current state, the other state or the third direction (the nearest of the three within 45°), or elsewhere.

Pull toward the other state. When token 1 goes to the current state and the other state receives no token in the trial, the deviation of the token-1 trajectory toward the other state measures how strongly the unchosen alternative competes for the response (Freeman & Ambady, 2010): maximum deviation toward the other state (0 if none), and the signed area toward it.

Spatial entropy. Shannon entropy (bits) of the cursor’s angular position in 32 sectors of the circle, weighted by the time spent at each sample, separately for the anticipation phase and the placement phase. Samples within radius 3 of the centre are left out. 0 means the cursor stays in one sector, 5 that it spends equal time in all sectors. In the anticipation phase the cursor stays near the centre on 38 % of the trials, which then have no anticipation entropy.

Anticipation position. Angle and radius of the cursor at the end of the anticipation phase, before the reset.

Trial phases. Event trial: a transition (first trial of a new episode) or an oddball trial; the nets are placed before the displaced attack is shown. After event: the trial directly after an event trial. Stable: all other trials.

Events. For transitions and oddballs, the placements at t+1 and t+2 are analysed when they show the same cue as the event trial and no further event occurred in between; old is the circular mean of the participant’s own nets at the event trial, new the direction of the displaced attack. Events at which the participant’s own nets were already within 45° of the displaced attack are left out (1,857 event placements). Token 1 is classified as at old or new (the nearer within 45°) or elsewhere. When the anticipation position lies at old or new (within 45°), token 1 goes to the same location in 85 % (new) and 65 % (old) of the placements.

Reliability. The participant means of the trajectory and entropy measures are stable within the session: the split-half reliability (odd vs even trials, Spearman–Brown corrected) is .89 to .99 for token 1 at the current and at the other state, pull, curvature, direction changes, response time and spatial entropy (

Figure 15, A; mouse_reliability.csv). The share of transitions with token 1 at the previous state rests on eight transitions per participant and has a reliability of .46 (95 % CI .23–.63), so single participants’ values of this measure are imprecise even though the group association with the scores is strong.

Pull toward the other state. 

Figure 13 shows the deviation of the movement to token 1 toward the unchosen other state for each participant, ordered by STICSA trait within the condition. Without instructions, the deviation of higher scorers is larger over the middle of the movement (+0.050 per SD, p = .005); with partial and full instructions, the deviation is larger in most participants regardless of the score, and the slopes are near zero (Partial −0.005, p = .89; Full −0.005, p = .83). The pattern is carried by many participants with a moderate pull rather than by a few extreme ones.

Token 1 after transitions. On the first trial of a new episode, token 1 goes to the previous state in a median of 75 % (None), 88 % (Partial) and 88 % (Full) of the eight transitions. One and two trials later, the share at the old location falls to about 30 % and 15 %, with large differences between participants (

Figure 14). Within the conditions, the upper third of STICSA trait starts from a higher share at t0 in None and Partial; from t+1 on, the thirds of the score do not differ systematically.

The attack window covers the 2.3 s animation. The mosquito approaches from the attack direction and either stops at the nets and flies back, or flies through to the centre. The result is therefore visible during the animation (see

State uncertainty couplings. Leaving out only the first trial of the session (83 trials with a baseline, 0.6 %) reduces the three couplings about as much as leaving out all post-pause trials. On the first trial the model’s state uncertainty is at its maximum: +3.4 SD of the within-participant deviation on average, where 1.2 % of the other trials exceed ±3 SD. The cue baseline is +1.9 z above the participant mean, after the rating screen and before any task experience. These trials contribute 42 % of the within-participant cross-product of baseline and state uncertainty. The pooled within-participant slope (in z per SD) is 0.091 with them and 0.057 without them.

Transition baseline. No transition trial follows a pause, so the regular trials, the reference of the contrast, contain all post-pause trials with their raised baselines. Leaving out the post-rating trials within the task or the post-break trials each reduces the contrast; leaving out both gives −0.10.

Score moderation of the update coupling. The post-rating trials within the task change it most (general factor −2.00° → −1.71°); the first trial and the post-break trials change it little. The pause covariates leave it unchanged, because they shift the level of these trials, not their slope. 1. ISI pupil and state uncertainty.

The larger ISI pupil with higher scores is present in None and Partial (general factor +0.079 and +0.101, both q = .050; 

Figure 14), not in Full (+0.037, q = .41); the conditions do not differ (pairwise q ≥ .69).

The ISI pupil does not follow the state uncertainty more strongly or more weakly with higher scores in any condition (moderation −0.002 to +0.004, all q ≥ .90).

The cue baseline follows the state uncertainty more strongly with higher scores in Partial than in Full (general factor: Partial +0.039, q = .062; Partial vs Full +0.066, q = .021; STICSA trait in Partial +0.042, q = .044; per participant, general factor r = +0.43, p = .013; 

Figure 15), but not in Full (−0.027, q = .18).

2. Couplings and fitted parameters (

Figure 16; q: family of the six parameters of one model).

The feedback response to surprise does not go with noise reactivity in the λ variant (r = −0.10, q = .43); in the adopted model r = −0.23 (p = .031, q = .062); within the conditions all q ≥ .55 (

Figure 17).

It goes with a higher cue sensitivity (adopted model r = +0.35, q = .003) and a lower placement noise (r = −0.37, q = .003).

The feedback response to the belief update goes with a lower noise reactivity (adopted model r = −0.27, q = .035) and a lower belief momentum (r = −0.28, q = .035; in None −0.46, q = .052).

The coupling of the update with the attack pupil does not relate to any parameter (all p ≥ .078).

3. Oddball attribution.

The feedback pupil is larger when the model attributes the attack to an oddball, most strongly in Full (+0.104 z per SD, q < .001; None +0.045, q = .021; Partial +0.033, q = .057; Partial vs Full −0.071, q = .079).

This tracking does not change with the general factor in any condition (Full +0.050, q = .12; Partial +0.013, q = .52; 

Figure 18).

The ISI pupil on the next trial does not follow the oddball attribution more strongly with higher scores in any condition (all q ≥ .33).

4. Noise vs change on the next trial.

The separation of transitions from oddballs at t+1 does not change with the scores in any condition, in the attack window or in the ISI (all q ≥ .75; 

Figure 19).

In Partial, the attack pupil at t+1 tends to be smaller with higher scores at both event types (general factor −0.082, p = .093; STICSA trait −0.083, p = .091; q ≥ .27).

5. Arousal over the episode and the session.

The cue baseline declines over the session in all conditions (−0.51 to −0.68 z per 100 trials, all q < .001), with no score moderation (all q ≥ .28).

Over the trials of an episode, the baseline declines more steeply with higher STICSA trait in Partial (−0.077 per 10 trials per SD, q = .010; Partial vs Full −0.086, q = .031; Partial vs None −0.087, q = .031), but not in None or Full (+0.010 and +0.009). For the general factor the same direction does not pass the correction (Partial −0.055, q = .13).

With higher scores in Partial, the baseline is higher in the middle of an episode (general factor +0.082 at trial 10, p = .031, q = .093), more so in its first trials, and comes close to that of lower scorers toward its end (

Figure 20). Per participant, the slope over the episode correlates with STICSA trait at r = −0.52 in Partial (p = .002; 

Figure 21).

The same holds for the feedback response to oddball attribution (r = −0.33, q = .007; Partial −0.52, q = .006) and to the belief update (r = −0.37, q = .002) (

Figure 22).

The mean ISI pupil does not relate to stable-trial accuracy (r = +0.07, q = .81; 

Figure 22).

The feedback response to surprise is larger with higher scores (general factor r = +0.36, p < .001; STICSA trait +0.38, p < .001), in None and Partial (STICSA trait +0.44 and +0.45, p = .011 and .009) and less so in Full (+0.23, p = .35).

In Full, the feedback response to the belief update is larger with a higher general factor (r = +0.48, p = .039), and the coupling of the update with the attack pupil is more negative (r = −0.56, p = .012; n = 19).

Relation to the working reading of the behaviour

records.content:
The working reading of the behaviour has two parts:

Higher scores go with relying more on internal structural representations to interpret new evidence, and with attributing surprising outcomes to noise until they are confirmed. This would help under structural ambiguity (Partial Instructions).

With explicit structure (Full Instructions), higher scorers may build larger hypothesis spaces, try to track all rules and reduce irreducible uncertainty, and end up more uncertain and slower.

The behavioural signs are higher noise reactivity in the λ variant of the model, splitting at t+2, and less following of transitions at t+1. Against this reading, the pupil results are:

Pupil response to surprising outcomes. In the attack window, the coupling with surprise is near 0 and does not change with the general factor or any scale. In the feedback window, the coupling with surprise and with the belief update is larger with a higher general factor (q < .001 and q = .021) and with higher STICSA scores. For the general factor this is clearest in Full Instructions (feedback ~ surprise +0.060, q = .018), but the conditions do not differ; for STICSA trait it is present in all three conditions. A smaller response to surprise with higher scores is not seen in either window.

Pupil–update coupling. With a higher general factor, the update toward the attack goes less with the attack pupil (−1.64° per SD, q = .027; IU, OCI and STICSA trait in the same direction, q ≤ .043). With lower scores a larger attack pupil goes with a slightly larger update; with higher scores, with a smaller one. This is in the direction of discounting outcomes that evoke a larger response. Part of this moderation is carried by the trials after a rating screen (see 

Trials after a pause).

Updating after a bite that is pure noise. With a net on the attack slot, a bite is a random outcome. After such a bite the next placement moves toward the attack in None (+3.6°) and Partial (+5.8°, q = .057), but not in Full (−0.2°; Full vs None + Partial −5.0°, p = .15). This pattern fits a reading in which explicit instructions let participants attribute the bite to the stochastic barrier rule (aleatoric uncertainty), while without them the bite is treated as possibly informative about the attack direction (epistemic uncertainty); the condition difference does not pass the tests here. With higher IU scores the shift after an unlucky bite is smaller (−3.4° per SD, p = .031, q = .062). The general factor does not change the shift (−0.9°, p = .52), in no condition.

Within the conditions (

Pupil, model and scores within the conditions).

Partial: higher scores go with a cue baseline that follows the model’s state uncertainty more closely than in Full, and (STICSA trait) with a baseline that declines more steeply over the trials of an episode. Across participants, a larger feedback response to surprise goes with higher stable-trial accuracy, most clearly in Partial. This pattern is in the direction of the first part of the reading (structure used where it has to be inferred).

Full: higher scores go with a larger feedback response to surprise and to the belief update (general factor), with no decline of the baseline over the episode; the oddball tracking of the feedback pupil does not change with the scores. This is weakly in the direction of the second part; the feedback moderation is not specific to Full.

Not seen: the ISI pupil does not follow the state uncertainty more strongly with higher scores in Full. The signature “surprise registered but attributed to noise” is not seen either: a larger feedback response to surprise goes with lower noise reactivity in the adopted model (r = −0.23, q = .062), not with a higher one.

Before the outcome. The ISI pupil, the last window before the attack is known, is larger with a higher general factor (+0.073 z per SD, q = .015), STICSA state and OCI, in None and Partial.

The EyeLink recorded the pupil size of one eye at 1000 Hz together with the gaze (

Eye-Tracking Preprocessing). This chapter describes the cleaning of the pupil signal, its normalisation, the event-locked epochs and the data quality.

Script (analysis repository): tambi_pupil_preprocessing.py (pipeline step pupil, after eyequal; reproducing step 8.9). Input: the 50 Hz gaze and pupil stream stats_results/eye_tracking/converted/<pid>/samples.parquet, the trial, phase, drift and geometry tables of tambi_eye_quality.py, and the result files. Output: stats_results/pupil/. Settings: pupil_settings.json.

The steps are applied to each recording block (trial) of each participant:

Step

Rule

1. Missing

bins with any invalid 1000 Hz sample (blink or tracking loss)

2. Margin

bins within 100 ms before and 160 ms after a missing bin are removed; the pupil signal is distorted while the lid closes and opens

3. Dilation speed

speed = larger of the absolute changes to the previous and the next bin, per 20 ms; bins above the participant median + 10 × MAD are removed (Kret & Sjak-Shie, 2019)

4. Interpolation

gaps up to 500 ms within a trial are interpolated linearly; longer gaps and gaps at the start or end of a trial stay missing

5. Smoothing

4 Hz low-pass filter (Butterworth, third order, zero phase) on stretches of at least 500 ms without missing bins

pupil_z: the cleaned pupil size z-scored over all trial bins of the participant. The epochs and the trial measures use this scale.

pupil_rel: the cleaned pupil size divided by the participant median.

A video eye tracker measures a smaller pupil when the eye rotates away from the camera (pupil foreshortening). Per participant, pupil_z is regressed on the drift-corrected gaze position (x, y, x², y², xy; bins that are not interpolated). The gaze position explains a median R² of .048 of the variance of pupil_z (.005–.233;

The outcome phase starts with a 2.3 s attack animation (mosquito_outcome_phase of conrad_fixed.py): the mosquito approaches from the attack direction toward the circle with the nets. A blocked mosquito reaches the nets 0.71 s after the animation starts and flies back; a mosquito that gets through flies at constant speed, crosses the nets at 1.59 s and reaches the centre. The result is therefore visible during the animation, and BLOCKED! or BITE! is shown with a sound 2.3 s after the animation starts. In the data, fixations reach the attack direction 250–500 ms after OUTCOME_START and return to the centre about 2 s later. The outcome message (OUTCOME_BLOCKED, OUTCOME_NOT_BLOCKED) is sent when the feedback screen ends, 6.3 s after MOSQUITO_ANGLE; it is not used as an event. Trials without an attack have no attack or feedback event. The epochs (pupil_epochs.parquet, one row per participant × trial × event, columns t_<ms>) hold pupil_z in 20 ms steps; bins outside the trial’s recording are missing. The baseline of each epoch is the mean of −200 to 0 ms (column baseline), and baseline correction is subtractive.

A trial is usable for pupil analyses when at most 25 % of the bins from the cue onset to the end of the ISI are missing after interpolation and the cue baseline is present. Of 16,008 trials, 13,602 are usable (85 %). The cue baseline lies in the first 200 ms of the recording and is missing in 10.8 % of the trials; 6.9 % of the trials have more than 25 % missing bins. Per participant the median share of usable trials is 89 % (28–100 %); below 50 % are 16381 (28 %), 15289 (43 %), 15265 (48 %, excluded) and 13855 (49 %). This section checks how the questionnaires were answered, using the item-level LimeSurvey export rather than the scored totals. It covers the answers to the questions on the time window of each section, the agreement of the STICSA trait and state items, the interval between the questionnaire and the lab session, completion times, attention checks, uniform answers across a scale, the answer format of the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II), the reverse-keyed items of the Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (SIAS), internal consistency, and the distributions and correlations of the totals. All numbers refer to the 85 participants with behavioural and questionnaire data of run 13_11 (None, 31; Partial, 33; Full, 21). Script tambi_questionnaire_quality.py (pipeline step qquality), outputs in stats_results/13_11/questionnaire_quality/ (report questionnaire_quality_report.txt, participant-level flags in quality_flags_participant.csv).

Before six of the sections, participants were asked to which time window the following questions refer, with the options “Genau jetzt, in diesem Moment”, “In der letzten Woche”, “Im letzten Monat”, “Im letzten Jahr” and “Seit der Geburt”. For the State-Trait Inventory for Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA), the trait items ask how the participant feels in general and the state items how the participant feels right now; the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI) and the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) refer to the last month; the BDI-II refers to the last two weeks including the day of completion; the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IU) has no time window and describes the person in general. Because the options contain neither “in general” nor “two weeks”, the answers counted as matching are “Seit der Geburt” for the STICSA trait and IU sections, “In der letzten Woche” for the BDI-II, and the literal time window for the other sections.

Twenty participants matched all six sections, 16 missed one, 18 two, 18 three and 13 four or five. The number of non-matching answers differed between conditions (Kruskal–Wallis H = 7.01, p = .030; matching answers for the STICSA trait section, None .52, Partial .33, Full .48) and increased with the OCI score (Spearman ρ = .33, p = .002), but not significantly with any other total (all p ≥ .085).

The non-matching answers to the STICSA trait question are not only a matter of the missing “in general” option. Of the 34 participants who answered “Genau jetzt” before the trait section, 31 gave the same answer before the state section, and their trait items were more similar to their state items. The difference between the trait and the state total was 0.4 points in this group and 3.9 points in the group answering “Seit der Geburt”, and at the same state score it was 3.4 points smaller (linear regression with the state total, HC3, p = .014). The share of the 21 items answered identically on both scales was 0.79 against 0.66 (Mann–Whitney p = .003; with both totals as covariates, +0.08, p = .063). Internal consistency of the trait scale was similar in both groups (Cronbach’s α .85 and .89).

As a check of the consequences for the behavioural results, the participant-level associations of the STICSA scales with the selectivity at t+1 and with the share of transitions followed at t+1 (see 

Responses to Events and Placement Duration) were estimated separately for the participants answering “Seit der Geburt” before the trait section and for the others (linear regressions with condition, HC3, standardized). For the STICSA trait total and the selectivity at t+1, the association was −0.22 SD per SD (p = .012) in all participants, −0.05 (p = .67, n = 37) in the matching group and −0.36 (p = .010, n = 48) in the others (interaction p = .089). The STICSA state total showed the same pattern (−0.09, n = 36, and −0.33, n = 48; interaction p = .33), as did the share of transitions followed. The difference between the groups is therefore not specific to the trait scale and cannot be attributed to the misreading of the trait instruction; it may reflect other differences between the participants who chose the two answers, or chance, given the subgroup sizes.

Interval between questionnaire and lab session

records.content: The questionnaires were completed online before the lab session, a median of 6.9 days earlier (quartiles 3.9 and 10.8 days, range 0 to 41.5 days); 13 participants completed them more than 14 days before the session and one shortly after it. The interval was not associated with any questionnaire total (all |ρ| ≤ .14) or with condition (Kruskal–Wallis p = .63).

hierarchy.lvl2: Completion times, attention checks and uniform answers
Completion times, attention checks and uniform answers

records.content: The median completion time was 24 minutes (10 to 103). No participant took less than 1 s per item in any section; four participants took less than 2 s per item in one section. Six participants failed one of the seven attention checks (IU, ACE, EAT-26 and SIAS one each, ERS two), and none failed more than one; their other indices (completion time, answers to the time-window questions, uniform answers) were unremarkable. The ac_* columns of the scoring are FALSE also for unanswered checks, as in the incomplete response of 15265, which did not fail any answered check. Identical answers to all items of a scale occurred only as “not at all” on the symptom scales (STICSA trait 2, STICSA state 3, OCI 1, PCL-5 3) and as “no” on all items of the Adverse Childhood Experiences questionnaire (ACE; 33 participants), which correspond to low symptom levels and to the absence of adverse experiences rather than to inattentive answering; no participant answered the SIAS, the Eating Attitudes Test (EAT-26), the IU or the Emotion Reactivity Scale (ERS) uniformly.

The BDI-II items were presented with one checkbox per statement, so that several statements of an item could be ticked. Thirteen participants ticked more than one statement on at least one item (22 items in total). Until 14 November 2026, the scoring script took the first ticked statement, which is the lowest value, whereas the BDI-II instruction is to choose the highest statement when several apply. The scoring now takes the highest ticked statement (questionnaire_scoring_pipeline.R, score_bdi_item_4 and score_bdi_item_7; backup questionnaire_scoring_pipeline.R.bak_2026-11-14). This raises the totals of these 13 participants by 1 to 7 points, the number of participants with a total of at least 14 from 20 to 22 (at least 20, 11 in both scorings), and the two scorings correlate with ρ = .985. For one participant, the previous scoring gave 0 on item 9 (suicidal thoughts) although a higher statement was also ticked; the participant is identified in quality_flags_participant.csv (columns bdi_item09_lowest and bdi_item09_highest) for the procedure of the lab. The text of the second statement of item 17 (irritability) repeats the first (“Ich bin reizbarer als sonst”) instead of “viel reizbarer”, so that the two cannot be distinguished by the participants.

All totals and subscale scores of the R scoring (questionnaire_scoring_pipeline.R) were recomputed independently from the item-level export in Python for all 172 responses, with the item assignments and keys of the published scales (STICSA somatic and cognitive items after Ree et al., 2008; reverse keying of SIAS items 5, 9 and 11 and of the EAT-26 item on trying new rich foods). All totals and subscale scores agreed exactly, apart from the BDI-II totals of the participants with several ticked statements before the fix described above. All answer labels in the export were covered by the recoding of the scoring. The subscale assignment of the IU (prospective and inhibitory) follows the IUS-12 and is not a published assignment for the German IU-18.

Internal consistency was high for all symptom scales (Cronbach’s α: STICSA trait .88, STICSA state .87, BDI-II .91, OCI .83, PCL-5 .94, IU .89, SIAS .91, EAT-26 .88, ERS .94) and low for the ACE checklist (.50), which counts different kinds of events rather than indicators of one construct. In the SIAS, the three reverse-keyed items had lower item-rest correlations (.31, .25 and .48) than the other items (.31 to .75).

The totals cover a broad range of symptom levels. Of the 85 participants, 22 (26 %) had a BDI-II total of at least 14, 11 of at least 20 and 3 of at least 29; 10 had a PCL-5 total of at least 33 and 13 met the DSM-5 symptom criteria of the PCL-5; 23 had a SIAS total of at least 34 and 11 of at least 43; 5 were at or above the EAT-26 cut-off of 20; and 5 reported four or more adverse childhood experiences. Thirty-five participants had an OCI-12 total of at least 11, the cut-off of the OCI-12 validation (Abramovitch et al., 2021). The distributions of the BDI-II (skewness 1.24), PCL-5 (1.39), EAT-26 (1.80) and STICSA state (1.12) were right-skewed, and the IU total was symmetric (0.01). The totals of the anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive and posttraumatic scales correlated between .55 and .74 (Spearman), whereas the IU correlated more strongly with the OCI (.61) and the ERS (.56) than with the STICSA state total (.41).

In the pipeline these are the steps rq3table, rq3, figs_rq3 and results of tools/run_pipeline.ps1. They replace symptom_parameter_models_v4.py and symptom_parameter_models_v3.py (archived in old_scripts/archived_2026-10-12/).

Parameters. The six parameters of the adopted model (

Model Selection and Validation): precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum, switch probability, cue sensitivity and placement noise. The outcome of each model is the participant’s posterior mean, standardised within the analysed sample. Slopes are therefore in parameter SDs per questionnaire SD, which makes them comparable across parameters; the means and SDs of the standardisation are reported, so that every slope can be expressed in the units of the parameter.

Questionnaires. STICSA state, STICSA trait, IU, BDI and OCI totals, each z-scored within the analysed sample. Each questionnaire enters its own model, as in RQ2; the questionnaires are not adjusted for each other.

Instruction condition. Unordered factor with the two planned sum-to-zero contrasts C3_vs_C1C2 = (−1/3, −1/3, 2/3) and C2_vs_C1 = (−1/2, 1/2, 0). With this coding the questionnaire term is the slope averaged over the three conditions, and its interactions with the two contrasts describe how the slope depends on the condition.

For each parameter, questionnaire and sample, two linear models are fitted with one row per participant:y_{z} = \beta_0 + \boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{cond}}^\top \mathbf{c} + \beta_q\, q_z + \boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{cond} \times q}^\top \mathbf{c}\, q_z + \varepsilon \qquad \text{(condition × questionnaire model)}y_{z} = \beta_0 + \boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{cond}}^\top \mathbf{c} + \beta_q\, q_z + \varepsilon \qquad \text{(across-condition model)}

where \mathbf{c} holds the two contrast codes. In the first model, \beta_q is the unweighted mean of the three condition-specific slopes. In the second, the slope is pooled over participants, so that each condition contributes in proportion to its size.

Tested terms. Three terms are tested for each parameter and questionnaire: q_z in the across-condition model (1 numerator df), and q_z (1 df) and cond:q_z (2 df) in the condition × questionnaire model. Each term is tested with an F-test against the model without it, which with the sum-to-zero coding is the Type III test. The slopes within each condition, in the two condition groups (None and Partial together, Full) and the two planned contrasts between conditions are estimated with emmeans::emtrends and reported unadjusted.

Multiple testing. For each of the three terms, the Benjamini-Hochberg correction is applied across the five questionnaires, separately for each parameter and sample (18 sets of five tests per sample). This mirrors the RQ2 models, in which the correction runs across the questionnaires within each model and term.

Distribution of the parameters and residuals. The posterior means of cue sensitivity and placement noise are bimodal within None and Partial and concentrated near the upper prior bound in part of the sample (cue sensitivity in Full, where the instructions state the cue offset of 70°, which the model represents as a value of 1; placement noise for participants with the most variable placements, whose estimates reach the bound of 50°), and precision weighting, belief momentum and the switch probability are right-skewed. tambi_rq3_parameter_table.py writes these distributions to parameter_descriptives.csv (quartiles, skewness and the number of estimates and posterior intervals at each prior bound, by sample and condition), and fig_rq3_0_parameter_distributions shows them. As a consequence, the residuals are not normal in most models. The three tested terms are therefore also tested with Wald F-tests based on a heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance matrix (HC3; 

MacKinnon & White, 1985). The Shapiro-Wilk test of the residuals and the largest Cook’s distance are reported for every condition × questionnaire model.

Uncertainty of the estimates. The posterior mean treats each participant’s parameter as known. To carry the uncertainty of the estimates into the group-level analysis, both models are refitted on each of 100 posterior draws per participant, standardised with the mean and SD of the posterior means, and the coefficients are pooled with Rubin’s rules (

Rubin, 1987), with the degrees of freedom of 

Barnard & Rubin (1999). This treats the posterior draws as plausible values. The fraction of missing information shows how much of the variance of a pooled coefficient is due to the uncertainty of the participants’ estimates.

Both models are fitted in two samples:

Hand-written section

This section is written by hand from the outputs of tambi_post_task_analyses.py (pipeline step posttask, run 13_11, 86 participants; all files in stats_results/13_11/task_questions/). It is included into the generated chapter and has to be updated by hand after a new run. All analyses are at the participant level.

Methods. Condition differences in the yes/no answers were tested with χ² tests over the three conditions and with Fisher’s exact test of C3 against C1 and C2. The aversiveness ratings of the two halves, their mean and their change (second minus first half) were modelled with linear models with the two planned contrasts (C3 versus C1 and C2, C2 versus C1) and heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors; the change was also tested against zero (Wilcoxon). Each of the ten questionnaire totals (z-scored) was related to the answers in models adjusted for condition (logistic regression for “rules noticed”, linear models with HC3 for the ratings), and in a second model with the interaction of the questionnaire with the two contrasts; p-values were corrected with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure across the five core questionnaires (STICSA state, STICSA trait, IU, BDI-II, OCI) and, separately, across the five further questionnaires, for each outcome and term (q). Because only 8 participants found the instructions unclear, this answer was compared between groups with Mann–Whitney tests. “Rules noticed” was related to behavioural measures and parameters (difference between participants who answered yes and no, in SD of the measure, adjusted for condition; BH across the 13 measures).

The share of participants who reported noticing rules (C1, 16 of 31; C2, 24 of 33; C3, 12 of 22; χ² p = .18), who found the instructions clear (27, 30 and 21; p = .59) and who had consumed caffeine on the day of the session (16, 13 and 11; p = .58) did not differ between conditions. The aversiveness of the task did not differ between conditions (median of both halves 52, 51 and 49; C3 versus C1 and C2, p = .84; C2 versus C1, p = .80), and it did not change from the first to the second half, overall (median change 0.0; 39 participants rated the second half as more aversive, 41 as less aversive, 6 as equal; Wilcoxon p = .65) or in any condition (all p ≥ .39).

Only 12 of the 22 participants in C3, who had been told the rules, answered that they had noticed rules. These participants probably read the question as asking whether they had discovered rules themselves. In C3, the answer therefore does not measure the same as in C1 and C2.

No questionnaire was associated with the report of noticed rules (all q ≥ .39), with the clarity of the instructions (all p ≥ .10) or, across conditions, with the mean or the change of the aversiveness (all q ≥ .44).

The association of the questionnaires with the change of the aversiveness depended on condition (interaction of the questionnaire with the contrast C3 versus C1 and C2) for IU (q = .006), STICSA state anxiety (q = .017) and OCI (q = .037), and among the further questionnaires for PCL-5 (q = .006) and ERS (q = .047). In C3, higher scores were associated with a more aversive first half and a stronger decrease of the aversiveness in the second half (change per SD of the questionnaire: IU −20.4 points, p < .001; PCL-5 −26.7, p < .001; STICSA state −17.9, p = .001; first half: IU +14.5, p < .001; PCL-5 +12.0, p = .011), whereas the slopes in C1 and C2 were between −5 and +10 points (post_task_aversiveness_slopes_by_condition.csv). A change score depends in part on its starting value, so that part of this association can reflect regression to the mean; the association with the first half alone was significant for IU and PCL-5. The estimates in C3 rest on 21 participants.

hierarchy.lvl3: Rules noticed, behaviour and model parameters
Rules noticed, behaviour and model parameters

records.content: Participants who reported noticing rules differed from those who did not on several measures (adjusted for condition, in SD of the measure): lower error relative to the hidden-state target on regular trials (−0.86, q < .001; medians in C1 39° versus 61°, in C2 43° versus 54°), a higher proportion of intercepted attacks (+0.98, q < .001), a greater additional weight on state error (+0.51, q = .001), higher cue sensitivity (+0.66, q = .004; median in C1 0.85 versus 0.16), lower placement noise (−0.61, q = .001), a smaller shift of the placement centre after oddballs (−0.65, q = .004) and larger |I_e| (+0.59, q = .015). Precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum and the switch probability did not differ (all q ≥ .079). In C1 and C2, the report thus agrees with the behaviour and with the parameters that describe the use of the colour cue and the selectivity for state error (post_task_rule_noticed_behaviour.csv).

hierarchy.lvl3: Cross-cue transfer and the learned cue offset
Cross-cue transfer and the learned cue offset

records.content:
The larger |I_e| of participants who noticed rules led to a closer look at the measure. |I_e| is the angular deviation of the first placement for the second colour cue after an episode transition from the placement that full transfer of the transition would predict, that is, from the previous placement for this cue rotated by 120° (0° = full transfer; random placement gives 90° on average). 

Figure 4 shows where these placements went, classified by structural_signatures.py (nearest of four candidate directions within 25°, otherwise “elsewhere”).



Figure 4:Cross-cue transfer by strategy. (a) Placement of the first trial of the second colour cue after each episode transition: full transfer (the new direction of this cue), no transfer (the previous direction of this cue), the new or previous direction of the other cue, or elsewhere (none of these within 25°). C1 and C2 are split by the learned cue offset (cue sensitivity above or below 0.5). (b) Mean |I_e| per participant; bars, medians; dashed line, 90°.

In C1 and C2, the participants who had not learned the cue offset (cue sensitivity ≤ 0.5; 22 participants) placed the nets for the second cue most often at the new direction of the first cue (43 % of transitions), which they treat as the same direction. These placements give |I_e| of about 51°, because the direction of the first cue lies 70° from the full-transfer direction of the second cue, and the mean |I_e| of this group (80°) is therefore below 90° without any cue-specific transfer. The participants who had learned the cue offset (42 participants) kept the second cue most often at its previous direction (44 %, |I_e| about 121°), which gives a mean |I_e| above 90° (104°). In C3, 37 % of the placements showed full transfer (mean |I_e| 75°). Of the C1 and C2 participants who reported noticing rules, 32 of 42 had learned the cue offset, against 8 of 22 of those who did not report it. Across participants, |I_e| increased with cue sensitivity (37° per unit, adjusted for condition, p < .001).

In C1 and C2, |I_e| therefore mixes two strategies, treating both cues as one direction and treating them as two independent directions, and values around 90° do not indicate random placement. The difference between C3 and the other conditions (section 2.1.4 of the results chapter) is carried by the share of full transfer (C1, 7 %; C2, 11 %; C3, 36 % of transitions per participant on average). For the questionnaire associations of |I_e| (Model D), the association with OCI arose from a higher share of placements at the previous direction of the second cue (+0.066 per SD, p = .008) and a lower share at the new direction of the first cue (−0.057, p = .012), not from a lower share of full transfer (p = .19); adjusted for cue sensitivity, it was weaker (from 6.8° to 5.0° per SD, p = .073). For STICSA trait anxiety, the share of full transfer was lower (−0.042 per SD, p = .043), and the association with |I_e| remained after the adjustment (4.3° per SD, p = .040) (transfer_questionnaire_check.csv).

The answers of all participants, one row per participant, are written to stats_results/23_11/task_questions/task_questions.csv.

The Adverse Childhood Experiences questionnaire (ACE) is not part of the core questions of this study. It was included to give a first, broad view of which aspects of structural inference could be worth focusing on in planned studies of structural inference after childhood adversity. The ACE is a coarse instrument (ten yes/no items on abuse, neglect and household dysfunction before age 18) compared with the MACE or the CTQ, which record type, timing and severity.

This chapter runs the questionnaire-dependent analyses of the study with the ACE total score as the only score. All numbers refer to run 23_11 (96 participants, 95 with ACE scores; pupil data for 84 of them, gaze data for 86). Slopes are per SD of the ACE score. Because the ACE correlates with current symptoms (section 1), every participant-level effect is also reported with the general questionnaire factor (gf_item_sl_g_oos_total, chapter 

A General Questionnaire Factor) and its interaction with condition as covariates.

Analyses.

Trial-level models with ACE total: the R model scripts with TAMBI_QSET=factor and TAMBI_QCOL=ace_total (RQ2 models A–D, RQ3 models of the Nexus parameters, of the action-rule variant lam and of the two alternative models, use of the task structure, replayed uncertainty, entropy decomposition, colour-cue learning, relative fit, in-task affect) and tambi_hybrid7_factor.py --score ace_total for the hybrid switch model.

Participant-level models (tambi_ace_effects.py): 64 measures from all modules (behaviour, Nexus parameters, alternative and hybrid models, relative fit, pupil, gaze, mouse tracking, affect and task questions), each regressed on ACE: y ~ ACE_z × (c3 + c21) for the slopes within None, Partial and Full and their differences, and y ~ ACE_z + c3 + c21 across conditions; OLS with HC3 standard errors, outcome in SD units. Adjusted models add the general factor (z) and its interaction with the condition contrasts. Benjamini–Hochberg q within module × score × adjustment. Scores: ACE total (main), ACE abuse and neglect, ACE household dysfunction.

Pipeline steps acerq2 to acefigs of tools/run_pipeline.ps1. Outputs: stats_results/23_11/questionnaire_factor/ace_total/ (one folder per analysis; participant-level results in ace_effects/ace_slopes.csv, participant table in ace_effects/ace_participant.csv). Figures: tambi_ace_figures.py.

RQ2 models (trial level). Placement error (A1): ACE slope p = .105, across conditions p = .17; interception (A2): p = .64. Transition-versus-oddball response (B1, error; event × trial × ACE): across conditions p = .084, condition dependence p = .13; net entropy (B2): event × trial × ACE p = .091 (cluster-robust CR2 p = .041), across conditions p = .11. Weighting of state error (C): the additional weight on state error increases with ACE (se × ACE F = 6.18, p = .013; slope per SD 0.082 in None, 0.059 in Partial, 0.100 in Full; condition dependence p = .31); with cluster-robust standard errors p = .26, and in the sensitivity model with random slopes p = .11. Transfer to the second cue (D): |I_e| increases by 5.1° per SD across conditions (p = .071; CR2 p = .053).

Placement strategies. The share of split placements at t+2 after transitions increases with ACE (0.27 SD per SD, p = .008, q = .10; Spearman on the condition residuals ρ = .21, p = .043), with similar slopes in the three conditions (None 0.24, Partial 0.38, Full 0.18; all differences p > .50). The slope is unchanged with the general factor (0.29, p = .010). The entropy decomposition of the nets after events gives the same direction: the probability that the nets are split over two clusters increases with ACE at t+1 after oddballs (0.59 log-odds per SD, p = .035) and at t+2 after oddballs (0.56, p = .048) and after transitions (0.57, p = .053). Both ACE subscales show the split-placement slope (abuse and neglect 0.27, p = .010; household dysfunction 0.17, p = .090).

Use of the task structure. Among the structure models, one term relates to ACE: in the model of following the new position at t+1 (S5), the change from the first to the second half of the session in the transition-minus-oddball difference depends on ACE (event × half × ACE −0.83 log-odds per SD, SE 0.24, p < .001). The other structure terms (oddball type, alternative directions, temporal structure, commitment, correctness at t+2) have p > .10. Shifts after transitions and oddballs, switching and following at t+1, net entropy, the stable-trial distance, replayed uncertainty and placement duration, the change of the stable-trial distance over the session and the cue transfer gap do not relate to ACE (participant level, all p > .10). The colour-cue learning measures do not relate to ACE (all p > .09).

Nexus. The switch probability h_switch increases with ACE (

Figure 3, 

Figure 4): RQ3 model with plausible values 0.33 SD per SD (SE 0.11, p = .004; F = 9.23, q = .003), in the latent-state sample F = 8.62, p = .004. Within conditions (participant level) 0.29 in None (p = .037), 0.25 in Partial (p = .27) and 0.46 in Full (p = .003); the conditions do not differ (all p > .40). With the general factor the slope is 0.37 (p < .001, q = .002); Spearman on the condition residuals ρ = .22 (p = .029). The slope is carried mainly by abuse and neglect (0.29, p = .004) and less by household dysfunction (0.20, p = .084). The action-rule variant lam gives the same result for h_switch (0.36, p = .001; Full 0.68, p = .004) and a positive noise-reactivity slope in Full (0.49, p = .047). The other five Nexus parameters do not relate to ACE (all p > .10).



Figure 3:RQ3 models of the Nexus parameters with ACE total (plausible values, all participants): slope per condition and across conditions (parameter SD per SD of ACE, 95 % CI). Filled: p < .05.

Alternative models. No parameter of the change-point observer or of the n-state model relates to ACE (RQ3 models: all p > .08; smallest p for the n-state precision weighting, F = 3.04, p = .085).

Hybrid switch model (hybrid7f). Noise sensitivity v, the probability of four states and the reliance on the structure w do not relate to ACE (across conditions all p > .44; within conditions all p > .30).

Relative fit. The advantage of the n-state model over simple tracking increases with ACE across conditions (0.21 SD per SD, p = .044; HC3 p = .081); the advantage of Nexus over simple tracking and over the change-point observer increases with ACE in Full (0.57, p = .030 and 0.56, p = .032) but not in None and Partial.

The participant slopes of the feedback pupil on model surprise (controlled for the model-free prediction error) increase with ACE for all three models, most clearly for the n-state model: 0.35 SD per SD (p = .003, q = .028; ρ = .28, p = .010), 0.32 with the general factor (p = .008). For Nexus (0.27, p = .083) and the change-point observer (0.25, p = .043) the slopes are carried by None (0.55, p = .069 and 0.49, p = .004) and are halved by the general factor (0.13, p = .24 and 0.13, p = .22). The n-state slope is carried by household dysfunction (0.34, p = .001) more than by abuse and neglect (0.20, p = .22). The coupling of the feedback pupil with the Nexus belief update, the baseline pupil, the coupling of the baseline pupil and of the pupil before the outcome with replayed uncertainty, and the pupil difference between bites and blocked attacks do not relate to ACE (all p > .25).



Figure 4:Measures with an across-condition ACE effect. Top: participants by condition (colours as in 

Figure 1) with the least-squares line per condition; ACE values jittered horizontally. (a) Nexus switch probability (posterior mean). (b) Share of split placements at t+2 after transitions. (c) Participant slope of the feedback pupil on the surprise of the n-state model, controlled for the model-free prediction error. Bottom (d–f): slope per condition and across conditions (SD of the measure per SD of ACE, 95 % CI), without (circles) and with the general factor (squares). Filled: p < .05.

Gaze: location entropy, the share at the third location and the share beyond the task locations in the prediction and anticipation windows do not relate to ACE (across conditions all p > .11; with the general factor all p > .09). Mouse tracking: placement entropy, curvature, direction changes of the first movement, the number of nets and the time to the first net do not relate to ACE (all p > .15).

The trial-level models of the six in-task ratings have no ACE term with p < .10. At the participant level, mean in-task anxiety, stress, valence, arousal and fatigue do not relate to ACE (all p > .18); with the general factor, stress is lower with higher ACE (−0.21 SD per SD, p = .050). Participants with higher ACE rate the instructions as clearer (0.19, p = .022; mostly in Partial, 0.39, p = .069). The change of aversiveness over the session and noticing the rule do not relate to ACE.

ACE total relates to three aspects of structural inference, each robust to the general factor: a higher switch probability in the Nexus model (in all conditions), more split placements after transitions (nets on both the old and the new direction), and a stronger coupling of the feedback pupil with the surprise of the n-state model. The ACE does not relate to accuracy, to the other model parameters, to the hybrid model, to gaze and cursor measures or to in-task affect. For a study of structural inference after childhood adversity, these results point to the belief about how often the hidden state changes and to the hedging between states after a change as candidate targets, with the abuse and neglect items carrying the switch-probability effect.

This chapter shows the behaviour around transitions and oddballs descriptively, by instructions and by median splits of the questionnaire scores, together with the raw net placements of every participant. The figures are drawn by tambi_event_locked.py (pipeline step eventlocked). No model is fitted in this chapter: each curve is the mean across participants of the participant means at each trial relative to the event, with its standard error (shaded). The model-based tests of the same questions are in 

Results by Research Question and 

Results in Figures.

Open the interactive data explorer. In the explorer, every measure can be shown after transitions or oddballs, grouped by instructions or by a median split of any of the five questionnaires (within each instruction condition or across all participants), for all trials or the first and second half of the session, with two measures side by side. A second view shows the net placements of a single participant trial by trial.

Definitions.

Events. A transition is the first trial of a new episode (not the first episode of the session); an oddball is a trial with a displaced attack within an episode. The window runs from two trials before to four trials after the event trial (0). After the event, it ends at the next event; before it, trials that are events themselves are left out. 688 transitions and 1,356 oddballs of 86 participants.

Distance from target: absolute distance of the placement centre from the hidden-state target, in degrees. On the event trial of a transition, the target is already the new state’s direction, while the placement was made before the displaced attack was seen.

Shift from previous trial: distance between the placement centres of consecutive trials, in degrees, corrected for the offset between the two colour cues.

Net entropy: entropy of the distribution of the nets over the 32 directions, in bits.

Replayed state uncertainty: uncertainty of the fitted latent-state model about the current state before the placement, 1 − |2z − 1| (0 = certain, 1 = maximal), averaged over the posterior draws of the participant.

Placement duration: time from the start of the placement phase to its end, in seconds.

Median split: above the median of all participants with questionnaire data, or at or below it. Session halves: trials up to and after the participant’s median trial.

Instructions: None (no rules), Partial (rules mentioned), Full (structure explained).
