records.content:
The median-split figures above suggest that the questionnaire scores relate to the course of the error, the replayed state uncertainty and the placement duration differently in the three instruction conditions. These patterns are tested here with models (tambi_event_locked_scores.py, pipeline step elscores).

Model. For each measure, event type, score and lag (or window), a participant-level regression of the participant mean on the score (z) × condition (contrasts C3 vs C1+C2 and C2 vs C1), with HC3 standard errors. From it: the slope per SD within None, Partial and Full, and the three pairwise differences of the slopes; across conditions, the slope of the model with condition as a covariate. The windows are before the event (k = −2, −1), the event trial (k = 0), the first trial after it (t+1), the mean of t+2 to t+4 (late), and the recovery (late minus t+1). Scores: the general factor (one test per measure) and, alongside, the five questionnaires.



Figure 15:Distance from the target: slope per SD of the score within each condition, at each trial relative to the event (95 % CI; ring: p < .05, uncorrected). Top: transitions; bottom: oddballs.

Distance from the target after transitions: a condition-specific pattern in Partial. With the rules mentioned (Partial), higher scores go with a larger distance on the event trial and at t+1 and a smaller distance at t+2:

event trial (k = 0), whose placement was made before the transition was seen, so a larger distance means a placement closer to the old state: general factor +9.3° per SD (p = .006);

t+1: general factor +8.3° (p = .043), OCI +8.0° (p = .005), STICSA state +8.1° (p = .002);

the late window: STICSA trait −5.3° (p = .024), general factor −4.5° (p = .055).

The drop from t+1 to the late window is therefore larger with higher scores (recovery: STICSA trait −12.7° per SD, p = .008; STICSA state −12.1°, p < .001; OCI −11.6°, p = .003; general factor −12.9°, p = .014). In the profile the slope is largest at t+2 (STICSA trait −8.6° per SD, p = .009). At t+3 and t+4 it points the same way but is smaller and not significant (−4.0° and −3.5°, p ≥ .20). With the median split of STICSA trait in Partial, high scorers are closer to the target at t+2 (−17.3°, p = .024) and t+3 (−13.9°, p = .037), and at t+4 the difference is −7.0° (p = .43). They are also closer before the event (k = −1: −16.7°, p = .022). In None the slopes are close to zero at every lag. In Full the late distance is larger with higher scores (OCI +7.7°, p = .047), so the late slope and the recovery differ between Partial and Full (general factor, late: p = .012; recovery: p = .041; OCI, recovery: p = .008).

After oddballs in Partial the distance is smaller with higher STICSA trait before the event (k = −2: p = .037) and on the event trial (p = .028), so part of the Partial pattern is a general difference in accuracy rather than a response to the event.



Figure 16:Distance from the target: differences between the condition slopes by lag (STICSA trait and general factor; 95 % CI; ring: p < .05, uncorrected).



Figure 17:Replayed state uncertainty: slope per SD of the score within each condition by lag, as in 

Figure 15.

Replayed state uncertainty: a difference in level, not in the course. In Partial the uncertainty tends to be lower with higher scores, and in Full higher, already before the event (STICSA trait, before transitions: Partial −0.039 per SD, p = .10; Full +0.025, p = .23; difference p = .042; before oddballs: difference p = .035; OCI similar). The decrease after the event does not differ with the scores in Partial (recovery p ≥ .25). In Full, the uncertainty after transitions decreases less with higher OCI (recovery +0.12, p = .014). The replayed uncertainty is computed from each participant’s fitted parameters, so a difference in level reflects a participant-level property of the model (how the participant’s parameters weigh evidence) rather than the trial-by-trial response.

Relation of the two. Across participants within each condition, the late distance and the late uncertainty are correlated after transitions (Spearman ρ = .57, .37 and .48 in None, Partial and Full) and after oddballs in None (ρ = .65). With the late uncertainty as a covariate, the STICSA trait slope of the late distance in Partial changes little (−5.3° to −4.4° per SD), so the uncertainty level does not account for the faster recovery.



Figure 18:Placement duration: slope per SD of the score within each condition by lag, as in 

Figure 15.

Placement duration: longer in Full, mostly a general level. With full instructions, higher scores go with longer placements after transitions (general factor at t+1 +0.32 s per SD, p = .009; late +0.27 s, p = .005; differs from Partial, p = .049 and .038). The slope is of a similar size before the event (+0.23 s, p = .062) and after oddballs (t0 +0.19 s, p = .029; t+1 +0.22 s, p = .045), and the recovery does not change with the scores (p = .43). Higher-scoring participants with full instructions are thus slower throughout, slightly more so after transitions. In None and Partial the slopes are not significant (OCI in Partial on the oddball trial: −0.29 s, p = .016).

Further participant-level measures tested against the scores within each condition (tambi_structure_use_scores.py, pipeline step suscores; same model as above; slopes per SD of the score). Stable trials: not an event and at least five trials after the last one.



Figure 23:General factor: slope per SD within each condition for every measure, in SD units of the measure (95 % CI; ring: p < .05; F≠P: Full vs Partial p < .05). The STICSA trait version is fig_su_forest_sticsa_trait.png.

Present from the first episodes. The smaller distance on stable trials with higher scores in Partial is already there in episodes 1 to 4 (general factor −6.2° per SD, p = .002; STICSA trait −7.4°, p < .001; Full vs Partial p = .011 and .003) and of similar size in episodes 6 to 9 (general factor −6.1°, p = .20; STICSA trait −8.0°, p = .064). The change from the first to the second half does not depend on the scores in any condition (p ≥ .45).



Figure 24:Distance from the target on stable trials by episode, upper and lower half of STICSA trait, per condition (mean ± SE across participants). The general-factor version is fig_su_learning_gf.png.

Model parameters. With the rules mentioned, higher scores go with a lower precision weighting (Nexus: general factor −0.145 per SD, p = .023; lam: −0.167, p = .009) and a lower expected switch rate h_switch (Nexus: general factor −0.026, p = .042; Full vs Partial p = .019; STICSA trait −0.027, p = .025). With full instructions, noise reactivity of the lam variant is higher with the general factor (+0.233, p = .022). Within Partial, the score effect on the stable-trial distance is not carried by precision weighting: a higher precision weighting goes with a smaller distance (−13.3° per SD of the parameter, p = .003), so with it in the model the score effect becomes larger (general factor −5.8° to −8.5°). With the cue sensitivity (Nexus: −5.8° to −4.0°) or the placement noise of lam (−5.8° to −3.4°) in the model it becomes smaller; the score is not associated with these parameters (p ≥ .15).

Transfer to the other colour cue. On the first trial with the other cue after a transition, the distance from the new target is larger with higher scores across conditions (general factor +7.1° per SD, p = .014; STICSA trait +7.1°, p = .006), in None (STICSA trait +7.2°, p = .031) and Full (+11.3°, p = .016) more than in Partial (+3.4°, p = .48). On the first trial with the cue of the transition the scores make no difference (p ≥ .39).



Figure 25:Distance from the new target on the first trial with the other colour cue (coloured) and with the transition cue (grey) after transitions, against STICSA trait, per condition (participants; line: least-squares fit with 95 % CI). The general-factor version is fig_su_transfer_gf.png.

Hypothesis space. On stable trials with the rules mentioned, gaze is more confined to the task locations with higher scores: less gaze beyond the task locations in the prediction window (general factor −0.043, p = .004; Full vs Partial p = .017), less at the third location (−0.009, p = .017; Full vs Partial p = .011) and a lower gaze entropy in the anticipation window (−0.097 bits, p = .048). In Full these slopes are positive and not significant. The spread of the nets (circular variance) differs between Partial and Full with STICSA trait (p = .047; Partial −0.030, Full +0.029), and the number of nets with both scores (Full vs Partial p = .051 and .041). The cursor measures do not change with the scores in Partial or Full; in None, the first movement is more curved with STICSA trait (+0.12, p = .045) and the time after the first net is longer (+0.24 s, p = .026). The longer placements in Full are not clearly located in the time to the first net (+0.07 s, p = .35) or the time after it (+0.08 s, p = .37).

Model fit and post-task questions. The fit advantage of the Nexus model over simple tracking does not change with the scores in any condition (p ≥ .14). Rule noticed and instructions clear do not change with the scores (p ≥ .16). The aversiveness rises less from the first to the second half with higher general factor in Full (−17.8 points per SD, p = .001) and more in None (+10.2, p = .037; Full vs Partial p = .049).

Summary of the pattern. With the rules mentioned (Partial), higher scores go with a more accurate placement in stable phases and a lower replayed state uncertainty, with placements that stay at the old state on the event trial and t+1 and are back at or below the low scorers’ distance from t+2. With full instructions the direction reverses: higher uncertainty, a tendency to larger distances late after transitions, and longer placements throughout. Without rules the scores make little difference. This fits a stronger reliance on an internal representation of the structure that helps when the structure has to be inferred (Partial) but not when it is given explicitly (Full).

Generated chapter

Written by tools/build_model_results.py from the files diagnostics/model_diagnostics.csv and diagnostics/*.png of run 23_11, which each R script writes through tambi_model_diagnostics.R. Do not edit by hand.

This chapter reports, for every fitted model of the current analysis set, the checks of the assumptions on which its tests rest. The models themselves are not changed by these checks.

Gaussian linear mixed models (lmer). Conditional residuals (observation minus fitted value including the random effects), standardised by the residual SD: QQ plot and histogram against the normal distribution; skewness and excess kurtosis (0 for a normal distribution); share of standardised residuals beyond ±3 (.0027 for a normal distribution); Shapiro-Wilk test on at most 5,000 residuals; residuals and √|residual| against the fitted values, with the Spearman correlation of |residual| and fitted value; ratio of the largest to the smallest residual SD of the three instruction conditions. Participant random effects: QQ plots and the smallest Shapiro-Wilk p over the random-effect terms. Fit: singular fit and convergence messages. Collinearity: largest variance inflation factor of the main-effect terms (interaction terms are left out because their variance inflation factors are inflated by construction).

Generalised linear mixed models (glmmTMB, binomial and beta). Raw residuals of these models have no reference distribution. Simulation-based quantile residuals are used instead (

Dunn & Smyth, 1996; as implemented in DHARMa, 

Hartig, 2022): the fitted model is simulated 250 times, and the residual of an observation is the randomised proportion of simulated values below it. Under a correct model they are uniform. Reported are the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of uniformity, the dispersion ratio (variance of the observations around the simulated mean relative to the same quantity in the simulations; 1 if the dispersion is reproduced) with its simulation p-value, and the share of observations outside all simulated values.

Linear models (lm, RQ3). QQ plot, residuals and √|standardised residual| against fitted values, Shapiro-Wilk test, Koenker’s studentised Breusch-Pagan test, and Cook’s distance per participant.

Screening thresholds. A model is flagged for inspection of its figure when |skewness| > 1, |excess kurtosis| > 3 or more than 1 % of standardised residuals lie beyond ±3 (residual shape); when |ρ(|residual|, fitted)| > .2, the residual SD ratio between conditions exceeds 1.5 or the Breusch-Pagan p < .01 (residual variance); when the quantile residuals deviate from uniformity (KS p < .01) or the dispersion test has p < .05; when a participant random effect deviates from normality (Shapiro-Wilk p < .01); when a variance inflation factor exceeds 5; when the largest Cook’s distance exceeds 0.5; and for singular fits and convergence messages. With several thousand observations, the Shapiro-Wilk and KS tests detect departures that are too small to matter, so that the decisive information is the size of the departure in the figures and in the skewness, kurtosis and dispersion values. The thresholds are conventions for screening and are not decisions about the models.

hierarchy.lvl2: M3: split allocation within a trial
M3: split allocation within a trial

records.content:
Whether the nets of a trial were split between distant positions (circular variance of the net positions > 0.15, i.e. two equal groups more than about 63° apart), trial level. Binomial mixed model with logit link (glmmTMB). Coefficients are in log-odds. The circular variance is bimodal (stacked versus split allocations), so that no unimodal model of it passed the diagnostics; the planned contrasts for the thresholds 0.10 and 0.20 are listed below.

Formula. split ~ instruction_condition + tau + episode_index_c + instruction_condition:tau + instruction_condition:episode_index_c + episode_length_c + (1 + tau + episode_index_c | participant_id) + (1 | participant_id:episode)

Sample: 17241 observations; groups: participant_id, 96; participant_id:episode, 864. Singular fit: false.



Figure 2:M3: split allocation within a trial. Left: fixed effects without the intercept; the two condition contrasts and their interactions are drawn in blue, covariates in grey. Right: estimated means per condition with 95 % confidence intervals. Points are estimates, lines 95 % confidence intervals. Filled points: the interval excludes zero (unadjusted).

Trial-to-trial update of the placement regressed on the prediction error (pe, attack minus placement) and the state error (se, hidden-state target minus placement). The coefficient of pe is the weight on outcome noise, the coefficient of se the additional weight on state error. Slopes are evaluated at pair_switch = 0 (the next trial shows the same cue).

Formula. update ~ cond * (pe + se) + pair_switch * (pe + se) + (1 + pe + se | participant_id)

Sample: 12228 observations; groups: participant_id, 96.

Generated chapter

This chapter is written by tools/build_model_results.py from the output files of tambi_rq2_models.R (run 23_11). Do not edit it by hand: changes are overwritten at the next pipeline run. Interpretation belongs in 

Results by Research Question.

Instruction condition is an unordered factor coded with two planned sum-to-zero contrasts: C3_vs_C1C2 = (−1/3, −1/3, 2/3), structure explained (Full) against not explained (None, Partial), and C2_vs_C1 = (−1/2, 1/2, 0), rules mentioned (Partial) against not mentioned (None). Planned contrasts are reported unadjusted; pairwise comparisons are Holm-adjusted.

Each model is fitted separately for each of the five questionnaires, z-scored within the analysed sample (q_z). For every pre-specified questionnaire term, the Benjamini-Hochberg correction is applied across the five questionnaires; q-values below .05 are printed in bold. In the models with condition × questionnaire terms, the questionnaire term is the unweighted mean of the three condition-specific slopes; the across-condition models estimate the slope pooled over participants.

pe:q_z is the association of the questionnaire with the weight on outcome noise, se:q_z with the additional weight on state error (averaged over conditions), cond:se:q_z its dependence on the condition. Fixed part. update ~ cond * (pe + se) + q_z:pe + q_z:se + cond:q_z:se + pair_switch * (pe + se)

Generated chapter

This chapter is written by tools/build_model_results.py from the output files of tambi_rq3_models.R (run 23_11). Do not edit it by hand: changes are overwritten at the next pipeline run. Interpretation belongs in 

Results by Research Question.

Instruction condition is an unordered factor coded with two planned sum-to-zero contrasts: C3_vs_C1C2 = (−1/3, −1/3, 2/3), structure explained (Full) against not explained (None, Partial), and C2_vs_C1 = (−1/2, 1/2, 0), rules mentioned (Partial) against not mentioned (None). Planned contrasts are reported unadjusted; pairwise comparisons are Holm-adjusted.

One linear model per parameter and questionnaire, one row per participant. The outcome is the posterior mean of the parameter, standardised within the sample, so that slopes are in parameter SDs per questionnaire SD; the means and SDs are in the table below. The condition × questionnaire model (y_z ~ cond * q_z) tests the slope averaged over the three conditions (q_z) and its condition dependence (cond:q_z); the across-condition model (y_z ~ cond + q_z) estimates the slope pooled over participants. For each tested term, the Benjamini-Hochberg correction is applied across the five questionnaires, separately per parameter and sample; q-values below .05 are printed in bold. Two sensitivity analyses accompany every test of a questionnaire term: the same test with a heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance (HC3), and the slope pooled over posterior draws (plausible values, Rubin’s rules), which carries the uncertainty of each participant’s estimate. All results refer to pipeline run 13_11: 86 participants with behavioural data (None 31, Partial 33, Full 22), 85 of them with questionnaire data. The analyses address three research questions:

RQ1: Does instruction about the latent structure change how participants infer it?

RQ2: Are questionnaire scores associated with how participants infer the latent structure?

RQ3: Which computational account describes participants’ behaviour, and are the parameters of the latent-state model associated with questionnaire scores?

Instruction (RQ1). Full Instructions improve accuracy and interception and increase the selectivity of the response to events (transitions followed more than oddballs). Partial Instructions do not differ from None on most measures. Full Instructions also make the colour-cue offset more likely to be learned and applied.

Responses to events and questionnaire scores (RQ2). Higher scores on the five questionnaires, and on their general factor, go with split placements at t+2 after transitions (nets on both the old and the new direction), fewer transitions followed at t+1 and lower selectivity at t+1. Following oddballs and overall accuracy are not associated with the scores. The split association is largest with Full Instructions. Among the subscales, it is carried by STICSA cognitive, OCI obsessing and IUS inhibitory, and not by OCI ordering and washing or IUS prospective. It remains when the replayed state uncertainty of the model is included as a covariate.

Computational models (RQ3). Behaviour is best described by the latent-state model. None of its six parameters is associated with the questionnaire scores or the general factor. The relative fit of latent-state and single-state models is not associated with the scores. In the hybrid switch model, 79 of 86 participants switch from tracking to latent-state inference, mostly in the second episode (median 12 trials after the first transition with None, about 7.5 with Partial and Full; not tested); switch time and reliance are not associated with the general factor.

This chapter estimates the power of the score × condition results of 

Structural Inference Under Uncertainty for two designs: the final lab sample of 120 participants, with three ways to allocate the remaining participants to the instruction conditions, and an online study with two arms (Partial and Full). The generating effects are the slopes of run 23_11 (95 participants with questionnaire scores: None 37, Partial 36, Full 22).

Generating model. For each measure of the synthesis signature and each score (general factor, STICSA trait), the participant-level model y = a_c + b_c · q + e was fitted within each condition c, with y in SD units of the measure and q the z-scored questionnaire score. Simulated participants receive a score drawn from the observed scores and a residual drawn from the observed residuals of their condition. The condition slopes b_c were used as observed (× 1) and multiplied by 0.75 and 0.5, because slopes estimated in the sample in which they were selected overestimate the population slopes. For the eye-tracking and pupil measures, the share of participants with data in each condition was kept as observed.

Tests. In each simulated sample, the slope within each condition, the difference between the Full and the Partial slope, and the across-condition slope (y ~ condition + q) were tested with ordinary least squares and HC3 standard errors, as in the synthesis chapter. A test counts as a hit if p < .05 and the estimate has the observed sign. Each design was simulated 2000 times.

Designs.

Lab: the current sample alone; and 25 further participants allocated (a) equally to the three conditions (None 45, Partial 44, Full 30), (b) equally to Partial and Full (None 37, Partial 48, Full 34), or (c) to Full only (None 37, Partial 36, Full 47).

Online: Partial and Full with 50 to 400 participants per arm, for the behavioural and model measures. The residual SD was multiplied by 1 and by 1.5, to cover noisier online data.

The tests are participant-level. For measures that the synthesis chapter tests at the trial level (split placements at t+2: logistic GEE), the simulated power is therefore lower than the power of the reported test.

Allocating the remaining participants to Partial and Full gives higher power than an equal allocation to all three conditions for every Full − Partial difference (by .02 to .06 with the observed slopes) and for the split placements (.84 vs .73). Allocation to Full only gives higher power for all differences except the expected switch rate (.49 vs .50) and the drop of the distance after t+1 (.58 in both).

Allocation to Full only gives the highest power for the pupil and gaze differences and for the across-condition slopes, because Full is the smallest group (22). Allocation to Partial and Full gives the highest power for the slope within Partial and for the tracking and model measures.

With the observed slopes, the pupil differences and the split placements reach a power of about .80 with either allocation to Partial and Full or to Full only. The differences in distance, replayed uncertainty, expected switch rate and gaze reach .29 to .60. With the slopes × 0.75, no Full − Partial difference reaches .70.

For STICSA trait, the pattern is the same; the stable-trial distance has higher power (Full − Partial .67, slope in Partial .76 with allocation to Partial and Full), and the baseline–uncertainty coupling lower power (.53).

With 200 to 300 participants per arm, the Full − Partial differences in tracking and in the model parameters reach a power of .80 if the slopes are 0.75 of the observed slopes and the online data are as noisy as the lab data; with 50 % larger residual SD, 300 participants per arm are needed for the drop of the distance after t+1, the slope within Partial and the expected switch rate, and more than 400 for the distance on stable trials and the replayed uncertainty. The slope within Full is not estimable with adequate power at any of these sample sizes (general factor, distance on stable trials: observed slope +0.01 SD per SD).

The five questionnaires of the core battery (STICSA trait, STICSA state, BDI-II, OCI, IUS) correlate .41–.78. This chapter summarises them by one general factor and tests that factor with the questionnaire models of RQ2 and RQ3, the structure analyses, the placement strategies and the hybrid switch model. All numbers refer to run 13_11. Slopes are per SD of the score. Event indicators are tested with logistic GEE clustered by participant (log-odds); participant-level measures with OLS and HC3 standard errors. Condition is included as a covariate (contrasts Full vs None + Partial, Partial vs None), and slopes within conditions come from the model with the score × condition interaction.

records.content:
Factor analysis. Minres EFA on smoothed Pearson correlations of the items (N = 84), for the five questionnaires (93 items) and all ten questionnaires (188 items, adding PCL-5, ACE, SIAS, ERS, EAT-26). Solutions: one factor; the general factor of a Schmid–Leiman bifactor solution with one group factor per questionnaire; five oblimin factors (ten Berge scores).

Five questionnaires: the first eigenvalue explains 24 % of the variance; ω_h = .60, explained common variance (ECV) of the general factor .36. The five oblimin factors are roughly BDI, IUS, STICSA cognitive, STICSA somatic, and OCI with somatic items.

Ten questionnaires: ω_h = .59, ECV .24. The five oblimin factors are general distress (STICSA, BDI, OCI), ERS, PCL/ACE/somatic, SIAS and EAT. ACE and EAT load weakly on the general factor (mean .15–.20).

With more items than participants, the item structure is not reproducible: loadings estimated in two random halves of the sample correlate .41–.47.

The item-level general scores correlate .98 (five questionnaires) and .93–.94 (ten) with the scale factor.

Hierarchical clustering. Agglomerative clustering of the items (distance 1 − r; average linkage, Ward’s method, ICLUST). Stability of the item partitions for 2–10 clusters, as the adjusted Rand index (ARI) between two random halves of the participants: Ward .10–.18, EFA .12–.18 (five questionnaires); .12–.17 for both (ten questionnaires). Average linkage merges almost all items into one cluster. At this N, no item partition is reproducible; only the top splits are interpretable (Ward, five questionnaires, two clusters: STICSA + BDI + half of OCI + 5 IUS items vs most of IUS + half of OCI).

Self-reported internalizing symptoms and mental health … ? The questionnaire battery comprised nine questionnaires. Anxiety was assessed using the german version of the State-Trait Inventory for Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA; cite), with its state and trait scales. Intolerance of Uncertainty was measured with the german version of the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IU-18; cite). Depressive symptoms were assessed with the german version of the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II). Obsessive compulsive behavior was tested by the german verion of the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory (OCI). … Emotion Reactivity Scale (ERS) …  … the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) … …. the Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (SIAS) …. ACE. …. EAT …. Total scores were z-scored across participants. For a supplementary analysis of in-task valence, an internalizing composite was formed as the mean of the z-scored totals of the STICSA trait scale, IU, BDI, OCI, the Emotion Reactivity Scale (ERS), the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) and the Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (SIAS).

In-task affect. After each of the nine episodes, participants rated their current valence, arousal, anxiety, stress, frustration and fatigue on visual analogue scales from 0 to 100 (nine ratings per scale and participant). [EXACT GERMAN WORDING AND SCALE ANCHORS OF THE SIX ITEMS TO BE ADDED]

To get a single net placement location estimate per trial and participant (net placement center), we calculated the circular mean of the positions of the placed mosquito nets (0–7 nets) per trial and participant. Angles were wrapped … to avoid …  Error is the absolute circular distance in degree(°) between the placement centre and the hidden-state target. As described above, the hidden-state target is the center of the von Mises distribution and thus contains no outcome noise, unlike the observed attack direction. Analyses of how net placement centers were updated across trials use the observed attack direction. To compare placements across the two color cues, each participant’s learned cue-2 offset was subtracted from cue-2 placements. The offset was estimated, per episode, as the difference between the circular mean placements for the two cues on regular trials from the fourth trial of the episode onward, and averaged across episodes.

Net placements around each event are indexed as follows. The event trial (t0) is the trial in which the mosquito nets were placed before observing that the direction of the mosquito attack has shifted. The net placement in the event trial thus reflects a pre-event baseline. The first net placement after the displaced mosquito attack is t+1. The first net placement after the next attack is t+2; it is the first net placement at which an oddball and an episode transition can be distinguished – for an oddball, the target angle at t0 equals the target angle at t+2; for an episode transition, the target angle at t+1 equals the target angle at t+2. The following placement is t+3. After a transition, error is computed relative to the target angle of the new latent state, and after an oddball relative to the unchanged target angle.

Net entropy is the Shannon entropy, in bits, of the net allocation of the 7 nets over the 32 positions. It is 0 bits when all nets are stacked on one position and 2.81 bits when they occupy seven different positions, so that higher values indicate a wider spread of net allocation within a single trial.

Latent-state model. Net placement behaviour was described with a computational model in which an agent infers which of two latent states is currently active and allocates its nets according to its prediction (reduced_agent_v3.py; full specification in 

The Inference Agent). The agent represents the attack direction for each colour cue in each latent state, with the second state rotated by an estimated angle (initialized at 120°) and the second cue offset from the first by a learned cue offset. Observed attack directions are modelled as a mixture of a von Mises distribution around the direction of the current state (concentration \kappa = 4) and an oddball component displaced by the rotation angle, with oddball probability \rho_{\text{eff}} = 0.10 \cdot \text{nr}. Before each outcome, the belief that the second state is active is propagated with the switch probability h; after the outcome, it is updated by Bayes’ rule and then shifted back toward its previous value by the belief momentum \text{bm}. The estimated directions are updated by a delta rule whose step is reduced when the outcome is attributed to the oddball component. For the allocation, the agent forms a predictive distribution over the 32 positions as a mixture of the two states, with weights that commit to the more probable state (logistic function of the predicted state probability with gain 3), shifts it by a random circular displacement with standard deviation \text{pn} (placement noise), raises it to the power 1 + \text{pw} and converts it into seven nets. Precision weighting (pw) also scales the concentration of the predictive distribution and the learning rate of the direction estimates, so that a higher value yields a narrower, more concentrated allocation.

The model has six free parameters with independent uniform priors: precision weighting (pw, 0.1 to 5), noise reactivity (nr, 0.1 to 3), belief momentum (bm, 0 to 0.95), switch probability (h, 0.005 to 0.30), cue sensitivity (cs, 0 to 1; the learned cue offset approaches cs × 70°) and placement noise (pn, 0 to 0.873 rad). Precision weighting determines how concentrated the nets are; noise reactivity, how strongly outcomes far from the expected direction are attributed to oddballs rather than to a change of state; belief momentum, how slowly the state belief follows new evidence; the switch probability, how readily a change of state is expected on any trial; cue sensitivity, how fully the offset between the two colour cues is learned; and placement noise, how variable the placements are around the predicted direction. All fixed constants are listed in 

Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants; the choice of the commitment gain is described in 

Model Selection and Validation.

Alternative models. Four alternative models were specified to test whether behaviour required latent-state inference (

Model Comparison): nets placed at random positions; a single direction tracked by a delta rule without distinguishing the colour cues; the same with a learned cue offset; and an agent that knows both directions of each cue and covers both on every trial without inferring which state is active.

Estimation. Parameters and model probabilities were estimated by amortized simulation-based inference with BayesFlow 2.0 (

Radev et al., 2023). Each session was summarized by 54 behavioural features describing the spread of the allocation, accuracy and interception, the trial-to-trial change of the placement, the responses to oddballs and episode transitions, and the use of the colour cues (feature_extraction_v3.py; 

Feature Extraction). The posterior network (flow matching with a summary network) was trained on 100,000 sessions simulated with parameters drawn from the priors on the 20 trial schedules of the study, for 150 epochs; for each participant, 4,000 posterior samples were drawn. The model classifier was trained on 100,000 sessions simulated from the five models in equal proportions, for 200 epochs, and returns the posterior probability of each model for a participant’s session.

Statistical analyses were conducted in Python (version) and R/RStudio (version).

Trial- and episode-level data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models (LMM) fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) in lme4 and lmerTest, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Proportions (beta distribution) and binary outcomes (binomial distribution) were modelled with generalized linear mixed models in glmmTMB (ref), tested with Wald z-tests. Model terms are reported as Type III F-tests.

Instruction condition was entered in every model as an unordered factor with two orthogonal, sum-to-zero planned contrasts. The first compares participants told the structure with those not told it (Full versus the mean of None and Partial, weights −1/3, −1/3, 2/3); the second compares participants told that rules exist with those told nothing (Partial versus None, weights −1/2, 1/2, 0). With this coding, all other terms of a model are evaluated as the unweighted mean over the three conditions. Condition differences are reported as contrasts of the estimated marginal means (emmeans package in RStudio; ref), which average over the covariates of a model. Model coefficients are reported instead for interactions of condition with trial-level predictors, where they equal the difference between the contrasted conditions in the effect of that predictor. Planned contrasts are reported unadjusted. All pairwise condition comparisons are reported with Holm correction.

Random effects followed the design of each model, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the within-participant predictors and, where events or episodes were nested within participants, random intercepts for these units. Where this structure produced a singular fit, it was reduced stepwise, first by removing the correlations between random effects and then by removing random slopes. The structure used is reported with each model. Because the diagnostics (section 1.5.4) showed heteroscedastic or heavy-tailed residuals and non-normal random effects for several models, every test of a linear mixed model was repeated with cluster-robust standard errors (bias-reduced CR2 estimator, clustered by participant, with small-sample-corrected Wald tests; 

Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2018), which do not assume normally distributed or homoscedastic residuals or random effects.

For each model, pre-specified ‘main-interest’ terms (A and D, the questionnaire term of the across-condition form and the condition × questionnaire term of the moderation form; B, the event type × placement × questionnaire term and its interaction with condition; C, the questionnaire × prediction error, questionnaire × state error and condition × questionnaire × state error terms) were corrected for the five questionnaires with the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate (FDR), separately for each term, and are reported as q. Simple slopes and planned contrasts derived from a model are reported unadjusted. All p-values are two-sided.

hierarchy.lvl4: 1.5.1. The Effect of the Level of Instruction on Task Behavior
1.5.1. The Effect of the Level of Instruction on Task Behavior

records.content:
The effects of instruction condition on net placement behavior were estimated with six models:
To examine how … / the effect of instruction condition on the net placement error relative to the hidden-state target, we estimated the model (M1):

log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + cue + oddball on the preceding trial × condition + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),

which was fitted at trial level. Because oddball trials … they were excluded from this model (t+1), such that the error describes …  The model contained a random intercept for participant, random slopes for within-episode position and episode index, as well as a random intercept for episode within participant.

To examine the degree to which participants stacked multiple nets in a single location or distributed them across multiple locations within a trial, we computed the circular variance of the (up to) 7 net positions, cv = 1 − R, where R is the length of their mean resultant vector (cv ∈ [0, 1]). The circular variance was bimodal: on most trials the nets were stacked on one or a few neighbouring positions (cv < 0.10), and on the others they were split between distant positions. Because no unimodal distribution described this (a beta mixed model of cv did not pass the diagnostics described in section 1.5.4), the outcome was whether the allocation of a trial was split, defined as cv > 0.15, which for two equal groups of nets corresponds to a separation of more than about 63°; the distribution of cv has its minimum between 0.10 and 0.15. Whether the allocation was split was modelled with a binomial generalized linear mixed model with logit link (M2):

split ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),

which was fitted at trial level. The planned contrasts were also computed for the thresholds 0.10 and 0.20.

Furthermore, we examined the magnitude of change of the placement centre from one trial to the next, and how this is modulated by instruction condition, the different types of event trials (oddballs, episode transitions and outcome omissions). The change of the placement centre (shift) was calculated as the circular distance between the cue-offset-corrected placement centres of consecutive trials, in degrees. Because the placement centre did not change on 4.4 % of the trials, a constant of 1° was added before the logarithm, as for the error in M1. The model (M3):

log(shift + 1) ∼ condition + oddball + transition + omission on the preceding trial + condition × (oddball + transition) + within-episode position + episode index + number of oddballs so far in the episode + episode length + (1 + oddball + transition | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).

… the model comprises fixed effects of instruction condition and each event type, as well as an oddball–transition contrast per condition to examine whether the differential reactivity to oddball events versus the differential reactivity to episode transitions varies across conditions. Regular trials are the reference category.

Next, we examined whether participants transfer an episode transition shift observed in one cue to the second cue in the first trial in which the second cue occurs in the respective episode. This cross-cue transfer  was operationalized as the angular distance between two placements for the cue shown second in a new episode (|I_e|): its actual placement at its first appearance, and the placement expected had its previous placement been rotated by the episode’s 120° shift. The previous placement is the circular mean of the last three placements for that cue in the preceding episode, and |I_e| = 0° indicates complete transfer. The model (M4):

|I_e| ∼ condition × (episode index + transition direction) + number of trials of the first cue before the first trial of the second cue + (1 + episode index + that number | participant)

included … fixed effects … interaction contrasts … random effects … random slopes … and was fitted at episode level, with one estimate per episode and participant.

To examine how overall mosquito defense performance differed between instruction conditions and across the session, we fitted a binomial mixed model of whether a net intercepted the mosquito attack (M5):

intercepted ∼ condition × episode index + within-episode position + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).

… fixed effect of the level of instruction (condition), episode index, as well as their interaction, to test whether how mosquito defense performance varies across episodes differs between instruction conditions.   … random effects … random slopes …

The net placement error relative to the true hidden target at t0 to t+3 was modelled separately for episode transitions and oddballs, to investigate differences in net placement error patterns around the different events. An interaction effect between condition and trial (t0:t+3) operationalized how net placement error patterns around events differed across instruction conditions. The model (M6) was fitted as:

log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × trial + (1 | participant) + (1 | participant:event),

with trial as a four-level factor (t0:t+3). Planned contrasts between conditions were computed at each placement.

Finally, we examined the effect of the level of instruction on the relative weighting of state error relative to outcome noise in trial-by-trial updating of mosquito net allocation centers. On each regular trial with an observed attack, the prediction error (observed mosquito attack direction – net placement centre) is the sum of two components known to the experimenter: the outcome noise (observed mosquito attack direction – hidden-state target) and the state error (hidden-state target – net placement centre). The change of the net placement centre from that trial to the next was modelled as (M7):

update ∼ condition × (prediction error + state error) + next-trial cue switch × (prediction error + state error) + (1 + prediction error + state error | participant).

In this parameterization, the coefficient of the prediction error is the weight on outcome noise, i.e. on the irreducible stochasticity, and thus the irreducible component of the total uncertainty. The coefficient of the state error is the additional weight on state error (distance of the net placement to the hidden-state target) beyond the weight on noise; the estimate is zero for a learner that responds to every outcome alike. All angles were expressed in the participant’s own frame (after removing the learned cue offset), and pairs in which the next trial showed either cue were included. The update, the prediction error and the state error were entered in units of 10°, which leaves the weights unchanged and avoids a convergence warning that occurred with angles in degrees. Condition-specific additional weights were obtained as simple slopes with emtrends (ref), at pairs in which the next trial showed the same cue.

hierarchy.lvl4: 1.5.2 Models of the Questionnaire Score Associations
1.5.2 Models of the Questionnaire Score Associations

records.content:
To examine how internalizing symptoms modulate overall task performance and signatures of structural inference, we estimated four linear mixed-effects-models (A–D) per questionnaire scale (trait anxiety [STICSA-T], state anxiety STICSA-S], depressive symptoms [BDI-II], intolerance of uncertainty [UI-18] and obsessive compulsive behavior [OCI-R]). Model A asks whether questionnaire scores relate to overall performance, as a boundary condition for the remaining models. Model B asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the response to an episode transition differently than to an oddball, that is, to a displaced attack that does or does not signal a change of latent state. Model C asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the weighting of state error (i.e. angular error between the participant’s current placement and the hidden target angle) relative to outcome noise. Model D asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the transfer of an episode transition to the second (i.e. previously unseen within the new episode) color cue. Each model was fitted separately for each of the five questionnaires.
Each model was fitted in two forms. First, we fitted the models across instruction conditions, with the model containing the questionnaire but no condition × questionnaire interaction, so that the questionnaire slope is estimated from all participants, each condition contributing in proportion to its size. These models are estimated to examine whether a questionnaire is associated with the outcome irrespective of instruction (i.e. which information about the hidden structure was provided). Second, we fitted an extended form of this model, by adding the condition × questionnaire interactions. From these models, the questionnaire slopes were estimated in each condition, pooled over None and Partial (participants not told the structure), and as the two planned contrasts between conditions. In these moderation-form models, the questionnaire main effect is the unweighted mean of the three condition-specific slopes, in which the (current) 13 Full participants count as much as the (current) 29 Partial participants, and it is therefore not used as the across-condition estimate.

To examine whether questionnaire scores are associated with overall task performance (Model A), we extended  M1 and M5 by the questionnaire (A1, error relative to the hidden-state target, A2, interception), with the questionnaire term added to the fixed effects of M1 and M5 and the same random effects (A1, A2, (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode)).

Whether questionnaire scores are related to differences in response to oddballs compared to episode transitions was examined across the first (t+1) and second (t+2) post-event trial. For each episode transition and each oddball, the net placements in  t+1 and t+2 entered the model,

outcome ∼ condition × event type × trial × questionnaire + (1 + event type | participant) + (1 | participant:event),

with event type (oddball, transition) and placement (t+1, t+2) coded −1/2 and +1/2. The outcome was net placement error relative to the hidden-state target (B1) or net entropy (B2). The three-way interaction event type × trial × questionnaire tests whether the association of the questionnaire with the change of the outcome from t+1 to t+2 differs between episode transitions and oddballs. From the model, the questionnaire slope was estimated for each event type and placement, together with its change from t+1 to t+2 for each event type and the difference between event types at each placement.

In B2, the random slope for event type produced a singular fit and was removed. Because the three-way interaction term varies within participants, B1 was refitted as a sensitivity model with uncorrelated by-participant random slopes for event type, trial and their interaction (reduced to event type and event type × trial where singular). For B2, these random slopes were estimated at zero, so that the sensitivity model reproduced the primary model. MOVE THIS PARAGRAPH TO RESULTS?

Furthermore, we examined whether questionnaire scores modulated the relative weighting of state error (net placement error relative to the hidden state target) relative to outcome noise in trial-by-trial updating of mosquito net allocation centers, using the model (Model C)

update ∼ condition × (prediction error + state error) + questionnaire × prediction error + questionnaire × state error + condition × questionnaire × state error + next-trial cue switch × (prediction error + state error) + (1 | participant).

The questionnaire × prediction error term operationalized the effect of the questionnaire scores on the weight on outcome noise; the questionnaire × state error term operationalized the effect of questionnaire scores on the additional weight on state error. Condition-specific slopes of the additional weight on state error were computed as linear combinations of the fixed effects (lmerTest::contest). The model contains a by-participant random intercept; a sensitivity model added an uncorrelated by-participant random slope for the state error. The update, the prediction error and the state error were entered in units of 10°.

An extended version of the cross-cue transfer model (M4) described above to examine whether questionnaire scores differentially modulated cross-cue transfer across instruction conditions. The model was estimated (Model D) as

|I_e| ∼ condition × questionnaire + number of first-cue trials × questionnaire + condition × (episode index + transition direction) + (1 + episode index + number of first-cue trials || participant),

with the number of first-cue trials centred on its mean. The random-effect correlations were removed because the correlated structure was singular. The interaction between the number of first-cue trials after an episode transition and questionnaire score additionally tested whether questionnaire scores are associated with differences in cross-cue transfer for different numbers of consecutive observations of the first color cue after an episode transition. To assess the influence of single participants on the slope in Full, the moderation form was refitted leaving out each of the 13 Full participants with questionnaire data in turn. (ONLY FOR NOW AS A SENSITIVITY CHECK TO GET AN INTUITION FOR HOW MUCH THE RESULTS DEPEND ON SINGLE Full PARTICIPANTS BECAUSE N OF Full IS SO SMALL)

In-task affect (E0, E1). Each of the six ratings was analysed with linear mixed models of the rating (0 to 100) after each episode (tambi_affect_models.R), with condition coded as in the RQ2 models and the episode centred at the fifth episode and divided by 8, so that its coefficient is the change from the first to the last rating. The effect of instruction was estimated in all 68 participants with

rating ∼ condition × episode + (1 + episode | participant),

and the planned contrasts were computed for the mean rating and for its change from the first to the last episode (Benjamini–Hochberg across the six ratings, separately for each contrast and quantity). The association with each of the five questionnaires (65 participants, scores z-scored within this sample) was estimated in an across-condition form,

rating ∼ condition × episode + questionnaire × episode + (1 + episode | participant),

in which the questionnaire term is the association with the mean rating and the questionnaire × episode term the association with its change, and in a moderation form that adds the condition × questionnaire interaction. The random effects were to be reduced to uncorrelated slopes and then to intercepts in case of singular fits; no fit was singular. All questionnaire terms were tested with Type III F-tests (Satterthwaite) and with cluster-robust CR2 standard errors, and corrected with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure across the five questionnaires, separately for each rating, term and model form. Because 29 % of the anxiety ratings were at or below 1 and the conditional residuals of the anxiety models were strongly right-skewed, the across-condition models of the anxiety rating were repeated for log(rating + 1).

hierarchy.lvl4: 1.5.3 Analyses of the computational model and its parameters
1.5.3 Analyses of the computational model and its parameters

records.content:
Model comparison. Each participant was assigned the model with the highest posterior probability. Participants for whom random placement had the highest probability were flagged for exclusion from the analyses of the parameters. Because the exclusion rule is not yet final, the analyses of questionnaire scores and parameters are reported both for all participants with questionnaire data and for the participants assigned the latent-state model. The classifier was validated on 5,000 new simulated sessions (1,000 per model) by its accuracy, the expected calibration error of its probabilities, and the posterior probability assigned to the generating model. Because only the latent-state model contains placement noise, the comparison was repeated with a second classifier for which the three directed alternative models received the same placement noise (same prior and implementation), trained and validated in the same way; this classifier was applied to all participants, both classifiers were applied to simulated sessions of both model sets, and the model frequencies in the sample were compared by random-effects Bayesian model selection (

Rigoux et al., 2014).

Validation of the parameter estimates. Calibration of the posterior network was tested by simulation-based calibration (

Talts et al., 2018) on 1,000 sessions simulated from the priors, with 1,000 posterior samples each, using the empirical distribution function of the rank of the true value and simultaneous 95 % bands (

Säilynoja et al., 2022). Parameter recovery was quantified on 500 further simulated sessions as the Pearson correlation between true values and posterior means, the slope of the posterior means on the true values, and the correlations between the estimate of one parameter and the true values of the others.

Posterior predictive checks. For each participant, the model was simulated with 100 posterior draws on the participant’s own trial schedule, and the 54 features were computed from each simulated session. For each feature, two quantities were computed across participants: the mean difference between the observed value and the median of the participant’s posterior predictive distribution, in units of the between-participant standard deviation of the feature, and the Spearman correlation between observed values and posterior predictive medians. The correlation was compared with the correlation expected if the model had generated the data, obtained by correlating one simulated session per participant with the median of the participant’s remaining simulated sessions. Bootstrap 95 % intervals were computed over participants (2,000 resamples).

Construct validity of the parameters. Each parameter was correlated across participants with the behavioural measures that follow from its definition (twelve pre-specified pairs; parameter_behavior_models_v4.py), for example precision weighting with the mean net entropy, cue sensitivity with the learned cue offset and placement noise with the variability of the placements within a latent state. The behavioural measures were computed from the participants’ data and not from the model. The direction of each correlation follows from the definition of the parameter, and the twelve one-sided tests were Holm-corrected as one set.

Questionnaire scores and parameters. The association of each of the five questionnaires with each of the six parameters was estimated with linear models at the participant level (tambi_rq3_models.R; 

Questionnaires and Model Parameters). The outcome was the posterior mean of the parameter, standardzied within the sample, and the questionnaire score was z-scored within the sample, so that slopes are expressed in parameter standard deviations per questionnaire standard deviation. As for the questionnaire models of RQ2, each model was fitted in two forms with the planned contrasts for instruction condition: an across-condition form,

parameter ∼ condition + questionnaire,

whose questionnaire slope is pooled over participants, and a moderation form,

parameter ∼ condition × questionnaire,

from which the questionnaire slopes were estimated within each condition, pooled over None and Partial, and as the two planned contrasts between conditions. Terms were tested with F-tests against the model without the term (Type III with the sum-to-zero coding). For each parameter and questionnaire, three terms were tested: the questionnaire term of the across-condition model (1 numerator df), and the questionnaire term (1 df) and the condition × questionnaire term (2 df) of the moderation model. The p-values of each of these terms were corrected for the five questionnaires with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, separately for each parameter and sample (18 sets of five tests per sample), and are reported as q. Simple slopes and planned contrasts derived from a model are reported unadjusted.

The posterior means of several parameters were not normally distributed within conditions (section 2.3.5): cue sensitivity and placement noise were bimodal in None and Partial and concentrated near the upper prior bound in part of the sample, and precision weighting, belief momentum and the switch probability were right-skewed. The residuals of the moderation models were accordingly not normally distributed in 54 of 60 models (Shapiro–Wilk p < .05). The same three terms were therefore also tested with Wald F-tests based on a heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance matrix (HC3; 

MacKinnon & White, 1985), which does not assume normal or homoscedastic residuals.

The posterior mean treats each participant’s parameter as known. To include the uncertainty of the individual estimates, both models were refitted on each of 100 draws from each participant’s posterior distribution, with the outcome standardized by the mean and SD of the posterior means. The questionnaire coefficient of the across-condition model and the questionnaire coefficient and the two condition × questionnaire coefficients of the moderation model were pooled over the 100 fits with Rubin’s rules (

Rubin, 1987), with the degrees of freedom of 

Barnard & Rubin (1999), and tested with t-tests. The fraction of missing information of a pooled coefficient is the share of its variance that is due to the uncertainty of the individual estimates.

Instruction effects on the parameters and on behaviour. The effect of instruction condition on each parameter was estimated with a linear model of the posterior mean (standardized within the sample) with the two planned contrasts; the contrasts were corrected with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure over the six parameters, separately for each contrast and sample, and tested with HC3 standard errors as sensitivity analysis. To test whether the parameters describe the instruction effects found in RQ1, each RQ1 outcome was summarized per participant (mean log error relative to the hidden-state target on regular trials, proportion of intercepted attacks, proportion of split allocations, mean log shift after transitions and after oddballs minus after regular trials, mean |I_e|, and the participant estimate of the additional weight on state error from M7) and regressed, after standardisation, on condition alone and on condition and the six parameters. The planned contrast Full versus None and Partial of the two models and the F-test of condition given the parameters show how much of the instruction effect on the behaviour is carried by the dimensions that the parameters describe. Because the parameters are estimated from the same behaviour, this is a test of description, not of mediation.

Incremental validity. For the association of a parameter with a questionnaire, a linear model of the questionnaire score (z) on condition and the behavioural measures that define the parameter (markers) was compared with the same model including the parameter (F-test of the parameter, 1 df; change of R²; HC3 sensitivity). For belief momentum, the markers were the change of the placement centre on the trials after an episode transition, the slope of the recovery of the error after transitions and the error on the first placement after a transition (the participant-level counterpart of the association of STICSA state anxiety in Model B1). Because each parameter is a function of all 54 summary features, incremental validity can only be tested against a selection of interpretable measures.

Reliability. The posterior reliability of each parameter was computed as the variance of the posterior means divided by the sum of this variance and the mean posterior variance, that is, the share of the between-participant variance of the estimates that is not estimation uncertainty. Split-half reliability is estimated by splitting each session at the episode boundary closest to its middle trial and estimating the parameters of each half with a posterior network trained on simulated full sessions whose features were computed from the same half (split_half_networks.py); each network was validated by parameter recovery on 500 simulated sessions, the correlation between halves was corrected with the Spearman–Brown formula (bootstrap 95 % intervals over participants, 2,000 resamples), and it was compared with the split-half reliability of one behavioural marker of each parameter computed from the same halves. Because learning can change the level of a parameter between the halves, which a correlation ignores, and because several parameters have skewed distributions, the agreement between halves was also quantified with the Spearman–Brown corrected Spearman rank correlation and with intraclass correlations from a two-way model of participants and halves (

McGraw & Wong, 1996): ICC(C,1), single-half consistency, which ignores a change of level between halves; ICC(A,1), single-half absolute agreement, which counts such a change as disagreement; and ICC(C,2), the consistency of the mean of both halves (equal to the Spearman–Brown corrected correlation when the variances of the halves are equal). Bootstrap 95 % intervals were computed for all coefficients.

Misspecification in the space of the summary features. The posterior network and the classifier were trained on simulated sessions, so their output for a participant is an interpolation only if the participant’s summary features lie within the distribution of the simulated features (

Schmitt et al., 2023). The 54 features of each participant were therefore compared with those of the 100,000 sessions simulated from the prior of the latent-state model on which the posterior network was trained, and with the 105,000 sessions of the five models on which the classifier was trained (misspecification_check.py). One feature (the shift after oddballs early in an episode) is zero in all simulations and all participants and was excluded. Per feature, the percentile of the participant’s value among the simulated values was computed (values below the 0.5th or above the 99.5th percentile are expected for 1 % of features). Jointly, the squared Mahalanobis distance of the participant’s standardized features from the mean of the simulated features was computed with the covariance of one half of the simulations and referred to the distances of the other half (empirical p-value: proportion of held-out simulations with a larger distance). The distance was also computed within the 10 and 20 leading principal components of the simulated features, to separate atypical values on the main dimensions of simulated variation from violations of relations between features that are nearly deterministic in the model, and without the four statistics of trial-to-trial variability that the posterior predictive checks found to be underpredicted. The log distance was related to condition (Kruskal–Wallis), the parameters and the five questionnaires (Spearman correlations, Benjamini–Hochberg over the five questionnaires), and the association of belief momentum with STICSA state anxiety was repeated with the distance and condition partialled out and without the participants most atypical within the leading components. A test on the summary embeddings learned by the networks was not performed.

The assumptions of every fitted model were examined with the same procedure (tambi_model_diagnostics.R, called by each analysis script; all figures and values in 

Model Diagnostics). For the Gaussian linear mixed models, the conditional residuals (observation minus fitted value including the random effects) were inspected in QQ plots, histograms and plots against the fitted values, and summarized by their skewness, excess kurtosis and the share of standardized residuals beyond ±3; the homogeneity of the residual variance was assessed by the Spearman correlation of the absolute residuals with the fitted values and by the ratio of the largest to the smallest residual standard deviation of the three conditions. For the beta and binomial mixed models, whose raw residuals have no reference distribution, simulation-based quantile residuals were computed from 250 simulations of the fitted model (

Dunn & Smyth, 1996) and tested for uniformity (Kolmogorov–Smirnov) and for over- or underdispersion. For all mixed models, the predicted participant random effects were inspected in QQ plots and tested with the Shapiro–Wilk test, and singular fits, convergence messages and the variance inflation factors of the main-effect terms were recorded. For the participant-level linear models of the questionnaire and parameter analyses, the residuals were additionally tested for heteroscedasticity (Koenker’s studentized Breusch–Pagan test), and the influence of single participants was assessed by Cook’s distance. The diagnostics led to four changes of the models, each described with the model: the shift in M3 was log-transformed with a constant of 1° instead of 0.001; the outcome of M2 was changed from the circular variance to whether the allocation was split; and the angles of M7 and Model C were entered in units of 10°. For the remaining departures (heavy-tailed or heteroscedastic residuals, non-normal random effects), all tests of the linear mixed models were repeated with cluster-robust standard errors (section 1.5).

Error was significantly lower in Full than in None and Partial: planned contrast = −0.76 log units, SE = 0.146, t(74.5) = −5.21, p < .001. It did not differ significantly between Partial and None: planned contrast = −0.17, SE = 0.133, t(74.2) = −1.31, p = .196. Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons showed lower error in Full than in None (difference = 0.85, SE = 0.164, t(74.5) = 5.19, p < .001) and than in Partial (difference = 0.68, SE = 0.158, t(74.5) = 4.29, p < .001). The increase of error on the trial after an oddball was significantly larger in Full than in None and Partial (condition × oddball on the preceding trial coefficient = 0.37 log units, SE = 0.093, t(10640) = 4.02, p < .001).

Participant-level mean net placement error on stable regular trials was 53.6° in None, 47.1° in Partial and 19.4° in Full.



Figure 1:Estimated marginal means of the log absolute error by condition as estimated with M1.

The effect of instruction on how many mosquitos were intercepted (proportion) was estimated with a binomial mixed-effects model (M4) of …. . The proportion of mosquito attacks intercepted was significantly higher in Full than in None and Partial (planned contrast = 0.96 log-odds, SE = 0.168, z = 5.69, p < .001), and it did not differ significantly between Partial and None (planned contrast = 0.27, SE = 0.158, z = 1.70, p = .089). Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons showed higher proportions in Full than in None (difference = 1.09, SE = 0.190, z = 5.74, p < .001) and than in Partial (difference = 0.82, SE = 0.182, z = 4.53, p < .001). The model-estimated proportions were 0.20 (None), 0.25 (Partial) and 0.43 (Full). Mosquito attack interception depends jointly on the position of the nets, their spread and chance, so the defense rate is treated here as a summary measure of task performance.



Figure 2:Proportion of intercepted (blocked) mosquitos by condition (indicated by color) over episodes. Episode index was centerd at 0 for comparability with trial- and trial-within-episode indices.

The effect of instruction on the spread of the allocation of mosquito nets within a trial was estimated with a binomial generalized linear mixed model with logit link (M2) of whether the nets of a trial were split between distant positions (circular variance > 0.15). Split allocations were significantly less frequent in Full than in None and Partial (planned contrast = −1.98 log-odds, SE = 0.853, z = −2.32, p = .020), and their frequency did not differ significantly between Partial and None (planned contrast = 0.20, SE = 0.755, z = 0.27, p = .790). The change of mosquito net placements after events was estimated with a linear mixed-effects model (M3) of …. , (which also served as a manipulation check).

(As expected,) relative to a regular trial, the net placement moved significantly more after an oddball (coefficient = 0.50 log units, SE = 0.054, t(73.1) = 9.24, p < .001) and after an episode transition (0.58, SE = 0.076, t(74.8) = 7.74, p < .001), and significantly less after an omission (−0.22, SE = 0.041, t(11578) = −5.32, p < .001).

The increase of the shift after an episode transition was significantly larger in Full than in None and Partial (Full versus None + Partial × transition coefficient = 0.95 log units, SE = 0.172, t(65.0) = 5.55, p < .001; with cluster-robust standard errors, p < .001) and did not differ between Partial and None (−0.02, SE = 0.157, t(65.0) = −0.12, p = .901). The increase after an oddball was larger in Full than in None and Partial by about a quarter of that amount (Full versus None + Partial × oddball coefficient = 0.26, SE = 0.123, t(65.8) = 2.09, p = .041), but this difference was not significant with cluster-robust standard errors (SE = 0.131, t(20.1) = 1.96, p = .064); it did not differ between Partial and None (−0.07, SE = 0.111, t(63.3) = −0.59, p = .557). On regular trials, the placement moved significantly less in Full than in None and Partial (coefficient = −0.92, SE = 0.133, t(65.0) = −6.91, p < .001).

Participants thus responded to displaced mosquito attacks, and moved their net placement less after trials on which no mosquito attack had been shown (omission trials). With deeper instruction they moved more after episode transitions than after oddballs. On the first net placement after a displaced mosquito attack, an oddball and an episode transition present the same evidence: a single mosquito attack about 120° from the expected direction. records.content:
The condition effects (level of instruction) on net placement error relative to the target angle (hidden-state target) after events was estimated with a linear mixed-effects model (M6), as planned contrasts of the condition means at each net placement. After episode transitions, the difference between conditions depended significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 1618) = 15.48, p < .001) – on the transition trial itself (t0), placed before the first attack of the new latent state, net placement error did not differ significantly between conditions (Full versus None + Partial, 0.16 log units, SE = 0.139, t(235.9) = 1.16, p = .247; Partial versus None, −0.08, SE = 0.127, t(236.6) = −0.65, p = .517). From the first net placement after the episode transition onward, net placement error was significantly lower in Full than in None and Partial, by an amount that increased across trials.

The model-estimated mean net placement error was 3.98 (None), 3.80 (Partial) and 3.14 (Full) log units at t+1, 3.53, 3.36 and 2.39 at t+2, and 3.82, 3.63 and 2.48 at t+3. Descriptively, the net placement center at t+1 had moved 0.24 (None), 0.29 (Partial) and 0.61 (Full) of the 120° rotation toward the new latent state, and at t+2 0.34, 0.37 and 0.79. In all conditions, net placement error rose again from t+2 to t+3. This rise coincides with the first appearance of the other color cue after the episode transition, which carries higher error than a repeat appearance of the first color cue (supplementary analysis ADD).

After oddballs, the difference between conditions did not depend significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 2839) = 2.08, p = .052). Net placement error was lower in Full than in None and Partial in every trial, including the oddball trial itself (t0, −0.81 log units, SE = 0.172, t(96.9) = −4.72, p < .001; t+1, −0.58, p = .001; t+2, −0.91, p < .001; t+3, −0.96, p < .001), and did not differ significantly between Partial and None in any trial (all p ≥ .093). Because oddballs occur within stable phases, in which Full participants were more accurate, the Full advantage after oddballs reflects their accuracy before the oddball rather than a different response to it.

records.content:
The effect of instruction on cross-cue transfer was estimated with M4 (see above, ‘Statistical Analysis’), as planned contrasts of the condition means of |I_e|, that is, the angular difference between actual net placement at the first appearance of the second color cue after an episode transition (where the transition was accompanied by the first color cue) and the placement expected at the previous (pre-transition) target angle, before the latent state rotated 120°.

|I_e| was significantly smaller in Full than in None and Partial (planned contrast = −25.3°, SE = 7.27, t(66.5) = −3.48, p < .001), and it did not differ significantly between Partial and None (planned contrast = −1.1°, SE = 6.54, t(64.1) = −0.18, p = .861). Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons showed smaller |I_e| in Full than in None (difference = 25.9°, SE = 8.11, t(66.2) = 3.19, p = .007) and than in Partial (difference = 24.7°, SE = 7.82, t(66.2) = 3.16, p = .007).

|I_e| decreased significantly with the number of trials of the first color cue that had preceded the first trial of the second cue (coefficient = −6.1° per trial, SE = 2.83, t(58.9) = −2.14, p = .036).

The difference in |I_e| between episode transitions away from and back to the first state was significantly larger in Full than in None and Partial (Full versus None + Partial × transition direction coefficient = 19.8°, SE = 9.71, t(396.6) = 2.04, p = .042). The model-implied |I_e| for episode transitions away from and back to the first state was 96.1° and 95.8° in None, 96.8° and 92.7° in Partial, and 85.3° and 65.1° in Full.

The additional weight on state error (updating based on the hidden state target) compared to weight on noise was estimated with the weighting model (M7) described above. Condition-specific weights were obtained as simple slopes, and condition differences as planned contrasts of those slopes.

The additional weight on state error did not differ significantly from zero in None (0.07, SE = 0.095, t(60.9) = 0.72, p = .476), and it was significantly greater than zero in Partial (0.25, SE = 0.088, t(43.2) = 2.80, p = .008) and in Full (0.66, SE = 0.184, t(658.0) = 3.56, p < .001). It was significantly greater in Full than in None and Partial (planned contrast = 0.50, SE = 0.188, t(386.3) = 2.65, p = .008), and it did not differ significantly between Partial and None (planned contrast = 0.18, SE = 0.118, t(41.8) = 1.52, p = .137).

The weight on outcome noise was significantly greater than zero in None (0.37, SE = 0.094, t(57.8) = 3.87, p < .001) and Partial (0.30, SE = 0.088, t(41.6) = 3.36, p = .002), but not in Full (0.08, SE = 0.181, t(562.3) = 0.44, p = .663). The planned contrasts of the weight on outcome noise were not significant (Full versus None + Partial, −0.25, SE = 0.185, t(334.3) = −1.36, p = .176; Partial versus None, −0.07, SE = 0.118, t(39.8) = −0.58, p = .564).



Figure 4:Note.

Expressed as percentages, participants in None followed on average 37% of the outcome noise and corrected 43% of the state error, participants in Partial followed 30% and corrected 54%, and participants in Full followed 8% of the noise and corrected 73% of the state error. The weight on outcome noise thus decreased descriptively with instruction, but only the additional weight on state error differed significantly between participants told and not told the structure. Participants in None corrected their error about the hidden state no more than they followed outcome noise, whereas participants in Full corrected state error selectively.
