records.content:
The associations of the questionnaires with the change of mosquito net placement error from the first to the second trial after an event were estimated with Model B1. The three-way interaction of event type × trial × questionnaire, tested whether the association of a questionnaire with the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 differs between episode transitions and oddballs.

In the across-condition form, this interaction was significant for OCI (F(1, 1432) = 7.76, p = .005, q = .022), STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 1416) = 6.92, p = .009, q = .022) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 1433) = 4.91, p = .027, q = .045), at the threshold for IU (F(1, 1422) = 3.84, p = .050, q = .063), and not significant for BDI (F(1, 1419) = 0.61, p = .435). For the two STICSA scales, the association of the questionnaire with the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2, averaged over event types, was also significant (trial × questionnaire, STICSA state F(1, 1433) = 8.92, p = .003; STICSA trait F(1, 1416) = 8.52, p = .004).

The simple slopes of the questionnaires show where this interaction arises. After episode transitions, net placement error decreased more steeply from t+1 to t+2 with higher STICSA trait scores (change of the slope = −0.25 log units per SD, SE = 0.072, t(1358) = −3.50, p < .001), STICSA state scores (−0.24, SE = 0.072, t(1361) = −3.28, p = .001) and OCI scores (−0.17, SE = 0.072, t(1361) = −2.32, p = .021), and not significantly with IU (−0.10, p = .18) or BDI scores (−0.11, p = .15). After oddballs, the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 was not associated with any questionnaire (STICSA trait −0.01, STICSA state −0.03, OCI 0.09, IU 0.08, BDI −0.03, all p ≥ .12).

The steeper decrease in net placement error after episode transitions for higher STICSA trait, STICSA state and OCI scores arose from higher net placement error at t+1. On the first placement after an episode transition, higher STICSA state scores were significantly associated with higher error relative to the new target (simple slope = 0.20 log units per SD, SE = 0.074, t(103.6) = 2.76, p = .007), and descriptively, higher STICSA trait (0.14, SE = 0.075, t(102.2) = 1.89, p = .062) and OCI scores (0.14, SE = 0.075, t(103.3) = 1.91, p = .059) showed the same tendency, but without reaching significance. At t+2, none of these slopes was significant (STICSA state −0.03, STICSA trait −0.11, OCI −0.02, all p ≥ .15). At t+1, the slope after episode transitions exceeded the slope after oddballs significantly for OCI (difference = 0.19, SE = 0.083, t(114.6) = 2.30, p = .023) and at the threshold (“AT THE THRESHOLD” IS WEIRD FOR p = .058 OR AT LEAST NOT BEST PRACTISE BUT I GOT STUCK FINDING A BETTER WORDING (for now)) for STICSA state anxiety (0.16, SE = 0.083, t(114.0) = 1.91, p = .058). After oddballs, the slopes at t+1 were close to zero for all questionnaires (between −0.05 and 0.05, all p ≥ .47).

In the sensitivity form with by-participant random slopes for event type, placement and their interaction, the focal interaction remained significant for STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 69.3) = 5.59, p = .021) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 69.1) = 5.19, p = .026), and was at the threshold (SEE ABOVE) for IU (F(1, 67.9) = 3.86, p = .054) and OCI (F(1, 68.9) = 3.57, p = .063). With cluster-robust standard errors, the event type × trial × questionnaire term of the across-condition form remained significant for STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 22.0) = 7.57, p = .012), STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 16.7) = 6.24, p = .023) and OCI (F(1, 15.6) = 5.61, p = .031; q = .052 for all three), and was not significant for IU (p = .106).

In the moderation form, the four-way interaction (i.e. the three-way interaction described above + questionnaire as a fourth term; condition × event type × trial × questionnaire) did not depend significantly on instruction condition for any questionnaire (condition × event type × trial × questionnaire, all F(2, ≈1410) ≤ 0.81, all p ≥ .44). For STICSA trait anxiety, the difference between episode transitions and oddballs in the change of the slope from t+1 to t+2 was of the same size in None and Partial (−0.24, SE = 0.119, t(1416) = −2.04, p = .042) as in Full (−0.25, SE = 0.166, t(1392) = −1.53, p = .127), and the same held for STICSA state anxiety (None and Partial, −0.30, p = .020; Full, −0.23, p = .30) (NOTE. NOTICE THE DIFFERENCES IN P VALUES WHICH ARE LIKELY DUE TO SAMPLE SIZE DIFF. EFFECT COULD REACH SIGNIFICANCE AT (MUCH) LARGER N). For OCI, it (SPECIFY) was present in None and Partial (−0.25, SE = 0.101, t(1417) = −2.49, p = .013) and smaller in Full (−0.15, p = .56), without a significant difference between them (p = .71).



Figure 5:Note.

Descriptively, the division of the nets between the two directions showed the same delay (Fig. X). On the first placement after an epsisode transition, participants in the lowest tertile of STICSA state scores already placed a larger mean share of their nets within one position of the new direction than of the old direction (0.36 versus 0.25). Participants in the highest tertile did not (0.26 versus 0.31). On the second placement, both tertiles placed 0.38–0.40 of their nets at the new direction and about 0.20 at the old direction. These values are descriptive; no statistical tests were computed on these descriptive differences.

Across individual episode transitions, about a third of net placements in the first trial after the respective episode transition (t+1) had no net at the new direction in either tertile, and net placements with all or nearly all nets at the new direction were less frequent in the highest tertile. The higher error at t+1 therefore reflects fewer nets moved (placed at?)  to the new direction, rather than a net placement at an intermediate direction.



Figure 6:Note.

Two further patterns in the moderation form were not part of the analyses based on the interaction terms (SPECIFY). First, the association of the questionnaire with the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 differed between conditions for OCI (condition × trial × questionnaire F(2, 1416) = 8.49, p < .001), BDI (F(2, 1410) = 5.22, p = .005) and STICSA trait anxiety (F(2, 1408) = 4.74, p = .009). These interactions were carried by the contrast between Partial and None. In Partial relative to None, higher scores were associated with a steeper decrease of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 after oddballs (Partial versus None, STICSA trait −0.39, p = .008; BDI −0.37, p = .013; OCI −0.28, p = .024; STICSA state −0.33, p = .034) and, for BDI and OCI, also after episode transitions (BDI −0.41, p = .036; OCI −0.40, p = .013). Second, in Full, net placement error after oddballs increased from t+1 to t+2 with higher IU (change of the slope = 0.27 log units per SD, SE = 0.132, t(1510) = 2.07, p = .038) and OCI scores (0.32, SE = 0.157, t(1518) = 2.07, p = .039), but not with STICSA or BDI scores (all p ≥ .68).

Participants with higher STICSA and OCI scores thus placed the mosquito nets further from the new target on the first trial after an episode transition and fully closed this gap by the second trial, whereas their net placement locations (relative to the target) after an oddball did not differ. This pattern was present irrespective of instruction for the STICSA scales. Where the structure had been instructed, participants with higher IU and OCI scores moved further from the target in the placement after an oddball, consistent with their higher net placement error in Full in Model A1.

The associations of the questionnaire scores (ACTUALLY, MAYBE “INTERNALIZING SYMPTOMS” OR SMTH LIKE THAT INSTEAD OF QUESTIONNAIRE SCORES COULD BE BETTER?) with net entropy after events were estimated with Model B2 (SPECIFY). In the across-condition form, the event type × trial × questionnaire interaction was significant for OCI (F(1, 1405) = 8.26, p = .004, q = .021), STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 1395) = 6.10, p = .014, q = .034) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 1407) = 4.42, p = .036, q = .060), and not significant for IU (F(1, 1399) = 3.01, p = .083) or BDI (F(1, 1397) = 0.50, p = .48). The residuals of this model had heavier tails than the normal distribution (section 2.4); with cluster-robust standard errors, the interaction remained significant for OCI (F(1, 15.9) = 11.11, p = .004, q = .021), STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 22.0) = 7.97, p = .010, q = .025) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 16.8) = 5.44, p = .032, q = .054).

For STICSA trait anxiety and OCI, the interaction arose at t+1. On the first placement after an event, higher scores were associated with a wider allocation after oddballs than after episode transitions (difference of the slopes, transition minus oddball, STICSA trait −0.054 bits per SD, SE = 0.025, t(2213) = −2.21, p = .027; OCI −0.052, SE = 0.025, t(2216) = −2.12, p = .034). At t+2, this difference was absent (STICSA trait 0.006, p = .80; OCI 0.019, p = .45), because the allocation after episode transitions widened from t+1 to t+2 with higher OCI scores (change of the slope = 0.048 bits per SD, SE = 0.020, t(1357) = 2.43, p = .015) and, at the threshold, higher STICSA trait scores (0.034, SE = 0.019, t(1356) = 1.73, p = .084).
STICSA state anxiety showed a different pattern. Higher state scores were associated with a wider allocation at both placements and after both events (simple slopes between 0.10 and 0.13 bits per SD; oddball t+1, 0.13, SE = 0.048, t(66.4) = 2.72, p = .008; transition t+2, 0.13, SE = 0.050, t(78.5) = 2.64, p = .010; transition t+1, 0.10, p = .057; oddball t+2, 0.11, p = .022).

In the moderation form, the difference between oddballs and episode transitions at t+1 was present in None and Partial for STICSA trait anxiety (−0.098 bits per SD, SE = 0.033, t(2211) = −3.00, p = .003), OCI (−0.065, SE = 0.028, t(2212) = −2.33, p = .020) and IU (−0.056, SE = 0.027, t(2212) = −2.05, p = .040), and close to zero in Full (STICSA trait 0.006, OCI 0.040, IU 0.046, all p ≥ .43). The planned contrast between Full and None + Partial was not significant (STICSA trait 0.10, p = .066; OCI 0.10, p = .17; IU 0.10, p = .12), and the four-way interaction was not significant for any questionnaire (all p ≥ .51).

After a single displaced mosquito attack, participants with higher STICSA trait, OCI and, in None and Partial, IU scores thus spread their nets more widely when the mosquito attack was an oddball than when it was an episode transition. After an episode transition, their allocation on the first trial after the respective epsidoe transition (t+1) was not wider than that of participants with lower scores, and it widened on the second trial (t+2). Participants with higher STICSA state scores spread their nets more widely after both kinds of event.

The associations of the questionnaires with the weights on state error (net placement error relative to the hidden state target) relative to outcome noise (von Mises noise around the hidden state target) were estimated with Model C (SPECIFY). In the across-condition form, higher OCI and STICSA state scores were significantly associated with a lower weight on outcome noise (questionnaire × prediction error coefficient, OCI −0.091 per SD, SE = 0.028, t(8264) = −3.20, p = .001, q = .007; STICSA state −0.088, SE = 0.030, t(8267) = −2.93, p = .003, q = .009). The associations for STICSA trait anxiety (−0.047, p = .13), IU (−0.049, p = .14) and BDI (−0.038, p = .26) were in the same direction but did not reach significance.

Higher scores on four questionnaires were significantly associated with a greater additional weight on state error (questionnaire × state error coefficient, STICSA trait 0.096 per SD, SE = 0.032, t(8266) = 3.02, p = .003, q = .006; OCI 0.093, SE = 0.028, t(8252) = 3.27, p = .001, q = .005; STICSA state 0.077, SE = 0.030, t(8266) = 2.55, p = .011, q = .018; IU 0.069, SE = 0.033, t(8266) = 2.09, p = .037, q = .046). The association for BDI was in the same direction but did not reach significnance (0.043, SE = 0.034, p = .20).

In the moderation form, the association with the additional weight on state error depended significantly on condition for OCI (condition × questionnaire × state error F(2, 8254) = 10.70, p < .001, q < .001), IU (F(2, 8257) = 8.87, p < .001, q < .001), BDI (F(2, 8194) = 4.98, p = .007, q = .012) and STICSA trait anxiety (F(2, 8183) = 4.63, p = .010, q = .012), and not significantly for STICSA state anxiety (F(2, 8077) = 2.68, p = .069).

Participants with higher anxiety, OCI and IU scores thus followed outcome noise less and, where the structure had to be inferred (i.e. in conditions 1 and 2), corrected state error more, so that their weighting in None and Partial lay closer to that of participants told the structure. records.content:
Associations between transfer inferred structure across color cues (|I_e|) and questionnaire scores were estimated with Model D. In the across-condition form, higher OCI scores were significantly associated with larger |I_e|, that is, with less transfer of the hidden-state change (i.e. the episode transition with it’s 120° environment shift) to the second color cue (6.3° per SD, SE = 2.92, t(61.1) = 2.16, p = .035, q = .17). Descriptively, STICSA trait anxiety showed the same tendency (5.0°, SE = 2.94, t(61.3) = 1.70, p = .094), without reaching significance. STICSA state anxiety, IU and BDI were not associated with |I_e| (all p ≥ .36). With cluster-robust standard errors, the association with OCI was of similar strength (F(1, 15.3) = 4.71, p = .046, q = .13).

In the moderation form, the association did not depend significantly on condition for any questionnaire (condition × questionnaire, IU F(2, 59.2) = 2.29, p = .110; BDI F(2, 60.0) = 2.15, p = .125; OCI, STICSA trait and STICSA state, all p ≥ .36). In Full, the simple slope was positive for IU (13.7° per SD, SE = 6.97, t(58.9) = 1.96, p = .055) and OCI (16.9°, SE = 8.27, t(58.8) = 2.04, p = .046), and the planned contrast between Full and None + Partial showed a trend for IU (14.4°, SE = 7.69, t(59.0) = 1.88, p = .065) and was not significant for OCI (12.5°, p = .16). In None and Partial, the pooled slopes were close to zero (IU −0.8°, OCI 4.3°, both p ≥ .19). For BDI, the slope was larger in Partial than in None (Partial versus None, 16.3°, SE = 7.97, t(60.0) = 2.05, p = .045), with slopes of opposite sign in the two conditions (None −9.3°, Partial 7.0°, both p ≥ .14).

When each of the 13 Full participants with questionnaire data was left out in turn, the Full slope remained positive in every refit, ranging from 7.7° to 17.2° per SD for IU and from 6.6° to 23.3° for OCI. Its significance varied with the omitted participant (IU, p = .021 to .343; OCI, p = .009 to .614). (CAN BE REMOVED WITH HIGHER N)
Descriptively, |I_e| in None and Partial was distributed around the 90° expected for random net placement across the whole range of IU scores (Fig. 4a). In Full, participants with lower IU scores showed |I_e| of about 35°–55°, whereas participants with the highest scores showed |I_e| at or above 90°, the level of the uninstructed conditions (Fig. 4b).

Higher OCI scores were thus associated with less transfer of the change to the second cue across conditions, and higher IU and OCI scores with less transfer in Full, where the structure had been instructed. The Full estimates rest on 13 participants and depend on individual participants (ATM).

Across the session, valence decreased from the first to the last rating by 16 to 22 points in the three conditions, while fatigue increased by 28 to 37 points (

Figure 17; E0). Stress and frustration increased in None (15 and 16 points) and Partial (6 and 12 points), whereas in Full stress decreased by 10 points and frustration increased by 5 points. The change of stress differed between Full and None and Partial (planned contrast of the slope over episodes, −20.3 points [−34.3, −6.3], p = .005, q_BH = .031; CR2 p = .002); the lower mean frustration in Full (−13.5 points [−26.1, −0.8], p = .037) did not survive the correction across the six ratings (q_BH = .21), and no contrast between Partial and None reached p < .05 (affect_condition_contrasts.csv).

Higher questionnaire scores were associated with lower mean valence during the task and with higher mean anxiety ratings (

Figure 18; across-condition models E1, coefficient in rating points per standard deviation of the questionnaire, 95 % CI). For valence, the associations were −4.8 [−8.8, −0.7] for STICSA trait anxiety, −5.1 [−9.1, −1.0] for the IUS and −5.0 [−9.1, −0.9] for the BDI-II (each p ≤ .023, q_BH = .038), −4.3 [−8.5, −0.2] for the OCI-R (p = .041, q_BH = .051) and −2.9 [−7.1, 1.3] for STICSA state anxiety (p = .17). For the anxiety rating, the association was 5.3 [1.4, 9.2] for STICSA state anxiety (p = .009, q_BH = .044), 4.5 [0.6, 8.5] for STICSA trait anxiety and 4.4 [0.4, 8.5] for the BDI-II (p = .026 and .031, q_BH = .051), 4.0 [−0.02, 8.06] for the OCI-R (p = .051) and 3.3 [−0.8, 7.4] for the IUS (p = .11). On the log scale, which removed most of the skew of the residuals of the anxiety models, the associations with STICSA state (p = .007, q_BH = .033) and STICSA trait anxiety (p = .016, q_BH = .041) were significant after correction, those with the BDI-II and the OCI-R had p = .042 and .040 (q_BH = .052), and with CR2 standard errors all four had q_BH ≤ .042 (affect_anxiety_log_sensitivity.csv). Higher IUS scores were associated with higher mean frustration (5.9 [0.7, 11.2], p = .027, q_BH = .13). The associations of STICSA trait anxiety, the IUS, the BDI-II and the OCI-R with mean valence held with CR2 standard errors (q_BH ≤ .038). records.content: The computational analyses ask, first, whether net placement behaviour is better described by inference of the latent state than by tracking of a single direction or by covering both possible directions, second, whether the parameters of the latent-state model can be estimated reliably from one session and describe the behaviour they are defined on, and third, whether these parameters are associated with the questionnaire scores (see ‘Computational modeling’, section 1.4.3, and ‘Statistical analysis’, section 1.5.3). records.content:
The posterior probabilities of the five models were estimated for each of the 68 participants with the model classifier. The latent-state model had the highest posterior probability for 59 participants (87 %; None, 21 of 24; Partial, 25 of 30; Full, 13 of 14), random placement for 5 participants (7 %) and the model that covers both directions of each cue without inferring the active state for 4 participants (6 %). Neither of the two models that track a single direction had the highest probability for any participant (largest posterior probability of any participant below 10⁻⁸). For 66 participants, the highest posterior probability exceeded .99; for the remaining two, random placement was more probable than the latent-state model (.65 versus .35 and .82 versus .18).

On 5,000 simulated sessions, the classifier assigned 4,999 to the model that had generated them (accuracy 0.9998), and the expected calibration error of its probabilities was below 0.001 for every model. Its probabilities lie almost exclusively near 0 and 1, so that this validation shows that the five models can be separated on the 54 features when one of them generated the data. It does not show which of them comes closest to data that none of them generated. Of the five models, only the latent-state model contains placement noise and cue sensitivity. A sensitivity analysis in which the alternative models receive the same placement noise is implemented and has not yet been run (ADD RESULT; see 

Model Comparison).

records.content:
Calibration and recovery were evaluated on sessions simulated from the priors. In simulation-based calibration with 1,000 sessions, the rank distribution of the true value within the posterior remained inside the simultaneous 95 % band for all six parameters; the mean ranks deviated from their expected value by at most 1.4 standard errors, and the central 50 %, 80 % and 95 % posterior intervals contained the true value in 48 % to 50 %, 78 % to 82 % and 94 % to 96 % of the sessions. The posterior distributions were therefore neither systematically shifted nor too narrow or too wide.

Across 500 simulated sessions, the posterior means correlated with the true values at r = .998 for precision weighting, .988 for placement noise, .926 for belief momentum, .922 for cue sensitivity, .917 for the switch probability and .785 for noise reactivity. The slope of the posterior means on the true values was 0.82 to 0.99 for five parameters and 0.59 for noise reactivity, whose estimates are drawn toward the centre of the prior. In the range of precision weighting in which the participants’ estimates lie (1.5 to 3.5), the correlation for noise reactivity was .86 (206 sessions). The estimate of one parameter correlated with the true value of another at most at |r| = .21 (between noise reactivity and belief momentum). Within the posterior distributions, noise reactivity and belief momentum were negatively correlated (mean r = −.64), so that for a single participant a higher value of one is partly exchangeable for a lower value of the other.

records.content:
The model was simulated with 100 posterior draws per participant on the participant’s own trial schedule, and the 54 features of the simulated sessions were compared with the observed features of the 59 participants assigned the latent-state model (

Posterior Predictive Checks). For the 30 features that describe the level of a behaviour (means, rates and proportions), the mean difference between observed and predicted values had a median of 0.30 between-participant standard deviations, and the median Spearman correlation between observed and predicted values across participants was .76, which is 86 % of the correlation expected if the model had generated the data (median .91). The mean net entropy (ρ = .96; expected .97), the mean error relative to the hidden-state target (ρ = .92; expected .95), the proportion of intercepted attacks (ρ = .86; expected .93), the mean change of the placement centre from one trial to the next (ρ = .96; expected .96), the variability of the placements within a latent state (ρ = .92; expected .96) and the learned cue offset (ρ = .77; expected .89) were reproduced in this way. The fitted model therefore reproduced the differences between participants in the behaviours from which its parameters are estimated.

Two kinds of features were reproduced less well. The trial-to-trial variability of the behaviour, such as the standard deviation of the change of the placement centre from one trial to the next, was higher in participants than predicted by 1.0 to 1.7 between-participant standard deviations (four of five such features), while the ordering of participants was reproduced in part (ρ = .12 to .62). Differences, ratios and slopes, such as the change of the proportion of intercepted attacks over the session, were reproduced in value (median difference 0.57 standard deviations) but only partly in the ordering of participants (median ρ = .27, at 46 % of the expected correlation of .70). Within conditions, the rank correlations of the level features reached a median of 91 % (None) and 88 % (Partial) of the correlation expected within the same condition, but 63 % in Full (13 participants), although the expected correlation was as high in Full as in None and Partial (median .90); the largest differences concerned the error relative to the hidden-state target (ρ = .55, expected .86), the proportion of large changes of the placement centre (.46, expected .92) and the learned cue offset (.53, expected .88). A trial-level comparison located the first deviation: participants alternated between precise placements and discrete moves of the placement centre to the direction of the other latent state or to the location of a preceding oddball, which the model represents as a random displacement of the allocation on every trial (

Model Selection and Validation). Accordingly, the median error of the placement centre relative to the hidden-state target on regular trials was reproduced (median difference −0.5°), whereas its 90th percentile was higher in participants than predicted (median difference 29°; higher for 93 % of participants).



Figure 21:Mean difference between observed and predicted values of the 54 features, in between-participant standard deviations, with 95 % bootstrap intervals (59 participants).



Figure 22:Spearman correlation across participants between observed and predicted values of each feature (points, 95 % bootstrap intervals), and the correlation expected if the model had generated the data (vertical marks).

Position of the participants relative to the training simulations. Compared with the 100,000 sessions simulated from the prior of the latent-state model, each participant had a median of 4 of the 53 varying features below the 0.5th or above the 99.5th percentile (0.5 expected by chance; at least one for 62 of 68 participants). The most frequent were the standard deviation of the change of the placement centre from one trial to the next and the variability of the allocation direction within episodes (above the 99.5th percentile for 59% of participants) and the standard deviation of the net entropy (53%), the statistics of trial-to-trial variability that the posterior predictive checks found to be underpredicted (

Figure 23). Across all features jointly, the squared Mahalanobis distance from the mean of the simulated features exceeded the 95th percentile of held-out simulations for 66 of 68 participants and the 99th percentile for 59; without the four variability statistics, the numbers were 64 and 52, and relative to the simulations of all five models of the classifier, 62 participants exceeded the 95th percentile. Within the 10 leading principal components of the simulated features, which carry 80% of their variance, 22 participants exceeded the 95th and 8 the 99th percentile (3.4 and 0.7 expected by chance); within the 20 leading components (93%), 45 and 17. The participants’ features therefore lie mostly within the range of the simulations on the main dimensions along which the model’s behaviour varies, but combine in ways that the model does not produce, in particular more trial-to-trial variability than the mean level of the behaviour implies. To this extent, the parameter estimates are extrapolations of the networks beyond their training distribution, and their calibration in simulations (section 2.3.2) does not guarantee calibration for these participants.

In the latent-state sample, the distance was larger in None and Partial than in Full (medians 203, 181 and 116; Kruskal–Wallis H = 16.5, p < .001) and larger for participants with higher placement noise (Spearman ρ = .53, p < .001) and noise reactivity (ρ = .30, p = .019) and lower cue sensitivity (ρ = −.51, p < .001). It was not associated with any of the five questionnaire scores (|ρ| ≤ .16, all q_BH ≥ .85; 57 participants). The correlation of belief momentum with STICSA state anxiety (r = .36, p = .006) was unchanged with the log distance and condition partialled out (partial r = .36, p = .006) and when the 6 participants with p < .01 within the 10 leading components were excluded (r = .33, p = .018; partial r = .34, p = .014; n = 51).

(a) Squared Mahalanobis distance of the 53 varying features from the mean of the simulations (log scale): held-out simulations (grey histogram) and participants (marks, coloured by assigned model); dashed and dotted lines, 95th and 99th percentiles of the simulations. (b) Percentile of each participant’s value among the simulated values, per feature, ordered by the median percentile; red bands, below the 0.5th and above the 99.5th percentile; red labels, the four statistics of trial-to-trial variability underpredicted in the posterior predictive checks.

2.3 Which computational account describes participants’ behaviour, and are the parameters of the latent-state model associated with questionnaire scores? (RQ3)

records.content: The posterior means of the parameters were correlated with the behavioural measures that follow from their definitions (68 participants; one-sided tests, Holm-corrected over the twelve pairs). Precision weighting correlated with lower mean net entropy (r = −.89, p < .001), a higher proportion of trials with stacked nets (r = .63, p < .001) and lower circular variance of the net positions (r = −.32, p = .004). Placement noise correlated with the variability of the placement centre within a latent state (r = .95, p < .001), and cue sensitivity with the learned cue offset (r = .71, p < .001), but not with the proportion of episodes in which the first placement for the second cue was closer to the new than to the previous direction (r = .05, p = .35). Belief momentum correlated with a smaller change of the placement centre after episode transitions (r = −.37, p < .001) but not with the slope of the recovery of the error after transitions (r = −.05, p = .34). The switch probability correlated with a steeper decrease of |I_e| with the number of preceding first-cue trials (r = −.31, p = .005) and, without surviving the correction, with the proportion of episodes in which the first placement for the second cue was closer to the new direction (r = .27, p = .013). Noise reactivity did not correlate significantly with the size of the change of the placement after oddballs (r = −.15, p = .11) or with its ratio to the change on regular trials (r = −.19, p = .061). All p-values are one-sided. Five of the six parameters were thus associated with at least one behavioural measure of the process they describe, in the direction implied by their definition; for noise reactivity, the correlations had the expected sign but did not reach significance.

records.content:
Figure 24 shows the posterior mean and the 95 % posterior interval of each of the 68 participants by condition; the numbers below refer to the 59 participants assigned the latent-state model (parameter_descriptives.csv lists them for both samples). Median estimates (interquartile range) were 2.20 (1.86 to 2.69) for precision weighting, 1.00 (0.40 to 2.44) for noise reactivity, 0.20 (0.14 to 0.42) for belief momentum, 0.076 (0.035 to 0.133) for the switch probability, 0.84 (0.24 to 0.90) for cue sensitivity and 0.55 (0.25 to 0.77) rad for placement noise. The 95 % posterior intervals spanned a median of 8 % (precision weighting), 15 % (placement noise), 30 % (cue sensitivity), 34 % (switch probability), 37 % (noise reactivity) and 39 % (belief momentum) of the prior range. The posterior reliability of the estimates (variance of the posterior means relative to this variance plus the mean posterior variance) was 0.98 for precision weighting and placement noise, 0.92 for cue sensitivity, 0.88 for noise reactivity and the switch probability, and 0.82 for belief momentum; within Full, it was lower for noise reactivity (0.55) and cue sensitivity (0.53), whose estimates varied little between Full participants.

The split-half reliability was estimated from the first and the second half of each session (split at the episode boundary closest to the middle trial), with a posterior network trained for each half. From half sessions, parameter recovery on simulated sessions reached r = .996 to .997 for precision weighting, .977 for placement noise, .88 to .91 for cue sensitivity and belief momentum, .86 to .90 for the switch probability and .71 to .72 for noise reactivity (first and second half). In the 59 participants assigned the latent-state model, the Spearman–Brown corrected correlations between the halves (95 % bootstrap intervals) were 0.86 [0.74, 0.93] for precision weighting, 0.82 [0.69, 0.92] for cue sensitivity, 0.74 [0.55, 0.86] for placement noise, 0.73 [0.56, 0.85] for belief momentum, 0.72 [0.54, 0.84] for noise reactivity and 0.52 [0.14, 0.73] for the switch probability. For comparison, the behavioural marker of each parameter reached 0.88 (mean net entropy), 0.76 (learned cue offset), 0.70 (variability of the placements within a latent state), 0.37 (slope of the recovery after transitions), 0.27 (ratio of the shift after oddballs to the shift on regular trials) and 0.73 (rate of switches without an event). Belief momentum and noise reactivity were thus considerably more reliable than the behavioural measures of the same processes, whereas the switch probability was less reliable than its marker. Precision weighting (median 2.04 versus 2.38, Wilcoxon p < .001) and belief momentum (0.21 versus 0.35, p = .005) were higher in the second half. The rank-based Spearman–Brown coefficients were 0.83 for precision weighting and cue sensitivity, 0.73 for placement noise and noise reactivity, 0.72 for belief momentum and 0.42 for the switch probability, within 0.03 of the coefficients based on Pearson correlations except for the switch probability (0.42 against 0.52), whose estimates are the most skewed. The single-half intraclass correlations for consistency, ICC(C,1), were 0.72 (precision weighting), 0.70 (cue sensitivity), 0.59 (placement noise), 0.58 (belief momentum), 0.56 (noise reactivity) and 0.35 (switch probability); the corresponding values for absolute agreement, ICC(A,1), were identical to the second decimal or lower by at most 0.03, except for precision weighting (0.63). The change of precision weighting between the halves thus reduced the agreement of the values but not the ordering of the participants, and for belief momentum the change was small relative to the differences between participants. The mean of both halves, ICC(C,2), reached 0.84 [0.70, 0.92] for precision weighting, 0.82 [0.69, 0.92] for cue sensitivity, 0.74 [0.55, 0.86] for placement noise, 0.73 [0.55, 0.85] for belief momentum, 0.72 [0.54, 0.83] for noise reactivity and 0.52 [0.14, 0.73] for the switch probability (split_half_reliability.csv). Of the behavioural markers, the slope of the recovery after transitions changed sign between the halves (median 2.7 versus −3.2, p < .001) and had ICC(A,1) = 0.19.

The distributions of the posterior means were not normal, for reasons that follow from the instructions and from the definitions and prior ranges of the parameters.

Cue sensitivity. In the model, the believed offset between the attack directions for the two colours approaches cue sensitivity × 70°, so that a value of 1 corresponds to the true offset of the task and any learned offset of 70° or more is represented by values near 1. Participants in Full were told that attacks for one colour are offset by about 70° from those for the other, with an illustration adapted to their own trial schedule. All 13 of them had posterior means between 0.84 and 0.99 (median 0.96), and their observed learned cue offset had a median of 73°. Participants in None and Partial received no information on the colours, and their posterior means were bimodal: 23 of 46 had values above 0.7 and 18 below 0.3 (None, 9 and 10 of 21; Partial, 14 and 8 of 25), with observed learned cue offsets of 75° and 30° (medians), respectively. In the latent-state sample, the 95 % posterior interval reached the upper bound for 27 participants (Full, 10 of 13), so that differences between participants with offsets at or above the true offset are not resolved by this parameter.

Placement noise. Placement noise was lower in Full (median 0.18 rad, 10°; 12 of 13 below 0.4 rad) than in None and Partial (0.62 and 0.65 rad), where the distribution was again bimodal (13 of 46 participants below 0.4 rad). Participants with lower placement noise placed their nets with less variability within a latent state (observed within-state variability, median 24° against 40° in None and Partial) and with smaller error relative to the hidden-state target (50° against 66°). The prior was bounded at 0.873 rad (50°), and for 11 participants (all in None and Partial) the 95 % posterior interval reached this bound; these participants had the most variable placements (median within-state variability 45°, against 30° in the others), and their placement noise is therefore estimated with an upper limit.

Noise reactivity. Noise reactivity was lower in Full (median 0.33) than in None and Partial (1.70 and 1.37), and 5 of the 8 posterior means within 5 % of the prior range from the lower bound were in Full. In the model, a low value means that a displaced outcome is rarely attributed to an oddball and is instead treated as evidence for a change of latent state. Participants in Full had been told that the attack directions shift by about 120° at irregular intervals, but not that single displaced attacks occur. Noise reactivity is the least precisely estimated parameter (recovery slope 0.59; section 2.3.2), so that values in the centre of the prior are drawn toward it.

Precision weighting, belief momentum and switch probability. These three parameters were right-skewed (skewness 1.20, 1.26 and 0.97), without differences between the condition medians of a similar size as for the three parameters above. Precision weighting had three high values (3.6 to 4.9; two in None), belief momentum had values above 0.5 for 12 participants (all in None and Partial), and the posterior means of the switch probability lay within 5 % of the prior range from the lower bound for 6 participants.



Figure 24:Posterior means of the six parameters by instruction condition for all 68 participants. Filled points: participants assigned the latent-state model; open points: participants assigned another model. Thin vertical lines: central 95 % posterior intervals. Black bars: median and interquartile range of the posterior means. Dashed lines: bounds of the uniform prior.

Instruction effects on the parameters. In linear models of the posterior means (standardized) with the planned contrasts (59 participants assigned the latent-state model), participants told the structure (Full) had lower placement noise (planned contrast Full versus None and Partial = −1.49 parameter SDs, SE = 0.248, t(56) = −6.02, p < .001, q < .001), lower noise reactivity (−1.22, SE = 0.275, t(56) = −4.43, p < .001, q < .001), higher cue sensitivity (1.14, SE = 0.279, t(56) = 4.09, p < .001, q < .001) and lower belief momentum (−0.64, SE = 0.306, t(56) = −2.08, p = .042, q = .063; HC3, p = .007) than participants not told it. Precision weighting (−0.23, p = .47) and the switch probability (−0.30, p = .35) did not differ, and no parameter differed between Partial and None (largest, precision weighting, −0.56, p = .060). Instruction therefore changed how precisely and how consistently the nets were placed relative to the predicted direction, how fully the cue offset was represented and how readily a displaced attack was taken as a change of state, but not the expected rate of state changes.

Instruction effects on behaviour and the parameters. When the six parameters were added to linear models of the participant-level RQ1 outcomes, the planned contrast between Full and None and Partial decreased by 83 % for the error relative to the hidden-state target (from −1.62 to −0.28 SDs; with parameters, p = .12), by 89 % for the proportion of intercepted attacks (1.43 to 0.16, p = .40) and by 81 % for the shift after transitions relative to regular trials (1.34 to 0.26, p = .44), and condition no longer explained variance beyond the parameters (F-tests of condition given the parameters, p = .30, .70 and .60). For the proportion of split allocations, the contrast decreased by 36 % and remained significant (−0.88 to −0.56, p = .019). For the transfer of a transition to the second cue (|I_e|; −1.07 to −1.39, p < .001) and the additional weight on state error (1.97 to 1.42, p < .001), the instruction effect was not accounted for by the parameters (F-tests of condition given the parameters, p < .001 for both). The parameters thus describe the instruction effects on accuracy, interception and the response to transitions, but not those on the transfer of a change to the second cue and on the selective correction of state error.

2.3 Which computational account describes participants’ behaviour, and are the parameters of the latent-state model associated with questionnaire scores? (RQ3)

records.content:
The associations of the five questionnaires with the six parameters were estimated with the participant-level linear models described in section 1.5.3, in an across-condition form and a moderation form, in all 65 participants with questionnaire data and in the 57 of them assigned the latent-state model (None, 20; Partial, 25; Full, 12). Of the 90 tests per sample (six parameters × five questionnaires × three terms: the questionnaire term of the across-condition model, and the questionnaire term and the condition × questionnaire term of the moderation model), one remained significant after the Benjamini–Hochberg correction for the five questionnaires.

Belief momentum and STICSA state anxiety. In the participants assigned the latent-state model, the across-condition model of belief momentum showed a significant questionnaire term for STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 53) = 7.45, p = .009, q = .043): higher state anxiety was associated with higher belief momentum (slope = 0.34 parameter SDs per questionnaire SD, 95 % CI [0.09, 0.59]; 0.076 units of belief momentum per SD). The association was retained with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors (p = .015) and when the uncertainty of the individual estimates was included by pooling over posterior draws (slope = 0.33, SE = 0.163, t(38.1) = 2.05, p = .047; 24 % of the variance of the pooled coefficient was due to the uncertainty of the estimates). In the moderation form, the slope did not differ between conditions (condition × STICSA state F(2, 51) = 0.01, p = .99; slopes in None, Partial and Full = 0.38, 0.33 and 0.34). No single participant determined the association: when each participant was left out in turn, the across-condition slope remained between 0.28 and 0.42 (p = .001 to .029; largest Cook’s distance 0.17). In all 65 participants, the across-condition slope was smaller and did not survive the correction (0.26, 95 % CI [0.02, 0.50], F(1, 61) = 4.50, p = .038, q = .15).

Incremental validity of belief momentum. In a linear model of STICSA state anxiety (z) with condition and belief momentum, the standardized coefficient of belief momentum was 0.36 (p = .009; latent-state sample). When the three behavioural markers of belief momentum were added, it decreased to 0.24 (SE = 0.168, F(1, 50) = 2.00, p = .163; HC3, p = .217; change of R² = 0.032), whereas the markers together were associated with STICSA state anxiety (p = .039). Of the markers, the error on the first placement after an episode transition was correlated with both belief momentum (r = .45) and STICSA state anxiety (r = .36, p = .005); the change of the placement centre after transitions was correlated with belief momentum (r = −.52) but not significantly with STICSA state anxiety (r = −.20, p = .14). The association of belief momentum with STICSA state anxiety is therefore largely shared with the higher error on the first placement after a transition, the participant-level counterpart of the association of STICSA state anxiety in Model B1 (section 2.2.2), and the parameter does not carry information about STICSA state anxiety beyond these markers. In the model, this higher error corresponds to a belief about the active state that follows the evidence of the displaced attack more slowly. In the model, higher belief momentum means that the belief about the active latent state moves less toward the evidence of each new outcome, that is, that the belief is revised more slowly.

Further associations that did not survive the correction. In all 65 participants, the questionnaire term of the moderation model of belief momentum was significant for OCI before correction (F(1, 59) = 7.04, p = .010, q = .051), with the steepest slope in Full (0.83 parameter SDs per questionnaire SD, 95 % CI [0.15, 1.52], against 0.21 in None and 0.12 in Partial; condition × OCI F(2, 59) = 1.78, p = .18); in the participants assigned the latent-state model, this term was not significant (p = .25). Higher STICSA state anxiety was associated with lower precision weighting in both samples (across-condition slope = −0.23 and −0.24, p = .064 and .067); with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors, this association was significant in all 65 participants (p = .009, q = .045) but not when the uncertainty of the estimates was included (p = .069). For the switch probability, the condition dependence of the OCI slope was significant before correction in all participants (condition × OCI F(2, 59) = 3.80, p = .028, q = .14), carried by the contrast between Partial and None (planned contrast of the slopes = −0.59, p = .038). For noise reactivity, cue sensitivity and placement noise, none of the three terms had p < .05 for any questionnaire in either sample.

The earlier analysis with partial correlations, in which each questionnaire was adjusted for the remaining scales, had shown a negative association between STICSA trait anxiety and the switch probability (partial r = −.34). In the models with one questionnaire at a time used here, this association was not present (across-condition slope, p = .17 in all participants and p = .52 in the participants assigned the latent-state model).



Figure 25:Questionnaire slopes of the six parameters from the across-condition models (parameter SDs per questionnaire SD), in all participants and in the participants assigned the latent-state model. Points are estimates and thick lines 95 % confidence intervals; filled points mark intervals that exclude zero (unadjusted). Thin lines are the 95 % intervals pooled over 100 posterior draws per participant.

2.3 Which computational account describes participants’ behaviour, and are the parameters of the latent-state model associated with questionnaire scores? (RQ3)

records.content: Net placement behaviour was best described by the latent-state model for 59 of 68 participants, and by neither of the two models that track a single direction for any participant. The six parameters of the latent-state model were calibrated and recovered from simulated sessions with correlations of .79 to .998, and the fitted model reproduced the differences between participants in the levels of the behaviours from which the parameters are estimated. Five of the six parameters correlated with the behavioural measure that follows from their definition. Of the associations between questionnaire scores and parameters, one survived the correction for the five questionnaires: higher STICSA state anxiety with higher belief momentum, in the participants assigned the latent-state model.

The diagnostics of all models are reported in 

Model Diagnostics, where the models carry the identifiers of the analysis scripts (given in parentheses below). For the models as reported here, the assumptions were met without relevant departures for the error relative to the hidden-state target (M1, M1, and A1; skewness of the standardized conditional residuals −0.31, excess kurtosis −0.10, 0.1 % beyond ±3; ratio of the residual SDs between conditions 1.05), for the binomial models of interception (M5, M7, and A2) and of a split allocation (M2, M3; quantile residuals consistent with uniformity, Kolmogorov–Smirnov p = .52 to .84, dispersion ratio 1.00 to 1.02), and for the change of the placement centre (M3, M4a; skewness −0.54, excess kurtosis −0.16, 0.1 % beyond ±3).

The diagnostics changed three models. (i) In M3, 4.4 % of trials without any change of the placement centre (None, 3.9 %; Partial, 3.4 %; Full, 7.6 %) had formed a separate cluster about four residual SDs below the other trials under log(shift + 0.001) (skewness −2.35, excess kurtosis 6.80, 4.1 % beyond ±3, singular fit); with log(shift + 1) this cluster disappeared and the fit was no longer singular. (ii) The circular variance of the net positions, the former outcome of M2, was bimodal (stacked versus split allocations); neither the beta model of the circular variance (quantile residuals not uniform, Kolmogorov–Smirnov p < .001; dispersion ratio 1.15, p = .008) nor Gaussian models of the circular variance or the circular SD (excess kurtosis up to 38) described it, whereas the binomial model of a split allocation did. (iii) M7 and Model C reported convergence warnings with angles in degrees, which disappeared with angles in units of 10°. In Model C, whose primary model contains a random intercept only, the questionnaire terms were not significant with cluster-robust standard errors (section 2.2.4).

The remaining departures were addressed by repeating every test of the linear mixed models with cluster-robust standard errors. They concerned heavy-tailed residuals in B2 (excess kurtosis 3.7 to 3.8; 0.7% beyond ±3) and, more moderately, in M7 and Model C (excess kurtosis about 2.0); residual variance that decreased with the fitted value for B1 (Spearman ρ = −.30), the cross-cue transfer (M4, M5, and D; ρ = −.21 to −.24) and the error profile after transitions (M6, profile_transition; ρ = −.40); and non-normal participant random intercepts in M4 and D (Shapiro–Wilk p = .001 to .012). The planned contrasts of the RQ1 models were unchanged in their conclusions with cluster-robust standard errors except for the condition dependence of the shift after oddballs in M3 (section 2.1.2). The prediction error and the state error remain correlated by construction (variance inflation factor of the state error about 7), so that the two weights are estimated with correspondingly larger standard errors.

In-task affect. In the models of the valence, arousal, stress, frustration and fatigue ratings, the skewness of the conditional residuals was between −0.62 and 0.26 and the excess kurtosis between 1.1 and 3.6. The anxiety ratings, of which 29% were at or below 1, gave strongly right-skewed residuals (skewness 2.3, excess kurtosis 15.9) and non-normal random intercepts (Shapiro–Wilk p < .001); on the log scale, the skewness was 1.0 and the excess kurtosis 4.4, and the results are reported for both scales (section 2.2.7).

Participant-level models of the parameters (RQ3). The residuals were not normally distributed in 109 of the 120 models (Shapiro–Wilk p < .05), mostly because of the skewed and bimodal distributions of the parameters (section 2.3.5), and the Breusch–Pagan test indicated heteroscedasticity in 34 models (cue sensitivity, 20; noise reactivity, 11), which is why all tested terms were also tested with HC3 standard errors. For the association of belief momentum with STICSA state anxiety in the participants assigned the latent-state model, no participant had a large influence (largest Cook’s distance 0.17), and the across-condition slope remained between 0.28 and 0.42 (p = .001 to .029) when each participant was left out in turn. The largest Cook’s distance of any model was 1.03 (noise reactivity, BDI, latent-state sample).

The three research questions meet in the response to a single displaced attack. Instruction about the structure (RQ1) lowered the net placement error relative to the hidden-state target, increased the proportion of intercepted mosquito attacks, reduced the proportion of trials with splitted net allocation centers (WE NEED A BETTER WORDING FOR THE NET PLACEMENT SPLIT BUT IDK YET), increased the change of the placement after episode transitions relative to oddballs, increased the transfer of an episode transition to the second color cue and increased the selective correction of state error relative to outcome noise; the planned contrast between Partial and None was not significant for any of these outcomes. Higher STICSA state and trait anxiety and OCI scores were associated with a higher net plaxement error on the first net placement after an episode transition, but not after an oddball, and with a wider allocation after oddballs than after episode transitions on the first net placement after the event (RQ2, Models B1 and B2; retained with cluster-robust standard errors). At the level of the computational model (RQ3), the latent-state model described the behaviour of 59 of 68 participants, and higher STICSA state anxiety was associated with higher belief momentum; this association was largely shared with the higher error on the first placement after a transition, so that the parameter describes the behavioural association of Model B1 as a slower revision of the belief about the active state, thereby providing one possible mechanism of belief updating giving rise to the observed behavioral tendencies. The parameters described the instruction effects on accuracy, interception and the response to episode transitions, but not those on the transfer to the second cue (because the current inference agent shares the latent state across cues, so it has no individual dimension for transfer --> TO BE DISICUSSED IF WE WANT TO TRY TO ADD A SEVENTH PARAMETER BUT PROBABLY ONLY WEAKLY IDENTIFIABLE) and the selective correction of state error (BECAUSE IT IS NO SIMPLE LR MODEL).

(INTERPRETATION AND DISCUSSION: see the draft in results/archiv/discussion_draft_until_2026-10-13.md; its quantitative statements partially refer to analyses that are no longer part of the analysis set and have to be replaced by the results above)

Structural Inference Under Uncertainty: A Multimodal Synthesis

records.content:
This chapter integrates the associations of a general worry factor with net placements, computational-model parameters, cursor movements, gaze, pupil size and self-reports. Every result is reported in detail in the chapters listed at the end. Each section below states one claim and the measures that bear on it. Effects are given as slopes per standard deviation (SD) of the questionnaire score; p-values refer to the models described in the linked chapters. All numbers are from run 23_11.

Task in brief. On each trial, participants place seven nets on 32 directions around a circle to block a mosquito attack. Attacks come from the direction of one of two hidden states (120° apart). The state switches at the start of each new episode (transition), and within an episode, single attacks come from the direction of the other state (oddball). Two colour cues alternate across trials; each cue has its own pair of directions. Three instruction groups received no rules (None, n = 37), a mention that rules exist (Partial, n = 36), or a full explanation of the structure (Full, n = 22); these are the 95 participants with questionnaire scores. Eye-tracking and pupil measures are available for 84 to 87 of them (Full: 19 to 20). Stable trials are trials that are not transitions or oddballs and lie at least five trials after the last such event. Distance from the target is the absolute angle between the centre of the nets and the direction of the current hidden state.

General worry factor. The five questionnaires (STICSA trait and state, BDI-II, OCI-12, IUS-12; 93 items) were submitted to a minimum-residual exploratory factor analysis with one group factor per questionnaire, and the general factor of the Schmid–Leiman transformation was extracted. The score of each participant is the sum of the z-scored item responses weighted by their general-factor loadings. The loadings used here were estimated in 83 online respondents without task data who passed all attention checks, and the task participants were scored with these loadings; this score correlates at r = .999 with the score whose loadings were estimated in all 178 respondents (

A General Questionnaire Factor). The loadings are highest for the cognitive STICSA items, the OCI obsessing items and the inhibitory IUS items, so the factor weights worry-related content more than somatic anxiety. Because one factor score replaces the five scale scores, each measure is tested once. STICSA trait is reported alongside because it carries the largest single-scale effects.

Overall accuracy (all trials: −1.4° per SD of the general factor, p = .31), accuracy two trials after a transition (p = .96) and the learning rate on regular trials (+0.11 SD per SD, p = .20) are unrelated to the general factor. The scores are instead associated with how unexpected outcomes are used. After an attack from an unexpected direction, higher scorers keep their first net and their first fixation at the previously correct state, and two trials later they more often split their nets between the old and the new state. Meanwhile, cursor and gaze show that the alternative state is represented: the first cursor movement curves towards it, and gaze shifts between the two states correlate with the splitting. Once a second attack confirms a change, higher scorers move to the new state.

The instruction condition moderates the consequences of this pattern. With partial instructions, higher scores are associated with a smaller distance from the target on stable trials from the first episodes on, gaze that stays on the task-relevant directions, a larger pupil before the outcome, and a baseline pupil that covaries with the model’s state uncertainty and declines within each episode. With full instructions, these associations are absent or reversed in sign, and several of these slopes differ significantly from the partial-instruction slopes; in addition, higher scores are associated with longer placements before and after events, a stronger pupil response to surprise, higher noise reactivity in the model and a decrease of the rated aversiveness over the session. Without instructions, the scores are associated with the cursor trajectories, a larger pupil before the outcome and an increase of the rated aversiveness. Mean state valence is lower with higher scores in all conditions.

We interpret this pattern as follows. Higher scores are associated with interpreting single outcomes through an internal model of the task structure, so that an unexpected outcome is treated as noise until a further outcome confirms a change. Accordingly, when participants know that a structure exists but have to infer it (Partial), this tendency is associated with more accurate tracking of the hidden state. Conversely, when the structure is fully explained and only stochastic outcome noise remains (Full), higher scorers may attempt to account for every instructed possibility, which is consistent with longer placements, more fixations at the alternative state, stronger pupil responses to surprise and stronger attribution of outcomes to noise.



Figure 1:Summary of the results. Top: sequence after an attack from an unexpected direction, with the measures that support each step. Bottom: associations of higher general-factor scores with partial and with full instructions. † slope within the condition not significant; difference between Partial and Full p < .05.



Figure 2:Slope per SD of the general factor within each instruction condition for one participant-level measure per finding, in SD units of the measure (95 % CI; filled: p < .05). Right margin: difference between the Full and the Partial slope. Model for every measure: measure ~ score × condition, ordinary least squares with HC3 standard errors. The STICSA-trait version is fig_syn_signature_sticsa_trait.png; a version with Partial and Full only is talk_syn_signature_gf.png.

Figure 2 summarises the condition dependence. With partial instructions, higher general-factor scores are associated with more split placements at t+2 (+0.43 SD per SD, p = .026), a steeper decrease of the distance from the target after t+1 (−0.56, p = .010), a smaller distance on stable trials (−0.28, p = .037), less gaze beyond the task-relevant directions (−0.33, p = .003) and at the third direction (−0.26, p = .012), lower gaze entropy in the anticipation phase (−0.42, p = .030), a larger pupil before the outcome (+0.44, p = .038), a stronger coupling of the baseline pupil with the model’s state uncertainty (+0.40, p < .001) and a stronger decline of the baseline pupil within episodes (−0.46, p < .001). With full instructions, the slopes for the tracking, gaze and baseline-pupil measures are near zero or opposite in sign, whereas higher scores are associated with more split placements (+0.47, p = .010), longer placements on stable trials (+0.35, p = .045), higher noise reactivity (+0.38, p = .022) and a decrease of the rated aversiveness (−0.52, p = .001). The Full–Partial differences reach p < .05 for the baseline–uncertainty coupling (p = .012), the within-episode decline of the baseline pupil (p = .038) and the change in aversiveness (p = .035), and p < .10 for the decrease after t+1 (p = .054), the expected switch rate (p = .052) and the gaze beyond the task-relevant directions (p = .056). Without instructions, higher scores are associated with a larger pupil before the outcome (+0.34, p = .005) and an increase of the rated aversiveness (+0.31, p = .002).



Figure 3:Net placements of four participants, 16 trials before to 24 trials after a transition. Top: partial instructions; bottom: full instructions; left: lower quartile, right: upper quartile of the general factor within the condition. In each group, the participant with the smallest maximum deviation from the group median over three features was selected: distance from the target and net entropy on stable trials, and distance at t+2 after transitions (deviations in SD units of the condition). The window was chosen so that the distance and entropy on its stable trials and the distance profile after its transition are closest to the participant’s own means. The panel titles give the participant’s values and the group medians. The values of all selected participants are in stats_results/<tag>/synthesis/followups/fig_syn_examples_selection.csv.

records.content:
On the trial after a transition, the attack has come from the direction of the new state, but single attacks from that direction also occur on oddball trials. Several measures indicate that higher scorers do not yet treat this attack as a state change.

Placements. Higher general-factor scores are associated with following transitions less at t+1 (−0.21 log-odds per SD, p = .042). On the first trial of a new episode, the first net is placed at the direction of the previous state more often with higher STICSA trait (+0.40 log-odds per SD, p < .001) and IUS (+0.32, p = .018) (

Figure 4).

Gaze. In the anticipation phase, the first fixation falls on the direction of the believed current state more often with higher STICSA trait (+0.13 log-odds per SD, p < .001) and general factor (+0.10, p = .007). For STICSA trait, the slope is similar in the three conditions (+0.12, +0.14 and +0.13) and present in the first and the second half of the session (

Figure 10).

Model parameters. In the variant of the latent-state model with an alternative action rule (lam), noise reactivity, which scales how strongly an outcome is attributed to the oddball component, is higher with the general factor (+0.19 SD per SD, p = .046) and with OCI (+0.27, p = .006). Within the conditions, this association is significant with full instructions (+0.38, p = .022) and not with partial instructions (+0.06, p = .78) or without instructions (+0.16, p = .38). In the adopted Nexus model, the expected switch rate h is lower with higher scores with partial instructions (−0.22 SD per SD, p = .17) and higher with full instructions (+0.24, p = .17; Full vs Partial p = .052).

Hybrid model. In the model in which participants switch from a cue-wise tracker to a latent-state system, the weight on the latent-state system after the switch is lower with higher scores (−0.023 per SD, p < .001; participants with high reliance on the latent-state system), whereas the type of structure used (two coupled states vs four independent states) is unrelated to the general factor (p = .60). The lower weight comes mainly from participants without instructions (None −0.029 per SD, p < .001; Partial −0.015, p = .20; Full −0.022, p = .36; differences between the conditions p ≥ .31). It does not account for the split placements: the weight is unrelated to the share of split placements at t+2 in these participants (p = .85), and the general-factor slope on split placements does not decrease when the weight is added (+0.034 to +0.040 per SD). Higher scorers thus appear to use the same structure but to rely on it less fully, and this is separate from their splitting of the nets. The weight result depends on the four Nexus parameters of the latent-state system being free, which the model does not recover: with them fixed at the medians of the Nexus fits (variant hybrid7f), the weight is unrelated to the general factor (−0.008 per SD, p = .12; None −0.010, p = .45).



Figure 4:First net of each trial. Left two panels: share of first nets at the direction of the previous state on the first trial of a new episode against STICSA trait and IUS, by condition. Right two panels: share of first nets at the direction of the other state on oddball trials, which is unrelated to the scores (from 

Mouse Tracking).



Figure 5:Noise reactivity of the lam variant against each questionnaire score and the general factor, across conditions. Points: posterior means of the participants, centred within condition; vertical bars: posterior SD; line: across-condition slope with 95 % CI.

Attacks that carry no information about the state. On trials with a net at the attack direction, the mosquito can still pass with a fixed probability. Such a bite therefore provides no information about the hidden state. After a bite on such a trial, compared with a blocked attack, the next placement moves towards the attack direction with partial instructions (+5.8°, p = .019), less without instructions (+3.6°, p = .19) and not with full instructions (−0.2°, p = .93; Full vs None and Partial p = .15). Higher IUS scores are associated with a smaller shift (−3.4° per SD, p = .031), most clearly without instructions (−4.9°, p = .050). In addition, the model surprise of these bites is lower with higher general-factor scores (−0.037 per SD, p = .021), mainly without instructions (−0.098, p < .001; None vs Partial p = .008, None vs Full p = .032): the fitted models of higher scorers expect such outcomes more. Two interpretations are compatible with these results: higher scores may go with less updating on outcomes that carry no information, or with a more accurate attribution of such outcomes to the stochasticity of the outcome.



Figure 6:Shift of the next placement towards the attack after a bite and after a blocked attack, on trials with a net at the attack direction, by condition (paired participant points, means and 95 % CI; from 

Pupil Analysis).

records.content:
The placements described in section 1 could reflect a failure to register the alternative state. Several measures argue against this possibility.

Split placements. At t+2 after a transition, higher scorers more often distribute their nets between the directions of the old and the new state (general factor +0.35 log-odds per SD, p = .009; STICSA state +0.33, BDI-II +0.33, OCI +0.31, STICSA trait +0.29, all p < .04; IUS +0.19, p = .21) (

Figure 7). A split placement distributes the belief over both hypotheses.

Cursor. Without instructions, the first cursor movement of a trial curves more towards the direction of the other state and changes direction more often with higher STICSA trait (curvature +0.13 per SD, p = .003; direction changes +0.09, p = .009; pull towards the other state +0.05, p = .005) (

Figure 8, 

Figure 10). With partial or full instructions, these slopes are near zero; the first movement is instead pulled more towards the other state in all participants (Partial vs None p = .001).

Gaze. Across participants, the frequency of gaze shifts between the two state directions during placement correlates with the frequency of split placements (ρ = .61). The share of gaze at the directions of the other colour cue increases more over the session with higher general-factor scores (+.023 per 100 trials and SD, p = .002).

Gaze at earlier outcome locations. In the anticipation phase, gaze returns to the direction of the most recent oddball attack more often than to a matched control direction (+2.5 percentage points of fixation time, p < .001). This difference is largest one trial after the oddball (+8.0 points), smaller two trials after it (+2.1 points) and absent from three trials on. Gaze also returns to the directions of the previous trial’s nets (+3.3 points, p < .001), more so with full instructions (+3.6 points, p = .007). These measures are unrelated to the general factor (all p ≥ .30); higher IUS scores are associated with less gaze at the last oddball location in the inter-stimulus interval (−1.1 points per SD, p = .035) (

Figure 9).

Accuracy. Accuracy at t+2 is unrelated to the general factor (p = .96).

Figure 8:First cursor movements without instructions for the lower and upper half of STICSA trait, aligned to the direction of the first net (from 

Mouse Tracking).



Figure 9:Fixation time at the direction of the most recent oddball attack (1–5 trials back) and at the directions of the previous trial’s nets, compared with matched control directions, in the anticipation phase and the inter-stimulus interval (ISI). Lines connect the target and control values of each participant (from 

Eye-Tracking Analysis).



Figure 10:Gaze and cursor measures for the lower and upper half of the general factor (median split) in each condition and pooled. Points: participant means; large points and bars: group mean and 95 % CI. Titles: GEE slope per SD of the score across conditions (pooled) and p within None (N), Partial (P) and Full (F); * p < .05. The STICSA-trait version is fig_syn_gaze_cursor_sticsa_trait.png.

records.content:
With partial instructions, the larger distance of higher scorers at the transition and at t+1 is followed by a steeper decrease of the distance.

On the transition trial, whose placement was made before the new attack direction was observed, higher scorers are further from the direction of the new state (general factor +8.8° per SD, p = .011), because their nets are more concentrated at the direction of the old state. At t+1, the difference remains (+8.4°, p = .047).

From t+1 to the mean of t+2 to t+4, the distance decreases more with higher scores (general factor −13.7° per SD, p = .011; STICSA trait −13.0°, p = .007; STICSA state −12.3°, p < .001; difference between Partial and Full for the general factor: p = .054). In the median split of STICSA trait, high scorers are closer to the target at t+2 (−13.6°, p = .062) and t+3 (−11.0°, p = .093) (

Figure 11).

High STICSA-trait scorers are also closer to the target one trial before the transition (−12.5°, p = .085). The smaller distance after confirmation is thus part of a more accurate tracking of the current state in general (section 4).



Figure 11:Distance from the target around transitions. Thin lines: participants (mean over their transitions); thick lines: mean ± SE of the lower and upper half of STICSA trait, by condition. The general-factor version is fig_syn_transition_lines_gf.png.



Figure 12:STICSA trait. Rows 1–2: distance from the target and replayed state uncertainty around transitions for the lower and upper half of the score (mean ± SE; * p < .05, Welch test). Row 3: slope per SD within each condition on stable trials and on the trials from t0 to t+4 after events (95 % CI). The general-factor version is in 

Event-Locked Behaviour.

hierarchy.lvl2: 4. With partial instructions, higher scores are associated with more accurate state tracking

records.content:
With partial instructions, participants know that rules exist but have to infer them. In this condition, and only in this condition, higher scores are associated with better performance on several measures of state tracking.

Distance on stable trials. Higher scorers are closer to the target on stable trials (general factor −6.1° per SD, p = .037; STICSA trait −7.6°, p = .004). The corresponding slopes are −1.1° (p = .74) without instructions and +0.2° (p = .95) with full instructions; the Partial and Full slopes differ for STICSA trait (p = .012) and not significantly for the general factor (p = .13) (

Figure 13, 

Figure 14).

Time course. The association is present in episodes 1 to 4 (general factor −6.5°, p = .002; STICSA trait −7.4°, p < .001) and has a similar size in episodes 6 to 9 (general factor −6.5°, p = .18); its change over the session is unrelated to the scores (p = .99) (

Figure 15). The information that rules exist may therefore suffice to elicit the association, without a gradual learning process. Consistently, the gaze associations with the scores are present in the first and the second half of the session.

Model-based uncertainty. The state uncertainty replayed from each participant’s fitted model on stable trials is lower with higher scores with partial instructions and higher with full instructions (STICSA trait: −0.035 and +0.033 per SD), but neither slope nor their difference is significant (Full vs Partial p = .13; general factor p = .24).

Parameters. With partial instructions, higher scores are associated with a lower precision weighting in the lam variant (−0.145 per SD, p = .039; Nexus −0.115, p = .12). The precision weighting does not account for the smaller distance: a higher precision weighting is associated with a smaller distance, so that the score effect increases from −6.1° to −7.6° when the Nexus precision weighting is added to the model. The score effect decreases when the cue sensitivity (Nexus: to −3.9°) or the placement noise of the lam variant (to −3.8°) is added, but these parameters are unrelated to the score (p ≥ .11).

Gaze. With partial instructions, higher scores are associated with less fixation time beyond the believed current state in the prediction phase (−0.33 SD per SD, p = .003; Full vs Partial p = .056), less fixation time at the third direction (p = .012), lower gaze entropy over the task-relevant directions in the anticipation phase (−0.111 bits per SD, p = .009) and in the outcome phase (−0.079 bits, p = .008), and more first fixations at the current and at the other state (current +0.154 log-odds, p = .030; other +0.155, p < .001). Gaze thus concentrates on the two state directions. Across conditions, higher scores are associated with less gaze at directions without nets (general factor −0.034, p = .016) and a longer lead of gaze over the cursor before the first net (+16 ms per SD, p = .049) (

Figure 10).



Figure 13:Distance from the target on stable trials against STICSA trait, by condition. Points: participants; line: least-squares fit with 95 % CI; titles: slope per SD and p of the score × condition model.



Figure 14:Slope per SD of the general factor for the distance from the target within each condition, on stable trials and on the trials from t0 to t+4 after events (95 % CI), with the difference between the Full and the Partial slope on stable trials.



Figure 15:Distance from the target on stable trials by episode for the lower and upper half of STICSA trait (mean ± SE). With partial instructions, the difference is present from the first episode on.

Pupil. In the inter-stimulus interval before the outcome, when the outcome cannot yet be known, the pupil is larger with higher scores with partial instructions (general factor +0.100 z per SD, p = .026) and without instructions (+0.078, p = .034), but not with full instructions (+0.038, p = .38) (

Figure 20). The baseline pupil before each trial covaries with the model’s state uncertainty more strongly with higher scores with partial instructions (+0.039 per SD, p = .021; per participant r = +.43; Full vs Partial p = .007) (

Figure 16). Within each episode, the baseline pupil of higher STICSA-trait scorers starts higher and declines faster (−0.077 z per 10 trials and SD, p = .003; Full vs Partial p = .020), so that it approaches the level of lower scorers towards the end of the episode (

Figure 17). Across participants, a larger pupil response to surprise after the feedback is associated with a smaller distance on stable trials (r = −.52; Partial: r = −.59), and with partial instructions this response is larger with higher STICSA trait (r = +.45, p = .009) (

Figure 18). Together, these results indicate that, with partial instructions, arousal in higher scorers is coupled to the model’s state uncertainty and decreases as the current state becomes established within an episode.



Figure 16:Coupling of the baseline pupil with the replayed state uncertainty (slope per participant) against the general factor, by condition.



Figure 17:Change of the baseline pupil over the trials of an episode (slope per participant) against STICSA trait, by condition.



Figure 18:Pupil response to surprise after the feedback against the distance from the target on stable trials, per participant.
