hierarchy.lvl2: 5. With full instructions, higher scores are associated with longer placements, stronger pupil responses to surprise and stronger attribution of outcomes to noise

records.content:
With full instructions, participants know the two states, the oddballs, the switches and the colour cues; only the timing of switches and the occurrence of oddballs remain unpredictable. In this condition, higher scores are not associated with more accurate tracking. The following associations are observed instead.

Placement duration. Placements take longer with higher scores, both on stable trials (general factor +0.24 s per SD, p = .045) and on the trials after events (+0.26 s, p = .018). The slope is positive at every lag from two trials before to four trials after transitions and oddballs, and is similar for STICSA trait, OCI and BDI-II (

Figure 19). Without or with partial instructions, the duration is unrelated to the scores. The additional time is not concentrated before the first net (+0.07 s, p = .37) or after it (+0.09 s, p = .27).

Attribution to noise. Noise reactivity in the lam variant is higher with the general factor (+0.38 SD per SD, p = .022). The feedback pupil covaries with the model’s oddball probability more strongly with full than with partial instructions (+0.104 vs +0.033, p = .026), and this coupling increases with the general factor in Full (+0.050 per SD, p = .041).

Pupil response to surprise. The feedback pupil scales with the surprise of the attack more strongly with higher general-factor scores (across conditions +0.042 per SD, p < .001; Full +0.060, p = .006; None +0.036, p = .040; Partial +0.036, p = .10) (

Figure 20), and its scaling with the belief update increases with the score in Full (+0.040, p = .006; per participant r = +.48).

Baseline pupil. The baseline pupil does not decline within episodes with higher scores (STICSA trait p = .73) and does not covary with the model’s state uncertainty (r = −.32, p = .18).

Transfer to the other colour cue. On the first trial with the other colour cue after a transition, the distance from the new target is larger with higher scores (STICSA trait: Full +11.1° per SD, p = .022; None +5.3°, p = .16; Partial +2.8°, p = .57). On the first trial with the colour cue of the transition, the distance is unrelated to the scores (p ≥ .08) (

Figure 21). Higher scorers with full instructions therefore apply a change observed with one cue to the other cue later.

Gaze in the prediction phase. Higher scores are associated with more fixations at the other state when no net is placed there (general factor +0.36 log-odds per SD, p = .022; Full vs Partial p = .089), more gaze shifts between the two states (+0.47, p = .023; Full vs Partial p = .058) and more later nets at the other state (+0.71, p = .009; Full vs Partial p = .025).

Aversiveness. The rated aversiveness increases less from the first to the second half of the session with higher scores (−18.0 points per SD, p = .001), whereas it increases more without instructions (+10.8, p = .002) and is unrelated to the scores with partial instructions (+1.2, p = .87; Full vs Partial p = .035) (

Figure 20). Higher scorers report having noticed a rule slightly more often across conditions (+0.09 per SD, p = .046), but not within any condition (p ≥ .16); the clarity of the instructions is unrelated to the scores (p ≥ .18).

These associations are consistent with a larger set of hypotheses that higher scorers attempt to monitor when all rules are given: longer deliberation, more fixations at the alternative state, stronger pupil responses to surprise and stronger attribution of outcomes to the oddball component. Accordingly, the tendency that is associated with more accurate tracking under partial instructions is associated with longer deliberation and stronger responses to surprise under full instructions.



Figure 19:Placement duration: slope per SD of each score within each condition at each trial from two trials before to four trials after transitions (top) and oddballs (bottom), with 95 % CI (ring: p < .05).



Figure 20:Change in rated aversiveness (top), pupil before the outcome (middle) and coupling of the feedback pupil with the surprise of the attack (bottom) against the general factor, by condition. Points: participants; lines: least-squares fit with 95 % CI; titles: slopes of the models reported in the text (aversiveness: participant-level OLS with HC3 standard errors; pupil: trial-level mixed models). The STICSA-trait version is fig_syn_tracking_sticsa_trait.png.



Figure 21:Distance from the new target on the first trial with the other colour cue (filled squares, solid line) and on the first trial with the colour cue of the transition (open circles, dashed line) after transitions, against STICSA trait, by condition (least-squares lines with 95 % CI).



Figure 22:Coupling of the feedback pupil with the model’s oddball probability by condition and score.

Across conditions, the pupil after the feedback increases with the surprise of the attack (+0.081 z per SD of surprise) and with the size of the model’s belief update (+0.061), both p < .001. On the trial after a transition, the pupil during the attack animation is larger than on the trial after an oddball (+0.08 z, p = .006); the pupil thus differentiates a confirmed change from an isolated oddball. With higher scores, the relation between the pupil during the attack animation and the subsequent shift of the placement changes sign (general factor −1.64° per SD, p = .027): in lower scorers, a larger pupil precedes a larger shift, whereas in higher scorers a larger pupil precedes a smaller shift. Higher scorers therefore show a pupil response to the attack that is not followed by a corresponding update of the placement.

records.content: Several gaze associations do not differ between the conditions and are present in both halves of the session. With higher STICSA trait, the first fixation in the anticipation phase falls on the current state more often (+0.13 log-odds per SD, p < .001), directions without nets are fixated less (−0.040, p = .002), the other state is fixated less when no net is placed there (−0.14, p = .026), gaze entropy over the task-relevant directions is lower in the anticipation phase (−0.055 bits, p = .030) and in the outcome phase (−0.045 bits, p = .020), and gaze precedes the cursor by a longer interval (gaze–cursor lag +22 ms per SD, p = .001). These associations describe a stable focus of gaze on the believed current state. The instruction condition determines whether this focus coincides with more accurate tracking (Partial) or not (None, Full).

records.content:
Participants rated their state once per episode, after trial 7 or 14. Mean valence is lower with higher scores (general factor −5.6 points on the 0–100 scale per SD, p = .001; STICSA trait −4.4, p = .005). The association is present in each condition and largest with full instructions (general factor: None −4.5, p = .16; Partial −4.9, p = .12; Full −7.8, p = .014); the conditions do not differ significantly (Full vs Partial p = .51). Valence decreases over the episodes in all groups, and this decrease is unrelated to the scores (−0.12 points per SD and episode, p = .69) (

Figure 24, 

Figure 25).

Within participants, valence covaries with tracking accuracy when the structure has to be inferred. After removing each participant’s linear trend over the episodes, valence is lower after episodes with a larger distance from the target with partial instructions (−1.3 points per SD of the distance, p = .009) and without instructions (−0.9, p = .068), but not with full instructions (+1.2, p = .098). With full instructions, valence tends to be lower after episodes with higher model-based state uncertainty (−1.2 points per SD, p = .12) (

Figure 26). The general factor does not modulate the coupling of valence with the distance in any condition (p ≥ .15). With full instructions, more distributed gaze in the anticipation phase is associated with higher valence in lower but not in higher STICSA-trait scorers (score × gaze entropy −1.4, p = .030).



Figure 24:State valence by episode. Thin lines: participants; thick lines: mean ± SE of the lower and upper half of the general factor, by condition. The STICSA-trait version is fig_syn_valence_trajectories_sticsa_trait.png.



Figure 25:Mean in-task valence (top) and its change per episode (bottom) against the general factor, by condition and pooled. Points: participants; lines: least-squares fit with 95 % CI; titles: slope per SD and p of the score × condition model (pooled: across-condition slope).



Figure 26:Within-participant coupling of valence with the distance from the target (top) and with the replayed state uncertainty (bottom) on the trials of the same episode before the rating, against the general factor, by condition. Points: slopes per participant (valence and predictor detrended over episodes); titles: mixed-model estimates.

hierarchy.lvl2: 9. Results that do not fit the interpretation, and open questions

records.content:
Model-based uncertainty. The replayed state uncertainty is lower with higher scores under partial and higher under full instructions, but the difference is not significant (STICSA trait p = .13). The condition dependence therefore rests on tracking, gaze, pupil, placement duration and self-report, not on the model’s uncertainty.

Expected switch rate. The lower expected switch rate of higher scorers with partial instructions is not significant within the condition (p = .17); only the Full–Partial difference approaches significance (p = .052).

Noise reactivity and pupil. The pupil response to surprise is unrelated to the fitted noise reactivity (lam: r = −.10, p = .35). Instead, it is associated with a higher cue sensitivity (Nexus: r = +.35) and a lower placement noise (r = −.37). Higher scores go with a stronger, not a weaker, pupil response to surprise after the feedback (section 5), so the pupil gives no direct physiological correlate of attributing surprise to noise.

Pupil before the outcome with full instructions. The pupil in the inter-stimulus interval does not covary more strongly with the model’s state uncertainty with higher scores under any condition (Partial −0.001, Full +0.004 per SD).

Transition vs oddball in the pupil. The pupil difference between the trial after a transition and the trial after an oddball is unrelated to the scores in all conditions.

Model fit. The fit advantage of the Nexus model over a simple tracking model is unrelated to the scores (p ≥ .12); the condition-dependent associations therefore do not reflect differences in which model describes the participants best.

Without instructions. Without instructions, higher scores are associated with a larger pupil before the outcome, a stronger pupil response to surprise, a lower model surprise of uninformative bites and an increase of the rated aversiveness over the session, but not with the distance from the target (p = .74). It is open whether these associations reflect the same tendency as in Partial without the information needed to turn it into more accurate tracking.

Mechanism of the tracking advantage. None of the fitted parameters accounts for the smaller distance of higher scorers with partial instructions; the cue sensitivity and the placement noise of the lam variant reduce the score effect but are themselves unrelated to the scores.

Sample size per condition. The condition-specific slopes rest on 22 to 37 participants per condition, and on 19 to 20 participants with full instructions for the gaze and pupil measures. The power of the Full–Partial differences in the final sample is estimated in 

Simulation-Based Power.

hierarchy.lvl2: 10. Implications for a multimodal account of structural inference in worry

hierarchy.lvl1: Structural Inference Under Uncertainty: A Multimodal Synthesis
hierarchy.lvl2: 10. Implications for a multimodal account of structural inference in worry

records.content:
The results support an account in which a transdiagnostic worry dimension relates to how evidence is interpreted rather than to overall accuracy or learning rate. Higher scorers register unexpected outcomes: the pupil responds to them, gaze returns to the location of the last oddball, and the cursor and the nets show that the alternative state is considered. Yet they interpret single unexpected outcomes through an internal model of the task structure and change their placement only after a second outcome confirms a change. Accordingly, whether this tendency is associated with better or worse performance depends on the information available. With partial instructions, the structure has to be inferred, and higher scores are associated with more accurate tracking, gaze concentrated on the two states, an arousal level that is coupled to the model’s state uncertainty and decreases within each episode, and a valence that covaries with tracking accuracy. With full instructions, only stochastic outcome noise remains to be explained, and higher scores are associated with longer deliberation, more fixations at the alternative state, stronger pupil responses to surprise, stronger attribution of outcomes to noise and a decrease of the rated aversiveness over the session.

Three implications follow for computational psychiatry. First, symptom dimensions may be described more precisely by how evidence for a change is weighed against an internal model than by a general tendency to update more or less. Second, the sign of an association between a symptom dimension and task performance can depend on the information provided about the task structure; tasks with and without explicit structure can therefore yield opposite associations in the same population. Third, distributional responses (seven nets) and continuous process measures (cursor, gaze, pupil) are required to detect this pattern: a single point estimate per trial would not reveal split placements, and without process measures the represented alternative and the within-episode decline of arousal would not be observable.

Event-Locked Behaviour and Data Explorer: event-locked analyses, stable trials, structure use and the scores

A General Questionnaire Factor: estimation of the general factor, item loadings, split placements

RQ3 Questionnaires and Model Parameters: parameter associations

Hybrid Switch Model and 

Action-Rule Variant (lam): the two model descriptions behind the reliance and noise-reactivity results

Mouse Tracking, 

Eye-Tracking Analysis, 

Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Analysis,

Simulation-Based Power: power of the score × condition tests for the final sample

Scripts of this chapter: tambi_synthesis_figures.py (pipeline step synthesis), tambi_synthesis_followups.py (state valence, participant-level figures, example participants, gaze and cursor by score; step synthfu) and tambi_synthesis_tracking.py (aversiveness and pupil by score and condition)

The latent-state model describes each participant by six parameters, and, given these parameters and the sequence of cues and attacks the participant saw, it implies on every trial a belief about which of the two latent states is active. This chapter uses this belief as a trial-by-trial measure of the uncertainty that the fitted model attributes to the participant, and asks whether the participant’s behaviour follows it in two respects that are not used to estimate the parameters (placement duration) or only in summarized form (net spread, nets on both directions), and whether it is associated with the questionnaire scores.

For each participant, the fitted model was replayed on the participant’s own trial sequence with 200 draws from the posterior of the parameters (belief_trace_replay.py). The state uncertainty on a trial is 1 − |2z − 1|, where z is the probability the model assigns to one of the two latent states before the placement of that trial, averaged over the draws; it is 0 when the model is certain which state is active and 1 when both states are equally probable. On the trial after an event (t+1), it therefore reflects the displaced attack of the event trial. The uncertainty was split into the participant’s mean over the session (between-participant component, standardized across participants) and the deviation of each trial from this mean (within-participant component, in SD of the deviations). The replay was computed for all 86 participants, including the nine assigned another model in the model comparison.

U1 to U3, uncertainty and behaviour (tambi_uncertainty_behaviour.R). Linear mixed models of the log placement duration (U1; sensitivity models with the number of positions used and the shift of the allocation centre as covariates, and without time-outs) and of the net entropy (U2) on both components, condition and trial index, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the within-participant component; a binomial mixed model of nets on both directions at t+1 and t+2 after events (U3; strategy class of the previous chapter) on both components, event type, trial and condition, with by-participant random intercepts. The net entropy enters the estimation of the parameters through its mean and SD over the session, so that U2 checks the consistency of the replay rather than providing independent evidence.

Q1, mean uncertainty and questionnaires (tambi_uncertainty_questionnaire.R). Linear regressions of the participant’s mean uncertainty (over all trials, over stable regular trials and over the placements at t+1 after events; standardized) on the questionnaire and condition (across-condition form) and on their interaction (moderation form), with heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors, in all participants and in those assigned the latent-state model, and with the six parameters as additional covariates. A regression on the six parameters and condition shows which parameters determine the mean uncertainty.

Q2, uncertainty around events and questionnaires. A linear mixed model of the trial-level uncertainty on position (regular trial, t0, t+1 and t+2 after transitions and after oddballs) × questionnaire, condition and trial index, with by-participant random intercepts, with tests of the questionnaire terms also with cluster-robust (CR2) standard errors, and participant-level regressions of the mean uncertainty at each position as a check.

Q3 and Q4, coupling with behaviour by questionnaire. The questionnaire forms of U1 and U2 (within-participant component × questionnaire), the corresponding form of U3, and the models of nets on both directions at t+1 and t+2 on the questionnaire with and without the two uncertainty components.

On regular trials, the mean replayed uncertainty was 0.28 in None, 0.23 in Partial and 0.14 in Full. It was lowest on the event trials (0.08 to 0.22) and highest on the first placement after an event, after transitions (None 0.49, Partial 0.53, Full 0.54) and after oddballs (None 0.39, Partial 0.35, Full 0.38). On the second placement, it remained high after transitions in None and Partial (0.40 and 0.43) and was lower in Full (0.24), and after oddballs it was 0.27, 0.21 and 0.15. In the model, the ambiguity of a single displaced attack at t+1 is thus of similar size in all conditions, and the conditions differ in how far it is resolved by the following attack.

The participant’s mean uncertainty was almost entirely determined by the parameters (linear regression on the six standardized parameters and condition, R² = .96). It was higher with higher belief momentum (0.79 SD per SD) and switch probability (0.35) and lower with higher cue sensitivity (−0.22) and placement noise (−0.09, HC3 p = .020); precision weighting and noise reactivity did not contribute (both p ≥ .91). The mean uncertainty at t+1 after events was determined less completely (R² = .57) and depended also on noise reactivity (−0.36), besides belief momentum (0.57) and the switch probability (0.46).

On trials on which the replayed uncertainty was higher than the participant’s own mean, the placement took significantly longer (within-participant component = 0.022 log units per SD, about 2.2 %, SE = 0.002, t(79) = 9.85, p < .001). The association was about half as large and remained significant with the number of positions used and the shift of the allocation centre as covariates (0.010, SE = 0.002, t(81) = 4.92, p < .001) and without time-outs (0.013, p < .001). Participants with a higher mean uncertainty did not place the nets significantly more slowly (between-participant component = 0.023, p = .16), and the conditions did not differ (both planned contrasts p ≥ .17) (

Figure 1).



Figure 1:Placement duration (mean) by decile of the within-participant component of the replayed state uncertainty, by condition.

The net entropy was significantly higher on trials with higher uncertainty than the participant’s mean (0.020 bits per SD, SE = 0.007, t(76) = 2.88, p = .005) and in participants with a higher mean uncertainty (0.14 bits per SD, SE = 0.036, t(86) = 3.94, p < .001). Nets on both directions at t+1 and t+2 after events were significantly more frequent on placements with higher uncertainty than the participant’s mean (0.18 log-odds per SD, SE = 0.062, z = 2.94, p = .003) and in participants with a higher mean uncertainty (0.52, SE = 0.184, z = 2.81, p = .005).

The replayed belief about the active state therefore predicted, within participants, how long the placement took and whether the nets were distributed across both directions, and, between participants, how widely the nets were spread and how often they were placed on both directions.

The participant’s mean replayed uncertainty was not significantly associated with any questionnaire in the across-condition form (all participants, slopes between −0.03 and 0.10 SD per SD, all p ≥ .34, all q ≥ .80; participants assigned the latent-state model, STICSA state anxiety 0.17, p = .067, HC3 p = .10, q = .33, all others p ≥ .42), and the same held for the mean uncertainty on regular trials (all q ≥ .49) (

Figure 2). In the moderation form, the association with OCI depended on condition in all participants (condition × OCI F(2, 78) = 4.12, p = .020, q = .10), with a positive slope in Full relative to None and Partial (0.53, p = .026; HC3 p = .11); within conditions, the Spearman correlations of OCI with the mean uncertainty were .12 (None), −.26 (Partial) and .30 (Full) (all p ≥ .14). In the participants assigned the latent-state model, no condition × questionnaire term was significant (all p ≥ .19). With the six parameters as covariates, all questionnaire slopes were close to zero (between −0.03 and −0.01, all p ≥ .19). The mean uncertainty at t+1 after events was associated with higher STICSA state anxiety in the participants assigned the latent-state model (0.23, p = .042, HC3 p = .012, q = .21, HC3 q = .062), but not in all participants (0.13, p = .24).



Figure 2:Mean replayed state uncertainty over the session against the five questionnaire scores, by condition (one point per participant; lines are least-squares fits within condition).

Around events, the trial-level model showed that the questionnaire slope of the uncertainty differed between positions for OCI (position × OCI F(6, 15021) = 5.00, p < .001, q < .001) and, without surviving the correction, for STICSA state anxiety (F(6, 15021) = 2.50, p = .020, q = .051). The slopes were positive at t+2 after transitions for OCI (0.044 uncertainty units per SD, SE = 0.019, t(116) = 2.34, p = .021) and STICSA state anxiety (0.040, SE = 0.019, t(116) = 2.14, p = .035), and close to zero at the other positions (

Figure 3); at t+2, the slope after transitions exceeded the slope after oddballs for OCI (0.044, p < .001, q < .001), STICSA state (0.033, p = .001, q = .003) and trait anxiety (0.026, p = .008, q = .014) and BDI (0.022, p = .026, q = .032). With cluster-robust standard errors, however, the position × questionnaire term was not significant for any questionnaire (all p ≥ .33), because the model tests a participant-level score against the variation between trials and events. In the participant-level check, the difference between the mean uncertainty at t+2 after transitions and after oddballs increased with OCI (0.23 SD per SD, HC3 p = .027, q = .13), with the same sign and without significance for the other questionnaires (0.06 to 0.16, all p ≥ .18).



Figure 3:Questionnaire slopes of the replayed state uncertainty at each position relative to events (trial-level linear mixed model with random intercepts; estimates and 95 % CI, uncertainty units per SD of the questionnaire). The confidence intervals do not reflect the cluster-robust tests, under which no position × questionnaire term was significant.

hierarchy.lvl2: Coupling of uncertainty and behaviour by questionnaire score
Coupling of uncertainty and behaviour by questionnaire score

records.content:
The association of the within-participant uncertainty with the placement duration did not depend on any questionnaire (within-participant component × questionnaire, all p ≥ .60), nor did its association with the net entropy (all p ≥ .51) or with nets on both directions after events (all p ≥ .09, all q ≥ .32). Participants with higher and lower questionnaire scores thus took longer and distributed their nets more when the model’s belief was more uncertain, to the same degree.

In the model of nets on both directions at t+1 and t+2 after events, higher STICSA state anxiety (0.46 log-odds per SD, p = .006) and BDI scores (0.37, p = .029) were associated with more placements on both directions. With the within- and between-participant uncertainty in the model, these coefficients were essentially unchanged (STICSA state 0.42, p = .012; BDI 0.38, p = .024), while the between-participant uncertainty retained its own association (0.50 to 0.56 log-odds per SD in all five models). The same held for STICSA trait anxiety (0.30 without and 0.31 with the uncertainty), OCI (0.24 and 0.19) and IU (0.12 and 0.09).

The replayed uncertainty and the questionnaire scores were therefore separate predictors of placing nets on both directions after an event. The more frequent placements on both directions of participants with higher state anxiety and depression scores did not arise from a more uncertain belief about the active state, as the fitted model reconstructs it, but occurred at the same level of that belief.

records.content:
This chapter describes what participants did on the first two placements after a single displaced attack (an oddball or the first attack of a new episode), and how long they took to place the nets on these trials. Both are reported by instruction condition and by questionnaire score. The analyses of net placement error (Model B1) and net entropy (Model B2) after events in 

Results by Research Question, section 2.2, describe the same trials by continuous measures; the strategies below decompose these measures into the discrete placements that produce them.

records.content:
Each placement at t+1 and t+2 was classified relative to the participant’s own placement on the event trial (t0), not relative to the hidden-state target, because participants in None and Partial were often far from the target before the event, so that a classification by target directions assigns many placements to none of the categories. Three anchors were defined for each event, the centre of the allocation at t0 (old direction), the direction 120° from it toward the displaced attack (new direction) and the direction 120° from it on the other side (third direction). For placements of the second color cue, the allocation was first rotated by the cue offset the participant had learned, so that both cues are expressed in the frame of the first. The share of the seven nets within two positions (±22.5°) of each anchor and the shift of the allocation centre from t0 defined six classes, assigned in the order nets on both directions (at least a quarter of the nets at the old and at the new direction), followed (at least half at the new direction, or a shift of at least 90° toward the attack), stayed (at least half at the old direction, or a shift of less than 30°), moved the other way (at least half at the third direction, or a shift of at least 90° away from the attack), moved part of the way (a shift between 30° and 90° toward the attack) and spread (all remaining placements). The classes refer to the location of the nets and not to the participant’s intention; a placement with all nets at the new direction after an oddball is classified as followed, although following an oddball is not adaptive.

The analysis comprised 2,030 events (1,345 oddballs and 685 transitions) of 86 participants. The probability of each class was modelled with logistic generalized estimating equations (GEE) clustered by participant with an exchangeable working correlation, with the planned condition contrasts (Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the strategies), and, for the questionnaires, with the standardized questionnaire score and condition as predictors, in an across-condition form and a form with the Full × questionnaire interaction (Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the five core questionnaires per strategy and term; the five further questionnaires of the battery were corrected separately and are not reported here). Two participant-level measures summarize the distinction between the events, the selectivity at t+1 (share of transitions followed minus share of oddballs followed) and the selectivity at t+2 (share of transitions at the new direction minus share of oddballs at the new direction), together with the share of correct placements at t+2 (at the new direction after transitions, at the t0 placement after oddballs); these were modelled with linear regressions with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors. The statistics of this analysis are computed in Python (tambi_event_strategies.py); moving them to R mixed models is an open item.

records.content:
After transitions, participants told the structure followed the displaced attack on the first placement significantly more often than participants not told it (shares of transitions followed, None .27, Partial .28, Full .47; planned contrast Full versus None and Partial = 0.86 log-odds, p = .001, q = .004), and the share did not differ between Partial and None (0.02, p = .95). After oddballs, participants told the structure stayed at their t0 placement significantly more often (None .32, Partial .35, Full .52; planned contrast = 0.78 log-odds, p < .001, q < .001), whereas the share of oddballs followed did not differ between conditions (None .24, Partial .21, Full .22; planned contrast = −0.05, p = .82). Moving part of the way after oddballs (None .10, Partial .14, Full .06; −0.86, p = .003, q = .008) and spread placements after both events (transitions, None .08, Partial .06, Full .01, −1.86, p = .009, q = .022; oddballs, None .13, Partial .09, Full .04, −1.12, p = .003, q = .008) were significantly less frequent in Full. Nets on both directions occurred after 12 % to 14 % of transitions and 6 % to 10 % of oddballs, without a significant difference between conditions (all p ≥ .20).

The selectivity at t+1 was significantly larger in Full than in None and Partial (mean selectivity, None 0.03, Partial 0.06, Full 0.25; planned contrast = 0.21, p = .001, q = .004). Participants not told the structure thus followed a displaced attack on the first placement with nearly the same probability whether it was an oddball or the first attack of a new episode, whereas participants told the structure followed transitions about twice as often as oddballs, although the two events present the same evidence at this point (

Figure 1).

On the second placement after transitions, the share of placements at the new direction was significantly higher in Full (None .41, Partial .38, Full .67; planned contrast = 1.15 log-odds, p < .001), and so was the share of placements back at the t0 placement after oddballs (None .39, Partial .43, Full .68; 1.10, p < .001). Participants told the structure kept the new direction at t+2 after following a transition at t+1 more often (None .58, Partial .62, Full .90; 1.79, p < .001), moved to it at t+2 more often when they had not followed at t+1 (None .34, Partial .29, Full .46; 0.63, p = .015, q = .035), and returned to the t0 placement more often after moving toward an oddball at t+1 (None .31, Partial .38, Full .57; 0.91, p = .001, q = .004). The share of correct placements at t+2 was .39 (None), .41 (Partial) and .67 (Full) (planned contrast = 0.27, p < .001), and the selectivity at t+2 was 0.21, 0.23 and 0.56 (0.34, p < .001). No contrast between Partial and None was significant for any strategy at t+1 or t+2 (all q ≥ .70).



Figure 1:Placement strategies after events. (a–d) Share of events by class of the placement at t+1 and t+2 after transitions and oddballs, by condition (2,030 events of 86 participants). (e) Questionnaire coefficients (log-odds per SD of the questionnaire; for the selectivity, difference of the rates per SD) from logistic GEE with condition as covariate (selectivity: OLS with HC3 standard errors); * p < .05, ** q < .05 (Benjamini–Hochberg across the five core questionnaires per strategy). (f–h) Questionnaire slopes within None, Partial and Full from the same models with the condition × questionnaire interaction (linear combinations of the fixed effects with robust standard errors); * p < .05, uncorrected.

records.content:
Higher STICSA state anxiety and BDI scores were significantly associated with following transitions less often at t+1 (STICSA state, −0.30 log-odds per SD, p = .008, q = .041; BDI, −0.27, p = .016, q = .041), and STICSA trait anxiety showed the same direction at the threshold of the correction (−0.24, p = .032, q = .054); the association did not depend on instruction (Full × questionnaire, all p ≥ .31). The share of oddballs followed at t+1 was not associated with any of the five questionnaires (coefficients between −0.07 and 0.05). Accordingly, the selectivity at t+1 was significantly lower with higher STICSA state (−0.059 per SD, p = .005, q = .026), STICSA trait (−0.051, p = .012, q = .029) and BDI scores (−0.053, p = .019, q = .031). For scale, the mean selectivity in None and Partial was 0.03 and 0.06, and the difference between Full and the other two conditions 0.21, so that one SD on these questionnaires corresponds to about a quarter of the instruction effect.

Higher BDI scores were significantly associated with nets on both directions at t+1 after transitions (0.33, p = .002, q = .008) and after both events together (0.26, p = .006, q = .032). At t+2 after transitions, nets on both directions were significantly more frequent with higher STICSA state anxiety (0.46, p < .001, q = .002), STICSA trait anxiety (0.33, p = .025, q = .031), BDI (0.36, p = .006, q = .010) and OCI scores (0.39, p = .006, q = .010); at t+2 after oddballs, they were more frequent with higher STICSA state anxiety (0.38, p = .001, q = .005). With windows of ±1 instead of ±2 positions around the anchors, the associations at t+2 were weaker, and the association of STICSA state anxiety was retained with a measure that requires no threshold (share of the nets on the less covered of the two directions; p ≤ .014). The share of placements at the new direction at t+2 after transitions, the share back at the t0 placement after oddballs and the share of correct placements at t+2 were not associated with any questionnaire. Among the transitions followed at t+1, higher IU (0.49, p = .004, q = .020) and OCI scores (0.43, p = .008, q = .020) were associated with keeping the new direction at t+2.

Participants with higher state anxiety, trait anxiety and depression scores thus followed a transition less often on the first placement, without following oddballs less often, and placed nets on both directions more often on the first and second placement. By the second placement, they were as often at the new direction after transitions and back at the old direction after oddballs as participants with lower scores. The strategies therefore show which placements underlie the higher net placement error at t+1 after transitions (Model B1) and the wider allocation after events (Model B2) in the results by research question.

records.content:
The placement duration is the time from the start of the placement phase until all seven nets are placed, or 7 s if they are not (4.7 % of trials). It was modelled on the log scale with a linear mixed model of condition × event type × trial (t0, t+1, t+2) with the trial index of the session as covariate and random effects for participants (intercept and trial) and for events within participants (tambi_placement_duration.R, P0). Two sensitivity models added the number of positions used and the log of the shift of the allocation centre (P0_adj), which index the amount of placement work, or excluded the time-outs. Estimates are given in log units, which for differences of this size correspond approximately to proportional changes (0.04 ≈ 4 %).

The median placement duration was 4.1 to 4.4 s at every trial type. The first placement after an event took significantly longer than the placement on the event trial, after oddballs (t+1 − t0 = 0.038 log units, SE = 0.009, t(140) = 4.19, p < .001) and after transitions (0.045, SE = 0.012, t(374) = 3.82, p < .001). After transitions, the second placement was again significantly shorter than the first (t+2 − t+1 = −0.035, t(508) = −3.26, p = .001) and no longer differed from t0 (0.010, p = .39). After oddballs, the second placement did not differ significantly from the first (−0.015, p = .083) and remained longer than t0 (0.023, t(171) = 2.64, p = .009), so that at t+2 placements after transitions were shorter than after oddballs (−0.024, t(5289) = −2.26, p = .024); the event type × trial interaction as a whole was not significant (F(2, 3731) = 1.24, p = .29). No term involving condition was significant (condition × trial F(4, 95.6) = 0.28, p = .89; condition × event type × trial F(4, 3731) = 0.83, p = .51), and none of the planned contrasts of the changes between trials (all p ≥ .22).

With the amount of placement work as covariate, the increase from t0 to t+1 was about half as large and remained significant (oddballs, 0.021, p = .017; transitions, 0.027, p = .020), the decrease from t+1 to t+2 after transitions remained (−0.026, p = .016), and the longer placement at t+2 than at t0 after oddballs was no longer significant (0.012, p = .19). Without time-outs, the estimates were similar to those of the primary model (t+1 − t0, 0.035 and 0.037; oddballs, t+2 − t0, 0.026, p = .002). Relative to regular trials, the event trials themselves were placed slightly faster, and the first placements after the event slightly slower (

Figure 2).



Figure 2:Placement duration on the event trial (t0) and the two following trials, relative to regular trials of the same participant (percent; mean and 95 % CI over participants), by event type and condition.

Classified by strategy at t+1, placements with nets on both directions took significantly longer than placements at the t0 position (0.065 log units, t(1977) = 3.50, p < .001), and followed placements were slightly shorter (−0.027, p = .039). With the number of positions used and the shift as covariates, the difference for nets on both directions disappeared (−0.005, p = .82), and followed placements were significantly shorter than stays (−0.077, t(1951) = −3.36, p < .001). The longer duration of placements on both directions thus reflects the larger number of positions to be filled, whereas a complete move to the new direction was faster than its placement work would imply.

records.content:
In the across-condition model with the questionnaire (P1), no questionnaire term was significant after correction (questionnaire main effects, all q ≥ .43; trial × questionnaire, smallest p = .073 for OCI and p = .094 for STICSA state anxiety; event type × trial × questionnaire, all p ≥ .35, all q ≥ .99). Of the simple contrasts of the questionnaire slopes, the increase of the duration from t0 to t+1 after oddballs was significantly larger with higher STICSA state anxiety (difference of the slopes = 0.025 log units per SD, SE = 0.009, t(143) = 2.84, p = .005; Benjamini–Hochberg across the five questionnaires for this contrast, q = .025) and OCI scores (0.022, SE = 0.009, t(140) = 2.43, p = .016, q = .041), but not significantly with STICSA trait anxiety (0.017, p = .067), BDI (0.015, p = .11) or IU scores (0.010, p = .27). After transitions, the corresponding slopes had the same sign and were not significant (STICSA state 0.010, OCI 0.016, all p ≥ .13). Because the event type × trial × questionnaire interaction was not significant, these contrasts do not show that the questionnaire association differs between oddballs and transitions. The general speed of placement on regular trials was not associated with any questionnaire (participant-level regressions with condition, all p ≥ .15, all q ≥ .46).

Descriptively (

Figure 3), participants with STICSA state scores above the median (above 30; n = 41) placed the nets 5.1 % longer at t+1 than at t0 after oddballs (mean 4.38 s versus 4.60 s), and participants at or below the median (n = 43) 2.7 % longer (4.26 versus 4.38 s); 78 % and 67 % of them, respectively, took longer at t+1 than at t0 on average. By tertile of the STICSA state score, the increase was 1.2 %, 5.0 % and 5.5 %. For OCI, the increase was 2.7 % at or below the median (9.5; n = 42) and 5.1 % above it (n = 42), and 1.7 %, 4.3 % and 5.7 % by tertile; 62 % and 83 % of the participants took longer at t+1. The participant-level Spearman correlations of the increase with the questionnaire scores were small (STICSA state ρ = .18, p = .11; OCI ρ = .21, p = .062; STICSA trait .11, BDI .13, IU .07). After transitions, the increase was 4.7 % and 4.3 % below and above the median of STICSA state anxiety and 2.7 % and 6.4 % below and above the median of OCI (ρ = .11 and .18, p ≥ .10).



Figure 3:Change of the placement duration from the event trial (t0) to the first placement after the event (t+1), per participant (mean over the participant’s events; percent), against the five questionnaire scores, after oddballs (top) and transitions (bottom). Lines are least-squares fits.

Higher state anxiety and OCI scores thus went with a somewhat larger slowing of the first placement after a displaced attack, of about 2.5 % of the duration per SD, but the trial-level model did not distinguish this slowing between oddballs and transitions, and the correlation at the level of participants was small.

Follow-up Analyses: Split Placements, Entropy and Colour Cues

records.content:
These analyses follow up on the placement strategies after events (

Responses to Events and Placement Duration) and on the entropy model B2 (

Model Results: RQ2). They are drawn by tambi_hedging_followups.py, tambi_entropy_decomposition.R and tambi_cue_learning.py (pipeline steps hedging, entropydec, cuelearn); all numbers refer to run 13_11 (86 participants, 85 with questionnaires). All measures are computed per participant; condition and questionnaire effects are estimated across participants.

Terms used on this page:

Split placement (nets on both directions). After an event, the class of a placement is defined relative to the participant’s own placement on the event trial (t0). A placement is split if enough nets lie within ±2 slots of both the t0 placement and the direction of the displaced attack. In the strategy analyses “enough” is a share of at least .25 of the nets, which with 7 nets means at least 2 nets on each direction.

Cluster of nets. A run of consecutive occupied slots on the circle. A placement with all nets in one run has one cluster.

Slopes of questionnaires are per SD of the questionnaire; log-odds for event indicators (logistic GEE clustered by participant), SD of the measure for participant-level measures.

The net entropy of a placement (bits) splits exactly into two parts:

between clusters: the entropy of how the nets are divided between separate clusters (0 if all nets form one cluster);

within clusters: the entropy of the nets within each cluster, weighted by the cluster’s share of the nets (how wide the clusters are).

First step for three questions about questionnaire scores, asked per participant: do participants with higher scores (A) find the latent states earlier, (B) rely on them more once found, or (C) find them more often at all?

Measure. The relative fit of 

Relative Model Fit and Questionnaires per episode: for each episode, the held-out log-likelihood per trial of a model with latent states minus that of the delta-rule tracker (nats per trial; positive = the model with states predicts the allocations better). hierarchy.lvl1: Use of the Two-State and Temporal Structure
Use of the Two-State and Temporal Structure

records.content: The strategies in the previous chapter describe the response to a single displaced attack. This chapter asks which structure that response, and the placement in stable phases, reflects. If a participant represents two latent states, the direction of the other state is a more plausible destination of a change than the direction that is never a state, both for following a displaced attack and for placing single nets in stable phases. If the participant represents the temporal structure, a displaced attack late in an episode is more likely to be taken as a transition than one shortly after the last transition. The speed with which all nets arrive at the new direction after a transition shows how quickly the participant commits to a new state once the evidence accumulates.

hierarchy.lvl1: Use of the Two-State and Temporal Structure
Use of the Two-State and Temporal Structure

records.content:
All placements were expressed in the frame of the first color cue, with the allocation for the second cue rotated by the participant’s learned cue offset, and the shares of nets were counted within two positions (±22.5°) of a direction (tambi_structure_measures.py). The models are binomial generalized linear mixed models with logit link and the planned condition contrasts (tambi_structure_use.R); session half is coded −½ (first) and +½ (second). Random effects were reduced to random intercepts where the fit was singular. For the questionnaires, the standardized score and its interaction with the term of interest were added, with the Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the five questionnaires per term.

S1, direction of the oddball. For each oddball, whether the placement at t+1 followed it (class followed, as in the previous chapter), as a function of condition, oddball type (pointing to the direction of the other latent state or to a direction that is never a state) and session half, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the oddball type.

S2, alternative directions in stable phases. For each regular trial without an event in the three preceding trials, whether any net was at the direction of the other latent state and whether any net was at the direction that is never a state (both relative to the participant’s own placement centre on that trial), as a function of condition, direction, session half and position in the episode (per 10 trials), with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the direction.

S3, temporal structure. Whether the placement at t+1 followed an oddball, as a function of the number of trials since the last transition (S3a, per 10 trials), and whether it followed a transition, as a function of the length of the preceding episode (S3b), each with condition and session half.

S4, time to full commitment. A discrete-time hazard model of the first placement after a transition at which the allocation was classified as followed (at least half of the nets at the new direction or a shift of at least 90°), for placements 1, 2, 3 and 4 or later, censored at the next oddball, the end of the episode or the tenth placement, with condition, session half and their interaction.

S5, change over the session. Following at t+1, and a correct placement at t+2 (at the new direction after transitions, back at the t0 placement after oddballs), as a function of condition, event type and session half.

Across the session halves, the difference between transitions and oddballs in following at t+1 was significantly larger in Full than in None and Partial (Full versus None and Partial × event type = 1.07 log-odds, SE = 0.290, z = 3.69, p < .001) and did not change from the first to the second half (event type × session half, −0.06, p = .80; condition × event type × session half, both p ≥ .38). At t+2, the share of correct placements was significantly higher in Full (planned contrast = 1.22, SE = 0.187, z = 6.56, p < .001), and its difference between the events changed over the session (event type × session half = −0.57, SE = 0.218, z = −2.60, p = .009). From the first to the second half, correct placements at t+2 after transitions became less frequent (None .47 to .34, Partial .44 to .32, Full .70 to .64), and correct returns to the t0 placement after oddballs more frequent in None (.35 to .43), slightly less frequent in Partial (.45 to .41) and unchanged in Full (.67 to .67).

Higher STICSA state anxiety (event type × questionnaire = −0.30 log-odds per SD, SE = 0.118, z = −2.54, p = .011, q = .034), STICSA trait anxiety (−0.27, p = .022, q = .036) and BDI scores (−0.29, p = .014, q = .034) were associated with a smaller difference between transitions and oddballs in following at t+1, the trial-level counterpart of the lower selectivity in the strategy analysis. For IU, the difference between transitions and oddballs at t+1 increased from the first to the second half with higher scores (event type × session half × questionnaire = 0.52, p = .028, q = .14). No questionnaire was associated with correct placements at t+2 or with their change over the session (all q ≥ .50).

hierarchy.lvl1: Use of the Two-State and Temporal Structure
Use of the Two-State and Temporal Structure

records.content: Participants in all conditions placed single nets in stable phases more often at the direction of the other latent state than at the direction that is never a state, and from the first to the second half of the session participants told the structure came to follow oddballs toward the other latent state more often than oddballs toward the direction that is never a state. Participants told the structure followed an oddball more readily the longer the episode had lasted, committed to the new direction after a transition at a higher rate, and placed fewer nets at alternative directions in stable phases. Over the session, the hazard of commitment after transitions decreased in all conditions, and correct placements at t+2 shifted from transitions toward oddballs. Of the questionnaire terms, those for the difference between transitions and oddballs on the first placement after the event were significant after correction. The terms for the measures of the two-state structure, of the dependence on the time since the last transition and of the time to full commitment were not significant individually, but had the same sign for all five questionnaires in three of the four measures. Higher scores went with a smaller preference for following oddballs toward the other latent state relative to the direction that is never a state (oddball type × questionnaire, −0.06 to −0.24 log-odds per SD), a weaker dependence of following oddballs on the trials since the last transition (−0.03 to −0.25) and a lower hazard of full commitment after transitions (−0.06 to −0.15), and, for four of the five questionnaires, with a slightly larger preference for the direction of the other latent state among the nets at alternative directions in stable phases (−0.02 to 0.11). Because the five questionnaires are correlated (Spearman ρ between .41 and .74), these signs are not independent observations.

This chapter relates the analyses of the representation of the task structure to each other and to the results by research question, and proposes how they can be read together. The interpretations are proposals for the discussion of the manuscript; the results they rest on are reported in the preceding chapters and in 

Results by Research Question (run 12_10, with the changes of run 13_11 noted where they bear on the argument).

hierarchy.lvl2: The decision at the first placement after a displaced attack
The decision at the first placement after a displaced attack

records.content:
On the first placement after a displaced attack, an oddball and an episode transition present the same evidence, and the replayed uncertainty of the fitted model about the active state was correspondingly high and of similar size in all three conditions (0.49 to 0.54 after transitions, 0.35 to 0.39 after oddballs). The placement duration rose from the event trial to this placement by about 4 % after both events, again without a difference between conditions. Whatever participants knew about the task, they thus registered a single displaced attack as surprising, and the model attributes to them a comparable ambiguity about its cause at this point. The conditions differed in what participants did with this ambiguity. Participants not told the structure followed a displaced attack with nearly the same probability whether it was an oddball or the start of a new episode (selectivity 0.03 in None and 0.06 in Partial), whereas participants told the structure followed transitions about twice as often as oddballs (selectivity 0.25), committed to the new direction after a transition at a higher rate, and stayed in place after oddballs more often.

Because the evidence of the displaced attack itself is identical for both events, a selective response on the first placement requires information that the attack does not carry, and the analyses of the temporal and two-state structure identify two such sources. First, participants told the structure followed an oddball more readily the longer the current episode had lasted, so that they treated a displaced attack late in an episode as more likely to be a transition, in the manner of an observer who expects a change with increasing time since the last one. Second, from the first to the second half of the session, participants told the structure came to follow oddballs pointing to the direction of the other latent state more often than oddballs pointing to the direction that is never a state, so that the identity of the displaced direction became informative about its cause once the set of directions occupied by latent states had been learned. Both sources rest on a representation of the task that goes beyond a single tracked direction, namely of the set of directions that latent states can occupy and of the time course of their changes, and instruction made both available. Instruction thus did not reduce the ambiguity of a single displaced attack, which is fixed by the design, but changed the prior information with which it was resolved.

The placements in stable phases show that participants did not represent only the direction they defended. In all conditions, single nets were placed more often at the direction of the other latent state than at the direction that is never a state, also in None and Partial, where nothing about the number or location of the states had been told. These nets were rare (about one trial in ten in None and Partial), became rarer the longer an episode had lasted, and were placed less often by participants told the structure, so that they behave like a hedge against a change whose probability is highest early in an episode and lower when the structure is known. The direction of such a hedge reveals the alternative the participant considers, and its preference for the other latent state over the third direction indicates that participants, with or without instruction, acquired a representation of two states rather than of an unstructured range of possible changes. This complements the model comparison of RQ3 (run 12_10), in which neither of the two models tracking a single direction described any participant, with evidence from the placements themselves that participants kept a specific alternative in view.

The changes over the session point in the same direction. In all conditions, the hazard of full commitment after a transition decreased from the first to the second half, the share of correct placements on the second trial after transitions decreased and the share after oddballs increased in None, and in Full the placement of nets at alternative directions in stable phases increased. Over the session, participants experienced about twice as many oddballs as transitions, and a representation that tracks the relative frequency of the two causes of a displaced attack would come to treat such an attack as more likely transient, commit to a new direction more slowly, and hedge more often. Fatigue, which increased over the session in all conditions (section 2.2.7 of the results by research question), offers an alternative account of slower commitment, but it does not explain why correct returns after oddballs became more frequent at the same time.

hierarchy.lvl2: The questionnaire scores and the response to ambiguity
The questionnaire scores and the response to ambiguity

records.content:
Against this background, the questionnaire associations are notably specific. Higher STICSA state and trait anxiety and BDI scores were associated with following transitions less often on the first placement, without following oddballs less often, and with placing nets on both the old and the new direction more often on the first and second placement after events; by the second placement, participants with higher scores were as often at the new direction after transitions and back at the old direction after oddballs as participants with lower scores. The measures of how the represented structure was used showed a weaker but consistent pattern. None of the questionnaire terms for the preference for following oddballs toward the other latent state, for the dependence of following on the time since the last transition, or for the hazard of full commitment was significant, but for each of these measures the coefficients of all five questionnaires had the same sign, and in each case the sign of a weaker use of the structure (smaller preference for the other latent state, weaker dependence on elapsed time, slower full commitment). The selectivity at t+1, which the instruction raised and higher STICSA and BDI scores lowered significantly (q ≤ .031), is itself a measure of this kind, since it requires distinguishing the two latent causes of a displaced attack. The general speed of placement was not associated with the questionnaires. The strategies thus resolve the continuous associations of RQ2 into their behavioural components. The higher net placement error at t+1 after transitions with higher STICSA scores (Model B1; in run 13_11, simple slope of STICSA state anxiety 0.19 log units per SD, p = .005), which was closed by the second placement, arises from fewer complete moves to the new direction and more placements that cover the old and the new direction together, rather than from moves to an intermediate direction, and the wider allocation after events with higher STICSA state anxiety (Model B2) is the same division of the nets seen as spread.

Read together, these results describe participants with higher anxiety and depression scores as entertaining more, or more complex, hypotheses about the structure that generates the attacks and as distributing their belief across these hypotheses more evenly. When an attack is displaced, they divide the nets between the old and the new direction, they wait for the next attack before committing fully, and they commit immediately once that attack singles out one hypothesis, reaching the new direction after transitions and the old direction after oddballs as often and as soon as participants with lower scores. Their reactivity therefore differs in two directions at once. They move less often immediately and completely to the direction of a displaced attack, follow oddballs no more often than participants with lower scores, and follow outcome noise less in the weighting analysis of Model C (section 2.2.4 of the results by research question; these terms were not significant with cluster-robust standard errors), while they cover the possible directions more broadly after a displaced attack. The consistent signs of the associations with the structure measures fit the same account. If the direction that has never been a state remains a possible state, an oddball pointing to it is less clearly an outlier than an oddball pointing to the other known state, which reduces the preference for following the latter; if alternative temporal structures are entertained, the time since the last transition is less diagnostic; and a belief spread over more hypotheses reaches the level that triggers full commitment later. In terms of the attribution of a displaced attack to an epistemic cause (a change of the latent state) or an aleatoric cause (a single outlier), participants with higher scores kept both attributions, and possibly further structural possibilities, in play until the next attack decided between them.

Two observations constrain this account. In stable phases, nets at alternative directions were about as frequent with higher as with lower scores, and among them the preference for the direction of the other latent state was, if anything, slightly larger (four of five questionnaires), so that the additional hypotheses do not show as a constant coverage of the third direction. The broader hypothesis space would thus be engaged by surprise, when a displaced attack calls the current structure into question, rather than held throughout. And the immediate move toward the third direction after oddballs was not associated with the five questionnaires, so that the additional hypotheses do not show as placements at that direction on the first trial after an event. Both observations are open to a direct test with a model that represents uncertainty over structures, such as the structural-switching agent, or with an analysis of the direction of the divided placements after oddballs pointing to the direction that has never been a state.

hierarchy.lvl2: Uncertainty about the state and the response to it
Uncertainty about the state and the response to it

records.content:
The replay of the fitted model allows a further distinction. Within participants, the uncertainty that the model attributes to the participant on a given trial predicted how long the placement took and whether the nets were divided between both directions, and placement duration is not among the quantities from which the parameters are estimated. The replayed belief therefore has behavioural validity as a trial-by-trial measure of the uncertainty about the active state, and participants took more time and divided their defence more when this uncertainty was higher, to the same degree whatever their questionnaire scores. Between participants, however, the questionnaire scores were not associated with the mean replayed uncertainty, and the association of state anxiety and depression scores with placing nets on both directions was unchanged when the replayed uncertainty was added to the model, while the replayed uncertainty retained its own association. The more frequent division of the defence with higher scores thus occurred at the same level of the belief about the state, as the model reconstructs it.

The account of a broader hypothesis space explains this dissociation without further assumptions. The fitted model represents exactly two latent states with a fixed relation between the cues, so that its replayed uncertainty is uncertainty about which of these two states is active, given that this structure holds. Uncertainty about the structure itself, about whether the third direction can be a state, whether the episodes follow another temporal regularity or whether more than two states exist, cannot appear in it. If participants with higher scores divide their defence because they distribute their belief over more structural possibilities, their hedging should be related to the questionnaire scores but not to the replayed uncertainty of a two-state model, which is the pattern observed. The mean replayed uncertainty is moreover almost entirely determined by the parameters (R² = .96, mainly belief momentum and the switch probability), so that it can carry only the questionnaire variance that these parameters carry.

A second reading is that the questionnaire scores relate to how a belief is translated into an allocation, rather than to the belief. An allocation proportional to the belief divides the nets in proportion to the probability of each state, whereas an allocation that weights the cost of leaving the active direction undefended more heavily divides them more evenly at the same belief. The two readings make different predictions. Under the first, a model that represents uncertainty over structures should carry the questionnaire association in its structural uncertainty, and the divided placements after oddballs pointing to the never-state direction should include that direction more often with higher scores. Under the second, a parameter for the mapping from belief to allocation, such as an exponent on the belief that ranges from proportional to maximizing allocation, should carry the association within the two-state model. The trial-level slopes of the replayed uncertainty at the second placement after transitions, which were positive for OCI and state anxiety but not significant with cluster-robust standard errors, do not distinguish between them.

hierarchy.lvl2: The breadth of the hypothesis space
The breadth of the hypothesis space

records.content: Taken together, instruction and questionnaire scores were associated with the breadth of the hypothesis space in opposite directions. Instruction narrowed the structure that participants used to interpret a displaced attack to the one that generates the attacks, namely the set of directions treated as possible states, the dependence of the expected change on elapsed time and the rate of commitment to a new state, and participants told the structure accordingly responded selectively to transitions and oddballs from the first placement on and committed earlier. Higher anxiety and depression scores went with the opposite pattern within each condition, a less selective first response, divided placements while the cause of an attack was undetermined, a slower full commitment and smaller dependence on the cues that the true structure offers, combined with less reactivity to noise and unimpaired accuracy once the ambiguity was resolved. In this task, internalizing symptoms are thus associated with a broader, more evenly weighted representation of the structures that could generate the observations, which participants act on by distributing their defence while the evidence leaves several of them open. Because this uncertainty concerns the structure rather than the state within a given structure, it does not appear in the replayed uncertainty of the two-state model, and testing it requires a model that represents structural uncertainty explicitly.

The strategy classes depend on thresholds for the share of nets at a direction, and the associations with nets on both directions at the second placement were weaker with narrower windows, although the association with state anxiety was retained with a measure that requires no threshold. The statistics of the strategy analysis are computed with generalized estimating equations in Python and remain to be repeated with mixed models in R. The questionnaire associations are corrected across five (or, for the strategies, ten) questionnaires for each term but not across the many measures analysed here, and several of them, such as the larger slowing of the first placement after oddballs with higher state anxiety and OCI scores, rest on contrasts of a three-way interaction that was not significant as a whole. The Full condition comprises 22 participants, so that the condition dependence of the questionnaire associations is estimated with little precision. The consistent but individually non-significant associations of the questionnaires with the measures of the use of the represented structure need the larger sample planned, or a joint model across these measures, before they can be stated as effects. Finally, the replayed uncertainty is a quantity of the fitted model, and its dissociation from the questionnaire scores is a statement about the belief as this model reconstructs it.

The analyses in this part address how participants represent the structure of the task and how they distribute their defence across the possibilities they consider. The task contains three kinds of structure that a participant can represent or ignore. The first is the set of possible attack directions, namely two latent states per color cue, about 120° apart, and a third direction 120° from both that is never the direction of a latent state but can be the direction of an oddball. The second is the temporal structure, in which the latent state persists for an episode of variable length and is interrupted by single displaced attacks (oddballs). The third is the coupling of the two color cues, whose attack directions are offset by about 70° and change state together.

A single displaced attack is ambiguous on the first placement after it (t+1), because an oddball and an episode transition present the same evidence, an attack about 120° from the expected direction. The second placement after the event (t+2) is the first at which the two can be told apart, because it follows the first attack after the event, which returns to the previous direction after an oddball and stays at the new direction after a transition. The response to the event at t+1 and t+2, and the time a participant needs before placing the nets, therefore show how the participant handles an ambiguity that the task structure resolves only on the next trial.

The analyses are organized in four chapters.

Responses to Events and Placement Duration classifies the placement at t+1 and t+2 into strategies (followed the displaced attack, moved part of the way, nets on both directions, stayed, moved the other way, spread) and relates them, together with the placement duration at the event trial (t0), t+1 and t+2, to instruction condition and questionnaire scores.

Use of the Two-State and Temporal Structure asks whether participants treat the direction of the other latent state differently from the direction that is never a state, whether their response to a displaced attack depends on the time since the last episode transition, how many placements they need before all nets are at the new direction after a transition, and how these measures change over the session.

Replayed State Uncertainty and Behaviour relates the trial-by-trial uncertainty of the fitted latent-state model about the active state to the placement duration, the spread of the nets and the placement of nets on both directions, and to the questionnaire scores.

Interpretation relates these results to each other and to the results by research question.

All results refer to run 13_11 (86 participants with behavioural data, 85 of them with questionnaire data; None, 31; Partial, 33; Full, 22). The instruction condition is coded throughout with the planned contrasts Full versus None and Partial and Partial versus None (see 

Results by Research Question, section 1.5). The questionnaire analyses use the five questionnaires of the main analyses, the State-Trait Inventory for Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA; state and trait scale), the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IU), the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI) and the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI), each standardized across participants, with the Benjamini–Hochberg correction (q) across the five questionnaires for each model term unless stated otherwise. The analyses of the response strategies and of the post-task questions additionally report the five further questionnaires of the battery, corrected separately from the five core questionnaires.

records.content:
The structure-use models, the placement strategies after events and the mouse-tracking analyses describe effects at the level of the group. This chapter estimates the same effects within each participant: the structure-use models with by-participant random slopes for every within-participant term, the strategies as participant profiles with their reliability, the persistence of a strategy after it worked, and the couplings of cursor and gaze with the model uncertainty before the outcome as within-participant slopes. The dependence of a within-participant effect on the questionnaire scores is tested as a cross-level interaction in the mixed model where participants contribute few observations, and as a regression of the participant slopes on the score where they contribute many. The participant estimates are saved as features for later analyses.

Participants differ detectably in how often they place nets at alternative directions (direction, position in episode, session half) and in how much more they follow transitions than oddballs at t+1. They do not differ detectably in the dependence of following an oddball on its direction or on the time since the last transition, or in the dependence of following a transition on the length of the preceding episode: for these terms the variance of the participant slopes was estimated at or near zero, so individual estimates of temporal-structure use cannot be obtained from these binary event outcomes with about 16 oddballs and 8 transitions per participant.

Score terms with the selected structure (general factor, log-odds per SD):

S2, position in episode × score. With random intercepts only, nets at alternative directions decreased more steeply over the episode in higher scorers (general factor −0.24, SE = 0.056, p < .001; STICSA trait −0.26, p < .001). With the selected random slopes the estimate is smaller and its standard error twice as large (−0.18, SE = 0.102, p = .072; STICSA trait −0.18, p = .081): the participants’ own slopes of position vary, and the score association is not separable from that variation.

S5, event type × score at t+1. The smaller difference between transitions and oddballs in higher scorers is of the same size with the random slope of the session half added (general factor −0.24, SE = 0.126, p = .055; STICSA trait −0.25, SE = 0.125, p = .043) as with random intercepts only (−0.23, p = .042; −0.24, p = .030). The same holds with the continuous trial (general factor −0.24, p = .059).

S1, oddball type × score. No random slope was supported, so both forms coincide: −0.27 (SE = 0.134, p = .042) for the general factor and −0.25 (p = .067) for STICSA trait, a smaller advantage of oddballs toward the other latent state in higher scorers.

The remaining cross-level terms (S2 direction, S3a, S3b, S4, S5 at t+2, and the change of following over the session or over trials) were all p ≥ .15. With BH correction over the 17 cross-level terms of the nine models (S1, S2, S3a, S3b, S4, S5 and S5c at t+1 and t+2), separately for each score and each random-effect form, no term is below q = .05 with the selected structure (smallest q = .31 for the general factor, .35 for STICSA trait).

The participant estimates are most reliable for the session-half and position terms of S2 (.66 and .62) and for the difference between transitions and oddballs in following at t+1 (.53 to .54), and less reliable for the difference at t+2 (.35 to .36), for direction in S2 (.31), for the change of commitment over the session (.30) and for the change of following over the session or the trials (.27 to .28). records.content:
For 2,165 pairs of consecutive events of 96 participants, repeat is whether the placement at t+1 of the next event has the same class as at the current event. Model: repeat ~ blocked_w + blocked_b + same event type + class + condition + (1 + blocked_w | participant), logistic, with blocked_w whether the attack on the t+1 trial was blocked, centred within the participant, and blocked_b the participant’s share of blocked t+1 attacks.

The class was repeated at 30 % of the next events (34 % after a blocked attack at t+1, 28 % after a bite). With the class and the event type in the model, a blocked attack did not make the repetition more likely within participants (0.11 log-odds, SE = 0.13, p = .40); repetitions were more frequent when the next event was of the same type (0.32, p = .003) and differed between the classes. The within-participant effect of a blocked attack did not depend on the scores (general factor × blocked_w 0.01, p = .91; STICSA trait 0.05, p = .70). The strategy chosen after an event thus does not follow a win-stay pattern across events.
